summary:
Mauwake intonation is generally low in pitch, with the most common sentence contour being falling: the first stressed syllable is highest, the pitch falls gradually, and there is a sharp terminal fall, a pattern used in statements, commands, non-polar questions, and some polar questions. Rising intonation is mainly found sentence-finally in polar questions when the speaker is uncertain, and more commonly in medial, subordinate, conditional, and left-dislocated phrases, where it marks non-finality or thematic prominence.

The passage also notes special intonation patterns for lists and for calling someone: non-final items in lists rise slightly or stay level, polite calls have a slight rise then sharp fall, and impatient or distant calls keep a high, level pitch with lengthening. Anger is expressed by shouting, with a fairly level, short, staccato delivery.

text:
The syllable in Mauwake consists of one or two vowels forming the nucleus, with optional onset and/or coda of one consonant, cv being by far the most frequent syllable structure. gives a short but good overview of syllable-final consonants in a number of tng languages. The syllable patterns are given in tab:2:syllablepatterns.

Any vowel can fill the simple nucleus slot of the syllable. The complex nucleus slot is filled either by a geminate vowel or a diphthong. Diphthongs can occur in non-initial syllables too, but geminate vowels cannot.

Any consonant can fill the onset slot, and all consonants except the voiced plosives, / / and /j/ can fill the coda slot of a syllable. The distribution of the voiced plosives and / / is also restricted in that they very seldom occur later than in the second syllable of a word and, except for /j/, do not appear in inflectional morphology. tab:5:consonantdistr shows the possible distribution of consonants in a syllable.
summary:
Mauwake syllables consist of a nucleus of one or two vowels, with an optional single-consonant onset and/or coda; the most common pattern is CV. The simple nucleus can contain any vowel, while the complex nucleus contains either a geminate vowel or a diphthong, though only diphthongs may occur in non-initial syllables.  

Any consonant can occur in onset position, but only consonants other than the voiced plosives, / /, and /j/ can appear in coda position. The voiced plosives and / / are also restricted in distribution, rarely occurring beyond the second syllable of a word and, except for /j/, not appearing in inflectional morphology.

text:
tab:6:vowelseq shows the possible two-vowel sequences in Mauwake. The only possible sequences beginning with either of the two mid vowels are geminate vowels; no other vowel sequences begin with a mid vowel. The other three vowels may combine with any vowel.

When the second vowel in a vowel sequence is articulatorily the same height or higher than the preceding vowel, the two form a diphthong, i.e., they are part of the same syllable ex:2:twovowel1.

/kae/ [ ˈkae] `my/our grandfather'

/kuina/ [ ˈkui.na] `woodborer'

/aowa/ [ ˈao.wa] `to tie around waist'

When the second vowel is lower than the first, the two vowels form the nuclei of two separate syllables ex:2:twovowel2.

/sier/ [ s.ˈer] `husking stick'

/luaka/ [ l.ˈa.ka] `whitebait'

/kia/ [ k.ˈa] `white'

The high back vowel /u/ is considered lower than the high front vowel /i/, as it behaves similarly to the non-high vowels when following /i/ ex:2:twovowel3.

/niuk/ [ n.ˈuk] `let them give you'

In an open syllable, all the diphthongs allowed by the language are possible. In a closed syllable, /ao/ is the only diphthong that has not been found; but it is very infrequent in an open syllable too.

Sequences with three vowels are rare: /uau/ and /uai/ are the only ones I have found, and these only occur at morpheme breaks (marked with a hyphen in the examples), and there is a syllable break within the sequence as well ex:2:threevowels. A syllable break does not need to coincide with a morpheme break; in the examples above it does not.

/kua-i-jem/ [ k.ˈai.jem] `I build'

/kua-uk/ [ k.ˈauk] `let them build'
summary:
Mauwake allows only certain two-vowel sequences: after the mid vowels, the only possible sequences are geminate vowels, while the other three vowels may combine with any vowel. If the second vowel is the same height or higher than the first, the sequence forms a diphthong within one syllable; if it is lower, the vowels form separate syllable nuclei, with /u/ treated as lower than /i/ in this respect.

Three-vowel sequences are rare and limited to /uau/ and /uai/, which occur only at morpheme breaks and include a syllable break. In open syllables, all permitted diphthongs can occur, but in closed syllables /ao/ is the only one not attested and is very rare overall.

text:
No consonant sequences occur word-initially or -finally. In words with three or more syllables there are some word-medial clusters, which I believe to have resulted from vowel elision. A vowel may be elided from a non-final syllable immediately following a stressed syllable, which is probably the least prominent syllable in the whole word. According to this is a common process in languages. It is mainly the high vowels that are dropped, since they are the least sonorant ex:2:vowelelision.

/ikemika/ [ iˈkemka] `wound (nn)'

/aakisa/ [ ˈaːksa] `now, today'

/pisikulaw/ [ piˈsiklaw] `grasshopper sp.'

A non-high vowel can also be elided if the adjacent stressed syllable has an identical vowel ex:2:vowelelisiontwo:

/kerekenam/ [ keˈreknam] `dollar bird'

/toonowaw/ [ ˈtoːnwaw] `honey eater'

Occasionally vowel elision takes place in a later syllable than that immediately following the stressed syllable ex:2:vowelelisionthree:

/o a ilika/ [ oˈ a ilka] `butterfly'

/aakuniwikin/ [ aːkuniwkin] `talk.2/3p. ds '

In some of these words the original vowel can still be perceived in slow pronunciation, but in others it has disappeared. Consequently, phonemic vowel clusters are currently developing in Mauwake, The present orthography reflects this development in that consonant clusters are written especially 1) where the quality of the elided vowel cannot be established, and/or 2) when the elided form is in very frequent use. and the distribution of cvc syllables is being extended to include word-medial position as well, and that of vvc and cvvc to include initial position in two-syllable words that have earlier had three syllables ( sec:2.3.2 ).

No clear rules have been found for the site of the vowel elision, but some tendencies are as follows. Nouns have more elision than verb stems. A vowel is dropped much more often between non-homorganic than homorganic consonants. The voiceless velar plosive /k/ is the most frequent phoneme on either side of the elided vowel.
summary:
The passage explains that Mauwake has no consonant clusters word-initially or word-finally, but some word-medial clusters have developed through vowel elision in polysyllabic words. Elision usually affects a high vowel in the non-final syllable after the stressed syllable, though it can also occur elsewhere under certain conditions, and this has led to the emergence of phonemic vowel clusters reflected in the orthography.

It also notes that vowel elision is more common in nouns than verb stems and is more likely between non-homorganic consonants, especially when /k/ is adjacent to the elided vowel. No firm rules determine exactly where elision occurs, but these tendencies are observed.

subsection: Defining a phonological word in Mauwake
text:
A phonological word is defined on the basis of a primary stress. Words are composed of one or more syllables. The number of syllables seldom exceeds ten, but compound words can be longer. A majority of the words have two or three syllables. Every word has one syllable with a primary stress, and usually one or more unstressed syllables.

In words of two or more syllables, the syllable containing the second vowel is stressed. Thus the first syllable is stressed if it contains a geminate vowel ( ex:2:stressone a) or a diphthong ( ex:2:stressone b). In all the other cases the second syllable is stressed ( ex:2:stressone c). When the stressed syllable is long, the stress falls equally on the whole vowel sequence ( ex:2:stressone d--e).

/aasa/ [ ˈaː.sa] `canoe'

/kuija/ [ ˈkui.ja] `it bites'

/a ura/ [ a.ˈ u.ra] `lime'

/siowa/ [ si.ˈo.wa] `dog'

/isaimija/ [ i.ˈsai.mi.ja] `(s)he heats (food)'

Both derivational and inflectional affixes may receive primary stress provided they are in a position where stress is normally placed ex:2:stresstwo:

/aw-om-e/\\
[ a.ˈwo.me] \\
weave- ben - bnfy1. imp.2s\\
`weave it for me'

/um-o-k/ \\
[ u.ˈmok] \\
die- pa -3s \\
`(s)he died'

Clitics, on the other hand, never receive stress placement. Grammatically they are words, but phonologically they attach to the preceding word. If the preceding word is monosyllabic and has a short vowel, it still takes the primary stress when a clitic is added. The unmarked pronouns are a case in point: they retain their stress when clitics are added. Some non-phonemic lengthening takes place in the vowel of the pronoun stem ex:2:stressthree.

/jo=ko/ [ ˈjo\..ko] ` I (with neutral focus)'

/jos=ke/ [ ˈjo\.s.ke] ` I (and not someone else)'

Compound words and some reduplicated words also have a secondary stress. In the second (and third) compound of a compound word, that syllable has a secondary stress which in a single word would receive primary stress ex:2:stressfour.

/soomare-jiawem-ikemik/ [ ˈsoːmare-j ˈˈawem-iˈˈkemik] `we were walking around'

/suuw-orom-ikua/ [ ˈsuːw-oˈˈrom-iˈˈkua] `he is pushing it down'

In those words where a long initial syllable is reduplicated as a whole, the second syllable is also long and receives a secondary stress ex:2:stressfive:

/kui-kuisow/ [ ˈkui.ˈˈkui.sow] `a few'

/suu-suusia/ [ ˈsuː.ˈˈsuː.sia] `thorny'
summary:
A phonological word is defined by primary stress, and most words are two or three syllables long, though compounds may be longer. In words of two or more syllables, stress normally falls on the syllable containing the second vowel, except when the first syllable has a geminate vowel or a diphthong; if the stressed syllable is long, stress is distributed over the whole vowel sequence.

Derivational and inflectional affixes can receive primary stress when they occur in a stressed position, but clitics never do and instead attach phonologically to the preceding word. Compound words and some reduplicated words also show secondary stress, with later compound elements or the repeated syllable receiving the secondary prominence.

subsection: Distribution of syllables in a word
text:
All syllable types except vc can form a monosyllabic word. In polysyllabic words, the occurrence of a certain syllable type is determined by both its position in the word and the stress.

tab:7:syllabletypes shows what syllable types occur in which positions in a word. A blank space indicates that the syllable type does not occur in that particular word position at all, and parentheses indicate a rare occurrence. Double parentheses indicate new positions for closed syllables formed as a result of vowel elision (see sec:2.2.3 ). ``2nd'' indicates the second non-final syllable, and ``3rd-'' stands for the third or later non-final syllable in a polysyllabic word.

`2nd' indicates the second non-final syllable, and `3rd-' stands for the third or later non-final syllable in a polysyllabic word.

Some distributional characteristics can be summarised as follows. The most frequent syllable type, cv, also has the widest distribution: a stressed initial syllable is the only position where it cannot occur, as an initial syllable with a single short vowel is always unstressed. The same reason accounts for the absence of v syllables in the same position. v syllables also never occur after a geminate vowel or diphthong, so they cannot occupy the second unstressed syllable position. A vv syllable in medial or final position is possible but very rare. The two previous statements may be combined to make the claim that there is some resistance towards vvv sequences in Mauwake. The syllables with a consonant coda only occur word finally, except where vowel elision has changed the syllable structure.
summary: All syllable types except vc can form monosyllabic words, but in polysyllabic words their distribution depends on both word position and stress. The commonest syllable type, cv, has the widest distribution, though it cannot occur in a stressed initial syllable; v syllables are likewise excluded there and also cannot follow a geminate vowel or diphthong, suggesting resistance to vvv sequences. Syllables with a consonant coda normally occur only word finally, except in cases where vowel elision has altered the syllable structure.

text: There are not many morphophonological alternations in Mauwake. The most important is the rule system governing the vowel of the past tense suffix and the medial verb same-subject sequential action and simultaneous action suffixes (called the medial verb suffixes There are also other medial verb suffixes, which are not affected by these morphophonological rules. in the discussion below). Others include the change in the verbaliser suffix and the form of the completive aspect marker.
summary: Mauwake has relatively few morphophonological alternations. The most important concern the vowel in the past tense suffix and in the medial verb same-subject sequential and simultaneous action suffixes, though other medial verb suffixes are not affected by these rules. Additional alternations involve the verbaliser suffix and the form of the completive aspect marker.

text:
The phoneme /a/ has a very high frequency as the word-final phoneme, particularly in the nouns and adjectives. It accounts for approximately 85% of all the vowel-final words. In normal and fast speech this /a/ is often dropped from an unstressed word-final cv syllable, especially when followed by a word with an initial vowel. The elision rule is in ex:2:elisionrule and examples in ex:2:elisionexample.

/koora unowa/ [ ˈkoːr uˈnowa] `many houses'

/takira aara/ [ taˈkir ˈ aːra] `boys' house'

/siiwa eliwa/ [ ˈsiːw eˈliva] `good/bright moon'

/ikoka uura/ [ iˈkok ˈuːra] `later at night'

In some cases even a stressed /a/ is elided, and the stress moves to the following vowel in the utterance. This mainly happens with the accusative pronouns, which tend towards cliticization ex:2:stressedelision ( sec:3.5.3 ).

/me ne a uru am/ [ ˈme ne ˈuru am] `I didn't see you'

In compound words the final /a/ is dropped from the first constituent even when the second begins with a consonant, except when the final syllable of the first constituent is stressed ex:2:compoundelision.

/aara muuka/ [ ˈaːr ˈmuːka] `chick'

/emera tapaka/ [ eˈmer taˈpaka] `sago cake'

/mera soo/ [ meˈra ˈsoː] `fish trap'
summary: The phoneme /a/ is very frequent word-finally, especially in nouns and adjectives, making up about 85% of vowel-final words. In normal and fast speech, unstressed final /a/ in a CV syllable is often deleted, especially before a vowel-initial following word; in some cases even stressed /a/ is elided, with stress shifting to the next vowel, particularly in accusative pronouns that behave like clitics. In compounds, final /a/ of the first member is usually dropped even before a consonant-initial second member, unless the first member’s final syllable is stressed.

text:
There are various patterns of reduplication in Mauwake. With a few exceptions, reduplication takes place at the beginning of the word. The meaning involves plurality in one way or another; with verbs it indicates repeated action and/or the object of the action ending up in several pieces. Occasionally with adjectives it also indicates enhanced quality ( sec:3.3 ).

How a word is reduplicated can to some extent be predicted from the phonological shape of the word. Type 1 below is the most common, 2 and 3 are the only possible ones for the words with a short and a long initial vowel respectively. Reduplication process does not always respect syllable boundaries.

Type 1

Everything up to and including the first vowel of the stressed syllable is reduplicated. Even with the reduplication these words retain the normal stress pattern: the second syllable of the reduplicated form is stressed, because regardless of whether one or two syllables are reduplicated the first syllable in this type is always short. When two of syllables are reduplicated, the originally stressed syllable of the word root gets a secondary stress ex:2:reduptypeone.

/pu-puukija/ [ pu.ˈpuː.ki.ja] `cut into pieces'

/pu-puija/ [ pu.ˈpui.ja] `break into pieces'

/pere-perekija/ [ pe.ˈre.pe.ˈˈre.ki.ja] `tear into pieces'

/kiri-kiripija/ [ ki.ˈri.ki.ˈˈri.pi.ja] `turn round & round, mix'

/mane-maneka/ [ ma.ˈne.ma.ˈˈne.ka] `(many) big (things)'

Type 2: v 1 c 1 v 1 - v 1 c 1 v 2 c 2 v ( v 3 ) x

In the words of the second type, the reduplication repeats the initial vowel and consonant of the word root, adding another vowel of the same quality after the consonant. In these words the stress shifts from the second syllable of the root to the final vowel of the reduplicated element. Phonetically this vowel usually merges into one with the following vowel, which always has the same quality ex:2:reduptypetwo. Stresswise this creates an interesting pattern, where a syllable with a primary stress is followed by one with secondary stress. Types 3 and 4 also have this kind of stress pattern.

/ele-eliwa/ [ e.ˈle.ˈˈli.wa] `(many) good (things)'

/ara-arow/ [ a.ˈra.ˈˈrow] `in threes'

/oko-okaiwi/ [ o.ˈko.ˈˈkai.wi] `this side and that'

Type 3: v 1 v 1 c 1 - v 1 v 1 c 1 v 2 x

A very small group of words has this type of reduplication, where the initial geminate vowel and the following consonant are reduplicated. The result is a word where both the first and the second syllable have a complex nucleus, a word type not allowed in the simple non-reduplicated words. In these reduplicated words the first syllable receives primary stress and the second syllable secondary stress. The first syllable has a syllable pattern ( vvc ) which is not possible for the first syllable in a non-reduplicated polysyllabic word ex:2:reduptypethree.

/iiw-iiwa/ [ ˈiːv.ˈˈ iː.va] `(many) short (things)'

/iin-iinan/ [ ˈiːn.ˈˈ iː.nan] `(the things) high up'

Type 4: c 1 v 1 v 2 - c 1 v 1 v 2 x

In this type the long first syllable is repeated entirely, but nothing else. The two vowels in the initial syllable may be identical or different in quality ex:2:reduptypefour. This is not a very common pattern.

/kui-kuisow/ [ ˈkui.ˈˈkui.sow] `a few'

/soo-soomarija/ [ ˈsoː.ˈˈsoː.ma.ri.ja] `amble, stroll'

Unusual reduplications

The word gelemuta `small' has two unusual reduplicated forms, where the end of the word is changed: gelemutitik and gelemutumut `(many) small (things)'. Type 1 reduplication rule can also be applied to these already reduplicated forms, although not to the root ex:2:redupgelemuta.

/gele-gelemutitik/ [ ge.ˈle.ge.ˈˈle.mu.ti.tik] `very small (pl.)'

*/gele-gelemuta/

The verb wafuriya `throw' also has an irregular reduplicated form: only the second syllable is reduplicated ex:2:redupwafuriya.

/wa u urija/ [ va.ˈ u. u.ri.ja] `throw around'

The reduplication for the word owowa `village' occurs at the beginning of the word, but it does not follow any of the patterns above ex:2:redupowowa. So far it is the only one of its kind found.

/owow-owowa/ [ o.ˈwo.woˈˈwo.wa] `(many/all) villages'

Mauwake has a number of nouns of the following the pattern c 1 v 1 c 2 v 2 c 1 v 1 c 2, which looks like reduplication, but with the word-final vowel deleted. However, these words do not have any semantic relationship with a corresponding c 1 v 1 c 2 v 2 word in cases where the latter may exist. Words of this type are not considered to have resulted from reduplication ex:2:nonredup.

/mulamul/ [ muˈlamul] `trevally'

/jawejaw/ [ jaˈvejav] `hunting magic'

Similarly, words of the pattern c 1 v 1 c 1 v 1 c 2 v 2 are not considered reduplicated forms ex:2:nonredup2. Firstly, there is no semantic relationship with a corresponding c 1 v 1 c 2 v 2 word, even if the latter exists. Secondly, in Mauwake there is a very strong tendency to have the same vowel in the first two syllables of trisyllabic or longer words, whether the consonant is the same or not.

/momora/ [ moˈmo.ra] `fool(ish)'

/sisina/ [ siˈsi.na] `edge'
summary:
Mauwake has several reduplication patterns, usually at the beginning of the word, and these forms generally express plurality: with verbs they can indicate repeated action or an object ending up in pieces, and with adjectives they may intensify the quality. The particular form of reduplication is partly predictable from the word’s phonological shape, with four main types differing in how much of the initial material is copied and how stress shifts.  

The passage also notes several irregular or unusual cases, including special reduplicated forms of *gelemuta*, an irregular verb form from *wafuriya*, and the exceptional noun *owowa*. It further distinguishes some words that only look reduplicated but are not treated as such because they lack a semantic relation to a simpler base form.

subsubsection: Past tense and medial verb suffixes
text:
There are three past tense verb suffixes for second and third person singular forms, - a, - e and - o. Which one is chosen for which verb is determined mainly by the phonemes in the stem final syllable. Most of these rules were originally worked out by Kwan Poh San.

The two basic allomorphs for the past tense suffix are \-a\ and \- e \. / -o/ is a subgroup of the allomorph \- e \. The subgrouping is based on the fact that the -a/ -e distinction runs through the whole past tense paradigms and occurs in the medial verb suffixes as well, whereas the - e/-o distinction only occurs in the second and third person past tense forms of some verbs. According to the rounding rule below ex:2:pasttenseruleEo, \- e \ is realized as /-o/ when both following a [+ labial] phoneme (either a labial consonant or the high rounded vowel /u/) and preceding a non-labial consonant ex:2:Eoex.

\ e \ /o/ / x lab __ c non-lab

/aaw-o-k/ `(s)he got (it)' cf. /aaw-e-m/ `I got (it)'

/mu-o-n/ `you swallowed' cf. /mu-e-m/ `I swallowed'

The discussion below only mentions the past tense suffixes. The vowels in the the medial verb suffixes are the same but do not have the allophonic variation between /-e/ and /-o/.

The morphophonological rules governing the choice of past tense suffixes are listed in their order of relative strength, with regard to the number of cases in the data The count included 273 verbs with the past tense suffix - a, 364 with the suffix - e. as well as the number of exceptions.

Rule 1. With a stem-final high vowel /i/ or /u/, the past tense suffix is always \ - e \ ex:2:rule1ex.

/waki- e-k/ `(s)he fell down'

/nepi- e-k/ `(s)he raised animals'

/mu- o-k/ `(s)he swallowed'

/karu- o-k/ `(s)he ran'

Rule 2. With a stem-final alveolar nasal /n/, the suffix is nearly always /-e/ ex:2:rule2ex.

/kekan- e-k/ `it hardened'

/peren- e-k/ `it tore'

/riirin- e-k/ `(s)he laughed'

/solon- e-k/ `it glided'

/uuwun- e-k/ `(s)he chatted'

In the data there are 128 verb stems ending in /n/, and only 15 take the suffix \ -a\. In some cases there is a conflict between rules 2 and 3 (below), and 13 of those exceptions follow Rule 3.

Rule 3. When the stem final syllable has a low vowel, there is dissimilation between the vowels in the stem final syllable and the past tense suffix. For these morphophonological rules the mid vowels are also considered low, so that there is height distinction only between high and low vowels.

The past tense suffix tends to be \-a\, when the last vowel in the stem is /e/ or /o/ ex:2:rule3ex.

/aner- a-k/ `(s)he aimed at'

/sirek- a-k/ `it scratched'

/imen- a-k/ `(s)he found

/on- a-k/ `(s)he did/made'

/soop- a-k/ `(s)he buried'

In words with /a/ as the last vowel in the stem, the past tense suffix tends to be \ - e \ ex:2:rule3exx. In the data there are 187 verbs that follow this rule and 19 that do not.

/serak- e-k/ `(s)he wiped'

/war- e-k/ `(s)he killed it'

/ma- e-k/ `(s)he said'

/ekap- o-k/ `(s)he came'

/aaw- o-k/ `(s)he got/took'

Rule 4. When a high vowel is followed by a stem-final consonant /k/, /t/, /s/, /r/ or /l/, the past tense suffix is \-a\. This group of consonants includes nearly all of the non-labial consonant phonemes; /n/ is handled in Rule 2, the voiced stops never occur stem-finally and /j/ hardly ever does ex:2:rule4ex.

/puuk- a-k/ `(s)he cut'

/mik- a-k/ `(s)he speared'

/itit- a-k/ `(s)he smashed'

/anetir- a-k/ `(s)he tied'

/ uur- a-k/ `(s)he blew'

/a ilil- a-k/ `it was sweet'

With the rest of the verbs, i.e. total of about 25% of all the basic verbs, it is very difficult to find any rules governing the choice of the past tense suffix ex:2:norule.

/tiim- a-k/ `(s)he touched'

/aru - a-k/ `(s)he hit'

/oosip- o-k/ `(s)he sweated'

/ iririm- o-k/ `(s)he squeezed'

/u - o-k/ `(s)he danced'

/iw- o-k/ `(s)he gave him/her'

A few verbs apparently have dropped the past tense suffix altogether. Most of these have the stem ending in the vowel sequence /ua/ ex:2:nopasttensesuffix:

/kua- -k/ `he built'

/wua- -k/ `(s)he put'

/piipua- -k/ `(s)he left'

Another verb where the past tense suffix vowel seems to have disappeared is /oro- -k/ `(s)he went down'. If the second vowel were to be taken as the suffix this verb would defy the basic rules, since the vowel /o/ is retained right through the past tense paradigm, and with the root vowel /o/ the suffix should be \-a\. Positing /oro-/ as the root solves the question why the present tense form is /ora-/: since /oi/ is not a permitted vowel sequence on Mauwake, the low back vowel /o/ has changed into the low central vowel /a/ when preceding the high front vowel /i/ of the present tense suffix.

The verbs in the Mauwake dictionary are marked as belonging to Class 1 or Class 2, the former taking \-a\ and the latter \- e \ as the past tense suffix. This is because of the following reasons: 1) the rules are rather complicated, 2) there are a number of exceptions to the main rules, and 3) there are pairs of homophonous verb roots that take a different past tense suffix each ex:2:homophonousroots.

/iw- a-k/ `(s)he went'

/iw- o-k/ `(s)he gave him/her'

/miim- a-k/ `(s)he heard'

/miim- o-k/ `(s)he preceded'

/op- a-k/ `(s)he held'

/op- o-k/ `it boiled'

/keen- a-k/ `it touched'

/keen- e-k/ `it was hot'
summary: Mauwake has three past tense suffixes for second and third person singular, -a, -e, and -o, but -o is an allomorph of -e conditioned by surrounding labial and non-labial sounds. The choice among these suffixes is governed by several morphophonological rules, especially the stem-final vowel and certain final consonants, though many verbs are exceptions or irregular. Because the system is complex and includes homophonous roots that take different suffixes, dictionary verbs are classified into two classes based on whether they take -a or -e in the past tense.

text:
The verbalizer for both adjectives and nouns is the inchoative suffix \-a r \, the root of the verb `to become' ( sec:3.8.2.2.2 ). In most environments it is realized as / -ar/, but becomes /-al/ when the last syllable of the root contains the lateral consonant /l/ ex:2:inchoative. An illustrative example is the word samora/damola `bad', which takes a different verbalizer depending on the root allomorph.

/supuk -ar-e-k/ `it got wet'

/duduw- ar-e-k/ `it became blunt'

/samor- ar-e-k/ `it broke/spoiled'

/damol- al-e-k/ `it broke/spoiled'

/memel- al-e-k/ `it became tame'

/masi- al-e-k/ `it became bitter'

In a few cases the inchoative suffix has the form /-al/ although there is no lateral consonant in the root. This might be expected, since there is some fluctuation between the liquids /l/ and /r/ in Mauwake: /eliwa/ /eriwa/ `good', /samora/ /damola/ `bad'. In Trans New Guinea, as well as other Papuan, languages it is also very common to have only one liquid, with /l/ and /r/ as allophones of the same phoneme (, ).
summary:
The verbalizer used with both adjectives and nouns is the inchoative suffix, historically from the verb meaning “to become.” It is usually realized as /-ar/, but changes to /-al/ when the final syllable of the root contains /l/, and in some cases /-al/ appears even without /l/ in the root.  

This alternation is connected to variation between /l/ and /r/ in Mauwake, where forms such as *eliwa/eriwa* ‘good’ and *samora/damola* ‘bad’ show fluctuation, and where /l/ and /r/ may function as allophones of a single liquid consonant.

text:
The completive aspect marker ( sec:3.8.5.1.1.1 ) has its origin in the verb for `put', wua -, The verb `put' is commonly used as a completive aspect marker in Papuan languages ( sec:3.8.5.1.1.1 ). but this connection has by now become opaque and the speakers consider it a morpheme on its own, pu- ex:2:completive. The initial /p/ results from assimilation with the final /p/ of the same-subject sequential action medial verb form obligatorily preceding the completive morpheme.

en-ep wu-a-k enep-pu-a-k \\
eat- ss. seq put- pa -3s eat- ss. seq - cmpl - pa -3s\\
`(s)he ate'
summary: The completive aspect marker comes historically from the verb *wua-* ‘put’, a development that is common in Papuan languages, but this origin is now opaque and speakers treat *pu-* as an independent morpheme. Its initial /p/ is explained as assimilation to the final /p/ of the same-subject sequential action medial verb form that must precede the completive marker.

text:
When words are borrowed from other languages, they are usually made to conform to the Mauwake phonology, if they do not originally do so. Thus Tok Pisin kikim `kick' becomes kiikim - in Mauwake; the word retains the original Tok Pisin word-initial stress, and the vowel in the first syllable becomes a geminate. The initial glottal fricative /h/ in the original becomes a lengthened vowel in Mauwake, e.g. Tok Pisin handet `hundred' changes into aandet in Mauwake.

The only non-native phoneme regularly retained in the loan word is the velar nasal / /, particularly prominent in the neighbouring language, Mala, and also used in personal names ex:2:Malaloan:

/nadi -ar-e-k/ `(s)he decorated him/herself'

Since consonant sequences are quite rare in Mauwake, loan words with consonant clusters tend to have vowels inserted between the consonants. With the ever-growing influence of Tok Pisin, vowel insertion is getting less common. A combination of a nasal plus a homorganic stop is always retained in a loan word ( tab:2:loanwords ).
summary:
Borrowed words are usually adapted to fit Mauwake phonology. Examples include Tok Pisin *kikim* becoming *kiikim* and *handet* becoming *aandet*, with original stress often preserved and certain sounds, such as initial /h/, replaced by vowel lengthening.

The only non-native phoneme regularly kept in loanwords is the velar nasal, especially from the neighboring language Mala and in personal names. Because consonant clusters are rare in Mauwake, vowels are often inserted between consonants, though this is becoming less common under Tok Pisin influence; a nasal plus a homorganic stop is always preserved.

text:
A grammatical word in Mauwake is defined on the basis of the following main criteria quoted from:

A grammatical word

When a grammatical word involves compounding or affixation, its component grammatical elements

The following supplementary criteria also apply: a word only allows one inflectional affix of any one type (ibid. 15), and in derivation recursiveness is blocked except in the case of causatives (ibid. 16--17). Even here the recursion is more ostensible than real, as it does not add another argument into the clause ( sec:3.8.2.3.1 ). Person/number suffixes act as word-final boundary markers in finite verbs (ibid. 17). Many words, especially those belonging to the major word classes, ``may constitute a complete utterance'' (ibid. 19) by themselves.

The boundaries of the grammatical and phonological words coincide, except in the case of clitics. Grammatically a clitic is a word but phonologically it is bound to the preceding word.

The classes of nouns, adjectives, personal pronouns, quantifiers, verbs and adverbials can be reasonably clearly defined both morpho-syntactically and semantically. The classes of question words and deictics include words with heterogeneous syntactic behaviour; question words have semantic and functional, and some morphological similarities as a group, whereas the category of deictics is based on strong morphological and semantic similarities. Connectives share the function of conjoining elements on the same level. As ``functor words'' postpositions and especially clitics are dependent on the preceding phrase. Interjections are different from all the other word classes in that they operate outside the normal syntax and often constitute a whole expression by themselves.

Nouns are naturally the largest category, but verbs are morphologically the most complex and interesting word class.

Although the great majority of the words in Mauwake can be assigned to one of the categories above, there is some indeterminacy with regard to some words that seem to belong to two or more word classes and the meanings of which are clearly related. In Austronesian languages it is common to have pre-categorial stems that may combine with affixation belonging to various word classes; only the whole word may be assigned to a particular word class. They are not homonyms, since they are semantically related. Some transitive verbs have been derived by zero derivation from nouns and adjectives, and even from adverbs (§ sec:3.8.2.2.1, sec:3.8.4.4.3 ). Nominalized verbs ( sec:3.2.6.1 ) function as nouns or adjectives. At the end of ( sec:3.2.2 ) there is a list of words that are originally nouns but have become adjectives as well. Some non-numeral quantifiers ( sec:3.4.2 ) also function as intensity adverbs ( sec:3.9.2 ). Besides these, there are individual words that function in more than one word class; these are mentioned where they occur.
summary:
Mauwake grammatical words are identified by morphological and phonological criteria, including limits on inflection, restrictions on recursive derivation, and the fact that person/number suffixes mark the end of finite verbs; many words can also stand alone as complete utterances. Grammatical and phonological word boundaries usually coincide except for clitics, which are grammatically words but phonologically attached to the preceding word.  

The language has relatively clear major word classes such as nouns, adjectives, pronouns, quantifiers, verbs, adverbials, connectives, postpositions, clitics, and interjections, though some categories are semantically or syntactically mixed. There is also indeterminacy where some words belong to more than one class, including zero-derived verbs, nominalized verbs, and words that shift between categories such as nouns, adjectives, quantifiers, and adverbs.

text:
Although the traditional semantic definition of the noun as the ``name of a person, place or thing'' is not valid as a basis for assigning members to the class, it still gives a good general description of the prototypical members of the class in Mauwake. In words, ``when the traditional definition is reversed, the definition turns out to be true. Nouns are not always persons, places or things, but persons, places and things always turn out to be nouns.'' See also,, and. Recognizing the semantic motivation of the class does not eliminate the need to define the class by its formal or functional properties.

No good morphological definition of nouns is possible in Mauwake, as there is no inflection for number ex:3:x1, gender or class, Gender or class systems are widespread in Papuan languages. Especially in the tng languages a covert system is common, where the noun class determines what existential verb is used with each noun. or case, in the noun itself. Especially the lack of plural marking is typical of the nouns in Trans-New Guinea languages. The glosses in ex:3:x1 indicate a singular/plural alternative in the nouns, but the singular form in the glosses of other examples is to be understood as neutral regarding number.

siowa wiawi\\
dog(s) father(s)\\
`The dog's/dogs' owner(s)'

Nouns are usually monomorphemic, with the exception of a small group of inalienably possessed nouns ( sec:3.2.4 ), nouns derived from verbs ( sec:3.2.6.1 ), reduplicated nouns ( sec:3.2.6.2 ) and compound nouns ( sec:3.2.5 ). The division into count and mass nouns is not very noticeable. It is mainly shown in the choice between the quantifiers unowa `many' and maneka `big, much', and to some extent in verb agreement morphology ( sec:3.4 ).

The syntactic function provides the best criterion for defining a noun in Mauwake. Nouns function mainly as the head of a noun phrase, often the head being the only element in the np. Sometimes an adjective, a quantifier or a genitive pronoun looks like a head of a np, but those cases are elliptical, and the head noun is recoverable. They can also function as a qualifier or, more rarely, as a modifier in a np. In ex:3:x2, the nps function as subject and object, and are manifested by just nouns.

Emeria=ke iwera fiirim-i-mik.\\
woman= cf coconut gather-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`(The) women gather coconuts.'

also maintain that ``from the discourse point of view, nouns function to introduce participants and `props' and to deploy them.'' Actually this is the function of a np rather than a noun. This is true in Mauwake as well, but it is not used as a criterion for defining the nouns.
summary:
In Mauwake, the traditional semantic idea of nouns as “persons, places, or things” is not sufficient for classifying nouns, but it does describe their prototypical members. The language provides no good morphological definition of nouns, since nouns do not inflect for number, gender/class, or case, and plural marking is generally absent.  

Instead, nouns are best defined syntactically: they mainly function as the head of a noun phrase, though they can also serve as qualifiers or, less often, modifiers. The passage also notes that discourse functions belong more properly to noun phrases than to nouns themselves.

subsection: Nouns and adjectives: one or two word classes?
text:
Since adjectives in Mauwake are phonologically, morphologically and syntactically very similar to nouns, the question must be asked whether the two form just one class of nominals or whether they belong to two separate word classes. In the following discussion they are treated on a semantic basis as if they were separate classes, i.e. certain words are called nouns and others adjectives, but a final conclusion as to their status is not drawn until the end of the section.

A phonologically interesting feature common to nouns and adjectives is that the majority of both end in the vowel <a>. In the other word classes words ending in <a> do occur but they are very infrequent. Inside noun phrases this vowel, when unstressed, is usually elided preceding a vowel and often also preceding a consonant. In cases like ex:3:x3, where there are two or more possible places for elision, the vowel most easily drops at the end of an adjective preceding an intensifier. Elision is also acceptable in two or more sites within one np; this is shown in ex:3:x3 and ex:3:x4.

koora eliw(a) akena also: koor(a) eliw(a) akena \\
house good very\\
`a very good house'

koor(a) kemena manek(a) akena nain \\
house inside big very that1\\
`the very big room'

Morphologically, nouns and adjectives resemble each other in that they lack inflection. There is no number, case, or gender marking in the adjectives, nor is there any inflection for comparison. (For comparison of adjectives, see sec:6.5.)

Both nouns ex:3:x7 and adjectives ex:3:x8 may be derived from verbs with the nominalizer suffix - owa.

mua soop-owa sira \\
man bury- nmz custom\\
`the burial custom (lit: the custom of burying men)'

Emi kekan-owa nain puuk-a-mik. \\
taboo be.strong- nmz that1 cut- pa -1/3p\\
`They broke the strong taboo rule.'

Verbs can be derived from both adjectives and nouns by zero verb formation ex:3:x482, ex:3:x484 or by the inchoative verbalizer - ar ( nx ). (See sec:3.8.2.2 for these processes and more examples.)

Miiw-aasa samor-a-k. \\
land-canoe bad- pa -3s\\
`He broke/ruined the car.'

Iwer(a) ififa palis-i-ya. \\
coconut dry pair.of.coconuts- nps - pr.3s\\
`He is tying dry coconuts into pairs.'

Miiw-aasa samor-ar-e-k. \\
land-canoe bad- inch - pa -3s\\
`The car broke.'

A clear morphological difference between nouns and adjectives is that adverbs may be formed from some adjectives by deleting the word-final <a> ex:3:x19, but they cannot be formed from nouns in the same way.

samora samor\\
`bad' `badly'\\

Syntactically, there are a few similarities between nouns and adjectives. Both can function as a modifier following the head noun in a np, although adjectives ex:3:x9 are much more common in this position. In terms, it is nouns whose categorial status has been reduced, i.e. nouns that are not fully individuated in the discourse ex:3:x10, that can function in this modifier position.

aasa awona fain \\
canoe old this\\
`this old canoe'

mua sira eliwa \\
man manner good\\
`a well-mannered man (=a good man)'

The intensifier akena `real(ly), very' can also modify both adjectives ex:3:x3 and nouns ex:3:x11.

mua akena \\
man real/true\\
`a real man'

Complete or partial reduplication of adjectives is a common strategy for indicating plurality in Austronesian languages, and it also occurs to some extent in many Papuan languages, including Mauwake. Reduplication is a more productive process in the adjectives ex:3:x12, ex:3:x481, but it is possible for a few nouns too ex:3:x13, ex:3:x1859 ( sec:3.2.6.2 ).

ifa samo-samora \\
snake rdp -bad\\
`bad snakes'

Maa ele-eliwa sesek-a-mik. \\
thing/food rdp -good sell- pa -1/3p\\
`They sold good foods (different kinds).'

Owow-owowa ikiw-e-mik. \\
rdp -village go- pa -1/3p\\
`They went to many villages.'

sira-sira \\
custom-custom\\
`many customs', `different kinds'

The syntactic differences between nouns and adjectives are as follows. Adjectives do not function as head of a noun phrase. The cases where they would seem to do so are in fact cases of ellipsis, and the head noun must be recoverable from the context, either linguistic or extra-linguistic ex:3:x14.

awona nain p-ekap-e! \\
old that1 bpx -come- imp.2s\\
`Bring the old one!'

Only a noun may occur as a qualifier in a noun phrase, preceding the head noun ex:3:x15. In some of these cases it is difficult to decide whether they are really nps with a qualifier and a head noun, or compound nouns. But if the latter is the case, then the restriction applies that an adjective cannot be the first element in a compound noun.

mera eka \\
fish water\\
`fish soup'

mera eka en-owa sira \\
[[fish water eat- nmz custom\\
`the custom of eating fish soup'

An adjective cannot be the only element following a genitive pronoun, but a noun can. Even in elliptical expressions an adjective following a genitive pronoun is not very acceptable ex:3:x17.

Yiena awona nain p-ekap-e! \\
1p. gen old that1 bpx -come- imp.2s\\
`Bring our old one(s)!'

An exception to this rule is the adjective maneka `big' ex:3:x105. The expression yiena Maneka `our Lord' (literally: our Big one), is probably formed following Tok Pisin Bikpela bilong yumi. Non-prototypical adjectives are discussed later in this section; `big' is a prototypical adjective, so its use in a typically nominal position is an exception.

wi Amerika maneka, unuma Magerka \\
3p. unm America big name MacArthur\\
`the leader of the Americans, whose name was MacArthur'

Only an adjective functions as the head of an adjective phrase. In that position it may be modified by intensity adverbs ( sec:3.9.2 ). Of these, lawisiw `rather' does not modify nouns at all ex:3:x18; akena `very' and pepek `enough' may modify nouns as well; wenup `very' can do that too, but as a noun modifier it has a somewhat restricted use and a different meaning: `many'.

Mera nain lawisiw maneka akena. \\
fish that1 rather big very\\
`That fish is rather huge.'
summary: The passage argues that Mauwake nouns and adjectives are highly similar phonologically, morphologically, and syntactically, so their status as one class or two separate classes is initially left open and discussed semantically before a final decision is made. Shared properties include frequent final <a>, lack of inflection, derivation from verbs by nominalization or verbalization, and some overlap in modification and reduplication, but adjectives differ in not serving as noun-phrase heads or as qualifiers before nouns, and in allowing adverb formation by dropping final <a>.

subsection: Nouns and adjectives: one or two word classes?
text:
What further obscures the area of nouns and adjectives is the fact that there are a number of words that sometimes function like nouns ex:3:x20, sometimes like adjectives ex:3:x21, and that also semantically could be like either.

Pina maneka kamenap? \\
weight big what.like\\
`What is the weight like?', `How big is the weight?'

Maa nain lawisiw pina. \\
thing that1 rather heavy\\
`The thing is rather heavy.

The prototype view offers a plausible solution for the problem. Starting from the study of basic colour terms it has been applied to other areas of semantics and also to linguistic categorization (e.g. and ). The main idea that categories have more central, or focal, members as well as more marginal members was also recognized by in his description of English word classes. The prototype approach allows for stability as well as flexibility, both of which are needed in an attempt to describe a human language.

If prototypical linguistic categories are focal, or optimal, instances on a continuum and maximally distinct from one another, what are prototypical nouns like as opposed to prototypical adjectives? According to, a noun indicates categor ization: most prototypical nouns identify a certain kind of person, thing or animal. Relative temporal stability is for Giv\'on what characterizes nouns, and the most prototypical nouns denote concrete, physical, compact entities ( Givon1984). Instead of time stability, claims it is relative atemporality that makes an entity an entity. Adjectives, or property concepts, indicate description, and they denote single properties unlike nouns which denote a cluster of properties.

In Mauwake, a prototypical noun occurs as a head in a np, as a pre-modifier or, less frequently, as a post-modifier in a np, or as any element in a compound noun. It does not occur as the head in an ap. It can be modified by adjectives or genitive pronouns but not by the intensity adverbs lawisiw `rather' and wenup `very'. Prototypical adjectives occur as the head of an adjective phrase. They do not pre-modify nouns or function as the first element in a compound noun.

It turns out that in Mauwake the most prototypical nouns include names of concrete non-human rather than human objects, when one would expect words referring to human beings to be nouns par excellence (see ). Some human nouns may be used as post-modifiers in a np: from the cluster of properties denoted by the noun one has been picked out, and the noun is used like an adjective ex:3:x23, ex:3:x24. The adjectival use of mua `man' in ex:3:x23 is particularly interesting, because the adjectives morena `male' and suwina `female' are used for animals.

labuel(a) mua \\
pawpaw man\\
`male pawpaw'

donki takira \\
donkey young.person\\
`young donkey'

The less prototypical status of human nouns also shows in words like apura `widow' and oosa `widower' which may occur by themselves as heads of a np, but which are most typically used as post-modifiers of emeria `woman' and mua `man', respectively. Other words in this group are muupera `visitor, guest' and especially weria, which as a human noun only occurs in the combination mua weria, `uncle/ male cross cousin/ nephew'. The mua weria' s are responsible for burying a dead person and dispensing of his/her belongings ( sec:1.3.6 ). As age in human beings tends to be treated as a crucial determinant of kind, even languages with large adjective classes often have special nouns for referring to old persons. In Mauwake, adjectives that indicate age in humans are non-prototypical, more noun-like than most adjectives: both iperowa `middle-aged' ex:3:x25 and panewowa `old' are used as the head of a np besides the typical adjectival use.

Iperowa opora wiar miim-i-yen. \\
middle-aged talk 3. dat hear-Np- fu.1p\\
`We will listen to the talk of the middle-aged (men).'

According to, if a language has adjectives at all, words expressing age, dimension, value and colour are likely to belong to the adjective class, however small the class. The most prototypical adjectives in Mauwake belong to these groups, with the exception of adjectives denoting human age. In the group of adjectives denoting either physical property or human propensity, some are ambiguous as to their basic category: anima is both `blade' and `sharp', and pina both `weight, burden' and `heavy'. Different groups of adjectives, as well as the use of adjectives, are discussed below in sec:3.3.

With the rules given above it is fairly straightforward to distinguish the nouns and adjectives in Mauwake. But a small group remains that seems to have a membership in both classes. Originally, they are are nouns that are now employed as adjectives as well. The claim is based on the fact that the noun category is the more basic and universally recognized, whereas the existence of the adjective category is disputed in some languages; in Mauwake the noun class is clearly established, large, and more easily definable. Also, there are at least two nouns in Mauwake that currently seem to be in the process of becoming regular adjectives: the meaning of the phrase stays the same with the pre-modifying noun and the post-modifying adjective ex:3:x107-- ex:3:x1823.

napum(a) mua\\
sickness man\\
`a sick man'

mua napuma \\
man sick\\
`a sick man', also: `human (lit: man's) sickness'

wadol(a) opora \\
lie/false talk\\
`a lie'

opor(a) wadola \\
talk lie/false\\
`a lie'

tab:3:nounadj gives a list of the most common of the words functioning both as nouns and as adjectives.
summary:
The passage explains that the boundary between nouns and adjectives is blurred because some words can function as either category and may be semantically compatible with both. It argues that a prototype approach is useful for handling this overlap, with prototypical nouns in Mauwake serving as heads of noun phrases and prototypical adjectives serving as heads of adjective phrases.

In Mauwake, prototypical nouns are often concrete, non-human entities, while some human nouns are less typical and can be used adjectivally as modifiers. Likewise, some adjectives denoting age, dimension, value, and colour are central to the adjective class, but a small group of words appears to belong to both classes or be in the process of shifting from nouns to adjectives.

text:
There is very little difference between common and proper nouns in Mauwake, and it can be questioned whether the two should be grouped separately as is traditionally often done in language descriptions. Proper nouns are sometimes classified separately because they are said to be unable to have modifiers, and in practice, they usually occur without any modifiers. This is related to the fact that they normally only have a referent, but no intension. In most of the cases where a proper noun is modified, ``it lacks a unique reference and is being used as a common noun'':

I mean the old and cranky Joe Smith, not the younger one.

The most common type of a proper noun is a name of a person. A proper noun may also become a true common noun, when one or more of the qualities of a person are used to characterise some other being. For example, the name of a well-known expatriate, Jooren, was borrowed by Mauwake speakers to mean `a stingy shopkeeper' (that is, one who does not sell things on credit and does not give discount to relatives).

In Mauwake, proper names can be modified without difficulty, especially by the demonstrative nain `that', but also by adjectives. In a culture where there are several namesakes, and surnames are rarely used, modifiers are occasionally needed to distinguish between people ex:3:x27.

Adek panewowa nain ma-i-yem. \\
Adek old that1 say-Np- pr.1s\\
`I am talking about the old Adek.'

But even proper names, that have a unique reference and do not need to be distinguished from any other referent can be modified ex:3:x106:

Dabe fain uuw-ow(a) mua=ke. \\
Dabe this work- nmz man= cf \\
`Dabe here is a hard worker.'

In this case, the behaviour of proper names is similar to that of the personal pronouns, which also have unique reference, but can be modified nevertheless. Van Valin and LaPolla (ibid. 59--60) note that languages may vary in how freely they allow proper nouns and pronouns to take modifiers.

Name taboos influence the use of personal names in several ways. A person is given many different names: at least one from each parents' side (as in-laws may not mention each others' names), a baptismal name, and possibly others as well. These names are used by different people. Name taboos may be avoided by calling someone by a teknonym like `Sarak's father', or by calling a wife by the husband's name when she is with the in-laws and the husband is not around. Nicknames, often referring to physical properties, are also very common: buburia `bald', mua kuuma `lame' (literally `stick-man'). The term `namesake' is very common and even used of people who have been named after different names of the same person. Two boys, Yoli and Wangali, were called namesakes of each other, as they were both named after the same ancestor.

Perhaps the most characteristic feature of personal names is discourse- pr agmatic: their token frequency is very low in texts. Especially the main participant, once (s)he has been mentioned by name -- if (s)he ever is -- (s)he is then usually referred to by other means: a np, pronoun, or just person marking on the verb.

Besides the names of people, place names form another large group of proper names. In Mauwake, the proper name often modifies a generic noun: Moro ( owowa) `Moro (village), Siburten ( ema) `Siburten (mountain/hill)', Nemuru ( eka) `Nemuru (river)' ( sec:4.1 ).

The place name is also used when the inhabitants are referred to. When reference is made to an individual or a select group, the place name is used as a qualifier in the noun phrase ex:3:x421:

Amiten mua oko ekap-o-k. \\
Amiten man other come- pa -3s\\
`A man from Amiten came.'

When the whole group is referred to, a plural pronoun is added to the place name ex:3:x422, ex:3:x423:

I Moro=ke uf-e-mik. \\
1p. unm Moro= cf dance- pa -1/3p\\
`We Moro people danced.'

(Wi) Lasen wia nokar-e-k. \\
3p. unm Lasen 3p. acc ask- pa -3s\\
`He asked the Lasen people'

The optional initial pronoun wi is part of the object here, not a subject pronoun.
summary:
In Mauwake, there is little difference between common and proper nouns, and proper names can freely take modifiers such as demonstratives and adjectives. The passage argues that proper nouns often behave like common nouns when modified, and notes that name taboos, alternative naming practices, and low token frequency in discourse all shape the use of personal names.

Place names are another major class of proper nouns, and they can modify generic nouns or refer to the people from that place. When referring to an individual or a subset, the place name functions as a qualifier, while reference to the whole group is marked by adding a plural pronoun.

text:
The Austronesian languages in Melanesia tend to have very elaborate semantically based possessive systems that indicate the relationship between the ``possessor'' and the ``possession'': kin relation, body part, food, etc. Inalienable possession is indicated by affixation on the noun, alienable possession by a separate possessive pronoun. Because of this, the simpler inalienable possession marking -- also evident in many tng languages -- could easily be attributed to influence from Austronesian languages. But claims it is likely that even Proto tng had inalienable nouns before there was any contact with Austronesian languages. On the time frames of tng occupation and Austronesian migration, see e.g.. In Mauwake the division into alienably and inalienably possessed nouns is along the lines of kinship terms (see sec:1.3.6 for a kinship chart). Most kin terms in tab:3:inalposs obligatorily indicate who the ``possessor'' is.

The possessive prefixes y-, n- and w- in the inalienably possessed nouns developed from the first, second, and third person pronouns. These prefixes are in the process of merging with the root. The terms (a-j) in tab:3:inalposs are somewhat more lexicalized than the ones in (k-t): the first person prefix is mostly lost, and in some cases there is suppletion in the stem. These are some of the socially most important and frequently used kinship terms. The frequent use probably accounts for the omission of the possession prefix in the first person: these terms are used more as terms of address, whereas the other kinship nouns are only needed as terms of reference. Also, there is a tendency to drop the first person prefix before the front vowel /e/ regardless of the closeness of the kinship relation.

The ``possessors'' are differentiated as first, second or third person but not as singular vs. plural. An unmarked ex:3:x1311 or a genitive pronoun ex:3:x28 and ex:3:x1312 may be used to either make this number distinction or to emphasize the kin relationship, when the relationship is used as a term of reference rather than as a term of address.

Kuuten wiawi iperowa, yo auwa kapa=ke. \\
Kuuten 3s/p.father firstborn 1s. unm 1s/p.father lastborn= cf \\
`Kuuten's father was the firstborn, my father the lastborn.' Both of these fathers could be called auwa `my/our father(s)' by the two men.

Aakisa yena auwa kapa fain=ke yia uruf-i-ya. \\
now 1s. gen 1s/p.father lastborn this= cf 1p. acc see-Np- pr.3s\\
`Now this lastborn of my ``fathers'' watches over us.'

Sa, a nena nie=ke, nena nepua=ke, niawi=ke.\\
intj intj 2s. gen 2s/p.uncle= cf 2s. gen 2s/p.brother-in-law 2s/p.father\\
`(Don't you understand,) those are your uncle(-in-law), your brother-in-law and father(-in-law).'

When a neutral, ``non-possessed'', kinship term is needed, the first person form is used. This is interesting, as the third person singular is typically considered the neutral, or unmarked, form. The terms `(my) mother' and `(my) father' are also used as respectful terms of address for almost any stranger regardless of age, or for anyone whose status in the kinship system is uncertain. I have been addressed as mother by an old man who temporarily forgot what my status according to their kinship system was - I was actually his granddaughter!

Four alienably possessed nouns, namely those for `man', `woman', `boy' and `girl', have been taken into the kinship system for terms of some nuclear family members, as seen in tab:3:alposs.

Also the term nembesir `ancestor (beyond grandparents)' or `descendant (beyond grandchildren)' is an alienably possessed noun, possibly because relatives so far removed in time are considered less relevant. It is used both for males and females. But the term for `namesake', yomawa, is included in the inalienably possessed kinship terms, as a child is named after some relatives, and the namesake relation forms an additional bond between them.
summary:
The passage describes a complex possessive system in Melanesian Austronesian languages and argues that although similar inalienable possession marking in TNG languages could reflect contact influence, Proto-TNG likely already had inalienable nouns. In Mauwake, kinship terms are divided into alienably and inalienably possessed nouns, with possessive prefixes derived from pronouns that are merging with the noun and sometimes omitted in highly frequent, socially important terms.  

The system marks possessor person but not number, though genitive forms can add number distinctions or emphasize kin relations, and some nouns such as `man`, `woman`, `boy`, and `girl` have been incorporated into the kinship system. The passage also notes that distant kin terms may be alienably possessed, while `namesake` is inalienably possessed because it creates a special social bond.

text:
The distinction between compound nouns and noun phrases is a problematic area in many languages, including Mauwake. Both are formed by combining independent elements into larger units, and their form and meaning are largely based on the form and meaning of those elements. Phonological, morphological, syntactic as well as semantic criteria have been called upon to differentiate between compounds and phrases.

In many languages, ``word accent'', i.e. stress and/or pitch, helps to distinguish compounds. In Mandarin Chinese, contrastive stress can only fall on the ``stress center'' of a word, including compounds. In Finnish, the primary stress is on the first, and only on the first, syllable of even very long compound words like kuluttajansuoja-asiamiesverkostokysymys `the question of consumer ombudsman network', but even in Finnish there are unclear cases like valveillaolo vs. valveilla olo `being awake', of which native speakers find hard to decide whether they are one or two words. The varying writing convention reflects the ambiguity.

Linguists differ in their views about the importance of stress placement in interpreting English compounds. and consider it criterial, and so do, although more cautiously. takes it as one premise for his study of compounds while admitting that the case is not very well substantiated. Others, like, and do not consider a single primary stress essential for compounds. According to, criteria for judging ``wordness'' in English, i.e. positional mobility and uninterruptability (or internal stability) do not distinguish between single- and double-stressed compounds.

Morphology may place constraints on compounding. In English, the genitive is common in phrases but rare in compounds: duck's egg vs. duck-egg. But note also women's lib(eration), a compound. In Finnish, the first part of a compound is often in the nominative or genitive case, whereas the other cases are infrequent in this position. In German, certain elements may serve as morphological ``glue'' between the parts of a compound (ibid. 42).

The two criteria for wordness by mentioned above are syntactic in nature: a word, hence also a compound, is moved as one unit, and cannot be interrupted by other words as a phrase often can. These criteria do not apply to all, and not only to compound words, but they are useful in trying to establish the difference between compounds and phrases in a given language. adds another one: a member of a compound generally cannot serve as a constituent in a syntactic construction. One can say a very black bird but not * a very blackbird.

The semantic interpretation of phrases is generally quite compositional: the meaning of the whole can be deduced from the meanings of the words. Compounds are more heterogeneous in their interpretation: some are compositional, whereas others involve special interpretive principles not applicable to phrases. Also, compounds as words are subject to changes of meaning, so many compounds may have meanings that are only vaguely or metaphorically related to that which is predicted on the basis of the parts (Anderson 1985a:42). Knowledge of the pragmatics of the situation may be needed for the interpretation of many compound words (Bauer 1983:58). The more fully lexicalized the compounds are, the more the meaning of the whole may deviate from the meaning of the parts. The same compound word may also be fully lexicalized in a certain context, and still be open for other interpretations in other contexts (Andrew Pawley, p. c.).

While there are languages where it is easy to distinguish between compound nouns and noun phrases, in others there is an intermediate area between the two. Thus doubts that the dividing line is always well-defined, and suggest the concept of ``partial compounding'' to account for the formal and semantic gradience between compounds and phrases in English. Bringing a historical viewpoint to the question, citing developments in English both from phrase to compound and from compound to phrase, offers a very liberal view: ``it is of no consequence whether we reckon [the] doubtful cases as one word or two words, for [...] a word group (like a single word) may be either primary or an adjunct or a subjunct''.

None of the criteria mentioned above can be easily applied in Mauwake. Semantically, there is a continuum between fully compositional noun phrases and fully lexicalized compounds. But warns that the greater specialization in meaning in the compound words as against phrases should not be used as a criterion, as ``we cannot gauge meanings accurately enough, and many a phrase is as specialized in meaning as any compound''. This warning is all the more relevant when one studies a language not one's own.

The basic stress pattern of noun phrases and compounds is similar, as one of the modifiers usually receives the phrase stress rather than the head noun ex:3:x29, ex:3:x30. Likewise, in compound nouns the modifying formative receives the main stress and the main formative is only weakly stressed ex:3:x31, ex:3:x32: the ``stress centre'' is on another element than the head.

yo auwa aasa \\
1s. unm 1s/p.father canoe\\
`my father's canoe'

aas(a) ge lemuta \\
canoe small\\
`a small canoe'

miiw(a)-aasa \\
land-canoe\\
`vehicle, car'

enow(a) ge lemuta \\
food/meal small\\
`feast'

In the examples ex:3:x29- ex:3:x32 only the phrase stress is marked by ' preceding the stressed syllable.
In Mauwake orthography, the parts of a compound word are usually written separately to help the new readers to identify the parts; miiw-aasa `vehicle' is one of the exceptions.
Enow gelemuta is not used with its literal meaning `small meal'.
However, the head noun in a np may receive the phrase stress if it is emphasized for contrast, clarification or some other reason, whereas the stress centre in a compound stays the same.
summary:
The passage argues that distinguishing compound nouns from noun phrases is difficult because phonological, morphological, syntactic, and semantic criteria often overlap or fail to give a clear boundary. In Mauwake, as in some other languages, compounds and phrases can show similar stress patterns, but compounds differ in that the main stress remains fixed on the modifier, their parts are usually written separately in orthography, and their meanings may be more lexicalized than those of ordinary noun phrases.

It also notes that no single criterion, especially semantic specialization, is reliable enough on its own, since meanings are hard to judge and many phrases can also be specialized. Overall, the text presents compounding and phrasal combination as a continuum rather than a sharp divide.

text:
Since there is hardly any morphology in nouns and noun phrases, one would not expect to find much help here in distinguishing between compounds and phrases. But there is a minor factor that is relevant in this respect: a phrase containing a noun and an adjective can be pluralized by adjectival reduplication when the adjective allows reduplication ex:3:x33, whereas a compound noun with a similar structure usually cannot ex:3:x34, even if it is possible in some rare cases ex:3:x35.

maa gelemuti-tik \\
thing small- rdp \\
`small things'

enow(a) gelemuti-tik \\
food/meal small- rdp \\
`feasts'

owow(a) mane-maneka \\
village rdp -big\\
`towns', `big villages'

Uninterruptibility is more typical of compounds than phrases. The noun phrase owow maneka means `a big village', as a compound it means `a town/city'. As a phrase it is interruptible ex:3:x1768, as a compound it is not.

owowa lawisiw maneka \\
village rather big\\
`a rather big village'

Likewise, as a compound kae sira `ancestral custom' (literally: `grandfather's custom') is uninterruptible. When a genitive pronoun is inserted between the two parts, the meaning cannot be `ancestral custom' ex:3:x1860:

kae ona sira \\
grandfather 3s. gen custom\\
`grandfather's custom/habit'

In Mauwake, word combinations are treated as compounds if they (1) have a specialized meaning, (2) have a stress centre not affected by contrastive stress, and (3) tend to be uninterruptible. However, this distinction is very tentative in some cases. Some examples are provided where the same combination may be either a compound noun or a noun phrase.

Morphologically, there are four compound noun types in Mauwake: n+ n, v NMZ + v, n+v NMZ and n+ adj. Syntactically these correspond to a head noun with a nominal pre- or post-modifier in a np, or a head noun with an adjective post-modifier in the np. In most compound nouns the last noun is the head. But in generic-specific compounds, as well as the n+ adj and n+v NMZ compounds, the first part is the main element, and the scope of its meaning is restricted by the second part. In coordinate compounds the two parts are equally important.

On the basis of the semantic relations between the parts the n+ n compounds can be divided into a few main groups. In the first one the relationship can be said to be characterized by origin understood very widely, e.g. in the sense of place of origin ex:3:x37, source ex:3:x1860, or ``possession'' ex:3:x40, ex:3:x41.

piip(a) mera \\
seaweed fish\\
`rainbow fish'

emeria napuma \\
woman sick(ness)\\
`menstruation'

ibiamun sama \\
dove ladder\\
`cross-beam (in a roof)'

The compound noun ex:3:x40 has the stress centre on the first part, but the noun phrase emeria napuma, with the phrase stress on napuma, may be used to mean either `a sick woman', or more commonly `a (dead) woman's body', a euphemistic expression.

The second relationship is a whole- part relationship: the first element states the whole, the second its part ex:3:x42, ex:3:x43.

mokok(a) oposia \\
eye meat\\
`pupil (of the eye)'

ekek(a) muuna \\
branch joint/projection\\
`bud'

The third relationship is that of container. As a compound muuk(a) sia ex:3:x45 has the stress centre on the first word. In a noun phrase ex:3:x1770, however, the phrase stress may also be on the second item if it is emphasized, and a third person singular genitive pronoun may be added between the parts as well. Example ex:3:x46 is an extended compound: iinan aasa is a ``sky canoe'', or vehicle, for flying in the sky, and iinan aasa epa a place for those vehicles.

muuk(a) sia \\
son netbag\\
`womb', `pouch (of a marsupial)'

muuk(a) sia \\
son netbag\\
`a son's/child's netbag (used for carrying the baby)'

iinan aasa epa \\
sky canoe place\\
`airstrip, airport'

As was mentioned above, the generic-specific relationship is different in that the modifying part follows rather than precedes the main part ex:3:x47-- ex:3:x49. In this respect these compounds resemble phrases where the head noun has an adjective rather than a noun modifier. A particularly common word for the first part in these compounds is the maximally generic word in Mauwake, maa ` thing' ex:3:x49. The scope of meaning for maa is like that of `thing ' in its widest sense in English.

mera nepa \\
fish bird\\
`eagle ray'

oon(a) tiretira \\
bone horizontal.cane (in roof structure)\\
`rib'

maa pela \\
thing leaf\\
`(edible) greens'

There are two compound types with nominalized verbs. When the nominalized verb follows the other noun, it behaves like an adjective and receives the phrase stress ex:3:x1521, ex:3:x1522.

maa en-owa \\
thing/food eat- nmz \\
`food'

emer(a) ik-owa \\
sago roast- nmz \\
`bread, roasted sago'

A compound type where the nominalized verb precedes the other noun is more common than the one above. When the second part is a human noun, it usually has to be the agent of the verb ex:3:x52, but when the noun is non-human, it is harder to find a common denominator for the semantic relationships between the parts in different compounds. Quite often the meaning centers around function, purpose or ``typical'' action, place, time, etc. ex:3:x53, ex:3:x54.

uuw-ow(a) mua \\
work- nmz man\\
`worker'

in-ow(a) koora \\
sleep- nmz house\\
`bedroom'

om-ow(a) eka \\
cry- nmz water\\
`tear'

This compound type particularly easily allows compounds with more than two roots ex:3:x55-- ex:3:x60:

ikemik(a) kaik-ow(a) mua \\
wound tie- nmz man\\
`doctor'

emer(a) en-ow(a) mua \\
sago eat- nmz man\\
`a Sepik man (lit: a sago eater)' Sepik province is known for its main staple, sago starch.

ama urup-ow(a) (epa/kame) \\
sun rise- nmz place/side\\
`east'

In the example ex:3:x61 the main noun epa/ kame can be dropped, and this happens in some other compounds as well:

epir(a) suruk-ow(a) (tetelka) \\
plate wipe- nmz finger\\
`forefinger'
summary:
Mauwake noun morphology provides limited help for distinguishing compounds from phrases, but compounds are more likely to show specialized meaning, fixed stress, and uninterruptibility. A phrase with a noun and adjective can sometimes be pluralized by adjectival reduplication, whereas similar compounds usually cannot.  

The passage classifies Mauwake compound nouns into four morphological types: n+n, v+NMZ+v, n+vNMZ, and n+adj, and notes that most are head-final except for generic-specific, n+adj, and n+vNMZ compounds, where the first element is the main semantic component. It also outlines major semantic relations among n+n compounds, including origin/possession, whole–part, container, and generic-specific relations, and illustrates that nominalized-verb compounds often express functions, purposes, or typical actions and can extend to more than two roots.

text:
The coordinate compounds are different from the other compounds in that neither of the parts modifies the other. The meaning of the whole is derived from the combined meaning of the two terms. Also, there is no stress centre: both parts of the compound are stressed equally. The number of these compounds is small ex:3:x50, ex:3:x51.

emeria mua \\
woman man\\
`people'

muuka wiipa \\
son daughter\\
`children'

The n+ adj compounds are as hard to distinguish from phrases as some of the other groups mentioned above ex:3:x57-- ex:3:x59. Again the uninterruptibility and lexicalized meaning are the main criteria. If the adjective sepa `black' is added between the two words in ex:3:x57, the meaning changes into `a small black man'.

mua gelemuta \\
man small\\
`a little boy'

mia yoowa \\
body/skin hot\\
`fever'

maa samora \\
thing bad\\
`mosquito'

Compounding is a productive process in Mauwake, and it is the most common language-internal means used for adding new lexical items to the language.
summary: Coordinate compounds in Mauwake differ from other compounds because neither element modifies the other; the meaning comes from combining both parts, and both are equally stressed. The language also has noun-adjective compounds that are hard to distinguish from phrases, with uninterruptibility and lexicalized meaning as the main diagnostic criteria. Overall, compounding is a productive process in Mauwake and the main language-internal way of creating new lexical items.

text: In this section I will discuss derivations where the end result is a noun. There are only two of these: nouns made out of verbs, and noun reduplications.
summary: The passage states that this section will discuss derivations whose final output is a noun. It notes that there are only two such types: nouns formed from verbs and noun reduplications.

text:
The process of nominalizing verbs is a straightforward and fully productive process of adding the nominalizing suffix - owa to the verb stem. The nominalized verbs most commonly function as nouns ex:3:x62-- ex:3:x1231, sometimes also as adjectives ex:3:x1247. In the Mauwake dictionary some of these nominalized forms have their own entry as if they were fully lexicalized as nouns, but this is to some extent a concession to other languages, where separate nouns may be required for the action nominals and more lexicalized deverbal nouns (for the distinction, see ). In Mauwake it is often difficult to establish which of the nominalizations are lexicalized.

uf- owa \\
dance- nmz \\
`(the act of) dancing', `(traditional) dance'

irak- owa \\
fight- nmz \\
`fighting', `fight/war'

Fiirim- owa=pa opaimika aakun-e-mik. \\
gather- nmz = loc talk talk- pa -1/3p\\
`In the meeting we talked.'

Amina puk -owa eliw(a) marewa=ke. \\
pot break- nmz good none= cf \\
`The pot is broken (and) not good' or: `The broken pot is not good.'

Action nominals function like any regular nouns in Mauwake. They can be, for example, a head ex:3:x64 or a qualifier ex:3:x65 in a np, and a first ex:3:x66 or last element ex:3:x67 in a compound noun.

Siowa alu-owa miim-ap ekap-o-k. \\
dog make.noise- nmz hear- ss. seq come- pa -3s\\
`He heard the dog's noise and came' or: `The dog heard noise and came.'

Irak-owa kerer-owa epa weeser-em-ik-eya \\
fight- nmz appear- nmz time finish- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds \\
`As the time of the war was getting close ' (Lit: `As the war-appearing time was coming to an end ')

Kererowa is both the head of irakowa kererowa and part of the qualifier phrase in irakowa kererowa epa.

Oram niir-ow(a) opora ma-e-m. \\
just laugh- nmz talk say- pa -1s\\
`I just said it as a joke.'

Kaul wafur-owa mera aaw-owa eliw. \\
hook throw- nmz fish get- nmz all.right\\
`As for throwing a hook, it is a good way of catching fish.' (Lit: `Hook-throwing is all right for fish-catching.')

The following expressions form an interesting pair, as ex:3:x424 is a np with a nominalized verb as its head, and ex:3:x425 is a compound noun with a nominalized verb as the first part.

mua aakun- owa \\
man talk- nmz \\
`talk(ing) of man/people', `people's talk'

aakun- ow( a) mua \\
talk- nmz man\\
`a talker', `a spokesman'

Action nominals keep their verb-like property of being able to take the same arguments and peripherals as the verb serving as the root of the noun. The result is a nominalized clause, which functions like a noun phrase. This is discussed further in sec:5.7 and sec:8.3.2.

list various kinds of other nominalization possibilities, calls all of these lexical nominalizations, and Ylikoski calls them deverbal nouns ( Ylikoski2003) to distinguish them from action nominals. but in Mauwake the corresponding expressions are compound nouns or noun phrases consisting of the nominalized verb (or clause) plus another noun ex:3:x1232, ex:3:x1233, rather than simple nominalizations.

ikemika kaik- ow(a) mua \\
wound tie- nmz man\\
`doctor, nurse'

maa eneka teek- ow(a) (maa) \\
thing tooth open- nmz (thing)\\
`can opener'

Maa eneka is a compound referring to edible animals; the very generic noun maa `thing' may be omitted from the end.
summary:
Verb nominalization in Mauwake is a fully productive process formed by adding the suffix **-owa** to the verb stem. These nominalized forms usually function as nouns, sometimes as adjectives, and they can retain their verb-like arguments and peripherals, creating nominalized clauses that behave like noun phrases.
