Wi feeke ika-uk, i iisow ikiw-i-yen. \\
3p. unm here. cf be- imp.3p 1p. unm 1p. isol go-Np- fu.1p\\
`Let them stay here, only we will go.'

When the first syllable of a plural isolative pronoun is reduplicated, the pronoun refers to individuals in the group ex:3:x603.

Ii-iisow pok-ap opora siisim-ep weeser-eya unow=iya aakun-e-mik.\\
rdp -1p. isol sit- ss. seq talk write- ss. seq finish-2/3s. ds many= com talk- pa -1/3p\\
`We sat and wrote separately, and then talked together.'

Although the pronouns in ex:3:x602 and ex:3:x603 sound rather similar, there is a stress difference between them. In the former, iisow gets stronger stress than the unmarked pronoun i, in the latter the first syllable of the reduplicated word is stressed.
summary:
The isolative pronouns are formed from the unmarked pronouns and use the ending -isow, which may be an older morpheme meaning “alone”; in singular forms, /o/ becomes /a/ because /oi/ is not allowed in Mauwake. Their basic meaning is “X alone” or “by himself/herself,” and they can function as subject by themselves or more commonly alongside an overt unmarked pronoun showing case.  

In the plural, the forms mean “only we/you/they as a group,” and reduplication of the first syllable shifts the meaning to individuals acting separately within the group. The passage also notes a stress contrast between the plain plural isolative form and the reduplicated form.

text:
The restrictive pronouns are formed by adding the limiting clitic - iw `only' either to a genitive pronoun or to a focal pronoun ( sec:3.12.6 ). When it is added to a genitive pronoun it means `on one's own' ex:3:x605-- ex:3:x607.

No nena=iw ma-i-n=i? \\
2s. unm 2s. gen = lim say-Np- pr.2s= qm \\
`Do you say it on your own?' (i.e. `Did you think of it yourself?')

O=ko me efa maak-e-k, yena=iw amis-ar-e-m.\\
3s. unm = nf not 1s. acc tell- pa -3s 1s. gen = lim knowledge- inch - pa -1s\\
`He/she didn't tell me, I learned it on my own.'

Yien=iw ikiw-ik-ua. \\
1p. gen = lim go-be- pa.3s\\
`Let's go on our own (as a group, or one by one).'

When the limiting clitic is added to the focal form of the free pronoun it adds the meaning of exclusiveness to the pronoun ex:3:x608, ex:3:x609.

Anane nos=iw nefa maak-i-ya. \\
always 2s. fc = lim 2s. acc tell-Np- pr.3s\\
`He always talks to you only.'

Wi anane is=iw yiam=iya irak-i-mik. \\
3p. unm always 1p. fc = lim 1p. refl = com fight-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`They always fight with us only.'
summary: Restrictive pronouns are formed by attaching the limiting clitic **-iw** ‘only’ to either a genitive pronoun or a focal pronoun. With genitive pronouns, it means **‘on one’s own’** or **‘by oneself’**, while with focal pronouns it adds an **exclusive** meaning, roughly **‘only’**.

text:
The reflexive-reciprocal pronouns have the unmarked pronouns as their basis, but the derivative suffix is slightly different for singular and plural. They are shown in tab:3:refl-recpron.

The singular forms are used as reflexives only ex:3:x610, ex:3:x1864, the plural forms both as reflexives ex:3:x611, ex:3:x1865 and as reciprocals ex:3:x612, ex:3:x1866.

Naap on-ap yame amukar-e-m. \\
thus do- ss. seq 1s. refl scold- pa -1s\\
`Having done so I scolded myself (i.e. was angry at myself).'

Iinan akena ikiw-ep wame pipilim-ep aakun-em-ika-i-non.\\
on.top very go- ss. seq 3s. refl hide- ss. seq speak- ss. sim -be-Np- fu.3s\\
`It (= a bird) will go very high up and hide itself and keep making its calls.'

Niam tuun-ap teeria erup wu-eka. \\
2p. refl count- ss. seq group two put- imp.2p\\
`Count yourselves and form two groups.'

Nainiw sande uura yiam fiirim-e-mik. \\
again Sunday night 1p. refl gather- pa -1/3p\\
`Again on Sunday night we gathered.'

Wiam fook-ap irak-e-mik. \\
3p. refl split- ss. seq fight- pa -1/3p\\
`They split from each other and fought.'

Sarir-ap yiam far-i-mik. \\
surround- ss. seq 1p. refl call-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`We surround (the fish) and call each other.'

In many contexts only the reflexive or the reciprocal interpretation is natural. But a potential ambiguity in some contexts is resolved by adding a genitive pronoun to mark the reflexive ex:3:x614 and an unmarked or restrictive pronoun to mark the reciprocal pronoun ex:3:x613.

Niena niam kookal-eka. \\
2p. gen 2p. refl like- imp.2p\\
`Like/love yourselves.'

Ni/nieniw niam kookal-eka. \\
2p. unm /2p. lim 2p. refl like- imp.2p\\
`Like/love each other.'

The reflexives are not very frequent in Mauwake, because they seem to be fairly strongly connected with [+Control]. If one hurts oneself unintentionally, the cause(r) or instrument occupies the subject position instead of the person hurt. Thus, ex:3:x617 is a semantically appropriate equivalent for the English clause `I cut myself with a knife':

Fura=ke efa puuk-a-k. \\
knife= cf 1s. acc cut- pa -3s\\
`A knife cut me.'

But a reflexive pronoun is used especially in expressions involving body parts when one does something to oneself, and the instrument is not known or mentioned ex:3:x618. In corresponding expressions English often uses possessive rather than reflexive pronouns.

Merena yame puuk-a-m. \\
leg 1s. refl cut- pa -1s\\
`I cut my leg.' (Or: `I cut myself in the leg.')

The plural forms of the reflexive pronouns have another, quite different use: when they are followed by numerals, especially by `two' or `three', they function as dual/trial etc. forms for the personal pronouns. They are considered to be in the nominative case when not followed by other pronoun forms ex:3:x615. Other cases need to be shown by appropriate additional pronouns ex:3:x616.

Yiam arow nain miim-ap soran-e-mik. \\
1p. refl three that1 hear- ss. seq be.startled- pa -1/3p\\
`The three of us heard that and were startled.'

Amia mua=ke wiam erup nain wia nokar-e-k, \\
bow man= cf 3p. refl two that1 3p. acc ask- pa -3s\\
`The policeman asked those two '
summary:
The reflexive-reciprocal pronouns in Mauwake are based on the unmarked pronouns, with slightly different suffixes in the singular and plural. Singular forms are used only as reflexives, while plural forms can function both as reflexives and as reciprocals, though in many contexts the meaning is clear from context; when ambiguity arises, genitive pronouns mark reflexives and unmarked or restrictive pronouns mark reciprocals.

Reflexives are relatively uncommon because they are strongly associated with control, and in some cases English reflexive meanings are expressed instead by clauses where the affected person is not the subject. The plural reflexive forms also serve as dual/trial personal pronouns when followed by numerals, and they are treated as nominative unless additional pronouns indicate another case.

text:
The comitative set of pronouns ( tab:3:comitativepron ) is a mixture as far as the basic forms are concerned. The first and second person singular forms have accusative pronouns, all the others have the reflexive pronouns as their roots. The ending is the comitative clitic - iya ( sec:3.12.1 ), which can also be added to nouns and is one of several ways of expressing accompaniment in Mauwake. The first and second person singular forms have a transition consonant - m- preceding the comitative clitic.

Lasen mua emeria wiam=iya me aakun-e-mik. \\
Lasen man woman 3p. refl = com not talk- pa -1/3p\\
`We didn't talk with the Lasen people.'

Liisa Poh San ikos yiam=iya soomar-emi \\
Liisa Poh San with 1p. refl = com walk- ss. sim \\
`Liisa and Poh San walked with us and '
summary: The comitative pronouns in Mauwake have mixed bases: first- and second-person singular forms use accusative pronouns, while all other forms are built on reflexive pronoun roots. They take the comitative clitic -iya, which is also used with nouns to express accompaniment, and the first- and second-person singular forms additionally insert a transition consonant -m- before the clitic.

subsection: Primary and secondary reference of personal pronouns
text:
Typically pronouns refer to the persons the form indicates: first person singular to the speaker, second person singular to the addressee etc. Besides this primary, or default, reference some pronouns may also have a secondary reference, if the person and/or number of the referent(s) is different from that indicated by the pronoun.

In Mauwake both the first and second person singular forms as well as the third person plural marking on verbs can be used for non-specific, or generic, reference. They occur particularly in explanations of customs or general principles, and in examples. The sentences are usually in the future tense and therefore hypothetical. In these texts the second person singular pronoun and the third person verb marking can alternate quite freely. Example ex:3:x621 is from a text describing the adoption process in general, and example ex:3:x622 was said to a person who does not even have a spirit name to call upon, nor does know how to spear pigs. Here the pronouns have acquired a non-deictic role: their correct interpretation does not depend on the non-linguistic context.

Yo muuka kookal-ep yena samapora wia maak-i-nen.\\
1s. unm son like- ss. seq 1s. gen clan 3p. acc tell-Np- fu.1s\\
`When I like to have a son/child I will tell my clan.' (Or: `When one wants a child he will tell his own clan.')

No waaya mik-ap inasina unuma me unuf-i-nan=na mua oko=ke nainiw mik-ap nefar aaw-i-non.\\
2s. unm pig spear- ss. seq spirit name not call-Np- fu.2s= tp man other= cf again spear- ss. seq 2s. dat take-Np- fu.3s\\
`If you spear a pig and don't call your spirit name, another man will spear it again and take it from you.' (Or: `If one spears a pig ')

When a maximally generic object is needed for a transitive verb, or when there is no overt object available, the first person plural accusative form is used ex:3:x623, ex:3:x624.

Ifa nain=ke yia keraw-i-ya. \\
snake that1= cf 1p. acc bite-Np- pr.3s\\
`That snake bites.'

Marasin fain yia girin-i-ya. \\
medicine this 1p. acc smart-Np- pr.3s\\
`This medicine smarts.'
summary: The passage explains that although pronouns normally refer to the speaker, addressee, or third person as expected, some forms in Mauwake also have secondary, generic uses where the reference is non-specific and independent of context. In particular, first- and second-person singular forms and third-person plural verbal marking can be used in hypothetical or general statements, especially in explanations, and first-person plural accusative is used when a maximally generic object is needed or no overt object is present.

subsection: Use of personal pronouns in text
text:
In Mauwake it is possible to leave the subject pronoun out, as the person and number of the subject are marked on the verb suffix. And this is not only possible but very common: approximately only 6% of all the clauses in narrative and descriptive texts have a pronominal subject, compared to about 30% of the clauses having a subject np of any kind. As the other arguments are not marked on the verb, except for a two-way distinction for beneficiary ( sec:3.8.3.1 ), other than subject pronouns need to be used for them if there is no full np, and they are often employed even when there is a np.

The frequency of subject pronouns depends on whether the person referred to is first, second or third, and on the type of text as well. The first person, both in singular and plural, is commonly referred to with a pronoun, instead of just a verb suffix. Second person pronouns are very frequent in hortatory texts and are used somewhat in conversations. Most narratives in the data have their main participants in third person, but pronouns are used to refer to them quite rarely.

A pronoun may be used for the second mention of a newly established topic ( sec:9.2.2 ). In particular when an important participant has been introduced by a proper name, in the next sentence (s)he can be referred to by a personal pronoun ex:3:x1867.

Eema=ke waisow amis-ar-e-k. Os=ke uuriw urup-emi \\
Eema= cf 3s. isol knowledge- inch - pa -3s 3s. fc = cf morning rise- ss. sim \\
`Only Eema knew. She got up in the morning and '

When a participant has been established as the topic, (s)he is referred to with a verb suffix only, or with a np if a better identification is needed. A pronoun is used mainly when the topic is re-activated after being inactive for a while ( sec:9.2.3 ). The example ex:3:x1922 is from a text where a couple goes down to the husband's village and then returns to the wife's village. The wife's relatives, inactive as a topic for the span of five clauses, are re-assigned the topic status with the pronoun wi `they'.

Or-op ik-ok nainiw urup-e-mik. Aria wi samapora maneka fook-ap \\
descend- ss. seq be-SS again ascend- pa -1/3p alright 3p. unm floor big split- ss. seq \\
`They (=the couple) went down and after a while they came up again. Alright they (=the wife's relatives) split (wood for) a big floor and '

In commands ( sec:7.3 ) the subject pronouns are more frequent than in statements. As many as 39% of commands in the text material have a pronoun subject, as against 6% in statements. The pronoun here is not a vocative; that would be separated from the rest of the clause by a pause, whereas a subject is not. The example ex:3:x685 is a fairly typical command in Mauwake. This is an unusual feature cross-linguistically, as languages tend to drop the subject pronoun in imperative clauses. The relatively high frequency of subject pronouns in imperative clauses may not be a peculiarity of Mauwake only. The grammatical descriptions of Papuan languages often state that the subject pronoun is optional in these clauses, but give no information as to their actual frequency. Personal communication with other field linguists working on Papuan languages gives reason to suggest that an overt personal pronoun with the imperative may be more common than is generally assumed.

Ni ikiw-eka! \\
2p go- imp.2p\\
`Go (2p)!'
summary:
In Mauwake, subject pronouns are often omitted because person and number are already marked on the verb, and only about 6% of clauses in narrative and descriptive texts contain a pronominal subject. Their use varies by person and discourse context: first- and second-person pronouns are relatively common, pronouns can introduce a newly mentioned participant or reactivate an inactive topic, and third-person reference in narratives is usually expressed by verb suffix alone.

Subject pronouns are much more frequent in commands than in statements, occurring in about 39% of imperative clauses. The passage notes that this is unusual cross-linguistically, since imperatives often drop subject pronouns, and suggests that overt pronouns in Papuan-language imperatives may be more common than previously assumed.

text:
This section brings together what are often called demonstrative pronouns and deictic locative adverbs. What is common to them is the spatial orientation based on the location of the speaker, as well as morphological similarity. The whole deictic system, which also includes personal and temporal deixis, is discussed briefly in sec:6.3.

Deictics operate on the scale of proximity, making reference to something else on the basis of location. The relative proximity may be measured either from the speaker or from the speaker and addressee. Papuan languages manifest both these types as well as a combination of the two. Elevation and visibility may be additional parameters, so the demonstrative systems range from a simple and rather common two-term system to quite complicated ones. Two-way distinctions are found in Siroi and Golin, three-way distinctions in Waskia, Bine and Korafe. Usan has four basic deictics, but derivations extend the system into an elaborate one. reports 19 locatives in Daga that are also used as demonstrative pronouns.
summary: The passage groups demonstrative pronouns and deictic locative adverbs together because both are organized around spatial reference from the speaker’s location and often show morphological similarity. It explains that deictic systems vary in how they mark proximity—sometimes relative to the speaker alone, sometimes to both speaker and addressee—and may also encode elevation or visibility, producing systems ranging from simple two-term contrasts to much more complex ones in different Papuan languages.

subsection: The basic spatial deixis in Mauwake
text:
The main factors dividing the deictic space in Mauwake are the relative proximity to the speaker, and visibility. There are four deictic roots, one of them proximal and three distal ( tab:3:deicticroots ).

The proximal deictic fa- indicates close proximity to the speaker: prototypically the referent marked with fain `this' can be touched by the speaker, and fan `here' indicates the speaker's location or close proximity to it. The distal-1 deictic na - indicates a distance that is out of touching distance to the speaker; the distance to the addressee is irrelevant. Na- is the most neutral and the least restricted of the three distal deictics, and its frequency is extremely high because of the various functions that the demonstrative nain has. On the other hand, the words formed with both the distal -2 root eef - and the distal -3 root een -, although available, are rarely used. They may be employed when the pragmatic situation meets the semantic specification for their occurrence, and they are needed when more than one far deictic is called for. Often the distance is a relative matter, and the speaker has a subjective choice between the different deictics.

The deictic roots suffixed with - in, marking given information, are used as demonstratives. When the roots are suffixed with - an `locative', the words function as locative adverbs. The distribution of both these suffixes is very restricted: they are only attached to deictic or question word ( sec:3.7.1 ) roots.

The deictic manner adverbs ( sec:3.6.4 ) are also based on the same roots.
summary: Mauwake deictic space is divided mainly by proximity to the speaker and by visibility, with four deictic roots: one proximal and three distal. The proximal fa- refers to things close enough to touch, while distal na- marks a non-touching distance and is the most common; the farther distal roots eef- and een- are rare and used only in more specific situations, especially when more than one far deictic is needed. These roots can take the suffixes -in to form demonstratives and -an to form locative adverbs, and the same roots also underlie deictic manner adverbs.

text:
The four demonstratives in Mauwake are formed by one of the deictic roots plus the suffix - in indicating given information.

In Mauwake the demonstratives are like the personal pronouns in that they can function as the sole head of a noun phrase. But they differ from the personal pronouns in that they do not have the case forms typical of the latter. In this respect the demonstratives are more like adjectives. Another feature that they share with adjectives is that they mainly function as modifiers in a np. But unlike the adjectives, which only occur alone in complement position (unless the np is elliptical), the demonstratives occur by themselves in several clause positions.

The numeral modifiers are positioned between an adjective and a demonstrative in a np ex:3:x631, but never between two adjectives ex:3:x632.

koora maneka arow nain \\
house big three that1\\
`those three big houses'

siowa sepa gelemuta erup \\
dog black small two\\
`two small black dogs'

There is a clear distinction in Mauwake between human and non-human reference, which shows in the choice of a pronoun vs. a demonstrative. A third person pronoun is not used for non-humans, whereas demonstratives in isolation Demonstratives are common as modifiers of nps referring to humans. are normally only used for non-humans. The only exception in my data is example ex:3:x633; nain `that' would not be acceptable even here.

No fain me nena niawi akena=ke. \\
2s. unm this not 2s. gen 2s/p.father true= cf \\
`This is not your true father.'

No `you' is an extra-clausal theme, not part of the subject.

Apart from the proximal demonstrative fain `this', the other demonstratives are not mutually exclusive. The distal-1 demonstrative nain `that' is the least restricted of the three, and it is extremely frequent, whereas both eefin `this/that' and eenin `that' are very rarely used. In ex:3:x1749 the distances of the two mountains fit the specifications for eefin and eenin, and more than one distal demonstrative is needed for contrastive purposes:

Ema eenin fikera=ke aw-o-k, aria eefin fikera=ke me aw-o-k.\\
mountain that3 kunai.grass= cf burn- pa -3s, alright that2 kunai.grass= cf not burn- pa -3s\\
`The kunai grass on that mountain (far away, invisible) burned, but the grass on this/that one (somewhat closer) did not burn.'

There is no number distinction in demonstratives. When they modify a [+human] noun, plurality is shown in the person/number marking of the verb and optionally by an additional personal pronoun ex:3:x635.

( Wi) takira fain=ke niir-e-mik. \\
3p. unm boy this= cf play- pa -1/3p\\
`It was these boys that played.'

With [-human] nouns, a quantifier in the np may be used ex:3:x636, or distributive suffix on the verb ex:3:x637 to indicate plurality, or the number may be left unspecified ex:3:x638.

Mera arow nain aaw-e-m. \\
fish three that1 get- pa -1s\\
`I caught those three fish.'

Mera nain aaw- omak-e-m. \\
fish that1 get- distr. pl - pa -1s\\
`I caught those (many) fish.'

Amina fain p-ekap-e-mik. \\
pot this bpx -come- pa -1/3p\\
`We brought this pot / these pots.'

Besides the exophoric (text-external) deictic use described above, another common function for demonstratives cross-linguistically is endophoric, or text-internal anaphoric and cataphoric reference. The proximity in the case of demonstratives relates to the participants in the text, rather than the speech situation.

Mauwake follows the typical pattern: the neutral distal demonstrative nain `that' is anaphoric: it only refers to the text preceding it, as in ex:3:x639, where the example sentence comes after the description of fishing with a fish trap. The proximal fain `this' is cataphoric, referring to the text following it ex:3:x640. The other two demonstratives, eefin and eenin, are not used for text-internal reference at all.

Nain soo era=ke. \\
that1 fish.trap way= cf \\
`That is the way (to catch fish) with a fish trap.'

Mua arow fain: Kuuten, Dogimaw, aria Olas \\
man three this: Kuten, Dogimaw, alright Olas\\
`These three men: Kuuten, Dogimaw and Olas '

The demonstrative nain `that' marks given/established information, and often has a similar function to a definite article (cf. Dryer 2007c:154). It has an important pragmatic function of marking topic continuity in Mauwake. A continuing [+human] topic, especially the main participant, is usually marked only by person/number inflection on the verb, whereas a minor participant or a [-human] established topic uses nps modified by nain.

Still another function for the demonstrative nain `that' is that of a nominalizer of otherwise finite verbal clauses ( sec:5.7.2 ). A nominalized clause of this type may be a relative clause ex:3:x687 ( sec:8.3.1 ), a complement clause ex:3:x689 ( sec:8.3.2 ) or a temporal subordinate clause ex:3:x688 ( sec:8.3.3.1 ). All these clauses have a function that is consistent with the core meaning of `givenness' or presupposition.

Merena ifa keraw-a-k nain RC puuk-a-mik. \\
leg snake bite- pa -3s that1 cut- pa -1/3p\\
`They cut the leg that the snake had bitten.'

Mukuna kerer-e-k nain CC i me paayar-e-mik. \\
fire start- pa -3s that1 1p. unm not understand- pa -1/3p\\
`We didn't know that a fire had started.'

Goron-ep ora-i-ya nain, maa muutitik iiwawun lalat-i-ya.\\
fall- ss. seq descend-Np- pr.3s that1 thing all.kinds altogether sweep-Np-3s\\
`When it goes down, it sweeps everything with it.'

The same demonstrative is also used as a strong adversative `but' ex:3:x690 ( sec:8.1.3 ). In that function it is placed clause-initially rather than clause-finally.

Wiawi eliw naak-e-k, nain me ikiw-o-k. \\
3s/p.father all.right say- pa -3s that1 not go- pa -3s\\
`He said yes (lit: all right) to his father, but didn't go.'
summary: In Mauwake, demonstratives are built from deictic roots plus the suffix -in and can function as the head of a noun phrase, though they do not take the case forms of personal pronouns. They are mainly NP modifiers, show a human/non-human distinction in use, and the common distal demonstrative nain marks given or established information, serves anaphoric and nominalizing functions, and can also express a strong adversative meaning “but.”

text:
The undebatable locative adverbs in Mauwake are all deictic ( sec:3.9.1.1 ). For each of the four deictic roots there are two corresponding locative adverbs ( tab:3:deicticlocadv ). The first set contains the deictic root and the locative suffix - an. The homorganic vowels in the root and affix have merged into one. The second set is suffixed with the contrastive focus clitic -( e) ke. When the clitic is added, the deictic adverb is in focus, but not necessarily contrastive. The morphophonological change that has taken place in the root is unusual: the vowel /a/ has assimilated with the initial /e/ of the contrastive focus clitic.

The difference in the usage between the neutral and focused member of each pair is that the first is only used with realis-type verb forms, i.e. past ex:3:x463, ex:3:x1213 and present tense ex:3:x1214, whereas the second one is mainly used with future ex:3:x464, imperative ex:3:x465, and counterfactual ex:3:x466, i.e. irrealis-type forms. Yet Mauwake does not differentiate between realis and irrealis in verbs, and a possible explanation here is that only locative adverbs that are in focus can make it into a future, imperative or counterfactual clause, whereas past or present clauses are less restrictive and use either focal or non-focal form.

Owowa=pa fan ik-emkun aasa maneka ekap-o-k. \\
village= loc here be-1s/p. ds canoe big come- pa -3s\\
`As I was here in the village the big ship came.'

Eliw feeke soop-i-yen. \\
well here. cf bury-Np- fu.1p\\
`We can bury him here.'

Yo fura belemuta eefan piipu-a-m. \\
1s. unm knife small there2 leave- pa -1s\\
`I left the small knife (somewhere) here.'

Ni koora epa eefeke ku-eka. \\
2p. unm house place there2. cf build- imp.2p\\
`Build a/the house over here in this place.'

Wi aakisa fain manina eenan on-i-mik. \\
3p. unm now this garden there3 make-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`Nowadays they make the garden(s) there (far away).'

Ni eeneke ikiw-ep momor naap niir-eka. \\
2p there3. cf go- ss. seq foolish thus play- imp.2p\\
`Go there (out of my sight) and play your foolish game.'

Neeke ik-ek-a-k=na iwer(a) ififa=ke ifakim-ek-a-k. \\
there1. cf be- cntf - pa -3s= tp coconut dry= cf kill- cntf - pa -3s\\
`If he had been there a (falling) dry coconut would have killed him.'

Soo nainiw muf-owa pun naap, aana=pa neeke muf-i-mik. \\
trap again pull- nmz too thus rattan= loc there1. cf pull-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`Pulling the trap again is also like that, we/they pull it there by the rattan.'

Malol=pa neeke nainiw suuw-urup-i-ya. \\
open.sea there1. cf again push-ascend-Np- pr.3s\\
` There from the open sea it (= tsunami wave) again pushes up (to the coast).'

In the following examples neeke and feeke are used with past ex:3:x1146 -- ex:3:x1200 or present tense verbs ex:3:x1572 and indicate a temporary rather than permanent location, but this is probably secondary, or related, to the adverbs being focal: there is less need to focus on a permanent location than on a temporary one. Note that in these clauses it is possible to have two constituents with contrastive focus marking ex:3:x1146, ex:3:x1572.

Miiw(a) aasa fa-ow(a) mua=ke neeke wia aaw-o-k. \\
land canoe drive- nmz man= cf there1. cf 3p. acc take- pa -3s\\
` There the truck driver picked them up.'

Or-op neeke ika-iwkin kokom-ar-e-k. \\
descend- ss. seq there1. cf be-2/3p. ds dark- inch - pa -3s\\
`When they had gone down and were there it became dark.'

Nainiw mukuna mamaiya neeke ikiw-o-k. \\
again fire close there1. cf go- pa -3s\\
`Again he went there close to the fire.'

The following example is a comment from a man after he sees Japanese bombers in the sky:

Fa, Yaapan=ke feeke ik-e-mik! \\
intj Japan= cf here. cf be- pa -1/3p\\
`Damn, the Japanese are here!'
summary:
Mauwake has four deictic locative adverbs, each with a neutral form ending in locative -an and a focused form marked by the contrastive focus clitic -(e)ke. The focused forms show unusual vowel assimilation, and while the neutral forms are used mainly with realis verbs, the focused forms are mainly found with irrealis clauses such as future, imperative, and counterfactual, though they can also occur with past or present forms.

The text suggests that focal marking may be required for locative adverbs in more restricted clause types, and that focused forms are also often associated with temporary rather than permanent location. Examples show both contrastive and non-contrastive focus uses, including cases where two constituents can bear contrastive focus in the same clause.

text:
The four deictic manner adverbs are based on the deictic roots, but their derivation is less regular than that of either the demonstratives or the deictic locatives, due to the restriction that a geminate vowel is only possible in an initial syllable ( tab:3:deicticmanneradv ). Again, the proximate ex:3:x701 and especially the distal-1 adverbs ex:3:x702 are common but the others are very infrequent.

Ikiw-e-mik=na feenap ma-em-ik-e-mik \\
go- pa -1/3p= tp like.this say- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`They went and (unexpectedly) kept saying like this '

Naap maak-iwkin naap ik-ua. \\
thus tell-2/3. ds thus be- pa.3s\\
`They told him like that, and he was like that.'

In ex:3:x1857 there is a long temporal distance between the hearing and the recounting of the story, which is apparently reflected in the choice of the adverbial.

Iiriw auwa-ke ma-iwkin eefenap miim-a-m. \\
earlier 1s/p.father= cf say-2/3p. ds thus2 hear- pa -1s\\
`The fathers spoke (about this) long ago and I heard it like that.'

In ex:3:x1858 there is both some temporal and a considerable locative distance between the original time and place of the quote and that of the rest of the example:

``Mua nain opora=pa wu-ami ifakim-e,'' eenap efa maak-e-mik.\\
man that1 talk= loc put- ss. sim kill- imp.2s thus3 1s. acc tell- pa -1/3p\\
` ``Accuse (lit: put to talk) that man and kill him,'' they told me like that.'

Location verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.3 ) are also based on the deictic roots, but directional verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.5 ), which also participate in the spatial deictic system in Mauwake, have different roots.
summary:
The four deictic manner adverbs are formed from deictic roots, but their derivation is less regular than that of demonstratives or deictic locatives because geminate vowels can occur only in an initial syllable. The proximate and especially the distal-1 forms are common, while the other forms are rare.  

The examples suggest that these adverbs can reflect temporal and locative distance from the original reported event, and the passage notes that location verbs also derive from deictic roots, whereas directional verbs use different roots.

text: Most of the indefinites in Mauwake are also question words, hence the treatment of both in the same subsection.
summary: Most Mauwake indefinites are also used as question words, so the two are discussed together.

text:
The question words are here grouped together because of their shared semantic features and their function and position in content questions, although on the basis of their syntactic function on clause level some are pronouns, others adjectives or adverbs.

The majority of the question words have an initial morpheme ka-, which indicates a question and is below in the derivations given the gloss `what', although it is unrelated to the question word mauwa `what'. The morphemes that make up the question words in tab:3:questionwords are given in parentheses when they can be reasonably clearly established.

Both the words translated with `which', kain and kaanin, have the suffix - in marking givenness. They are both morphologically and semantically related to the demonstratives fain `this' and nain `that' ( sec:3.6.2 ).

Kaan `where' is formed by the question root ka- and the same locative affix - an that is used in the deictic locative adverbs fan `here' and nan `there' ex:3:x1852 ( sec:3.6.3 ). The derivation with the contrastive focus marker -(e) ke is more frequently used than the non-focused form ex:3:x1854, possibly because the the other two most frequent question words, mauwa `what' and naarewe `who', so often take the contrastive focus clitic.

Mua nain unuf-ami ma-i-kuan, Mua nain kaan ik-ua? \\
man that1 call- ss. sim say-Np- fu.3p man that1 where be- pa.3s\\
`They call the man's name and say, ``Where is that man?'' '

Oo Sarak, no kaan=eke ik-ok kerer-e-n a? \\
intj Sarak 2s. unm where= cf be- ss arrive- pa -2s intj \\
`Oh Sarak, where have you been (lit: where were you and arrived)?'

Kaanin `which of two' also shares the locative morpheme an- with kaan- `where' as well as fan `here' and nan `there', although in its present meaning it is not a locative question.

There is also a morphological relationship between kamenap `how/ what like?' and kamin `how many/much?' and the deictic adverb naap `thus', but synchronically their semantic relationship is opaque. Kamenion `or what? / how is it?' has obviously developed from kamin `how many/much?' and the modal clitic -yon `perhaps' ( sec:3.9.3 ), but again, the relationship is not transparent any more.

The question words, except for kamenion and naap-i, occupy the same syntactic position and clausal function ex:3:x520, ex:3:x521 as the corresponding non-interrogative element would have ex:3:x647, ex:3:x648.

Mua nain iikamin ekap-o-k? \\
man that when come- pa -3s\\
`When did that/the man come?'

Mua nain unan ekap-o-k. \\
man that yesterday come- pa -3s\\
`That/the man came yesterday.'

Maa mauwa en-e-n? \\
thing/food what eat- pa -2s\\
`What did you eat?'

Maa oposia en-e-m. \\
thing/food meat eat- pa -1s\\
`I ate meat.'

Neither number nor case is marked on the interrogative words themselves. If either marking is required, it is done through personal pronouns, but for [+human] nps only ex:3:x522, ex:3:x523.

Mua naarew wia uruf-a-n? \\
man who 3p. acc see- pa -2s\\
`Whom (pl) did you see?'

Naarew wiar aaw-o-k? \\
who 3. dat get- pa -3s\\
`Who did he get it from?'

When an interrogative word is used as a subject, the contrastive focus marker - ke is added. This is natural since it is the question word that is the focal element in questions ex:3:x524-- ex:3:x526.

Mauwa =ke nefa aruf-a-k? \\
what= cf 2s. acc hit- pa -3s\\
`What hit you?'

Mua kain=ke nomak-e-k? \\
man which= cf win- pa -3s\\
`Which man won?'

Masin kaanin=ke samor-ar-e-k? \\
engine which.of.2= cf bad- inch - pa -3s\\
`Which engine (of the two) broke?'

Naarew (e) `who?' is only used for [+human] referents. When the contrastive focus maker - ke is suffixed to the question word, the last syllable is normally deleted. Mauwa `what', on the other hand, is used almost solely for [-human] nouns. The only natural expression with mauwa referring to humans that I have encountered is of the type ex:3:x649. When a person's name is inquired, either naarewe ex:3:x1855 or kamenap ex:3:x650 is used rather than mauwa.

Emeria nain no/nena mauwa=ke? \\
woman that 1s. unm /1s. gen what= cf \\
`What (relation) of yours is that woman?'

O unuma naare=ke? \\
3s. unm name who= cf \\
`What is his/her name?'

Kaanin `which of two?' is specified for number ex:3:x526, but kain `which?' is not ex:3:x691.

No kain kookal-i-n? \\
2s. unm which like-Np- pr.2s\\
`Which one (of two or many) do you like?'

The locative question word kaan( eke) `where' is often used as a phrase by itself ex:3:x1852, ex:3:x1854. but it is also employed as a modifier of a locative noun phrase rather than kain or kaanin ex:3:x1853.

Epa ara kaan=eke NP ikiw-e-mik? \\
place section where= cf go- pa -1/3p\\
`What/which area did they go to?'

Kamenap is a question word both for manner `how?' ex:3:x527 and for adjectives `what like?'. In the latter sense it usually modifies the noun sira `custom, kind' ex:3:x528.

No kamenap ik-o-n? \\
2s. unm how be- pa -2s\\
`How are/were you?'

O koora sira kamenap ku-a-k? \\
3s. unm house custom/kind what.like build- pa -3s\\
`What kind of house did he build?'

It is also used with the noun unuma `name' when the name of someone or something is inquired ex:3:x650, ex:3:x651:

O unuma kamenap? \\
3s. unm name what.like?\\
`What is his/her name?'

Nomokowa fain unuma kamenap? \\
tree this name what.like\\
`What is the name of this tree?'

In example ex:3:x650 kamenap is interchangeable with naare( we)- ke `who', but in ex:3:x651 it is not interchangeable with mauwa -ke `what'.

The interrogative kamenion forms a clause by itself and only occurs after the question clitic - i and/or the connective e `or' ex:3:x529.

Maa en-owa=ko p-ekap-e-mik=i kamenion? \\
thing eat- nmz = nf bpx -come- pa -1/3p= qm or.what\\
`Did they bring food, or what (happened)?'
summary:
The passage describes the morphology and syntax of question words in the language, noting that many begin with the question morpheme ka- and that some are related to demonstratives or locative forms. It explains how different interrogatives are used for human vs. non-human referents, how number and case are usually not marked on the question word itself, and how the contrastive focus marker -ke is added especially when the interrogative functions as subject.

It also shows that several forms have specialized meanings and distributions: kaan/kaanin for location and “which,” kamenap for “how” and “what kind of,” and kamenion as a clause-level expression meaning “or what?/how is it?” Some interrogatives can function as modifiers of noun phrases, while others occupy the same syntactic positions as the corresponding non-interrogative elements.

text:
The question word naap-i `like that?' is different from the other question words. It is formed by adding the question marker - i to the demonstrative naap `thus, like that', and it occurs by itself or sentence-finally after a statement, which often follows another question. It is mainly used in argumentation ex:3:x1194, ex:3:x1195.

Siiwa arow ikiw-eya maa en-owa perek-i-mik. Naap =i? \\
moon three go-2/3s. ds thing eat- nmz harvest-Np-1/3p thus= qm \\
`After three months we'll harvest the food, right?'

Feenap eliw ma-i-yen=i? Sira nain eliw marew, naap =i?\\
like.this well say-Np- fu.1p= qm custom that1 good none thus= qm \\
`Should we say that that custom is not good -- is that what you are saying?'

Question sentences are discussed in sec:7.2, which has more examples as well.
summary: The question word *naap-i* ‘like that?’ is formed from the demonstrative *naap* ‘thus, like that’ plus the question marker *-i*. It can occur alone or sentence-finally after a statement, often following another question, and is mainly used in argumentation.

text:
Indefinites are sometimes classified as pronouns, although they often are not very pronoun-like; sometimes they are grouped together with quantifiers. By definition they lack definiteness which is typical of other pronouns. Also their status as np substitutes is questionable.

In Mauwake, the indefinites behave syntactically very much like quantifiers ex:3:x641, ex:3:x642. The position of the indefinites in the np is after the adjective phrase and immediately preceding the demonstrative. They rarely co-occur with a quantifier phrase, but if they do, they follow the qp.

The number of indefinites in Mauwake is very small. The last four in tab:3:indefinites are actually question words ( sec:3.7.1 ) that also function as indefinites.

Iiriw muuka oko wiawi onak urera maa uup-e-mik.\\
long.ago boy other 3s/p.father 3s/p.mother evening food cook- pa -1/3p\\
`Long ago, a certain boy's father and mother cooked food.'

Ne wia, papako=ke ma-e-mik, \\
add no, some/other= cf say- pa -1/3p\\
`But no, some/others said, '

The indefinite oko `a certain, (an)other' also has the meaning `otherwise' when it introduces an apprehensive clause ex:3:x741 ( sec:8.1.6 ).

Gurun-owa epasia=pa miim-am-ika-i-kuan, oko mua papako maa ik-em-ik-owa nain kawus wiar uruf-i-kuan.\\
rumble- nmz far= loc hear- ss. sim -be-Np- fu.3p other man some thing/food roast- ss. sim -be- nmz that1 smoke 3. dat see-Np- fu.3p\\
`They (villagers) keep listening to the rumble from far away, otherwise/lest they (pilots) see the smoke from some men's/people's food-roasting fire.'

Those question words ( sec:3.7.1 ) that may function as indefinites behave similarly to question words as np constituents, but on the sentence level there are differences between them. The interrogatives occur either in a simple interrogative sentence or occasionally in a medial clause ex:3:x643. The indefinites can occur in a medial clause ex:3:x644, but they are more common in subordinate clauses, especially relative clauses ex:3:x645.

Naarew wia far-ep ekap-o-n? \\
who 3p. acc call- ss. seq come- pa -2s\\
`Who did you call, and then came?' A more natural translation into English would be `Who did you call before you came?', but it would hide the fact that medial clauses are coordinate.

Masin kaanin=ke samor-ar-eya oko fain=ke asip-i-non.\\
engine which.of.2= cf bad- inch -2/3s. ds other this= cf help-Np- fu.3s\\
`Whichever engine breaks down, this other one will help/substitute.' With question intonation it would mean: `Which engine i will this other one j help, if it i breaks down?'

Prais aaw-ep uf-owa kain=ke nomak-e-k nain RC wi-e-mik.\\
prize take- ss. seq dance- nmz which= cf win- pa -3s that1 give.them- pa -1/3p\\
`They took the prize and, whichever dance won, they gave it (the prize) to them (the dancers).'

The indefinite mauwa `what' is also used as a generic substitute for any [ -human] np that is left unmentioned because the name of the particular thing is not known or is temporarily forgotten, like whatchamacallit in English ex:3:x646.

Mua nain mauwa nain akim-a-k=na weetak, mauwa nain me or-o-k.\\
man that1 what that1 try- pa -3s= tp no, what that1 not descend- pa -3s\\
`The man tried the thing (press button), but the thing (lift) didn't go down.'

The locative question word kaaneke is also used as an indefinite locative adverb ex:3:x1869.

No kaaneke ikiw-i-nan=na, yos pun nook-i-nen. \\
2s. unm where. cf go-Np- fu.2s= tp 1s. fc too follow.you-Np- fu.1s\\
`Wherever you go, I will follow you.'
summary:
Mauwake indefinites are few in number and often overlap with question words, some of which also function as indefinites. Syntactically, they behave much like quantifiers: they occur after the adjective phrase and before the demonstrative, and if a quantifier phrase is present they follow it.

Several indefinites have special uses beyond simple indefiniteness: *oko* can mean “otherwise” in apprehensive clauses, *mauwa* serves as a generic substitute for an unmentioned nonhuman noun, and *kaaneke* functions as an indefinite locative adverb meaning “wherever.” Unlike interrogatives, these indefinites are more common in subordinate clauses, especially relative clauses.

text:
The verb category can be defined morphologically, syntactically, semantically and pragmatically. Of these, the first criterion is the most critical in Mauwake and covers the whole class; the others are less definitive, but help define a prototypical verb.

According to the morphological, or structural, criterion, a verb is a word that can be inflected for tense as well as the person and number of the subject. The derivational suffix categories of verbalizer, distributive and benefactive are not as useful in defining the class of verbs, as these can be used in the nominalized forms of verbs as well. also adds aspect and mood into inherent verbal inflections, but in Mauwake aspect is coded syntactically ( sec:3.8.5.1.1 ), and modal categories either morphologically, syntactically or lexically.

Syntactically a verb functions as the nucleus of a predication independently or as part of a verbal cluster ( sec:3.8.5 ). Since single verbs and verbal clusters have such similar functions, the latter are described in the morphology chapter immediately after the verbs, and not in the chapter on phrase. Also, the term verb is often used below as a generic term to cover both a single verb and a verbal cluster, unless specifically the verbal cluster is meant. The verb is the last element in a pragmatically neutral clause.

The verbal predicate is the only obligatory element in an intransitive clause. A transitive clause does require an object, but even it can often consist of a verb only, as the third person singular accusative pronoun, used for object, is zero ex:3:x177. The directional verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.5 ) often co-occur with a goal, but when it is left implied the verb can be the only element ex:3:x178. In a verbless clause the predicate is a noun, adjective, possessive pronoun or adverb.

Aaw-e-m. \\
get- pa -1s\\
`I got it.'

Urup-e-mik. \\
go/come.up- pa -1/3p \\
`We went/came up.'

The predicate verb selects the arguments in a predication. This argument selection can be used as an important basis for the division into different verb classes ( sec:3.8.4 ).

Semantically, according to, a prototypical verb encodes ``less time-stable experiences, primarily transitory states, events and actions''. In Mauwake this lack of time-stability feature shows in the strong tendency to use inchoative verbs ex:3:x179 ( sec:3.8.2.2.2 ) instead of adjectives to describe non-permanent states.

supuk-ar-e -k vs. supuka `wet' \\
wet- inch - pa -3s \\
`(it) is wet' (lit: `has become wet')

But it is also possible to express less prototypical, time-stable states and events with verbs. In words, ``verbs require temporal fixing'', when compared with the ``relative atemporality'' of an entity. So the relative temporality is the main defining factor for verbs, regardless of the time-stability.

add a discourse perspective to the definition of verbs by suggesting that ``verbs which do not report discourse events fail to show the range of oppositions characteristic of those which do'', and are therefore less prototypical. According to them, categoriality is only weakly associated with the root forms, and the discourse use determines how clearly the verbhood manifests itself (ibid. 747). Theirs is an important viewpoint for the study of language in general and of those languages in particular that have plenty of root forms that can be used for different word classes. But for Mauwake I assume the existence of rather discrete categories of noun and verb, which the root forms belong to, rather than just having ``a propensity or predisposition to become N's or V's'' (ibid. 747). The number of roots that can be used across categories without special derivational suffixes is small.
summary:
In Mauwake, verbs are defined most decisively by morphology: they can inflect for tense and for the person and number of the subject, while other derivational suffixes are less useful because they also occur in nominalized forms. Syntactically, verbs function as the nucleus of a predication, can appear alone or in verbal clusters, and are the only obligatory element in an intransitive clause; semantically, prototypical verbs express relatively time-unstable events, states, and actions, though more stable states can also be expressed verbally.

The passage also notes a discourse-based view that verbhood is clearer when forms are used to report discourse events, but rejects this as the main account for Mauwake. Instead, the author treats noun and verb as fairly discrete categories, with only a small number of roots used across categories without special derivation.

subsubsection: General characteristics of verbs in Mauwake
text:
Mauwake is a strongly verb-oriented language, and often a verb is the only element in the clause. In running text, there are roughly three words per clause, so approximately one word in three is a verb, as most of the clauses are verbal clauses.

The verb morphology is agglutinative; this shows mainly in the structure of the verbs. Suffixing is the basic strategy, but a few prefixes are used as well. Reduplication is of the prefixing type, with few exceptions.

Although the verb morphology in Mauwake is quite extensive, for a Papuan language it is not very complex, and the patterns are quite transparent. The verb morphology marks features of the event itself: tense, mood, sequentiality vs. simultaneity of actions, but also features related to the participants in the clause: subject, beneficiary, and distributive indicating the number of S, O or rec. Aspect is expressed through verbal groups ( sec:3.8.5.1.1 ).

To enlarge its verb inventory, Mauwake uses serial verbs ( sec:3.8.5.1.2 ) or adjunct Adjunct is here used in the sense of ``a secondary element in a construction [, which] may be removed without the structural identity of the rest of the construction being affected''. plus verb constructions ( sec:3.8.5.2 ). The serial verbs are mostly formed by a productive process, whereas the adjunct plus verb constructions tend to be lexicalized forms.

Some verbs have roots that are very similar to nouns. Especially in Austronesian languages the question arises whether these roots are originally nouns, verbs, or unspecified as to the grammatical category. This question for Mauwake is discussed in the section on verb derivation ( sec:3.8.2 ).

Mauwake has no passive voice. The subject demotion strategy is described in sec:3.8.4.3.3.

There is a distinction in Mauwake between medial ( sec:3.8.3.5 ) and final verbs ( sec:3.8.3.4 ). Sometimes they are also called dependent and independent verbs (e.g. Foley 1986:11). This distinction is very important on both sentence and discourse levels.

The verbs can be divided into two conjugation classes based on the past tense suffix vowel. Semantically these classes are arbitrary; the division is made on the basis of morphophonology and is discussed in sec:2.3.3.3. But the classification done according to transitivity ( sec:3.8.4.2 ) and that based on semantic characteristics ( sec:3.8.4.4 ) are more interesting grammatically and reveal more of the nature of the language.
summary:
Mauwake is a strongly verb-oriented, mostly verbal-clause language with highly transparent, agglutinative verb morphology that is mainly suffixing, though some prefixing and prefix-type reduplication also occur. Its verbs mark event properties such as tense, mood, and sequentiality, as well as participant-related features like subject and beneficiary, and the language expands its verb inventory through serial verbs and adjunct-plus-verb constructions.

The language has no passive voice, distinguishes medial from final verbs, and divides verbs into two conjugation classes on morphophonological grounds. The passage also notes that transitivity-based and semantic classifications are more revealing than the arbitrary conjugation classes.

text:
A verb consists of a root optionally preceded by a derivational prefix ex:3:x180 and followed by various derivational and inflectional suffixes ex:3:x181, ex:3:x182, as shown in the diagram below ( fig:3:verbstructure ). Only tense and person/number suffixes are obligatory in a finite verb in the indicative mood. The obligatory elements are bolded in the diagrams.

Soomia wia amap-ep-om-i-ya. \\
spoon 3p. acc bpx -go- ben -Np- pr.3s\\
`He takes spoons to them.'

Iwera pun wiar aw-omak-e-k. \\
coconut too 3. dat burn- distr / pl - pa -3s\\
`Many of his coconut palms burned too.'

Lawiliw akena um-ek-a-m. \\
nearly very die- cntf - pa -1s \\
`I very nearly died.'

The imperative verb structure fig:3:imperativeinflection is understandably different in that it cannot take counterfactual, tense or indicative person/number suffixes. Instead, an imperative person/number suffix needs to be attached as the final suffix of the verb ex:3:x183, ex:3:x184.

Ni ekap-omak-eka. \\
2p. unm come- distr / pl - imp.2p\\
`Come!' (said to several people together)

Muuka arim-ow-e. \\
son grow- caus - imp.2s \\
`Bring up the boy.'

Medial verbs likewise can have only the medial suffix after the derivational suffixes, if there are any. The medial suffix distinguishes between sequentiality ex:3:x409 and simultaneity ex:3:x186 of the actions when the subject stays the same; with a different subject ex:3:x187 the actions are understood to be sequential, and simultaneity needs to be marked through continuous aspect form ( sec:3.8.5.1.1.2 ).

Oposia pu-puuk-ap uup-e-mik. \\
meat rdp -cut- ss.seq cook- pa -1/3p\\
`They cut the meat in many pieces and cooked it.'

Ewar=ke wuun-ow-ami epia faker-a-k, mukuna. \\
wind= cf blow- caus - ss. sim firewood raise- pa -3s fire \\
`The wind blew and raised the fire(wood), the fire.'

Kees-om-a-ya en-e-k. \\
spit- ben - bnfy 2-2/3s. ds eat- pa -3s \\
`He spat/regurgitated it for her and she ate.'
summary:
The passage describes the structure of the verb as a root that may be preceded by a derivational prefix and followed by derivational and inflectional suffixes. In finite indicative verbs, only tense and person/number suffixes are obligatory, while imperative verbs instead require an imperative person/number suffix and cannot take counterfactual, tense, or indicative person/number suffixes.

It also explains that medial verbs take only a medial suffix after any derivational suffixes, and that this suffix marks whether linked actions are sequential or simultaneous when the subject is the same. With different subjects, actions are normally interpreted as sequential, and simultaneity must then be marked by a continuous aspect form.

text: This section deals with derivational processes in which the end result is always a verb. Verbs can be derived from other word classes through two category- changing strategies. In category- maintaining derivations affixes are added to the verb root to change the semantics of the root. Among the latter, the semantic changes can be considerable especially in cases where the valence changes, whereas in category-changing derivations the semantic difference is not always so great.
summary: The passage explains that derivational processes can produce verbs as their final result, and that verbs may be derived from other word classes by two category-changing strategies. It also notes that in category-maintaining derivations, affixes are added to a verb root to alter its meaning, sometimes substantially when valence changes, whereas in category-changing derivations the semantic difference is not always as large.

text:
According to, ``an inflectional morpheme is a bound non-root morpheme whose appearance in a particular position is compulsory.'' It is ``required by syntax''. In contrast, derivational affixes are non-obligatory. In Mauwake, all the derivations are non-obligatory. Of the inflections, the beneficiary suffix and the counterfactual suffix as such are not required by syntax like the tense and person marking, but they have an interdependence relationship with other suffixes: the beneficiary suffix has to occur in a past tense or imperative form of a verb that also has the benefactive suffix, and the counterfactual suffix restricts the tense marking to past tense.

In Mauwake verb structure the derivational suffixes always precede the inflectional ones. This agrees with one of Greenberg's universals: ``If the derivation and inflection follow the root the derivation is always between the root and the inflection'' ( Greenberg1966).

Inflectional suffixes in Mauwake form paradigms, even if in some cases the paradigms only have two members.

The greater syntagmatic freedom of derivational affixes is shown in Mauwake by the fact that a verb with any of the derivations can be nominalized with the nominalizing suffix - owa, whereas one with inflectional suffixes cannot. It is possible to nominalize whole clauses where the main verb has inflectional suffixes, by adding the demonstrative nain `that' after the clause, but this strategy is not available for individual verbs ( sec:5.7.2 ). This ability of verb stems with derivational suffixes to be nominalized is the main distinction between derivation and inflection in Mauwake.

A special feature in Mauwake is the dividing point between the derivational and inflectional suffixes: the benefactive suffix is derivational, whereas the beneficiary suffix is inflectional. The latter can only be present when there are other verbal suffixes following, whereas the former can also be followed by a nominaliser suffix. Other differences between the two suffixes are described below ( sec:3.8.2.3.3 ), ( sec:3.8.3.1 ). In the following section, the derivational suffixes are introduced in the order that they occur following the verb root; the prefixes are discussed last.

There is clear iconicity in the linear ordering of the derivational suffixes ( tab:3:verbderivation ): the closer the suffix is to the root, the more profound the change it effects on it. The verbalizing suffixes change the word class; the causative adds an argument; the distributive pluralizes an argument, and the benefactive adds a peripheral.
summary:
The passage distinguishes inflectional from derivational morphology in Mauwake: inflectional morphemes are compulsory and syntax-required, while derivational affixes are optional. It notes that derivational suffixes precede inflectional ones, that inflectional suffixes form paradigms, and that derivational suffixes are more freely combinable, especially because stems with derivational suffixes can be nominalized but those with inflectional suffixes cannot.

A special case is the contrast between the derivational benefactive suffix and the inflectional beneficiary suffix, which differ in where they can appear and what follows them. The passage also says the ordering of derivational suffixes is iconic, with suffixes nearer the root producing more fundamental changes in meaning or word class.

text:
There are two strategies in Mauwake whereby words from other word classes can be changed into verbs. Zero verb formation is less productive than the inchoative. Also the meanings of the verbs resulting from zero verb formation are in some cases more lexicalized, or less transparent, than the meanings of the verbs formed with the inchoative suffix. Often roots can be used for both the strategies, but not always: words like amisa ` knowledge' and ewur ` quickly, fast' only allow the inchoative suffix.

Zero verb formation

Mauwake has a number of verbs where the root is originally a noun, an adjective or an adverb, and the verb is formed without any overt morpheme to mark the category change. remark that ``languages often possess rather elaborate morphology whose sole function is to convert verbal roots into N's, but no morphology whose sole function is to convert nominal roots into V's''. Zero verb formation is here understood, not as adding a zero morpheme, but as a lexical process (following ). A noun ( tab:3:verbsfromnouns ), an adjective ( tab:3:verbsfromadjectives ) or an adverb ( tab:3:verbsfromadverbs ) is used as a root for the verb, and in this process it becomes a true verb, unlike nominalizations which are nouns but retain a lot of their verbal nature as well. propose that a word root is unspecified as to the grammatical category, and that discourse function assigns categoriality. This fits many Austronesian languages in which there are plenty of words where only the non-root morphology, or else syntactic behaviour, shows what class the word belongs to. Mauwake has relatively few forms like this and it is reasonable to assign words to specific word classes even without reference to discourse function.

The resulting verb is usually transitive ex:3:x188, with a few exceptions. The final vowel of a noun or an adjective, usually /a/, is deleted before the verbal inflection ex:3:x189.

Yo aakisa inasina Rubaruba nanar-i-yem.\\
1s. unm now spirit Rubaruba story-Np- pr.1s \\
`Now I tell about spirit Rubaruba.'

Aruf-ami me samor-eka!\\
hit- ss. sim not bad- imp.2p \\
`Don't hit/beat and destroy it.'

Semantically the resulting verb is usually very close to the word that serves as the root, but in a few instances like ex:3:x190 the semantic link is not very strong.

Nefa ikum-am-ika-iwkin nan kerer-e-n. \\
2s. acc illicitly- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds there appear- pa -2s \\
`They were just speculating about you when you arrived.'

Inchoative suffix

The second verb formation process in Mauwake takes a noun, adjective or adverb root and adds an inchoative suffix - ar ( sec:2.3.3.4 ) to form a new verb usually meaning `become n'. The term `inchoative' is used for derivation; `inceptive' for aspect, following. Although in the majority of the cases a word from one of the other word classes is made into a verb, the basic meaning is inchoative rather than verbalizing, as the same suffix can also be added to a few verbs. The suffix has been grammaticalized from the verb ar - `become', `enter into a state', and there are a few cases where it is difficult to decide with certainty which one it is. The differences between the full verb and the suffix are listed below.

The full resultative verb ar - `become' is more common with nouns, and the meaning of the verb is transparent ex:3:x191. It is also used with numerals ex:3:x192. Both words retain their word stress.

Arim-emi mu'a ar-'e-k. \\
grow- ss. sim man become- pa -3s \\
`He grew up and became man/adult.'

Aruf-owa e 'repam ar-'e-m. \\
hit- nmz four become- pa -1s \\
`I hit it four times.' (Lit: `Hitting it I became four.')

The inchoative suffix - ar can occur with nouns ex:3:x193, but is more common with adjectives ex:3:x194 and adverbs ex:3:x195, and can attach to a few verb roots too ex:3:x196. Since the result is one word it only has one word stress.

Yiena opaimika me baliwep a'mis-ar-e-mik. \\
1p. gen talk not well knowledge- inch - pa -1/3p \\
`They don't know our language well.'

Miiw-aasa sa'mor-ar-ek. \\
land-canoe bad- inch - pa -3s \\
`The car broke.'

Miiw-aasa samor-a-k `He broke the car' would be a corresponding sentence with zero verbalization.

Kau pun weeser-owa e'wur-ar-ek. \\
cow too finish- nmz quickly- inch - pa -3s \\
`The beef finished quickly too.'

Mua i'men-ar-ep opora pun i'men-ar-ek. \\
man find- inch - ss. seq talk too find- inch - pa -3s\\
`When man appeared, talk/language appeared too.'

Verbs derived from adjectives are often used rather than adjectives in the predicative position ex:3:x82, ex:3:x1764. And instead of a modifying adjective, a whole relative clause with a verb derived from an adjective may be used ex:3:x83. This happens especially when the property denoted by the adjective is not static.

Sia nain senam pin(a)-ar-e-k. \\
netbag that1 too.much heavy- inch - pa -3s\\
`The netbag is/was (lit: became) very heavy.'

Muuka nain op-iya dubil (a)- al - e - k. \\
boy that1 hold-2/3s. ds slippery- inch - pa -3s\\
`When he 1 held the boy 2, he 2 was slippery.'

Konima supuk(a)-ar-e-k nain yasuw-e. \\
cloth wet- inch - pa -3s that1 wash- imp.2s\\
`Wash the wet cloth.' (Lit: `Wash the cloth that has become wet.')

The consonant /r/ in the suffix is lateralized into /l/ when the root has /l/ in the immediately preceding syllable. Lateralization takes place arbitrarily in a few other cases as well ex:3:x199.

Yo damol(a)- al-e-m oo. \\
1s. unm bad- inch - pa -1s oh \\
`I feel terrible.' (Lit: `I'm destroyed/ruined.')

Epa dabel(a)- al-ek. \\
place cold- inch - pa -3s \\
`It is cold.'

Opaimika efa masi(a)- al-i-ya. \\
mouth 1s. acc bitter- inch -Np- pr.3s \\
`It tastes bitter to me / in my mouth.'

If two preceding syllables contain /l/, the consonant in the verbaliser is not lateralized ex:3:x200. This rule is very tentative, as ilelar - is the only example found so far.
summary: Mauwake has two ways to turn nouns, adjectives, and adverbs into verbs: zero verb formation, which adds no overt morphology, and an inchoative suffix -ar. Zero verb formation is less productive and often more lexicalized, while -ar usually means “become X” and is more common with adjectives and adverbs, though both processes can apply to some of the same roots.

text:
Aasa puuk-ap ilel(a)- ar-i-ya. \\
canoe cut- ss. seq gouge- inch -Np- pr.3s \\
`He has cut the canoe (length from a tree) and is gouging/carving it'

The suffix ar- often retains its original verbal meaning `become' when adjectives are made into verbs ex:3:x201, but when the other word classes are used as the root the original meaning tends to become more opaque or get lost ex:3:x202.

Dubil (a)-al-e-k. \\
slippery/smooth- inch - pa -3s \\
`It became slippery/smooth.'

No wadol (a)-al-i-n. \\
2s. unm lie- inch -Np- pr.2s \\
`You are lying.'

Most of the verbs formed with the inchoative suffix are intransitive, but some are active, transitive verbs ex:3:x203, ex:3:x204:

Muuka kuisow muuk (a)-ar-e-k. \\
son one son- inch - pa -3s \\
`She gave birth to one son.'

Epa mores-ar-ep ikiw-o-k. \\
place like( adv )- inch - ss. seq go- pa -3s \\
`He made the place ready and went.'

The inchoative verb formation is also used with verb loans from other languages ex:3:x488, especially Tok Pisin ex:3:x487. The Tok Pisin loans often originally come from English. Both of the loan words below also have a vernacular synonym.

Muuka wia was-ar-e-mik. (from Tok Pisin was `look after') \\
son 3p. acc look.after- inch - pa -1/3p\\
`They were looking after the boys/children'

Nading-ar-ep uf-e-mik. (from Mala nading `decoration') \\
decoration- inch - ss. seq dance- pa -1/3p\\
`We decorated ourselves and danced.'
summary: The passage explains that the inchoative suffix **-ar-** usually preserves its original meaning “become” when attached to adjectives, but this meaning becomes less transparent when attached to other word classes. Most inchoative verbs are intransitive, though some are active transitive verbs, and the same verb-forming process is also used with loanwords, especially from Tok Pisin, even when vernacular synonyms exist.

text:
Causative suffix

The causative suffix - ow (or - aw) transitivizes an intransitive verb: the clause gets a new subject, and the subject of the intransitive verb becomes the direct object. Usually it adds a causative meaning `cause someone to do something', or `cause something to happen'. The object of a causative construction has no control, or only minimal control, over the action or event indicated by the verb.

In many verbs there is free variation between - ow and - aw. Some verbs seem to prefer one or the other, but there is no clear pattern. There is also some dialectal and possibly age-based variation depending on the speaker. - ow is taken here as the basic form, since it is the more common of the two, and because in ``double causatives'' it is always used at least as the first one. tab:3:causverbsnbases lists some causative verbs.

Sometimes the causative suffix occurs reduplicated as a ``double causative'', but these still add only one argument. Many of the short directional verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.5 ) take a double causative instead of a single one ex:3:x205.

Eewua ir -ow-aw-ap osaiwa ar-e-k. \\
wing climb- caus - caus - ss. seq bird.of.paradise become- pa -3s \\
`She put the wing up (on herself) and became a bird of paradise.'

A single or double causative can be added to the intransitive verb reen- `(become) dry' with the result of two different meanings, but both of these still only add one more argument: reenow- `dry (something)', reenowaw- `smoke (something)'.

The only two transitive verbs that have been found to take the causative are mik- `spear/hit' and op- `hold/grab', with the causative forms mik-ow-aw- `join (the ends of two long items)' and op-aw- `accuse falsely'.

tab:3:pseudocausatives lists some verbs that have are derived from other verbs with the causative suffix but which do not have any causative meaning ex:3:x991, ex:3:x489. The causative as a valence-increasing device is discussed in sec:3.8.4.3.1.

Mukuna kuuf-ap kirir-e-k. \\
fire see- ss. seq shout- pa -3s\\
`She saw the fire and shouted.'

Yiok-ami naap yia kirir-ow-am-ik-ua. \\
follow.us- ss. sim thus 1p. acc shout- caus - ss. sim -be- pa.3s\\
`She was following us and shouting about us like that.'

Distributive suffix

A distributive suffix pluralizes one of the verbal arguments. There are two distributive suffixes: - urum `all' and - omak `many'. They are fully productive in the whole verb class, as long as the semantics of the verb allows multiple arguments.

The hierarchy of which argument the distributive applies to is as follows: if there is a recipient ex:3:x209 or beneficiary ex:3:x429, the distributive applies to that; if there is no recipient or beneficiary but an object, the distributive applies to the object ex:3:x492; and in case the clause has neither a recipient or beneficiary nor an object, the distributive applies to the subject ex:3:x491. Since transitive verbs need an object, the subject can be pluralized with the distributive only when the verb is intransitive.

rec/ben o s

Mua teeria opaimika wia sesek- omak-e-mik. \\
man family talk 3p. acc send- distr / pl - pa -1/3p \\
`They sent word to (many members of) the man's family.'

Wiena wiawi=ke amia wia keraw-om- omak-e-mik. \\
3p. gen 3s/p.father= cf spear 3p. acc carve- ben - distr / pl - pa -1/3p\\
`Their fathers carved spears for them ( many beneficiaries).'

Emeria unowa fain nia aaw- urum-i-kuan. \\
woman many this 2s. acc take- distr / a -Np- fu.3p\\
`They will take all you women.'

Emeria teeria koka ikiw- urum-e-mik. \\
woman group jungle go- distr / a - pa -1/3p\\
`The whole group of women / all the women went to the jungle.'

In verbal groups ( sec:3.8.5.1 ) the distributive suffix usually attaches to the last verb root ex:3:x207, ex:3:x490, but it can occasionally also attach to the first root, i.e. the main verb in a verb+ aux combination ex:3:x208.

Iinan aasa ikiw-emi paran-em- mi-omak-e-k. \\
sky canoe go- ss. sim rumble- ss. sim -go.around- distr / pl - pa -3s\\
`Many planes went rumbling around.'

Iinan aasa fan or-om -ik-omak-eya \\
sky canoe here1 descend- ss. sim -be- distr / pl -2/3s. ds \\
`When many planes were coming down here '

Wi ifa saarik in-urum-ep-ik-e-mik. \\
3p. unm snake like sleep- distr / a - ss. seq -be- pa -1/3p \\
`They all slept/lay like snakes.'

Both suffixes can be attached to the same verb but it is rare. In that case - urum precedes - omak ex:3:x206.

Wia ifakim -urum- omak-e-mik. \\
3p. acc kill- distr / a - distr / pl - pa -1/3p \\
`They killed each and every one of them.' (There were many of those killed.)

Benefactive suffix

The benefactive suffix, indicating the fact that the action of the verb is done for someone, for their benefit or detriment, is a borderline case among the derivations. It is the last one of the derivational suffixes, and the beneficiary suffix ( sec:3.8.3.1 ) following it and marking the person that the action is done for, is inflectional even if the two suffixes go together semantically. The position of the benefactive is not as stable as that of the other suffixes: it comes after the distributive when the beneficiary is first person singular ex:3:x210, ex:3:x1925 but occurs preceding it with the other persons ex:3:x211, ex:3:x1926.

Mua Maneka=ke maa maneka on-omak- om-e-k. \\
Man Big= cf thing big do- distr / pl - ben - bnfy 1. pa -3s \\
`God did great things to/for me.'

The vowel of the beneficiary suffix deletes the vowel of the past tense suffix. The relationship between the beneficiary suffix and the suffix following it is discussed in detail in sec:3.8.3.1, and the medial suffix forms are discussed in sec:3.8.3.5.

Buk aaw-omak- om-e! \\
book get- distr / pl - ben - bnfy 1. imp.2s\\
`Get the books for me!'
summary:
The causative suffix -ow/-aw transitivizes intransitive verbs by adding a new subject and making the original subject the direct object, usually with the meaning ‘cause someone/something to do or happen.’ It can appear as a double causative without adding more than one argument, and some transitive verbs also take it, though many related forms are causative only in form and not in meaning.

The distributive suffixes -urum ‘all’ and -omak ‘many’ pluralize a verbal argument according to a hierarchy: recipient/beneficiary first, then object, and finally subject if no object is present. The benefactive suffix marks that an action is done for someone’s benefit or detriment, is less stable in position than other derivational suffixes, and interacts with the beneficiary suffix and past tense morphology.

text:
Buk aaw- om-omak-e! \\
book get- ben - distr / pl - imp.2s \\
`Get the books for him!'

Wiena wiawi=ke amia wia keraw- om-omak-e-mik. \\
3p. gen 3s/p.father= cf bow 3p. acc carve- ben - distr / pl - pa -1/3p \\
`Their fathers carved bows for them.'

In verbal groups the benefactive suffix is usually attached to the finite verb or auxiliary ex:3:x212 but can occasionally occur on the non-finite root ex:3:x213 or even on both of the two ex:3:x214.

Iwera wia uruk-am-ik- om-a-mik. \\
coconut 3p. acc drop- ss. sim -be- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p\\
`We kept dropping coconuts for them.'

Maamuma wia p-ikiw- om-ap-pu-ap \\
money 3p. acc textscbpx-go- ben - bnfy 2. ss. seq - cmpl - ss. seq \\
`Having taken money to them, '

Moro mua wia wu- om-am-ik- om-a-mik. \\
Moro man 3p. acc put- ben - bnfy 2. ss. sim -be- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p\\
`They put them (=carts) for the Moro men.'

The benefactive form does not always mean that something happens for someone's benefit. The benefactive may be strengthened with the adverb orawin `for the benefit' ex:3:x215, which makes it unambiguous.

Iwera orawin kais- om-e-mik. \\
Coconut for.the.benefit husk- ben - bnfy 1. pa -1/3p \\
`They husked coconuts for me (for free).'

By using a suffix completely unrelated to the verb `give', Mauwake shows itself different from all of those reasonably closely related languages that have grammatical descriptions available. A serial verb construction involving the verb `give' is a very common way of expressing benefactive in Papuan languages. Waskia (Ross and Paol 1978:45) and Maia employ this strategy, and in Usan it is behind one of the two strategies: the benefactive verb form has been grammaticalized from a serial verb with the verb `give' (Reesink 1987:110--111). The other strategy for Usan is to use a postposition with the appropriate noun phrase (ibid. 154). Bargam is similar to it (Hepner 2002:65--66, 99), but Amele utilizes an indirect object clitic attached to the verb to express the beneficiary as well as other semantic relations.
summary: The passage explains that Mauwake marks benefactive meaning with a special suffix attached mainly to the finite verb or auxiliary, though it can also appear on the non-finite root or on both parts of a verbal group. This form does not always clearly mean “for someone’s benefit,” so the adverb *orawin* “for the benefit” can be added to make the meaning explicit. It also notes that Mauwake differs from several related Papuan languages because its benefactive is not derived from a verb meaning “give,” unlike common strategies in languages such as Waskia, Maia, Usan, Bargam, and Amele.

text:
Although Mauwake is very strongly a suffixing language, it makes use of some derivational prefixes as well. Reduplication is the most common among these.

Reduplication

The morphophonological aspect of reduplication was already described in sec:2.3.3.2. In sec:6.4.2, reduplication is discussed as one of the many quantification strategies in Mauwake.

Reduplication in verbs is used in Mauwake to indicate continuity or iterativity of action and/or plurality of the resulting object. Mostly the reduplication is done only once, but especially motion verbs can have several identical reduplicative prefixes.

In verbs of motion reduplication means continuity ex:3:x218, and the passing of time may be shown by the number of reduplications ex:3:x216.

Biri-birin-emi wia akim-omak-e-mik. \\
rdp -fly- ss. sim 3p. acc try- distr / pl - pa -1/3p \\
`They were flying and teasing them.'

Ne oro-oro-oro-oro-mi oro-oro-or-o-k, onoma.\\
and rdp - rdp - rdp -descend- ss. sim rdp - rdp -descend- pa -3s horizon.\\
`And it went down and down and down all the way to the horizon.'

In other intransitive verbs reduplication indicates either iterative action ex:3:x217 or occasionally continuity ex:3:x692.

Nomokowa ku-ku-ep or-om-ik-ua. \\
tree rdp -break- ss. seq descend- ss. sim -be- pa.3s\\
`The timber (in a bridge) kept breaking and falling down.'

Epa wii-wiim-ik-ua, \\
place rdp -dawn-be- pa.3s\\
`It was dawning, '

Both of these meanings fit in well with description of the various meanings that reduplication in verbs can have. In transitive verbs reduplication indicates iterative action as well as the plurality of an inanimate object ex:3:x219. The form is used especially when the action results in a plural object ex:3:x220.

Iinan aasa=ke maifa fu-fuurk-ikiw-o-k. \\
sky canoe= cf paper rdp -throw-go- pa -3s \\
`The plane went throwing paper slips down'

Oposia nain pu-puuk-ap uup-e-mik. \\
meat that1 rdp -cut- ss. seq cook- pa -1/3p \\
`We cut up the meat (into many pieces) and cooked it.'

Usan differs from Mauwake in that it does not use reduplication very much in verbs, and never in main clause final verbs. Also, when reduplication is used to indicate duration or repetition the whole verb word is reduplicated (ibid. 117). In Bargam reduplication occurs but is not very productive. In transitive verbs reduplication indicates plurality of objects, in intransitive verbs plurality of subjects. In Maia ``verb roots may be partially or completely reduplicated. Verb reduplication broadly indicates an augmented action which may include a greater, more massive, more intensified or very often repetitive form of the action''.

Bring-prefixes

The prefixes in this group change the directional verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.5 ) into transitive verbs with the meaning `bring' or `take'. p - is a neutral prefix and by far the most common one ex:3:x221, amap - is used when something is brought out in the open, often with the meaning `bring forth'. Usually there is a clear goal, a person or a place, which may not be mentioned in the clause itself but occurs in an earlier one ex:3:x430, or is understood from the context ex:3:x222. If the goal is explicitly mentioned in the clause, the neutral prefix is used ex:3:x221, ex:3:x223. The prefix aap - ex:3:x224 is very rare and I have been unable to establish whether it really differs from amap - or whether it is just a matter of idiolectal use. The bring - pr efixes may have been grammaticalized from a medial verb construction involving the verb aaw - `take'. It is easy to see how aawep ekap - `take (and) come' could have developed into aapekap - `bring' and possibly also into pekap -. Another possibility is that it is a result of a related process to that in Usan where the verb ba `take' has contracted into b -, which has combined with verbs of motion and been lexicalized with the meaning of bringing or taking (Reesink 1987:144--145). The amap - pr efix may have its origin in the expression ama- pa `in the sun', which implies `in the open'. There is also a very slight possibility that the p -prefix might be an Austronesian loan, as p(V ) - is a common causative or transitivizer prefix in Austronesian languages. But all of this is just conjecture at this point.

Amina aaw-ep Liisa ame wia p-er-om-a.\\
