pot take/get- ss. seq Liisa others 3p. acc bpx -go- ben - bnfy 2. imp.2s\\
`Get the pot and take it to Liisa and the others.'

Pita pensil wiar or-op ik-ua nain aaw-ep amap-ikiw-om-aka.\\
Pita pencil 3. dat fall- ss. seq be- pa.3s that1 take- ss. seq bpx -go- ben - bnfy 2. imp.2p\\
`Take to Pita his pencil that has dropped.'

Wiipa oko amap-ora-iwkin ma-e-k \\
daughter other bpx -descend-2/3p. ds say- pa -3s \\
`When they took another daughter down (from the house out in the open), he said '

Ni auwa maa p-urup-om-aka. \\
2p. unm father food bpx -ascend- ben - bnfy 2. imp.2p \\
`Take food (up) to father.'

Iwera ir-ap erup op-ap aap-or-e. \\
coconut go.up- ss. seq two grab- ss. seq bpx -descend- imp.2s \\
`Climb the coconut palm, grab two coconuts and bring them down.'
summary:
Mauwake is strongly suffixing, but it also uses a few derivational prefixes, especially reduplication. In verbs, reduplication signals continuity or iterativity, and in transitive verbs it can also indicate plurality of an inanimate object; motion verbs may show repeated reduplication to mark extended movement or the passing of time.  

The language also has a set of “bring-” prefixes that turn directional verbs into transitive verbs meaning ‘bring’ or ‘take.’ The neutral prefix p- is most common, amap- is used when something is brought out into the open, and aap- is very rare and possibly not distinct from amap-.

text: The inflectional suffixes are discussed in the order that they occur following the verb stem.
summary: The inflectional suffixes are presented in the same sequence in which they follow the verb stem. The discussion therefore proceeds from the first suffix position outward in order of occurrence.

text:
The beneficiary suffix indicates the person the action is done for. Its position is directly after the benefactive suffix, or after the distributive suffix in those few cases where the benefactive comes before the distributive ( sec:3.8.2.3.3 ). It is inflectional rather than derivational because 1) when it is used, nominalization is blocked and 2) it has a paradigm for different persons, even if the paradigm only consists of two members.

The only two forms for the beneficiary are - e for first or second person singular ex:3:x225 and - a for all the other persons ex:3:x226. The context often provides more person distinctions, as the plural requires accusative pronouns to precede the verb to indicate the beneficiary, like third person plural in ex:3:x227.

Wafur-om- e! \\
throw- ben - bnfy 1. imp.2s \\
`Throw it to me!'

Marasin wu-om- a-mik=na weetak. \\
medicine put- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p= tp no \\
`They put medicine on him but no (it didn't help).'

Na-iwkin wia uf-om- a-mik. \\
say-2/3p. ds 3p. acc dance- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p \\
`They said so and we danced for them.'

When the beneficiary suffix is followed by a vowel, a mid vowel is deleted adjacent to a low vowel ex:3:x228 and both a mid and a low vowel are deleted preceding a high vowel ex:3:x444. In the latter case the person distinction gets neutralized in the singular ex:3:x1750, but not in the plural where the obligatory accusative pronouns maintain the distinction ex:3:x445. The examples ex:3:x494- ex:3:x496 below show how the beneficiary suffix affects the past tense suffix. In ex:3:x496 a sequence of two identical vowels is reduced to one vowel.

aaw-om- ak-a-m aaw-om- a-ek-a-m \\
get- ben - bnfy 2. cntf - pa -1s \\
`I would have gotten it for him'

aaw-om- i-non aaw-om- e-i-non, aaw-om- a-i-non \\
get- ben - bnfy. nps - fu.3s\\
`he will get it for me/you/him/her'

aaw-om- uk aaw-om- e-uk, aaw-om- a-uk \\
get- ben - bnfy. imp.3p\\
`let them get it for me/you/him/her'

Panewowa maa wia p-ikiw-om- uk. \\
old food 3p. acc bpx -go- ben - bnfy. imp.3p\\
`Let them take food for the old people.'

Uf- o-k. \\
dance- pa -3s\\
`He danced.'

Uf-om- e-k. \\
dance- ben - bnfy 1. pa -3s\\
`He danced for me/you.'

Uf-om- a-k. \\
dance- ben - bnfy 2. pa -3s\\
`He danced for him.'
summary:
The beneficiary suffix marks the person for whom an action is performed and occurs immediately after the benefactive suffix, or after the distributive suffix in a few cases. It is treated as inflectional because it blocks nominalization and has a person paradigm, though this paradigm is limited to two forms: **-e** for first/second singular and **-a** for all other persons.

The passage also notes several phonological effects: vowel deletion can occur when the beneficiary suffix is followed by another vowel, sometimes neutralizing singular person distinctions, while plural distinctions are preserved by obligatory accusative pronouns. Examples show that the beneficiary suffix can also affect the form of the past tense suffix and reduce identical vowel sequences to one vowel.

text:
The counterfactual modality is the only modal distinction made in the verb morphology. It is an expression of the truth value of the statement: something could or would have happened, but did not, or something might be the case but for some reason is not. The counterfactual is marked by the suffix - ek ex:3:x234 and is only used with the past tense suffix even if the verb refers to the present ex:3:x433 or future ex:3:x434 time. The counterfactual is used in both hypothetical and counterfactual conditional clauses ( sec:8.3.5 ).

Lawiliw akena waki- ek-a-m. \\
nearly very fall- cntf - pa -1s \\
`I very nearly fell.'

Yena aamun aakisa uruf- ek-a-m=na kemel- ek-a-m. \\
1s. gen yonger.brother now see- cntf - pa -1s= tp rejoice- cntf - pa -1s\\
`If I saw my younger brother now, I would be happy.'

Morauta fan ik- ek-a-k=na uurika ikiw-ep maak- ek-a-mik.\\
Morauta here be- cntf - pa -3s= tp tomorrow go- ss. seq tell- cntf - pa -1/3p\\
`If Morauta were here, tomorrow we would go and tell him.'

If there is a beneficiary suffix -a preceding the counterfactual, the vowel /e/ of the counterfactual suffix is deleted ex:3:x235:

Maifa yia aaw-om- ak-a-k=na \\
paper 1p. acc get- ben - bnfy 2. cntf - pa -3s= tp \\
`If he had gotten tickets for us '
summary: The passage explains that counterfactual modality is the only modal distinction expressed in the verb morphology, marking situations that would or could have happened but did not, or might be true but are not. It is formed with the suffix **-ek** and always occurs with the past tense suffix, even when referring to present or future time, and it is used in both hypothetical and counterfactual conditional clauses. If a beneficiary suffix **-a** comes before it, the vowel **/e/** of the counterfactual suffix is deleted.

text:
Mood in Mauwake is defined as a morphological category of the verb, relating to the pragmatic function of the sentence. Mauwake has a mixed tense-mood system, where the indicative present, past and future, and the imperative are in contrast.

The mood distinctions only show in the finite verb. Same-subject medial verbs take the interpretation of their mood from the following finite verb, but different-subject medial verbs may be independent of the final verb as to their mood.

Indicative

The indicative is the neutral, morphologically unmarked mood. It is characterized by the tense distinctions between present, past ex:3:x693 and future ex:3:x694, and the person/number distinctions of first, second, and third person in singular and plural.

I me yia damol-a-mik. \\
1s. unm not 1s. acc harm- pa -1/3p\\
`They didn't harm us.'

Aria, iperowa opora wiar ook-i-yen. \\
alright, middle-aged talk 3. dat follow-Np- fu.1p\\
`Alright, we'll follow the advice of the middle-aged men.'

Imperative

The term imperative is used for ``mands'' Lyons borrows the term from B.F. Skinner as a useful cover term, without subscribing to Skinner's behaviouristic position. showing in the verbal morphology, regardless of person. In Mauwake the imperatives form a full paradigm (with the first person singular being replaced with the first person dual), and their syntactic behaviour is similar. So there is no valid reason to divide them into different categories such as imperatives, jussives and hortatives, just because semantically giving orders to oneself differs from giving orders to an addressee or to a third person ex:3:x229-- ex:3:x230. For a discussion on this question, see.

There are no tense distinctions in the imperative forms. The initial (or only) vowel in the second person imperatives is usually <e>, but in very few cases it is <a>. The only verbs found with - a in the imperative are iw - `go', mik - `spear, hit', op - `hold' and pok - `sit'. The imperative suffixes are listed in tab:3:imperative.

Or-op mua nain uruf- e. \\
descend- ss. seq man that1 see- imp.2s \\
`Go down and see that man.'

Ikoka amap-urup-eya op- ikua. \\
later bpx -ascend-2/3s. ds hold- imp.1p\\
`Later when he comes up, let's hold/grab him.'

Wi urup-ep mukuna nain umuk- uk. \\
3p. unm ascend- ss. seq fire that1 extinguish- imp.3p\\
`Let them go up and extinguish the fire.'

The imperative differs from the other moods in that in the first person it has a dual form, rather than a singular form ex:3:x446, ex:3:x1196.

Aria, i owowa=ko or- u. \\
alright, 1p. unm village= nf descend- imp.1d\\
`Alright, let's (d.) go down to the village.'

Yiena ikos akena iw- u. \\
1p. gen two.together truly go- imp.1d\\
`Let's just the two of us go together.'

The initial (or only) vowel in the second person imperative forms is deleted after the beneficiary suffix ex:3:x432-- ex:3:x233.

Iwera ir- e. \\
coconut ascend- imp.2s\\
`Climb up the coconut palm (to get coconuts).'

Iwera ir-om- e. \\
coconut ascend- ben - bnfy 1. imp.2s\\
`Climb up the coconut palm for me.'

Iwera ir-om- a. \\
coconut ascend- ben - bnfy 2. imp.2s \\
`Climb up the coconut palm for him.'

Iwera yia ir-om- aka. \\
coconut 1p. acc ascend- ben - bnfy 2. imp.2p \\
`Climb up (plural) the coconut palm for us.'

The semantics of the imperative and the functional aspects of commands are discussed in sec:7.3. On the use of subject pronouns with imperatives, see sec:3.5.11. The imperative forms of the verbs are also used in desiderative and conative ( sec:8.3.2.1 ) constructions.
summary:
Mauwake mood is a morphological verb category tied to the pragmatic function of the sentence, and the language has a mixed tense-mood system in which indicative present, past, and future, plus imperative, contrast. Mood is expressed only in finite verbs: same-subject medial verbs take their mood from the following finite verb, while different-subject medial verbs can have mood independent of the final verb.

The indicative is the neutral, unmarked mood and shows tense and person/number distinctions. The imperative is a full paradigm used for commands or other “mands,” has no tense distinctions, includes a first-person dual form instead of a first-person singular, and its forms are also used in desiderative and conative constructions.

subsubsection: Tense and person/number in final verbs
text:
Tense is a ``grammaticalized expression of location in time''. Mauwake has a straightforward three-tense system in the finite verbs marking past, present and future time reference. The tense system is simple compared with most other Papuan languages, many of which have more than three genuine tense distinctions and/or interaction between tense and status `Status' here refers to the distinction between realis and irrealis. resulting in several ``tenses'' (Foley 1986:158--163). Of the most closely related languages well studied so far, Usan has five tenses out of which one, uncertain future/subjunctive, is semantically related to irrealis. Maia has a complete status system instead of a tense system, and temporal relations are inferred from the realis or irrealis status and the aspects. According to Foley, ``most Papuan languages are tense-dominated [rather than status-dominated]'' Foley1986. In Mauwake the status hardly plays any role at all.

Portmanteau morphemes of the tense and person/number markers are very common in Papuan languages, but having the two distinct from each other is not uncommon either. The tense and person suffixes are separate morphemes in Mauwake, but have an interesting interplay with each other.

The speech event is taken as the reference point. The tense suffixes in themselves only distinguish between two tenses, past and non-past, and the further distinction between present and future is made by the person/number suffixes ex:3:x1029. The person/number suffixes, on the other hand, are the same in past and present tense except for the first and third person singular forms.

Unan aakun-e-mik, aakisa aakun-i-mik ne uurika nainiw aakun-i-yen.\\
yesterday talk- pa -1/3p now/today talk-Np- pr.1/3p add tomorrow again talk-Np- fu.1p\\
`Yesterday we talked, now/today we talk and tomorrow we'll talk again.'

The non-past marker in the second person plural future form is - o instead of - i possibly because of assimilation to the labial consonant /w/ in the person/number suffix.

The verb conjugation classes determining the past tense suffix vowels are discussed in the section on morphophonology ( sec:2.3.3.3 ). The beneficiary and the counterfactual suffixes influence the past tense suffix in the following way. After the counterfactual the past tense suffix is always - a. When the beneficiary suffix is present, the vowel of the past tense suffix is assimilated to it. tab:3:tenseperson presents the full paradigms for the tense and person/number suffixes.

The person/number marking in the verb distinguishes three persons in both singular and plural. There is no dual number, nor is there inclusive-exclusive distinction in the first person plural form. The plural is marked only for humans, spirits and important animals. The singular form is used for less important and small animals as well as all inanimates ex:3:x236.

Waa muuka arow ekap-o- k. \\
pig boy three come- pa -3s \\
`Three piglets came.'

Besides their primary meaning, the present and future tenses also have secondary meanings. The present tense form of the first or third person plural is used for generic or time-neutral statements ex:3:x1034. For the habitual aspect in the present, the simple present tense ex:3:x1035 is an alternative to the full habitual aspect form. Continuous aspect form is required for the past habitual ( sec:3.8.5.1.1.2 ).

Ifa yia keraw-i-ya nain miira saawirin-i-mik. \\
snake 1p. acc bite-Np- pr.3s that1 face become.round-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`When a snake bites us, we become dizzy.'

Nos=ke anane urema efar ikum-ar-i-n. \\
2s. fc = cf always bandicoot 1s. dat illicitly- inch -Np- pr.2s\\
`You always steal bandicoots from me.'

The future tense in any person form is used for habitual or generic conditionals ex:3:x1640 ( sec:8.3.5 ). The example ex:3:x1641 refers to a traditional custom and is generic, even if the first person form of the verb is used, and the first person pronoun as well.

Waaya ika-i-non, waaya uup-i-nan, naap. \\
pig be-Np- fu.3s pig cook-Np- fu.2s thus\\
`If there is a pig, you will cook it - it is like that.'

Ikoka yo um-i-nen, muuka nain nainiw wiena aaw-i-kuan.\\
later 1s. unm die-Np- fu.1s son that1 again 3p. gen take-Np- fu.3p\\
`Later, if I die (without paying the bride price) they will take the son back.'

The second person singular form of the future tense has two other usages as well. It can be used when referring to generic or habitual situations, especially in process descriptions which can also be understood as instructions. For these, the first person plural form of the present tense is much more common, but often the two alternate. The following example ex:3:x1038 describes work involved in harvesting taro roots (and the addressee that the story was told to, had no garden, so the speaker did not refer to her personally).

Perek-ami en-ow(a) gelemuta on-i-nan. \\
harvest- ss. sim eat- nmz little make-Np- fu.2s\\
`When you harvest it, you make a feast.'

It is also used for a command, or a statement of obligation ex:3:x1039:

Ikoka kuisow kuuma kuisow yi-i-nan. \\
later one stick one give.me-Np- fu.2s\\
`Very soon you have to give me 10 kina.' Or: `Give me 10 kina very soon.'
summary:
Mauwake has a simple three-tense system in finite verbs, marking past, present, and future, and status plays little role compared with many other Papuan languages. Tense and person/number are expressed by separate suffixes, but they interact so that the tense suffixes mainly distinguish past vs. non-past, while person/number suffixes help determine present vs. future; there is no dual or inclusive-exclusive distinction.

The present and future forms also have secondary uses: present forms can express generic, time-neutral, or habitual meanings, and future forms are used in habitual or generic conditionals. The second person singular future additionally can function as a generic/process form or as a command or statement of obligation.

text:
The distinction between medial and final verbs is common in Papuan languages. Especially in the TNG languages the medial verbs are ``very common, universal over a wide area [and the] systems often highly complex'' (, also ). The medial verbs typically lack the full tense and person/number marking of the finite verbs. Instead, they usually indicate whether the subject is the same as the subject of the following verb, and/or whether the action of the verb is simultaneous or sequential with the action of the following verb. This is called the ``switch-reference system''. The question whether the system really tracks the topic (pragmatic subject) or the syntactic subject is discussed further in sec:8.2.3. As for person reference, the verbs in the simplest systems only show whether the two subjects are the same or different, but in the most elaborate systems the subjects of both the medial verb and that of the following verb are shown in the medial verb, which is thus even more specific than the finite verb. Usan makes a distinction between neutral and future medial verbs, and in both of these there is a division between same-subject and different-subject forms, but not between sequentiality and simultaneity (Reesink 1987:87--92). Maia only uses medial verbs when a clause has the same subject as the following clause; a distinction is made between simultaneous and sequential actions. When the following clause has a different subject, finite forms plus the contrast clitic -( d)i is used. Amele makes the basic distinction between the same-subject and different-subject medial verbs, and has simultaneous and sequential forms in both. But it also has different-subject simultaneous irrealis forms. Particularly the East New Guinea Highlands languages are known for marking the anticipatory subject in their medial verbs. See for a succinct list of switch-reference characteristics in Papuan languages, and for a more comprehensive overview.

In Mauwake the medial verb system is relatively simple. The suffixes indicate whether the subject of the medial verb stays the same in the following verb as well, and in the ``same subject following'' ( ss) verbs there is a further distinction between simultaneous and sequential action. The ``different subject following'' ( ds) verbs indicate sequential action; for simultaneous action one needs to use the continuous or stative aspect ( sec:3.8.5.1.1 ). The ds verbs also have some person marking but not as detailed as the finite verbs have.

The two sections below give a general outline of the person reference in medial clauses, but it is discussed in more detail in sec:8.2.3.

Typically, medial verbs have much fewer inflectional possibilities than finite verbs. This is the case in Mauwake too: mood or tense and full person/number marking cannot be suffixed to the medial verbs. Derivational suffixes, on the other hand, can freely occur on the medial verbs. In Tail-Head linkage a new sentence begins with a medial verb copy of the finite verb that ended the previous sentence ( sec:8.2.3.5 ). Often the derivational morphology of the two verbs is the same, and sometimes the medial verb has less derivation than the final verb; very rarely it has even more ex:3:x237:

Ikiwosa wiar pepekim-ep kaik-a-m. Kaik- om- a p \\
head 3. dat measure- ss. seq tie- pa -1s tie- ben - bnfy 2. ss. seq \\
`I measured her head and tied it (=headdress). I tied it for her and '

Same-subject marking

When the subject of the medial clause is the same as that of the following clause, the verb itself does not give any indication of the person and number of the subject, only that the same subject continues in the next clause. For exceptions to this, see sec:8.2.3 where the functional aspects of switch reference are discussed. If the actions are sequential, i.e. the action indicated by the verb in the medial clause precedes that of the following clause, the suffix is - ap or - ep ex:3:x238 depending on the conjugation class ( sec:2.3.3.3 ). For the second conjugation class verb or - `descend' the suffix is - op.

Owowa or- op, wuailal- ep akia ik-e-k. \\
village go.down- ss. seq be.hungry- ss. seq banana roast- pa -3s \\
`He went (down) to the village, was hungry and roasted bananas.'

If the verb has the beneficiary suffix -a or -e ( sec:3.8.3.1 ), the vowel of the medial verb suffix gets assimilated to it ex:3:x1930, ex:3:x1929.

eka=pa merena yasuw-om- ep... (cf. yasuw- ap) \\
water= loc foot wash- ben - bnfy.1- ss. seq \\
` she washed my feet in water (and) '...waaya nain uup-om- ap samapora=pa wu-ap maak-e-mik... (cf. uup- ep)\\
pig that1 cook- ben - bnfy 2. ss. seq floor= loc put- ss. seq tell- pa -1/3p\\
` they cooked the pig for him, put it on the floor and told him, '

When the medial clause subject is the same as the subject in the following clause but the two actions are simultaneous, or at least overlapping, the suffix is - ami or - emi (or - omi) according to the conjugation class of the verb. Even if the action of the medial verb may often be interpreted as continuous ex:3:x239, the suffix in itself only indicates simultaneity ex:3:x240. Continuous aspect marking may be needed for clarity when continuity is in focus ex:3:x241.

Wi sawur ir- ami fan yiar pok-a-mik. \\
3p. unm spirit go- ss. sim here 1p. dat sit.down- pa -1/3p \\
`As the spirits were going they sat down here with us.'

ekap- emi koora=pa yia wua-i-mik. \\
come- ss. sim house= loc 1p. acc put-Np- pr.1/3p \\
` coming (=upon arrival) they put us in the house.'

Soomar-em-ik -ok ifara oko uruf-a-k. \\
walk- ss. sim -be-SS vine other see- pa -3s \\
`He was walking and saw another vine. '
summary:
The passage explains that Papuan languages, especially TNG languages, often use a medial/final verb system in which medial verbs lack full tense and person marking and instead encode switch-reference: whether the subject is the same as or different from the following clause, and whether the actions are simultaneous or sequential. Mauwake has a relatively simple version of this system, with same-subject medial verbs marking either sequential or simultaneous action and different-subject forms mainly marking sequential action, while full mood/tense and detailed person-number marking are reserved for finite verbs.

It also notes that medial verbs allow derivational suffixes but not the full inflectional range of finite verbs, and that in tail-head linkage a sentence may begin with a medial copy of the previous clause’s final verb. In same-subject clauses, the medial verb itself does not mark person and number, only continuity of subject and, depending on the suffix, sequence or overlap of actions.

text:
The verb ik- `be' is different from other verbs in that there is no differentiation between the simultaneous and sequential forms in the same-subject medial verb: in example ex:3:x242 the actions are simultaneous, in ex:3:x243 sequential. Also, the verb does not take either one of the normal same-subject suffixes.

Owowa=pa neeke ik-ok mua maak-ek \\
village= loc there. cf be-SS man tell- pa -3s \\
`While they were there in the village she told her husband, '

No kaaneke ik-ok kerer-e-n? \\
2s. unm where. cf be-SS appear- pa -2s \\
`Where have you been and now come?'

Different-subject marking

If the subject of the medial clause is different from that of the following clause, the suffix of the ds verb reflects this. There are some person/number distinctions in these suffixes, even though not as many as in the finite verbs. The first person singular and plural are distinguished from all the other forms; in the other persons the distinction is based on the number: second and third person singular share the same suffix, and second and third person plural likewise ex:3:x244, ex:3:x245. There is great variation in this area in Papuan languages. Some only have one form to indicate that the subject changes, others have partial or full differentiation according to the person, some even show the subject of the following clause in the medial verb. tab:3:differentsubject shows the different subject suffixes.

Imen-ap maak- iwkin o miim-o-k. \\
find- ss. seq tell-2/3p. ds 3s. unm precede- pa -3s \\
`They found him and told him, and he went ahead of them.'

Mik- amkun me um-o-k, wiowa onaiya ikiw-em-ik- eya Olas=ke war-ek.\\
spear-1s/p. ds not die- pa -3s spear with go- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds Olas= cf shoot- pa -3s\\
`When I speared it, it didn't die, (but) as it was going with the spear Olas shot it.'

The suffix is - aya instead of - eya in a few short conjugation class 1 verbs ( sec:3.8.4.1 ) ex:3:x493 The vowel -a is somewhat more common in the Muaka dialect group where the 2/3s. ds marker is - era instead of - eya. and in those benefactive verbs where the first vowel of the suffix is assimilated to the preceding vowel of the beneficiary suffix ex:3:x695.

Iw- aya nan miira saawirin-e-k. \\
enter-2/3s. ds there face become.round- pa -3s\\
`As [the poison] entered [his liver], he became dizzy.'

Aaya=ko yia aaw-om- aya enim-i-yan. \\
sugarcane= nf 1p. acc get- ben - bnfy 2.2/3s. ds eat-Np- fu.1p\\
`Get us sugarcane and we'll eat it.'

The different-subject marking - eya is also used with some non-verbs. This seems to be uncommon in png languages: in ' (1997:137) survey the very few examples where the switch-reference marking was on non-verbs these were pro-clausal substitutes like a demonstrative or vocative. In Mauwake the ds suffix can be added to nouns ex:3:x250 or adjectives ex:3:x251, or the negative adverbs weetak and marew ex:3:x252 functioning as predicates in verbless clauses. When it is added to words ending in - a, the first vowel in the suffix gets assimilated to this vowel ex:3:x250.

Enakiwa- ya me aaw-e-m. \\
half-2/3s. ds not take- pa -1s \\
`There was (only) half (left), so I didn't take any/it.'

Mauwow maneka- ya=na yia maak-i-non. \\
work big-2/3s. ds = tp 1p. acc tell-Np- fu.3s \\
`If the work is big, she will tell us.'

Soomia marew- eya amap-ep-om-a-m. \\
spoon none-2/3s. ds bpx -come- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1s \\
`She has/had no spoons (lit: there are/were no spoons) so I brought them to her.'

When the different subject marking - eya is added to the adverb naap `thus', the outcome is a consecutive connective `therefore, so' ( sec:3.11.2 ).

Tense and medial verbs

The medial verbs have no tense marking, so the tense in a medial clause is interpreted in relation to that of the next finite clause. When the finite clause is in the past tense, both a simultaneous ex:3:x1025 and a sequential medial clause ex:3:x1023 are also understood to be in the past tense.

Iwera uruk-am-ika-iwkin wi ikiw-emi aaw-em-ik-e-mik.\\
coconut drop- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds 3p. unm go- ss. sim take- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`They i kept dropping coconuts, and they j went and got them.'

Owowa or-op, wailal-ep, akia ik-e-k. \\
village descend- ss. seq be.hungry- ss. seq banana roast- pa -3s\\
`He came down to the village, was hungry and roasted bananas.'

Since a sequential verb indicates that the action takes place before another action, a sequential medial clause preceding a present tense final clause has to be interpreted to be in the past tense, whereas a simultaneous clause is interpreted to be in the present tense like the final verb ex:3:x1024.

Iperuma nain=ke mua puuk-ap owora en-emi afura buan-em-ika-i-ya.\\
eel that1= cf man change.into- ss. seq betelnut eat- ss. sim lime.container knock- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.3s\\
`The eel has become man, and is eating betelnut and knocking the lime container.'

Both a sequential and a simultaneous medial clause preceding a future final clause are also understood as future clauses. The action in a sequential medial clause takes place before that in the final clause, but it is still in the future ex:3:x1026. The action in a simultaneous clause is partly or fully overlapping with that in the final clause ex:3:x1027.

Is=ke maa uup-emkun wi ekap-ep enim-i-kuan. \\
1p. fc = cf food cook-1s/p. ds 3p. unm come- ss. seq eat-Np- fu.3p\\
`We'll cook the food and they'll come and eat it.' Or: `When we have cooked the food they will come and eat it.'

Wi ir-ami nia aaw-emi efa ifakim-i-kuan. \\
3p. unm come- ss. sim 2p. acc take- ss. sim 1s. acc kill-Np- fu.3p\\
`They will come and take you and kill me.'
summary:
The passage describes Mauwake medial verbs, noting that the verb *ik-* “be” is exceptional because it does not distinguish simultaneous from sequential same-subject medial forms and does not take the usual same-subject suffixes. It then explains different-subject marking, where the suffix on the medial verb signals a change of subject with limited person/number contrasts, and notes that these suffixes can also appear on some non-verbs used predicatively.  

It also shows that medial verbs have no tense marking of their own, so their tense is interpreted relative to the following finite clause: sequential medial clauses are understood as preceding the final clause, while simultaneous clauses overlap with it. This interpretation holds across past, present, and future final clauses.

text:
The medial verb form cannot be used in the following example, because the first verb refers to time preceding the speech event and the second verb to time following it. Final verbs with different tenses have to be used, and in this case it is most natural to place the past tense verb in a relative clause ex:3:x1030.

Mukuna kerer-e-k nain kamenap umuk-i-yan? \\
fire appear- pa -3s that1 how extinguish-Np- fu.1p\\
`How shall we extinguish the fire that started?'

The medial verbs acquire more absolute-relative tense character of ``past in the past'' in those cases where sequential medial clauses are either right-dislocated and placed after the final clause ex:3:x1031 or placed inside another medial clause ex:3:x1032, or when there is a separate time expression referring to earlier time than that indicated by the final verb ex:3:x1033.

Rubaruba nain=ke ona emeria nain aaw-ep p-ikiw-o-k, iw-iwkin.\\
Rubaruba that1= cf 3s. gen woman that1 take- ss. seq bpx -go- pa -3s give.him-2/3p. ds \\
`That Rubaruba took his wife and took her (away), when they had given her to him.'

Um-eya merena ere-erup ifara aaw-ep kaik-ap nabena suuw-ap akua aaw-ep or-o-m.\\
die-2/3s. ds leg rdp -two vine get- ss. seq tie- ss. seq carrying.pole push- ss. seq shoulder take- ss. seq descend- pa -1s\\
`It died, and I tied its legs in pairs with a vine that I had gotten, and pushed it to the carrying pole and carried it down on my shoulder.'

Iiriw inasin mua nain=ke naap wia maak-eya wi naap on-a-mik.\\
earlier spirit man that= cf thus 3p. acc tell-2/3p. ds 3p. unm thus do- pa -1/3p\\
`The spirit man had earlier told them like that and they did so.'
summary: The passage explains that medial verb forms cannot be used when one verb refers to time before the speech event and the next to time after it; in such cases, final verbs with different tenses are required, often with the past-tense verb placed in a relative clause. It also notes that medial verbs can take on a more absolute-relative “past in the past” meaning when sequential medial clauses occur after the final clause, inside another medial clause, or alongside a separate time expression referring to an earlier time.

text: Verbs can be divided into classes on the basis of various criteria. Conjugation classes based on morphological/inflectional criteria are usually arbitrary and unrelated to other parts of the grammar. They are only touched on briefly in the next subsection. Transitivity as a basis of verb classes is discussed in sec:3.8.4.2, and valence-changing operations in sec:3.8.4.3. Verb classes based on semantic features are described in sec:3.8.4.4.
summary: Verbs may be divided into classes using different criteria. Conjugation classes based on morphological or inflectional properties are generally arbitrary and not connected to other parts of the grammar, while transitivity, valence-changing operations, and semantic features provide other bases for classifying verbs.

text:
In the Mauwake lexicon the verbs are divided into classes 1 and 2 depending on whether they have - a or - E as the past tense suffix. There are morphophonological rules for deriving the past tense marking for most verbs ( sec:2.3.3.3 ), but since some of the rules are rather complicated, and because they do not cover a number of cases like ex:3:x253 and ex:3:x254 below, the division into two separate classes is maintained.

miim- a-k \\
hear- pa -3s \\
`he heard'

miim- o-k \\
precede- pa -3s \\
`he went ahead'

In Class 1, transitive verbs outnumber intransitive verbs over four times, but Class 2 is divided almost equally between transitive and intransitive verbs. For this count, the verbs formed with the verbalizer -ar and the causative -ow were deleted from the total of 857 verbs, since both these suffixes influence the choice of the past tense vowel.

puuk- a-k vs. puk- o-k \\
cut- pa -3s burst- pa -3s \\
`he cut (it)' `it burst'

teek- a-k vs. ten- e-k \\
pluck- pa -3s collapse- pa -3s\\
`he plucked (it)' `it collapsed' (also: `it broke away')
summary: Mauwake verbs are divided into two classes based on whether the past tense suffix is **-a** or **-e**, even though morphophonological rules derive the marking for most verbs, because those rules are complex and do not cover all cases. Class 1 is dominated by transitive verbs, which outnumber intransitives by more than four to one, while Class 2 contains roughly equal numbers of transitive and intransitive verbs; verbs with the verbalizer **-ar** and causative **-ow** are excluded from this count because they affect the past tense vowel choice.

text:
With the term transitivity of a verb I refer to its syntactic transitivity, i.e. ``the number of overt morpho-syntactically coded arguments it takes''.

Intransitive verbs in Mauwake only require a subject, whereas transitive verbs require a direct object as well. This definition differs slightly from that of, who defines as transitive verbs those that can take a direct object, and as intransitive those that cannot (emphasis mine). Crystal's definition works for Mauwake when considering prototypical patient/undergoer objects, but it fails in the cases where the syntactic object manifests other roles not required by the semantic structure of the verb. The syntactic transitivity of a verb can differ from both its semantic and macrorole transitivity.

In some languages verb roots can be neutral as to transitivity, but in Mauwake each verb has a basic transitivity value. Most verbs are either intransitive ( sec:3.8.4.2.1 ) or transitive ( sec:3.8.4.2.2 ). There are only a few ambitransitives ( sec:3.8.4.2.3 ). Mauwake does not have a regular class of ditransitive verbs that would require two objects. Instead, some verbs that are transitive easily allow a second object. And in the small class of the object cross-referencing verbs ( sec:3.8.4.2.4 ), in which the pronominal object is in the verb root, two of the verbs require a second object as well.

The basic transitivity of a verb can be changed with valence-changing strategies ( sec:3.8.4.3 ). Causative ( sec:3.8.2.3.1 ) and benefactive morphology ( sec:3.8.2.3.3 ) as well as possessor raising ( sec:5.3.2.3 ) are processes that increase the number of syntactic objects in a clause.

Intransitive verbs

In Mauwake the class of basic, or ``ordinary'', intransitive verbs consists of a semantically very diverse group including involuntary processes ex:3:x266, many motion verbs ex:3:x267, and some bodily function verbs ex:3:x269.

Fikera aw-o-k. \\
kunai.grass burn- pa -3s \\
`The kunai grass burned.'

Kuuten ikos karu-e-mik. \\
Kuuten with run- pa -1/3p \\
`I ran with Kuuten.'

Niir-emi pisi-e -k. \\
laugh- ss. sim fart- pa -3s \\
`He laughed and farted.'

Some experience verbs expressing physiological states are also regular intransitive verbs ex:3:x1485:

Maa enowa nopa-yiaw-ep wuailal-ep ma-e-mik, ``...''\\
food eat- nmz search-move.around- ss. seq get.hungry- ss. seq say- pa -1/3p\\
`They searched around for food and got hungry and said, `` '' '

The verbs derived with the inchoative suffix - ar ( sec:3.8.2.2.2 ) are mostly intransitive ex:3:x271, ex:3:x1486, but a few of them are transitive ex:3:x1836.

Uuw-ap uuw-ap lebum-ar-e-m. \\
work- ss. seq work- ss. seq lazy- inch - pa -1s \\
`I worked and worked and got tired.'

Nan teeria manek-ar-e-k, owowa pun manek-ar-e-k. \\
there family big- inch - pa -3s village also big- inch - pa -3s\\
`The family grew big there, and the village grew big too.'

Maa unowa oram me amis - ar - i - mik, weetak. \\
thing many just not knowledge- inch -Np- pr.1/3p no\\
`We don't just gain knowledge of many things (without learning them), no.'

Climate expressions often use intransitive verbs. There is no separate class of verbs for climate expressions ex:3:x270. Climate expressions also use directional verbs ( ipia oraiya `the rain descends'), inchoative verbs ( kokomarek `it got dark') and transitive verbs ( ama fookak `the sun split (tr.)').

Aapereka paran-em-ika-i-ya. \\
cloud rumble- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.3s\\
`It is thundering.'

Intransitive clauses are discussed in sec:5.4.

Transitive verbs

Transitive verbs require a subject and an object. A [+human] object needs to be marked with an accusative pronoun ( sec:3.5.3 ) regardless of the presence or absence of a separate object np ex:3:x294.

Yaapan wia ifakim-e-mik. \\
Japan 3p. acc kill- pa -1/3p \\
`They killed the Japanese.'

Besides the prototypical transitive verbs with an agent subject and a patient-of-change object like ex:3:x295 and ex:3:x296, also many verbs of perception ex:3:x297, cognition ex:3:x298 and emotion ex:3:x299 are transitive.

Wiipa erup wia sesek-a-mik. \\
girl two 3p. acc send- pa -1/3p \\
`They sent the two girls.'

Yo me efa enim-uk. \\
1s. unm not 1. acc eat- imp.3p \\
`Let them not eat me.' This was said in a traditional story by a spirit that was able to change into a man or into an eel, which the people in the story were preparing to eat.

Nomokowa unowa aakisa wia uruf-i-n. \\
2s/p.brother many now 3p. acc see-Np- pr.2s \\
`Now you see many brothers of yours.

Nefa amis-ar-ep ma-i-yem. \\
2s. acc knowledge- inch - ss. seq say-Np- pr.1s \\
`I am saying (this) because I know you.'

Yena mua=ke efa kookal-ep manin(a) uuw-owa efa asip-i-ya.\\
1s. gen man 1s. acc like- ss. seq garden work- nmz 1s. acc help-Np- pr.3s\\
`My husband likes me and helps me in the garden.'

If there is no other overt object available for a transitive verb, the maximally generic noun maa `thing' The semantic area of maa is at least as wide that of its English equivalent `thing'. Because it is used so often with verbs denoting eating and preparing food, it has acquired a secondary meaning `food'. is used as a dummy object ex:3:x300, ex:3:x1825. Compare the next two examples: in ex:3:x300 maa is added because of syntactic requirements, whereas in ex:3:x301 the lack of an overt object indicates a third person singular object.

(Yo) maa uruf-i-yem. \\
I thing see-Np- pr.1s \\
`I see.' (=I see something, or: I can see.)

(Yo) uruf-i-yem. \\
I see-Np- pr.1s \\
`I see him/her/it.'

Iir oko maa enim-i-yem, iir oko maa me enim-i-yem. \\
time other thing eat-Np- pr.1s time other thing not eat-Np- pr.1s\\
`Sometimes I eat, sometimes I don't eat.'

The language-specific characteristic of syntactic transitivity is illustrated by a number of verbs that are transitive in Mauwake but intransitive in English: aner- `aim (at), refer (to)' ex:3:x302, ikum- `wonder (about)' ex:3:x303, kerew- `be angry (at)'.

Wi wia amukar-emi me nefa aner-a-m. \\
3p. unm 3p. acc scold- ss. sim not 2s. acc refer.to- pa -1s \\
`When I scolded them I didn't refer to you.'
summary:
The passage defines transitivity in Mauwake as the number of overt morphosyntactically coded arguments a verb takes, distinguishing this from semantic and macrorole transitivity. In Mauwake, verbs have basic transitivity values: most are either intransitive, requiring only a subject, or transitive, requiring a subject plus a direct object, while only a few are ambitransitive and there is no regular class of ditransitives, though some transitive verbs can take a second object.

The text also notes that transitivity can be increased by causative, benefactive, and possessor-raising processes. It then illustrates that Mauwake intransitives and transitives cover a semantically wide range, including motion, bodily functions, perception, cognition, emotion, and even some verbs that are transitive in Mauwake but intransitive in English.

text:
Nefa ikum-am-ika-iwkin nan kerer-e-n. \\
2s. acc wonder.about- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds there arrive- pa -2s\\
`As they were wondering about you, you arrived there.'

There are a few verbs that require an undergoer object, but usually have recipient object as well. The verbs ofakow- `show, teach' ex:3:x1838 and maak- `tell' ex:3:x943 are the most common of these. The verb `send' is cross-linguistically typically ditransitive, but in Mauwake it requires the benefactive suffix in order to be able to take a second object.

Tunde urera Liisa ame=ke epa O yia O ofakowa-y i aw - e - mik.\\
Tuesday afternoon Liisa assoc = cf place 1p. acc show-move.around- pa -1/3p\\
`On Tuesday afternoon Liisa and the othes showed us around the place.'

Nena panewowa pun wadol opora O yia O maak-i-n. \\
2s. gen old also lie talk 1p. acc tell-Np- pr.2s\\
`You yourself -- an old person too! -- tell us lies.'

The verb wu- `put' requires both an undergoer object and a locative adverbial ex:3:x1837:

Sosora nain O pona=pa AdvP wu-a-mik. \\
grass.skirt that1 riverbank= loc put- pa -1/3p\\
`They put those grass skirts on the riverbank.'

The directional verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.5 ) could be treated as weakly transitive, in which case the goal np, which is never marked with the locative clitic - pa, could be a locative object. There are two main reasons against this analysis. When the goal of a directional verb is a personal pronoun, the dative case is used rather than the accusative ex:3:x1870.

ona wiawi wiar ikiw-o-k. \\
3s. gen 3s/p.father 3. dat go- pa -3s\\
` she went to her father.'

Also, if the directional verbs were considered weakly transitive and the the goal a locative object, the locative adverb nan `there' in the following clauses would be treated as a locative adverb in ex:3:x1871 but as a locative object in ex:3:x1872:

Kerer-ep nan soomare-miaw-e-mik. \\
arrive- ss. seq there walk-move.around- pa -1/3p\\
`They arrived and walked around there.'

Or-op nan ikiw-ep wia uruf-a-k. \\
descend- ss. seq there go- ss. seq 3p. acc see- pa -3s\\
`He went down and went there and saw them.'

Ambitransitive verbs

Although most verb roots in Mauwake are clearly transitive or intransitive, there are a few that are ambitransitive ex:3:x1827-- ex:3:x1060. Many of their English equivalents would be intransitive. Only the following roots have been found to be neutral with regard to transitivity ( tab:3:ambitransitives ). Of them ofof- and taan- are of the S=O type, where the intransitive subject is an undergoer; the others are of the S=A type, where the intransitive subject is an actor.

Ifar(a) makena wulewul ofof-i-ya. \\
vine fruit wulewul shake-Np- pr.3s\\
`The vine fruit (called) wulewul shakes.'

Maa-ofofona saarik wia ofof-a-k. \\
earthquake like 3p. acc shake- pa -3s\\
`It shook them like an earthquake.'

Ifa uruf-ap baurar-ep karu-or-o-mik. \\
snake see- ss. seq flee- ss. seq run-descend- pa -1/3p \\
`We saw a snake and fled and ran down (to the village).'

Epasia=pa ik-omkun me efa karu-e-mik. \\
far= loc be-1s/p. ds neg 1s. acc run/visit- pa -1/3p\\
`When I lived far away, they didn't visit me.'

En-em-ika-eya ona wiamun=ke uruf-ap om-o-k.\\
eat- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds 3s. gen younger.sibling= cf see- ss. seq cry- pa -3s\\
`When he was eating it his younger sibling saw it/him and cried.'

Efa om-em-ik-eya epa wiim-o-k. \\
1s. acc cry- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds place dawn- pa -3s\\
`While she was mourning for me it dawned.'

The subject of the adjunct plus verb pepek er- `be enough, suffice' is typically inanimate ex:3:x1058, whereas the object, when there is one, is usually human ex:3:x306.

Kemuka nain pepek er-eya onak ona wiar puuk-a-k.\\
string that1 enough go-2/3s. ds 3s/p.mother 3s. gen 3. dat cut- pa -3s\\
`When the string was (long) enough, their mother herself cut it.'

Wia pepek er-a-k. \\
3p. acc enough come/go- pa -3s \\
`It was enough for them.'

Object cross-referencing verbs

One feature very common to a small group of verbs in the Trans-New Guinea languages is that the ``verb stem undergoes changes according to the person of the object or beneficiary''. Wurm actually seems to be referring to recipient rather than beneficiary, as `give' is the most common of these verbs, and the verb stem changes according to the recipient. In Mauwake this group consists of only five members.

I call these verbs object cross-referencing because, besides marking the subject with a suffix like all other verbs do, they also obligatorily mark the object in the verb root. What has clearly been a prefix Phonetically this prefix is closer to the unmarked pronouns than the accusative pronouns. earlier has been grammaticalized as part of the verb itself: there is no neutral root that would not be linked to any particular person ex:3:x334-- ex:3:x336. When a ``neutral'' form is required, the third person singular is used. In this respect these verbs differ from all the other verbs in Mauwake. In the case of `give' the verb root i- has assimilated into the prefix, so currently the person marking of the recipient object is the only root that there is. Four of the object cross-referencing verbs are listed in tab:3:crossreferencingverbs.

Maa fain me iw-o-k. \\
thing this not give.him/her- pa -3s \\
`He did not give this thing to him/her.'

Waaya pun enak-e-mik. \\
pig too feed.me- pa -1/3p \\
`They also gave me pork to eat.'

Amia=iya nenar-e-mik=i? \\
bow= com shoot.you- pa -1/3p= qm \\
`Did they shoot you with a gun?'
summary: The passage describes several transitive patterns in Mauwake, including verbs that require both an undergoer object and sometimes a recipient or locative element, as well as directional verbs whose goal arguments are not best analyzed as locative objects because they take dative marking with pronouns. It also notes a small set of ambitransitive verbs, distinguishing S=O and S=A types, and explains that certain “object cross-referencing” verbs obligatorily encode the object or recipient in the verb root itself rather than using a neutral stem.

text:
The cross-referenced objects are semantically quite different. In the verbs iw- `give (him)' and onak- `feed (him)' it is the recipient, onak- `feed (him)' requires a food term as the undergoer object, so a better translation, but longer, would be `give him (something) to eat'. in war- `shoot (him)' and ook- `follow (him)' the undergoer. The verb wionar- A possible origin for this is pron +onaiya+ar- `become together-with pron ' (Kwan, p.c.) `hide among (them)' is a special case in two ways: the cross-referenced argument `among a group' is quite untypical as a verbal argument; and only plural forms of this verb can be used because of semantic restrictions: yionar- `hide among us', nionar- `hide among you (pl)', wionar- `hide among them' ex:3:x337.

Wi wionar-ep pok-ap ik-ua. \\
3p. unm hide.among.them- ss. seq sit.down- ss. seq be- pa.3s \\
`He sat hiding among them.'

Maia does not have any verbs behaving like this, and only reports one for Bargam: -g `give' (2002:87). Usan has three verbs involving a stem change of this kind: ut\^ab `give (him)', w\^ab `shoot' and w\^aramb `hit'. Ut\^ab, which coreferences the recipient, has quite strict co-occurrence restrictions with other arguments or even with peripheral elements in the same clause (ibid. 129--30).

Unlike Usan, in Mauwake the clauses with object cross-referencing verbs can easily have a locative or instrument phrase, and the verb itself can take a benefactive suffix. A sentence like ex:3:x338 would be possible for instance when sending money to people travelling in the same vehicle as the addressee.

Miiw-aasa=pa wi-om- e. \\
land-canoe= loc give.them- ben - bnfy 1. imp.2s \\
`Give it to them for me in the car.'
summary: The passage notes that cross-referenced objects can play different semantic roles depending on the verb: in some verbs they are recipients, in others undergoers, and in *hide among them* the cross-referenced argument is unusually “among a group” and is restricted to plural forms. It also compares languages, saying that Maia lacks such verbs, Bargam has only one reported example, Usan has three verbs with this type of stem change and strict argument restrictions, while Mauwake allows these verbs to co-occur more freely with locative, instrumental, and benefactive markings.

text:
The term valence refers to the number of arguments that have a grammatical relation with the verb. As was mentioned above, almost all of the verb roots in Mauwake have a basic valence of one or two: they take either a subject only (intransitive verbs sec:3.8.4.2.1 ) or a subject and an object (transitive verbs sec:3.8.4.2.2 ) as their arguments. There are some ways to change the valence of verbs, even if strategies like passivization and dative shift are not possible in Mauwake. The valence is increased, when an intransitive verb is made into transitive or a transitive verb into causative with the addition of an causative suffix, or when a benefactive suffix is added to a verb. There are no processes to decrease the syntactic valence of a verb. The semantic valence is decreased when the object of a transitive verb is a reflexive or reciprocal pronoun, since the subject and object have the same referent(s). Subject demotion is another way to decrease the semantic valence.

Causatives

The causative always increases the number of arguments a verb can take: the subject of an intransitive verb ex:3:x997 becomes the object of a transitive verb ex:3:x998, and a new subject is added. The causative suffix - ow was described above in sec:3.8.2.3.1. In most cases the meaning of a causative is `to cause someone or something to do something'. The caused `doing' is usually not agentive ex:3:x992.

Iwera nainiw kaken iimar-e-k. (Intransitive) \\
coconut again straight stand- pa -3s\\
`The coconut palm stood straight again.'

Eka napia O koor miira=pa iimar- ow-a-mik. \\
water bamboo house face= loc stand- caus - pa -1/3p\\
`We made the bamboo water containers stand in front of the house.'

Wiowa erup O ar- ow-amkun um-o-k. \\
spear two become- caus -1s/p. ds die- pa -3s\\
`I speared it a second time and it (=the pig) died.' (Lit: `I caused a spear to become two and it died.')

The mental state of being angry is expressed via a verb in Mauwake ex:3:x993, and it can take the causative suffix ex:3:x994.

Kema bagiwir-a-m. \\
liver be.angry- pa -1s\\
`I was angry.'

Yo kema efa O bagiwir- ow-a-n, yaa! \\
1s. unm liver 1s. acc be.angry- caus - pa -2s intj \\
`Boy, have you made me angry!'

In some cases the causative suffix acts simply as a transitivizer. The subject in ex:3:x995 does not actually cause the children to grow. Also in this case the suffix increases the valency of the verb: arim- `grow' in ex:3:x996 is intransitive, but arimow- in ex:3:x995 is transitive and takes an object.

Aakisa arim-o-n, aakisa muew-o-n. \\
now grow- pa -2s now marry- pa -2s\\
`Now you have grown, now you have married.'

No nena maa fariar-ep muuka nain O arim- ow-e.\\
2s. unm 2s. gen food abstain- ss. seq son that1 grow- caus - imp.2s\\
`You yourself have to abstain from (certain) food(s) and bring the son up.'

When the causative suffix is added to the intransitive verb sail- `(tell a) lie', its meaning changes into `lie to someone', `cheat' ex:3:x448.

Opor(a) makena ma-i-yem, me nia O sail- ow-iyem. \\
talk true say-Np- pr.1s not 2p. acc lie- caus - pr.1s\\
`I am telling the truth, I am not cheating you.'

Bring-prefixes ( sec:3.8.2.4.2 ) are another causative strategy, used only with the directional verbs ex:3:x999, ex:3:x1001 ( sec:3.8.4.4.5 ) and a couple of other motion verbs ex:3:x1000. The subject of the verb causes the object to move by undertaking the transfer himself/herself.

Maa unowa ifer aasa=ke p-urup-o-k. \\
thing many sea canoe= cf bpx -ascend- pa -3s\\
`A lot of things were brought/taken up by ships.'

O mua imen-ap=na feeke wia p-ekap-eka. \\
3s. unm man find- ss. seq = tp here. cf 3p. acc bpx -come- imp.2p\\
`If/when you find a/any man, bring them/him here.'

Gomi kawus p-irapar-i-ya. \\
east.wind smoke bpx -move.to.and.fro-Np- pr.3s\\
`The east wind moves the smoke around.'

Forming a causative from an agentive verb ( inducive causative, ) is not done morphologically with an affix but syntactically with a verbal construction involving the nominalized form of the main verb and suuw- `push' as the causative auxiliary ex:3:x1003, ex:3:x1002 ( sec:5.7.1 ).

O uruf-ap op-ap Yeesus nomokowa moke akua-aaw-om-owa suuw-a-mik.\\
3s. unm see- ss. seq hold- ss. seq Jesus tree slanting shoulder-take- ben - nmz push- pa -1/3p\\
`They saw him and took hold of him, and made him carry Jesus' cross on his shoulder.'

Sira enuma ook-owa nia suuw-i-mik. \\
custom new follow- nmz 2p. acc push-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`They make you follow new customs/ways.'

In the following examples the three different causative strategies have been applied to the same verb ikiw- `go', and in all of them the patient is [+human]. In ex:3:x1016 and ex:3:x1829 the object of the causative verb has no influence on what happens to him/her, but in ex:3:x1873 the object of the inducive causative is active and becomes the actor of the verb resulting from the causation.

Ipamsika mua=ke ikiw-ow -a-k. \\
nail man= cf go- caus - pa -3s \\
`A sorcerer (lit: nail man) killed him (lit: caused him to go).'

Kes tepak=pa wu-ap p-ikiw-e-mik. \\
coffin inside= loc put- ss. seq bpx -go- pa -1/3p\\
`They put him inside the coffin and took him (away).'

Yo mua oko ikiw-owa suuw-amkun ikiw-i-non. \\
1s. unm man other go- nmz push-1s/p. ds go-Np- fu.3s\\
`I make a man go and he goes.'

Benefactive

The benefactive form of a verb ( sec:3.8.2.3.3 ) is used when an action is done for someone, for their benefit ex:3:x1004, or in some cases for their detriment ex:3:x1005. With the addition of the benefactive suffix to the verb, the beneficiary becomes an obligatory argument. The beneficiary is always animate, and usually human.

Wi owow mua=ke wilkar wia muf-em-ik- om-a-mik.\\
3p. unm village man= cf cart 3p. acc pull- ss. sim -be- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p\\
`The village men kept pulling carts for them.'
summary: Mauwake verbs generally have a valence of one or two arguments, and while the language lacks processes such as passivization and dative shift, valence can be increased through causatives and benefactive marking. Causatives add a new subject and can turn intransitive verbs into transitive ones or make transitive verbs causative; they may also function as simple transitivizers or as a syntactic construction with an agentive verb plus *suuw-* ‘push’. The benefactive suffix adds an obligatory animate beneficiary argument, sometimes indicating action for someone’s benefit and sometimes for their detriment.

text:
Epia wilin-owa uruf-ap bom yia fuurk- om-i-kuan.\\
fire(wood) shine- nmz see- ss. seq bomb 1p. acc throw- ben -Np- fu.3p\\
`When they see the light from the fire(s), they will throw bombs at us.'

More than one valency-increasing strategy can be applied to a verb simultaneously. In both ex:3:x1007 and ex:3:x1008 the valency of the verb increases from one to three: besides the subject of the original verb, the derived verbs also have both an object and a beneficiary.

Koor poka iimar- ow- om-e. \\
house post stand.up- caus - ben - bnfy 1. imp.2s\\
`Stand up the house posts for me.'

Ona soomia marew-eya amap-ep- om-a-m. \\
3s. gen spoon no(ne)-2/3s. ds bpx -come- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1s\\
`She has/had no spoons of her own, so I brought them for her.'

Decreasing semantic valence

There are no morphological means in Mauwake for decreasing syntactic valence. A verb that is inherently reflexive, like yaki- `wash oneself', is intransitive. But the semantic valence of transitive verbs is decreased when they are made either reflexive ex:3:x1834 or reciprocal ex:3:x1835. Syntactically the reflexive/reciprocal pronoun is an object, but the pronoun refers to the same referent(s) as the subject.

Birin-ep nomokowa iinan akena ikiw-ep wame pipilim-ep aakun-em-ika-i-non.\\
fly- ss. seq tree top very go- ss. seq 3s. refl hide- ss. seq speak- ss. sim -be-Np- fu.3s\\
`It will fly and hide (itself) in the very top of a tree and keep making noise.'

Osaiwa aalbok ikos uf-owa na-ep ofa wiam if-e-mik.\\
bird.of.paradise black.cuckoo-shrike together dance- nmz say- ss. seq colour 3p. refl paint- pa -1/3p\\
`A bird of paradise and a black cuckoo-shrike wanted to dance together and painted each other with colour.'

A common valence-decreasing device in many languages is the passive voice, which demotes or deletes the subject. In Mauwake verbs there is no passive voice. The standard way of demoting the subject is to have the verb in third person plural form and leave the subject np unexpressed ex:3:x1009, ex:3:x1010. Cf. the English impersonal ``they'': They say it is going to be cold tomorrow. None of the arguments change their syntactic function. The example ex:3:x1009 comes from a story where the main point was that the people responsible for the fire were never found, and it was not known if only one person was involved or many.

Fikera ikum kuum-e-mik nain ma-i-yem. \\
kunai.grass illicitly burn- pa -1/3p that1 say-Np- pr.1s\\
`I tell about when the kunai grass was burned (by arson).'

Nefa war-iwkin naap ma-e. \\
2s. acc shoot-2/3p. ds thus say- imp.2s\\
`If/when you are shot, then say like that.' (Or: `If they shoot you, then say like that.')

Another strategy to demote the subject is to use the same-subject sequential form of the main verb and the auxiliary ik- `be' agreeing with the object of the verb ex:3:x1011. This can only be used when the end result is a state.

Nomokowa puuk-ap ik-ua. \\
tree cut- ss. seq be- pa.3s\\
`The tree is cut.'
summary: The passage shows that Mauwake can increase valency by combining strategies such as causative and benefactive morphology, raising a verb from one argument to three; in these cases the derived verb has the original subject plus an object and a beneficiary. It then notes that Mauwake has no morphological passive or other dedicated valence-reducing device: reflexive and reciprocal forms reduce semantic valence, while subject demotion is expressed by leaving the subject unspoken with a third-person plural verb, or by using a sequential form with the auxiliary *ik-* ‘be’ when the result is a state.

text:
Even though the following classification is based on semantic characteristics of the verbs, the verbs within the resulting groups tend to have similarities in their syntactic behaviour as well.

Stative/existential verb ik -

The basic meaning of the stative verb ik( a)- is `be'. The vowel /a/ gets deleted elsewhere except in the present tense and the medial different-subject non-first plural form; in the corresponding singular form the vowel may be optionally deleted ex:3:x257.

Nan mukuna=pa ik(a)-eya o nan samor aaw-o-k. \\
there fire= loc be-2/3s. ds 3s. unm there badly get- pa -3s\\
`They (=bananas) were there on the fire and he really got bad there.'

Like intransitive verbs, it may form a complete clause by itself. Example ex:3:x1455 is from a situation where the speaker was in a plane for the first time, refused to eat and declined any help offered to him.

Ika-i-nen. \\
be-Np- fu.1s\\
`I will just be (like this).'

Often it is used for `be/live (somewhere)', and in this use it naturally co-occurs with a locative adverbial ex:3:x497:

I naap koora=pa ik-e-mik. \\
1p. unm thus house= loc be- pa -1/3p\\
`We were in the house like that.'

Together with the dative pronouns ik- is used to form possessive constructions ex:3:x258 (§ sec:3.5.5, sec:5.5.2 ).

Yo waaya arow efar ik-ua. \\
1s. unm pig three 1s. dat be- pa.3s \\
`I have three pigs.'

The function of ik- as a copular verb is very restricted. In equative or descriptive clauses it is normally not used in the present tense finite form, but in the past ex:3:x259 and future ex:3:x1070 tenses it is employed. It could be said, following, that in these clauses its primary function is to be the carrier of the tense.

Yo um-ep ik-owa saarik ik-e-m. \\
1s. unm die- ss. seq be- nmz like be- pa -1s\\
`I was like dead.'

Ikoka maa marew, eliw manek=iw ika-i-nan. \\
later thing none well big= lim be-Np- fu.2s\\
`Later there will be no problem, you will just be very well.'

In Mauwake it can also be used when the non-verbal predicate is understood to be transitory ex:3:x499 rather than stable over time:

No kamenap ika-i-n? \\
2s. unm how be-Np- pr.2s\\
`How are you?'

The verb ik- `be' is in a class of its own for several reasons. Its morphology is irregular, and so are the semantics of some of its morphology. In ex:3:x258 the past tense and the person/number marker in the third person singular form are merged into one portmanteau morpheme. An alternative form for the different-subject first person form ikemkun is ikomkun ex:3:x1931. The same-subject medial form is ikok ex:3:x260, not * ikep and * ikemi. ikep and ikemi are the same subject medial forms of the homophonous verb ik- `roast'. There is no formal differentiation between a simultaneous ex:3:x260 and a sequential ex:3:x262 form in the same-subject medial verb.

Siowa nain kakalt-am- ik - emkun arim-o-k. \\
dog that1 look.after- ss. sim -be-1s/p. ds grow- pa -3s\\
`I was looking after the dog and it grew.'

Naap ik-ok uruf-am-ika-iwkin wia. \\
thus be-SS see- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds no\\
`As he was/stayed like that they were watching him (but) no (=he didn't get better).'

Owowa ekap-o-k, amia mua=pa ik-ok. \\
village come- pa -3s bow man= loc be-SS \\
`He came to the village, having been in the police (force).'

It also differs from ordinary intransitive verbs in that in a verb+auxiliary construction it cannot be the main verb, but can be used as the aspectual auxiliary ex:3:x1931 (see also sec:3.8.4.5 ). But it is like other intransitive verbs in that it can take an causative suffix ex:3:x261. notes that in Usan the corresponding verb igo `be' cannot occur with the causative suffix. In Mauwake there is no similar restriction.

Nomokowa war-ep miiwa=pa ik-ow-a-mik. \\
tree cut- ss. seq ground= loc be- caus - pa -1/3p\\
`We cut trees and laid them on the ground'

The tense distinction is partly neutralized: the past tense form is used for past ex:3:x263 and present ex:3:x264. The present tense form is not very common and is mainly used for less time-stable situations ex:3:x499, ex:3:x1028, or to replace the missing continuous aspect form ex:3:x265. The verb ik- is used as the regular continuous aspect auxiliary ( sec:3.8.5.1.1.2 ), and as a main verb ik- `be' cannot take this auxiliary.

Yo unan koka=pa ik-e-m. \\
1s. unm yesterday jungle= loc be- pa -1s \\
`Yesterday I was in the jungle.'

Ni kaaneke ik-e-man oo, ni ekap-omak-eka oo! \\
2p. unm where be- pa -2p oh 2p. unm come-DISTR- imp.2p oh \\
`Wherever you are, come!'

Mesa asia fiker gone=pa ika-i-ya nain aaw-em-ik-e-m.\\
winged.bean wild kunai.grass middle= loc be-Np- pr.3s that1 take- ss. sim -be- pa -1s\\
`I was picking wild winged bean that was (lit: is) in the middle of the kunai grass.'

Yo nan ika-i-yem nain yo nia asip-i-yem, \\
1s. unm there be-Np- pr.1s that1 1s. unm 2p. acc help-Np- pr.1s\\
`Now that I am living there I help you, '

The verb ik- mainly functions in intransitive clauses, but it is also needed as a copula for those cases where a non-verbal predicate is in a non-present tense ex:3:x969.

O ikoka somek mua maneka ika-i-non. \\
3p. unm later song man big be-Np- fu.3s\\
`He will later be the headmaster.'

An equative or descriptive medial clause requires ik- as a copula regardless of the tense of the final verb ex:3:x498.

Koora naap ik-eya uruf-i-mik. \\
house thus be-2/3s. ds see-Np- pr.1p\\
`We see the house as it is like that.'

Position-taking verbs

The three position-taking verbs are among the most frequently used verbs in Mauwake: pok- `sit down', iimar- `stand up' and in- `lie down/ fall asleep'. They are essentially punctiliar verbs with an inceptive meaning ex:3:x273, but they are most typically used in the same-subject sequential form together with the auxiliary ik- ( sec:3.8.4.5 ) to convey stative meaning: `sit' ex:3:x274, `stand', and `lie/sleep'.
summary: The passage explains that although the verb groups are classified by meaning, they also show similar syntactic behavior. The stative/existential verb **ik-** means “be,” is highly irregular, can function as a complete clause, express location and possession, and serve as a restricted copula and a regular auxiliary, especially in non-present or less time-stable situations. It also notes that the position-taking verbs **pok-** ‘sit down’, **iimar-** ‘stand up’, and **in-** ‘lie down/fall asleep’ are punctiliar in form but often combine with **ik-** in sequential constructions to express stative meanings like sitting, standing, or sleeping.

text:
Kokom-ar-eya in-e-mik. \\
darkness- inch -2/3s. ds lie.down- pa -1/3p \\
`When it got dark we went to bed.'

Ona koora=pa arew-ap pok-ap ik-e-mik. \\
3s. gen house= loc wait- ss. seq sit.down- ss. seq be- pa -1/3p\\
`We sat and waited (lit: waited and sat) in his house.'

The verb pok- is occasionally used even without the auxiliary to mean `sit' ex:3:x1824.

Neek(e) pok-aka. \\
there sit- imp.2p\\
`Sit there/Keep sitting there.' (Commonly used as a conversational ``filler'' for people that are already sitting, when there is a lull in the conversation.)

The continuous aspect form of the position-taking verbs is not used with progressive meaning, only with the meaning `habitual' ex:3:x275 ( sec:3.8.5.1.1 ).

Irak-ow epa=pa koka=pa in-em-ik-e-mik. \\
fight- nmz time= loc jungle= loc lie.down- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
`During the war we used to sleep in the jungle.'

Location verbs

The two verbs that have been verbalized from the demonstrative adverbs fan `here' and nan `there' ( sec:3.8.2.2.1 ), are very restricted in their use. The original meaning of the verbs must refer to arrival at some place, but since they are only used in the past tense, they currently tend to indicate presence at a place rather than movement ex:3:x1270-- ex:3:x1272. This may indicate that the past tense used to encode perfectivity (Malcolm Ross, p.c.) They can even be used with immobile objects ex:3:x1276.

No ikiw-e, irak-owa maneka fan - e - k a. \\
2s. unm go- imp.2s fight- nmz big here- pa -3s intj \\
`Go (home), the big war is here.'

Aakisa i fan-e-mik. \\
Now 1p. unm here- pa -1/3p \\
`Now we are / have come here.'

No niawi akena nan-e-k. \\
2s. unm 2s/p.father true there- pa -3s\\
`Your real father is there.'

Aa, o koora fan-e-k a. \\
intj 3s. unm house here- pa -3s intj \\
`Ah, his house is here.'

Resultative verbs

The resultative verbs with the meaning `become' are another small group of intransitive verbs. Besides the semantic similarity they also share the syntactic characteristic that, in addition to the subject, they require another argument expressing the result of change. This other obligatory argument is a noun with the verbs ar- `become' ex:3:x276, ex:3:x277 and puuk- `change into' ex:3:x278, This verb is homonymous with the transitive verb puuk- `cut'. They may be historically related, but synchronically the meanings are quite different. and a colour adjective with the verb kir- `turn' ex:3:x279.

Takira arim-ep mua ar-e-k. \\
boy grow- ss. seq man become- pa -3s \\
`The boy grew and became a man.'

Emeria nain afa ar-e-mik. \\
woman that1 flyng.fox become- pa -1/3p \\
`Those women became flying foxes.'

Inasin mua ifa puuk-ap solon-ep \\
spirit man snake change.into- ss. seq glide- ss. seq \\
`The spirit man changed into a snake, glided and '

Oona kia kir-em-ik-eya uruf-ap ma-e-k \\
bone white turn- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds see- ss. seq say- pa -3s \\
`She saw that the bones were turning white and said, '

The verb ar- is mostly used when the subject stays essentially the same but undergoes some change ex:3:x276. However, it can also be used when the subject changes into something else ex:3:x277. The verb puuk- is only used in the latter context ex:3:x278, and it is always an intentional action. It is most common in traditional stories where spirits change into various inanimate things or animate beings. The verb kir- is used with most colour terms ex:3:x279, but for `black' there is a separate verb formed with the inchoative suffix - ar: sepenar- This is related to the adjective sepa `black'. `become black'. The inchoative suffix ( sec:3.8.2.2.2 ) is the standard device used for verbalizing adjectives.

Directional verbs

The verbs indicating coming and going are among the most frequent verbs in Mauwake. These verbs have the direction inherent in the verb root. Verbs of this kind are quite common among Papuan languages: in some languages the directional is an affix, in others it is part of the meaning of the root itself; Mauwake is of the latter type. The directional verb group contains verbs that in many languages would be prototypically intransitive ex:3:x280, ex:3:x281. The directional verbs are listed in tab:3:directionals.

Most of these verbs can be translated into English as either `go' or `come', depending on the context. Since the elevation of the goal, the direction of the compass and the distance all influence the choice of the verb, and may conflict with each other, the speaker has some freedom of choice. Also, with regard to proximity, it is a very relative notion how close or far away something is.

Manina urup-ep nan uuw-ap owowa or-o-k. \\
garden ascend- ss. seq there work- ss. seq village descend- pa -3s\\
`She went up to the garden, worked there and came down to the village.'

Fofa er-ap ir-i-mik. \\
market go- ss. seq come-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`We are coming back from the market.' (Lit: `We went west to the market and are coming east.')

The deictic orientation of ikiw- `away from speaker/deictic centre' and ekap- `towards the speaker/deictic centre' is stricter in Mauwake than in many European languages where the deictic centre especially for `come' can vary considerably. The sentence ex:3:x282 is all right in Finnish regardless of the location of the speaker, but the corresponding sentence in Mauwake would be acceptable only if the speaker were in Tampere at the time of speaking.

Isois\"ani tuli Tampereelle vuonna 1912. (Finnish)\\ \\
`My grandfather came to Tampere in 1912.'

The equivalent of the English `come' in ex:3:x283 has to be `go' in Mauwake ex:3:x284. This is discussed further in ( sec:6.3 ).

I'll come to your place tomorrow. \\
\\

Uurika nefa uruf-owa ikiw-i-nen. \\
tomorrow 2s. acc see- nmz go-Np- fu.1s \\
`Tomorrow I'll go to see you.'
summary: The passage describes several small classes of intransitive verbs in Mauwake: position-taking verbs like *pok-* ‘sit’ and *in-* ‘lie down,’ location verbs derived from demonstratives that often indicate presence rather than movement, resultative verbs meaning ‘become,’ and directional verbs meaning ‘go’ or ‘come.’ It notes that some verbs have restricted aspectual or semantic uses, such as continuous forms of position verbs expressing habit rather than progressive aspect, and that directional verbs encode deictic orientation more strictly than in many European languages.

text:
When these verbs occur with a locative phrase containing the locative marker ( sec:3.12.4 ), the phrase almost always refers to either source ex:3:x285, or location/path ex:3:x447. The goal is very seldom marked with the locative marker - pa; this happens when the goal is important mainly as the location of the next event ex:3:x1878. Also, in ex:3:x1878 mukuna `fire' is an untypical goal for a directional verb.

Manina =pa ekap-ep maa uup-e-mik. \\
garden= loc come- ss. seq food cook- pa -1/3p \\
`We came from the garden and cooked food.'

Iinan aasa iinan=pa fan ekap-emi \\
sky canoe sky= loc here come- ss. sim \\
`The airplane came here in the sky and '

Ne soran-emi epia mukuna = pa or - omi aw-o-k.
\\
add get.startled- ss. sim firewood fire= loc descend- ss. sim burn- pa -3s\\
`And he got startled and fell on the fire and burned himself.'

The directional verbs differ from other verbs in Mauwake in that they can be transitivized with the bring-prefixes p- ex:3:x286, amap- and aap- ( sec:3.8.2.4.2 ) to indicate either bringing or taking something somewhere.

Ona owowa p-ikiw-ep soop-i-yan. \\
3s. gen village bpx -go- ss. seq bury-Np- fu.1p \\
`We'll take him (=his body) in his village and bury him (there).'

The causative suffix - ow ( sec:3.8.4.3.1 ) can be added to the roots; when following a one-syllable root the suffix is often reduplicated ex:3:x435, but the meaning is still the same as with a single causative suffix.

Purowa ir- ow-( ow)-eya siin-ar-e-k. \\
armband go.up- caus - caus -2/3s. ds tight- inch - pa -3s\\
`She pushed the armband up and it got tight.'

The directional verbs are very frequent as the second root in serial verbs ex:3:x287 ( sec:3.8.5.1.2 ) and as the main verb in verb plus auxiliary constructions ex:3:x288 ( sec:3.8.5.1.1 ). Some of them also enter into adjunct plus verb constructions ex:3:x289 ( sec:3.8.5.2 ).

Wi Amerika ``epa eliwa'' nae- ekap-e-mik. \\
3p. unm America time good say-come- pa -1/3p \\
`The Americans came saying, ``peace''.'

Wi Yaapan saa=iw ir-am-ika-i-mik. \\
3p. unm Japan sand= inst go- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`The Japanese are going along the beach.'

Kemuka pepek er-eya puuk-a-k. \\
string enough go-2/3s. ds cut- pa -3s \\
`When the string was (long) enough she cut it.'

The meaning of the verbs ekap- `come' and ikiw- `go' can be metaphorically extended to time, to signal time spans. The former is used when the time span is extended from the past to the present ex:3:x290, the latter is more common when the time extends from the present to the future ex:3:x437, but it can also refer to the past ex:3:x291.

Naap on-am-ik-e-mik, ekap-ep aakisa. \\
thus do- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p come- ss. seq now\\
`We have been doing like that (all the time) up until now.'

No naap ik-ok iki(w-e)p mokoma enuma iiwawun aakun-i-nan.\\
2s. unm thus be-SS go- ss. seq year new altogether talk-Np- fu.2s\\
`You will be like that (long time) but next year you will talk.'

Buren ife-iki ( w-e ) p aakisa arim-o-n. \\
ceremonial.liquid rub-go- ss. seq now grow- pa -2s \\
`You have kept rubbing the buren liquid on (for years), and now you have grown up.'

On the fringe of directional verbs are kerer- `arrive', yiaw-/ miaw- `walk/move around, wander' and irapar- `move back and forth (aimlessly)', which share some of their grammatical characteristics but not all of them. Of these three verbs, kerer- cannot be prefixed with the bring-prefixes, but it mainly occurs with an unmarked goal instead of a locative phrase ex:3:x292.

Emeria mua manina kerer-e-mik. \\
woman man garden arrive- pa -1/3p \\
`The people arrived in the garden.'

With the other two, a bring-prefix is acceptable ex:3:x293, but they do not take a goal/path argument. If a locative phrase occurs with them it requires a locative clitic ex:3:x436.

Gomi kawus p-irapar-i-ya. \\
east.wind smoke bpx -move.back.and.forth-Np- pr.3s \\
`The east wind moves/blows the smoke around.'

Soora=pa nan yiaw-e-mik. \\
jungle= loc there walk.around- pa -1/3p \\
`They walked around in the jungle.'

Utterance verbs

Utterance verbs may be either intransitive ex:3:x309, ambitransitive ex:3:x310, ex:3:x1927, or transitive ex:3:x311. They may be used to introduce a quote complement, but not to close it. They often occur with one of the `saying' verbs described below ex:3:x310.

Takira niir-emi kirir-i-mik. \\
boy play- ss. sim shout-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`The boys are playing and shouting.'

Wi iperowa=ke aakun-ep ma-e-mik, `` '' \\
3p. unm middle.aged= cf discuss- ss. seq say- pa -1/3p\\
`The middle-aged men discussed (it) / talked and said, `` '' '

Maapora kamenap aakun-i-yan? \\
feast how discuss-Np- fu.1p\\
`How shall we discuss the feast?'

Yena mua far-e-m, ``Sarak oo, '' \\
1s. gen man call- pa -1s Sarak oh \\
`I called to my husband, ``Oh Sarak, '' '

The ` saying verbs' described in this section below include three, or four, verbs that between them divide the semantic area of `tell/say/speak/think' ( tab:3:sayingverbs ). They are frequently used as frame verbs in quote formulas, but they have other functions as well.

The verb maak- `tell' is used in the same two main senses as its English equivalent: telling someone about something ex:3:x312 and telling someone to do something ex:3:x313. In direct quote formulas it is used mainly preceding a quote ex:3:x314, not directly following it as a short closing formula. It is not used in indirect quotes at all.

Ne maak-e-mik, ``Ifa yia keraw-i-ya nain, '' \\
and tell- pa -1/3p snake 1p. acc bite-Np- pr.3s that1\\
`And they told him, ``When a snake bites us, '' '

Moma yia maak-i-mik. \\
taro 1p. acc tell-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`They are telling us (to get them) taro roots.'

Efa maak-ek, ``Opora tep=pa wu-e.'' \\
1s. acc tell- pa -3s talk tape.recorder= loc put- imp.2s\\
`She told me, ``Put the talk on a tape recorder.'' '
summary:
The passage describes Mauwake directional verbs, noting that with locative-marked phrases they usually indicate a source or a location/path, while goal marking with =pa is rare and used only when the goal functions mainly as the site of the next event. These verbs can also take bring-prefixes to mean bringing or taking something somewhere, and can be causativized with -ow, which may be reduplicated after one-syllable roots without changing the meaning.

It also explains that directional verbs commonly appear in serial verb constructions, as main verbs with auxiliaries, and in adjunct-plus-verb constructions, and that their meanings can be extended metaphorically to time spans. Finally, the passage outlines utterance verbs and saying verbs, showing that utterance verbs can introduce quotes but not close them, while saying verbs such as maak- ‘tell’ have specific roles in direct quote formulas and do not occur in indirect quotes.

text:
When maak- closes a direct quote, it requires the manner adverb naap `thus' to precede it ex:3:x315:

``Aaw-ep p-ekap-eka,'' naap yia maak-em-ik-e-mik.\\
get- ss. seq bpx -come- imp.2p thus 1p. acc tell- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
` ``Bring it'', they were telling us like that.'

The default object for maak- is the addressee ex:3:x314 and a possible second object is the speech itself ex:3:x316.
