Wadol opora O yia O maak-i-n. \\
lie talk 1p. acc tell-Np- pr.2s \\
`You are telling us lies.'

The status of the verb naak- is unclear. It is infrequent, and in natural texts only occurs in closing formulas ex:3:x317. It may have developed as an analogy to the verb pair ma-/ na-.

``No bom fain=iw mera kuum-e,'' naak-e-mik. \\
2s. unm bomb this= inst fish burn- imp.2s tell- pa -1/3p \\
` ``Blast fish with this bomb,'' they told him.'

With the verb ma- `say/speak/tell' the addressee is not in focus, and is hardly ever even mentioned. Instead, the verb requires either an object referring to the speech content ex:3:x318 or an adverb naap `thus' ex:3:x319 preceding the verb, or a quote complement following it ex:3:x320.

Yo yena yaaya ifa ku-o-k nain opora ma-i-yem.\\
1s. unm 1s. gen 1s/p.uncle snake bite- pa -3s that1 talk say-Np- pr.1s\\
`I am telling a story about my uncle that was bitten by a snake.'

Momora, no naap me ma-e. \\
Fool 2s. unm thus not say- imp.2s \\
`Fool, don't say like that.'

En-e-mik na ma-e-mik, ``Eliwa, aara oposia saarik.'' \\
eat- pa -1/3p add say- pa -1/3p good hen meat like\\
`They ate it and said, ``It is good, like chicken meat.'' '

Tok Pisin na `and' is increasingly used instead of the vernacular additive connective ne.

Occasionally the verb can occur without any of the above objects ex:3:x321:

Yena oram ma-i-yem. \\
1s. gen just say-Np- pr.1s \\
`I'm just speaking (without any reason ).'

The difference between the verbs maak- and ma- in regard to the semantic role of a person object is shown clearly in ex:3:x322:

Naap yi a ma-i- kuan na-ep yo ariman nefa maak-i-yem.
\\
thus 1p. acc say-Np- fu.3p think- ss. seq 1s. unm openly 2s. acc tell-Np- pr.1s\\
`Thinking that they will say like that about us I'm openly telling you (this).'

The verb na- `say/speak/call/think' is the most interesting of the speech verbs. In quote formulas it is only used for closing the quote, with ex:3:x323 or without another utterance verb ex:3:x942 in an opening formula.

ma-em-ik-e-mik, ``Oo, '' na-em-ik-e-mik. \\
say- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p oh... say- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
`...they kept saying, ``Oh...'', they kept saying (like that).'

Amerika fan ``Epa eliwa'' nae-ekap-e-mik. \\
America here time good say-come- pa -1/3p\\
`The Americans came saying ``peace''.'

In a tail-head type construction ( sec:8.2.3.5 ) it is often used as a generic verb to replace another utterance verb, when normally the first verb would be repeated ex:3:x324. Other types of verbs, when not repeated in a tail-head construction, are replaced with the generic verb on- `do'.

Wia maak-e-mik, ``Yia uf-om-aka.'' Na-iwkin \\
3p. acc tell- pa -1/3p 1p. acc dance- ben - bnfy 2. imp.2p say-2/3p. ds \\
`They told them, ``Dance for us.'' When they said (that) '

When na- replaces another utterance verb in that way, the replaced verb may influence what semantic argument becomes the object. In ex:3:x325 maak- requires the addressee of the verb as the default object, and in the following sentence with na- the same accusative pronoun wia still refers to the addressees, even if with na- it would normally refer to the people spoken about.

Ekap-emi wia maak-e-mik, ``Maa iiw-eka.'' Wia na-iwkin ma-e-mik,...\\
come- ss. sim 3p. acc tell- pa -1/3p food dish.out- imp.2p 3p. acc say-2/3p. ds say- pa -1/3p\\
`They i came and told them j, ``Dish out food.'' They i said to them j like that and they j said, '

The verb na- is also used in a somewhat different sense `call (by some name)'. In ex:3:x326 the speaker tells that the word used by the Japanese soldiers for `coconut' was yasi, a foreign word for her. The verb unuf - is used when the calling by name or giving a name is emphasized.

Iwera ``yasi'' yia na-em-ik-e-mik. \\
coconut yasi 1p. acc say- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`They kept calling coconut (by the name) ``yasi'' to us.'

The ``speaking'' expressed by na- can also be internal speech, i.e., thinking ex:3:x327. This characteristic is quite common to speech verbs in Papuan languages. When the thinking process itself is more in focus, an adjunct plus verb construction kema suuw- `think' (literally: `push the liver') is used.

Maa eliwa=ke na-ep aaw-e-m. \\
thing good= cf say- ss. seq get- pa -1s \\
`I thought it was a good thing and got it.'

Related to the inner speech is another usage typical of verbs for `saying' in Papuan languages: to convey desire, intention or plan ex:3:x328-- ex:3:x1608. For this function only the same subject sequential form naep is used, and the verb that indicates the desired or intended action is in a preceding speech complement clause. This is discussed more fully in the section on complements of utterance verbs ( sec:8.3.2.1 ).

Yo manina urup-i-nen na-ep. \\
1s. unm garden ascend-Np- fu.1s say- ss. seq \\
`I want to go to the garden.'

Irak-u na-ep ikiw-e-mik. \\
fight- imp.1d say- ss. seq go- pa -1/3p\\
`They went to fight.' (Lit: ` ``Let's fight'' they said/thought and went.')

Ununa owowa p-or-owa na-ep maa eno-wa maneka on-i-kuan.\\
slit.gong village bpx -descend- nmz say- ss. seq food eat- nmz big make-Np- fu.3p\\
`When they want to take the slit gong down to the village they make a big feast.'
summary: The passage contrasts several speech verbs in the language: *maak-* typically takes the addressee as its default object and can also take the speech content as a second object, while *ma-* usually focuses on the speech content or a preceding adverb like *naap* rather than on the addressee. The verb *na-* is the most multifunctional: it closes quoted speech, can replace other utterance verbs in tail-head constructions, can mean ‘call’ or represent inner speech/‘think’, and is also used to express desire or intention when followed by a same-subject sequential form.

text:
In this function naep is becoming less like a regular medial verb. It can occur in sentence-final position, without being right-dislocated ex:3:x328. It usually does retain its word stress, but there is a tendency to un-stress and shorten it by dropping the vowel /a/ in speech ex:3:x1830. When the verb in the speech complement clause is in the counterfactual form, all that is sometimes left of na-ep is only the suffix, which is then added as a suffix to the other verb ex:3:x1609.

Ifana wu-am-ika-i-kuan, unuma wia miim-u n - ep.\\
ear put- ss. sim -be-Np- fu.3p name 3p. acc hear-1d. imp say- ss. seq \\
`They i are listening carefully (lit: putting their ear), wanting to hear their j names.'

Yo aakisa nanar nain ma-ek-a-m- -ep. \\
1s. unm now story that1 say- cntf - pa -1s- - ss. seq \\
`Now I would like to tell that story.'

The verb na- quite freely combines with sound words ex:3:x330, and a number of these combinations have been lexicalized ex:3:x331, ex:3:x332. The onomatopoeic word has become part of the verb, and the vowel /a/ has been deleted from the verb in the process.

Oro-mi bulak na-i-ya. \\
drop- ss. sim plop say-Np- pr.3s \\
`When it drops it says ``plop''.'

Siowa baun-i-ya. ( bau na-i-ya) \\
dog bark-Np- pr.3s ( bau say-Np- pr.3s)\\
`The dog barks.'

Ema buun-eya mua erup um-e-mik. ( buu na-eya) \\
mountain erupt-2/3s. ds man two die- pa -1/3p ( buu say-2/3s. ds )\\
`The mountain (=volcano) erupted and two men died.'

In fast speech na- is often reduced to a- when the verb follows a consonant-final word ex:3:x333.

``Uruf-a-mik'' a-e-k. \\
see- pa -1/3p say- pa -3s \\
` ``They saw it,'' he said.'

The medial form na-eya is also used as resultative connective `so, therefore' ex:3:x500 ( sec:3.11.2 ).

Iwera yia na-em-ik-e-mik. Naeya iwera wia uruk-am-ik-om-a-mik. \\
coconut 1p. acc say- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p So coconut 3p. acc drop- ss. sim -be- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p\\
`They kept speaking to us about coconuts /asking us for coconuts. So we kept dropping coconuts for them.'

Impersonal experience verbs

This very small group mainly consists of verbs indicating some kind of pain. They look like transitive verbs, but the syntactic subject is inanimate, usually a body part, and the human experiencer is the object ex:3:x1013, ex:3:x1014 ( tab:3:impersonalexperience ).

Maara efa tiitin-i-ya. \\
forehead 1s. acc hurt-Np- pr.3s\\
`My head hurts.'/ `I have a headache.' (Lit: `It hurts my forehead.')

Uuw-ap uuw-ap oona=ke efa sirir-i-ya. \\
work- ss. seq work- ss. seq bone= cf 1s. acc ache-Np- pr.3s\\
`I have worked and worked, and my bones ache.'

Most of the experience verbs in Mauwake are adjunct plus verb constructions ( sec:3.8.5.2.1 ), a few are ordinary intransitive verbs ( sec:3.8.4.2.1 ).
summary:
The passage describes how the medial verb na- is being reduced and grammaticalized: it can appear sentence-finally, lose stress or the vowel /a/, and in some counterfactual contexts survive only as a suffix attached to another verb. It also combines productively with sound words, producing lexicalized forms and further vowel loss, and in fast speech may reduce to a- after consonant-final words. 

In addition, na-eya is used as a resultative connective meaning “so, therefore.” The passage then briefly introduces a small set of impersonal experience verbs, mainly pain verbs, which behave like transitives with an inanimate body part as subject and the human experiencer as object.

text:
The small group of auxiliary verbs in Mauwake consists of two ordinary verbs that have also grammaticalized as auxiliaries indicating aspect. In this function the lexical meaning of the verbs is somewhat bleached. The auxiliary is the last verb in a verbal group ( sec:3.8.5.1 ).

The paradigms of the auxiliaries are similar to those of main verbs. tab:3:auxiliaries shows the auxiliary verbs.

The auxiliary ik- is very frequent and has several functions. When it is used with a main verb in the same-subject simultaneous form ( ss. sim ), it indicates continuous aspect, which can have either progressive ex:3:x339 or habitual ex:3:x340 meaning. For position-taking verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.2 ) and other semantically punctiliar verbs the habitual interpretation is the only possible one, but for other verbs the context is needed to determine the correct interpretation.

Fikera aw-em- ik-eya uruf-a-k. (progressive) \\
kunai.grass burn- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds see- pa -3s \\
`When the kunai grass was burning she saw it.' (Or: `She saw the kunai grass burning.')

I yabuela aaw-ep wi-em- ik-e-mik. (habitual) \\
1p. unm papaya get- ss. seq give.them- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
`We kept getting papayas and giving them to them.'

When the main verb is in the same-subject sequential form ( ss. seq ), the auxiliary ik- indicates stativity ex:3:x341. With non-punctiliar verbs this form can often be translated into English with a past perfect ex:3:x342.

Pok-ap- ik-emkun epa wiim-o-k. (stative) \\
sit.down- ss. seq -be-1s/p. ds place dawn- pa -3s \\
`As I was sitting it became light.'

Ikiw-ep- ik-eya ona emeria=ke ekap-o-k. (perfect) \\
go- ss. seq -be-2/3s. ds 3s. gen woman= cf come- pa -3s \\
``After he was/had gone his wife came.'

The auxiliary pu- `completive', is obviously derived from wu- `put' `Put' is one of the verbs commonly used in Papuan languages to indicate completion. through assimilation with the final /p/ of the same-subject sequential form in the main verb preceding it ex:3:x343, ex:3:x501. Synchronically, the Mauwake speakers do not recognise the origin of the auxiliary.

Maa en-ep- pu-ap soomar-eka. \\
food eat- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. seq walk- imp.2p \\
`Having finished eating you may go.' (Lit: `Eat the food and go'.)

Nan efa wu-ap- pu-ami o Ulingan ikiw-o-k. \\
there1 1s. acc put- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. sim 3s. unm Ulingan go- pa -3s\\
`He left (lit: put) me there and went to Ulingan.'
summary:
Mauwake has a small set of auxiliary verbs, consisting of two ordinary verbs that have grammaticalized to mark aspect, with their lexical meaning partly bleached and the auxiliary appearing as the last verb in a verbal group. The very frequent auxiliary **ik-** marks continuous aspect with same-subject simultaneous main verbs, stativity with same-subject sequential verbs, and in some contexts can be interpreted as progressive, habitual, or perfect.  

The auxiliary **pu-** means “completive” and is historically derived from **wu-** “put,” a common Papuan source for completive marking, though speakers no longer recognize this origin.

text:
The verbal clusters are described here under verb morphology, because they function as a unit very much like single verbs. There are two kinds of verbal clusters: verbal groups and adjunct plus verb constructions. The definition of a verbal group is from: ``a sequence of words in the primary class of verb'' ex:3:x347.

Ifara mokak-ikiw-em-ik-ok ifara oko uruf-a-k. \\
vine stare-go- ss. sim -be- ss vine other see- pa -3s\\
`He kept looking for a vine and saw one vine.'

Adjunct plus verb combinations calls these ``phrasal verbs''. contain a verb (or a verbal group) plus an element from another word class that is obligatory and contributes to the meaning of the verb ex:3:x348.

Owora efar ikum aaw-iwkin wia maak-e-m. \\
betelnut 1s. dat illicitly get-2/3p. ds 3p. acc tell- pa -1s\\
`They stole my betelnut and I talked to them.'

The status of a verb phrase in Mauwake is somewhat questionable. It is discussed in sec:4.5.
summary: The passage explains that verbal clusters in Mauwake are treated under verb morphology because they function like single verbs. It distinguishes two types: verbal groups, defined as sequences of words in the primary class of verb, and adjunct-plus-verb constructions, or “phrasal verbs,” which combine a verb or verbal group with an obligatory element from another word class that adds to the meaning of the verb. The status of the verb phrase in Mauwake is noted as uncertain and is discussed elsewhere.

text:
A verbal group consists of two or more verbs that function grammatically and semantically as one unit. The semantic unity within the group varies between different types of verbal groups.

The verbal groups containing a main verb plus auxiliary have developed by merging clauses as can still be seen from the verbs involved. But since they synchronically function as a unit very much like an individual verb they are treated on the word level. Features that identify them as one close-knit unit are as follows:

Mauwake has two kinds of verbal groups. The verbs in the first group consist of a main verb and an aspectual auxiliary. The second group consists of serial verbs, where all the verb stems contribute to the semantic, rather than grammatical, meaning of the verb.

Main verb plus auxiliary: aspect

The importance of tense as a verbal category in Mauwake shows in its obligatory morphological marking, but aspect is a relatively important category as well. Aspects are `different ways of viewing the internal temporal constituency of a situation'.

Aspect in Mauwake is expressed periphrastically, through verbal groups that have a main verb and an auxiliary. The main verb, which is in the medial form, largely gives the semantic content to the whole, and the auxiliary adds the grammatical meaning of aspect. In the continuous and stative aspects also the medial form of the main verb contributes to the aspectual meaning. What distinguishes these constructions from medial clauses ( sec:8.2 ) is that the two verbs function as a unit rather than individual verbs, and their phonological stress, intonation and pause pattern is that of a word or phrase rather than a medial clause.

As is typical of sov languages, the auxiliary follows the main verb (; ). The more common of the aspectual auxiliaries is ik - `be', which can combine with two different medial forms. The other aspectual auxiliary is pu - `completive' ( sec:3.8.4.5 ).

The neutral, aspectually unmarked verb form is used in Mauwake whenever the speaker chooses not to pay special attention to the internal structure of the situation. It could be claimed that this is a neutral perfective, since the situation is viewed as a whole, but that term would be confusing, as the neutral forms can also be used in clauses that are aspectually habitual. The majority of the verb forms used in all kinds of texts in Mauwake are aspectually neutral.

The marked completive aspect is only used when completion of an action is stressed. The continuous aspect is used for both progressive and habitual actions, and the stative aspect for a state continuing over some time.

Completive aspect

When the completion of an action is in focus, the completive aspect is used. It is formed by a main verb in the same-subject sequential form, followed by the auxiliary pu- `completive' ex:3:x361 ( sec:3.8.4.5 ).

Ifakim-ep nomokow ekeka=pa sererim-ep-pu-a-k. \\
kill- ss. seq tree branch= loc hang- ss. seq - cmpl - pa -3s \\
`He killed it and hung it on a tree branch.'

The completive aspect verb is often used in a medial same-subject sequential form, which in itself only indicates sequentiality but often implies completion of the first action as well ex:3:x362-- ex:3:x1042.

Sererim-ep-pu-ap owowa or-o-k. \\
hang- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. seq village descend- pa -3s\\
`He hung it up and went/came down to the village.'

Manina n op-ap-pu-ap nomokowa war-i-mik. \\
garden burn- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. seq tree cut-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`We burn (the undergrowth for new) garden and (when it is done we) cut the trees.'

Nomokowa war-ep-pu-ap arew-i-mik. \\
tree cut- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. seq wait-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`We cut the trees and wait.'

But it is not uncommon either to have the completive aspect with a simultaneous action medial form, when the second action coincides with the completion of the first one ex:3:x363-- ex:3:x1043.

Wia maak-ep-pu-ami i ikiw-e-mik. \\
3p. acc tell- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. sim 1p. unm go- pa -1/3p\\
`We told them and went.'

Aria yo nan efa wu-ap-pu-ami o Ulingan ikiw-o-k.\\
alright 1s. unm there 1s. acc put- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. sim 3s. unm Ulingan go- pa -3s\\
`Alright he put me there and he went to Ulingan.'

Maa en-owa wakesim-ep-pu-ami ikiw-o-k. \\
thing eat- nmz cover- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. sim go- pa -3s\\
`Covering the food she left.'

The completive aspect form is also used when momentaneity of the action is emphasized ex:3:x364:

En-ep-pu-ap ikiw-e! \\
eat- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. seq go- imp.2s\\
`Get done with your eating and go!'

The origin of the auxiliary, the verb `put', shows in the fact that it cannot be used with non-controlled actions ex:3:x365. In general, control vs. non-control is not a prominent feature in the verb system in Mauwake, unlike many other Papuan languages (, ).

Waki-ep-pu-a-k \\
fall- ss. seq - cmpl - pa -3s\\

In process descriptions a medial verb, followed by the verb weeser- `finish', which stresses the endpoint of the action, is used more than the completive aspect ex:3:x366. This, however, is a case of clause chaining ( sec:8.2 ), not a verbal group.

Uup-ep weeser-eya wienak-e-m. \\
cook- ss. seq finish-2/3s. ds feed.them- pa -1s\\
`I finished cooking it and fed it to them.' [Lit: `I cooked it and when it (=the cooking) was finished I fed it to them.']

Continuous aspect: progressive and habitual

Continuity, or duration, is the semantic component shared by the aspects called progressive and habitual in many languages: continuation of the same action or of repeated actions of the same kind. The continuous aspect form in Mauwake can have either progressive ex:3:x349, ex:3:x1044 or habitual ex:3:x350, ex:3:x1045 interpretation. The main verb is in the same-subject simultaneous medial form, but with the final /i/ deleted, and the auxiliary ik- `be' is inflected for tense and person/number ex:3:x350.
summary:
Mauwake has verbal groups in which two verbs function as a single grammatical and semantic unit, especially main verb plus auxiliary constructions and serial verbs. In main verb + auxiliary forms, aspect is expressed periphrastically: the main verb supplies most of the meaning while the auxiliary marks aspect, with the neutral form being most common and the marked aspects including completive, continuous, and stative.

The completive aspect is used when completion or momentaneity is emphasized and is formed with a sequential medial verb plus the auxiliary pu- “completive,” while the continuous aspect covers both progressive and habitual meanings and is formed with a simultaneous medial verb plus the auxiliary ik- “be.” The passage also notes that these verbal groups are phonologically and grammatically more like single words than clause chains.

text:
Maa en-em-ik-omkun ama or-o-k. \\
food eat- ss. sim -be-1s/p. ds sun descend- pa -3s \\
`As I was eating the sun went down.'

Fikera aw-em-ik-eya nain umuk-i-nen na-ep urup-o-k.\\
kunai.grass burn- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds that1 extinguish-Np- fu.1s say- ss. seq ascend- pa -3s\\
`The kunai grass was burning, and she went up in order to extinguish it.'

Iwera=ke wia aruf-eya ma-em-ik-e-mik, `` '' \\
coconut= cf 3p. acc hit-2/3s. ds say- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
`When coconuts hit them, they kept saying, ``...'' '

Wi Yaapan naap kuisow=iw ekap-em-ik-e-mik. \\
3p. unm Japan thus one= inst come- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`The Japanese kept coming like that, one by one.'

For punctiliar verbs the habitual interpretation ex:3:x351 is the only one possible, whereas for non-punctiliar ex:3:x1932 verbs both habitual and progressive interpretations are possible.

Koka=pa nan in-em-ik-e-mik. \\
jungle= loc there lie.down- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`We kept sleeping in the jungle'

Owowa oko wiam=iya irak-em-ik-e-mik. \\
village other 3p. acc = com fight- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`We were fighting (or: kept fighting repeatedly) with the other village.'

When the verbal group is in the medial form, the progressive interpretation ex:3:x353 is the more common:

Waaya urup-em-ik-eya mik-a-m. \\
pig ascend- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds spear- pa -1s\\
`As the pig was going/coming up I speared it.'

Often the context provides the only clue as to whether the continuous aspect form should be interpreted as progressive or habitual. The example ex:3:x354 describes a situation where the villagers kept feeding the Japanese soldiers who asked them for food; the sentence ex:3:x355 is from a text describing a coconut plantation fire and its consequences.

Waaya yia na-iwkin waaya wienak-em-ik-e-mik. \\
pig 1p. acc say-2/3p. ds pig feed.them- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`They asked us for pigs and we kept giving them pigs to eat.'

Kawus ir-am-ik-eya kuuf-a-k. \\
smoke rise- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds see- pa -3s\\
`The smoke was rising and she saw it.'

Cross-linguistically the habitual aspect more commonly receives overt marking in the past tense than in the present. In Mauwake the continuous aspect can be used for habitual in any of the three tenses. The example ex:3:x1063 was said about particular work that the speaker was not involved in continuously; he used to do it time to time because of his position as need arose. The example ex:3:x1064 refers to a couple needing to keep visiting an ailing father.

Yo anane maneka naap mauw-am-ika-i-yem. \\
1s. unm always very thus work- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.1s\\
`I always/forever keep working like that.'

O me sariar-i-non-(na) neeke in-em-ika-i-kuan. \\
3s. unm not get.well-Np- fu.3s-( tp ) there. cf sleep- ss. sim -be-Np- fu.3p\\
`If he doesn't get well, they will keep sleeping/staying there.'

For a clause to have habitual interpretation it is not obligatory to use the continuous aspect form in the verb. For instance in process descriptions, which tell how something is habitually done, the unmarked, aspectually neutral present tense form is more common than the continuous aspect. Three of the four verbs in ex:3:x1049 are aspectually unmarked, although all the clauses have habitual interpretation, describing seclusion customs.

Moma ik-owa enim-i-mik. Eka me enim-i-mik, iwer eka me enim-i-mik. Aaya muutiw en-em-ika-i-mik.\\
taro roast- nmz eat-Np- pr.1/3p water not eat-Np- pr.1/3p coconut water not eat-Np- pr.1/3p sugarcane only eat- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`We do not eat roasted taro. We do not drink water or coconut water. We only eat / keep eating sugarcane.'

Stative aspect

The same semantic component of continuity is also shared by the other aspect using the auxiliary ik - `be': this time it is a state rather than activity that continues the same over time. In the stative aspect, the auxiliary is combined with a main verb that is in the same-subject sequential form. This usage is most common with the position-taking verbs like pok- `sit down' ex:3:x356, iimar- `stand up' ex:3:x1046 and in- `lie down/ fall asleep'.

Pok-ap-ik-omkun epa wiim-o-k. \\
sit.down- ss. seq -be-1s/p. ds place dawn- pa -3s \\
`As we were sitting it dawned.'

Yena koor miira=pa iimar-ep-ik-e-m, \\
1s. gen house face= loc stand.up- ss. seq -be- pa -1s\\
`I was standing in front of my house, '

Other punctiliar verbs ex:3:x357, as well as non-punctiliar verbs, can be used in this aspect to indicate the state resulting from an action ex:3:x358, or process ex:3:x1047, but they are less frequent.

Ifakim-eya pu-ep-ik-eya om-em-ik-ua. \\
kill-2/3s. ds die- ss. seq -be-2/3s. ds cry- ss. sim -be- pa.3s\\
`When she killed him and he was dead, she was crying.'

Ikiw-ep-ik-eya ona emeria=ke ekap-o-k. \\
go- ss. seq -be-2/3s. ds 3s. gen woman= cf come- pa -3s\\
`While he was gone his wife came.'

Ewar pun wuun-e-k ne epa reen-ep-ik-ua. \\
west.wind too blow- pa -3s and place dry- ss. seq -be- pa.3s\\
`The west wind blew, too, and the ground was dry.'

In ex:3:x359 the continuous form indicates more active waiting process than is the case in ex:3:x360 with the stative aspect. In ex:3:x359 the people were getting impatient with the vehicle that should already have come to get them. The example ex:3:x360 is from a description of garden work, and part of the work process is the state of patiently waiting for the felled trees and undergrowth to dry.

Arew -am-ik-omkun ama ikur miiw-aasa kerer-ek. \\
wait- ss. sim -be-1s/p. ds sun five land-canoe arrive- pa -3s\\
`As we were waiting the car arrived at five.'

Nomokowa war-ep-pu-ap arew -ap-ika-iwkin reen-eya saama kuum-i-mik.\\
tree cut- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. seq wait- ss. seq -be-2/3p. ds dry-2/3s. ds cleared.bush burn-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`They cut the trees and while they are waiting it dries and then they burn the cleared bush.'

Serial verbs
summary:
The passage explains that Mauwake’s continuous aspect with auxiliary *ik* ‘be’ can express either habitual or progressive meaning, with punctiliar verbs allowing only habitual interpretation and non-punctiliar verbs allowing both. In medial clauses, the progressive reading is more common, and context is often needed to distinguish habitual from progressive; habitual meaning can also be conveyed by unmarked present-tense forms in process descriptions.

It then describes a related stative aspect, formed with *ik* plus a same-subject sequential verb, which expresses a continuing state rather than an ongoing activity. This form is common with posture verbs like ‘sit,’ ‘stand,’ and ‘lie down,’ but can also mark resulting states, processes, or patient waiting.

text:
Verbal groups called serial verbs are very common in Papuan languages. Finding a cross-linguistic definition for serial verbs has proved to be an extremely hard task (, ). Instead of one definition covering all the possible serial verbs, suggests defining these verbs within ``specific typological and linguogenetic groupings'' for comparative purposes.

For a working definition I borrow one given by describing the serial verbs in Siane, another Papuan language:

Typically, even if not obligatorily, one of the verbs in the series is finite and the other(s) more or less ``stripped-down''. In a verb-final language the finite verb is the last one in the series. After describing the serial verb construction in Mauwake, I will discuss the question whether serial verbs are actually compound verbs, and the relationship of the serial verbs to main verb + auxiliary verbal groups and medial clauses.

In Mauwake a non-final verb in a serial construction consists of a bare root without any inflection at all. This restriction is tighter than those given for serial verbs in many other languages (;; ). Each of the verbs in a serial construction contributes to the overall semantic meaning of the predicate. Even if the meaning is not exactly the same as the combination of the same verbs would have in a tight medial verb chain ex:3:x377, it does not get bleached either, like that of the auxiliaries. Since a serial verb construction has only one main stress it is written as one word in the orthography, but the verb stems are separated by hyphens to make reading easier.

Sama=pa oro-boon-ek. \\
ladder= loc descend-get.loose- pa -3s\\
`He fell from the ladder.'

The last verb in a series is either a finite verb with tense and person/number inflection, or a medial verb. The arguments are shared by the whole verbal complex, even if they would originally have been associated with only one of the verbs ex:3:x378. Also negation and obliques ex:3:x379 are shared. All this points to serial verbs being a nuclear-level phenomenon in Mauwake, rather than a core-level one.

Yo Amerika wia akup-ikiw-i-yem. \\
1s. unm America 3p. acc search-go-Np- pr.1s \\
`I am going to look for the Americans. / I go searching the Americans.'

Neeke aw(e)-or-om-ik-eya \\
there. cf burn-descend- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds \\
`As it was burning (towards) down there '

Semantically the verb combinations are of two types. In the more common one a directional or another motion verb follows another verb stem, giving the meaning of movement to the whole ex:3:x378- ex:3:x438, and often the meaning of directionality as well ex:3:x379- ex:3:x381. Cross-linguistically motion and location verbs are very common in serial verbs. This is a productive process, as long as the verbs are semantically compatible.

Wia mokak-urup-o-k, wia mokak-or-o-k. \\
3p. acc stare-ascend- pa -3s 3p. acc stare-descend- pa -3s\\
`He stared them up and down.'

Aasa suuw-or-o-mik. \\
canoe push-descend- pa -1/3p \\
`We pushed the canoe down (towards the sea).' Compare this with a medial construction: Aasa suuw-ap or-o-mik `We pushed the canoe and went down (to sea)'

If the first stem is also a motion verb, it indicates the manner of movement ex:3:x380:

Merena kir-ep segen-ikiw-o-k. \\
foot turn- ss. seq limp-go- pa -3s \\
`He twisted his foot and limped.'

A motion verb in a serial construction can also indicate temporal continuity over a long period of time. In ex:3:x439 the length of time is emphasized even more by the repetition of the motion verb.

Ife-iki(w-e) p iki(w-e) p aakisa arim-o-n. \\
rub-go- ss. seq go- ss. seq now grow- pa -3s\\
`You kept rubbing it (over the years) and now you have grown up.'

In the second type, any two verbs can, in principle, combine into a serial verb. But this process is less productive, and both the type and token frequency of this type is low when compared with the frequency of the first type. Usually, like in ex:3:x382 the meaning of the whole is transparent and can be inferred from the meanings of the component roots, but sometimes the semantics are more opaque ex:3:x383.

Emera kue-puuk-ap okaiwi siowa onak-e-k. \\
sago bite-cut- ss. seq other.side dog feed.him- pa -3s \\
`He bit off half of the sago cake and fed it to the dog.'

Aakun-emi mika-kof-a-m. \\
speak- ss. sim spear-knock- pa -1s \\
`I stumbled in my speech.'

This type of serialization in Mauwake is very close to what calls lexical serialization.

A special case among the roots forming serial verbs is afur- `do well'/`augmentative', which is not used as an independent verb, only as a second element in a serial verb structure ex:3:x384. See for the use of a similar verb, ito, in Siane.

Koora ku-owa amis-ar-afur-a-k. \\
house build- nmz knowledge- inch -do.well- pa -3s \\
`He really knew how to build a house.'

It is quite possible even if not very common to form a three-root serial verb by combining the two types ex:3:x385:

Mika-fien-ikiw-o-k. \\
hit-push.aside-go- pa -3s \\
`He went on countering (an attack).'

It is far more common to have three verbs in a combination where an auxiliary is attached to a serial verb ex:3:x386:

Naap amis-ar-ikiw-em-ik-o-wen. \\
thus knowledge- inch -go- ss. sim -be-Np- fu.2p \\
`That way you will gain more and more knowledge.'

Combining four or more roots into one verbal group is more of a theoretical possibility than a practical reality. Examples are easy enough to obtain through elicitation, but very rare in non-elicited texts.

Mauwake does not use serial verbs for a benefactive like many languages do; it utilizes benefactive morphology for that purpose ( sec:3.8.2.3.3, sec:3.8.3.1 ). Neither is the serial verb structure used for aspect, as a verb plus auxiliary construction takes care of that. Another function often associated with serial verbs is that of instrument marking, but for that Mauwake uses either an ordinary switch-reference construction or an adverbial phrase ( sec:4.6.3 ).
summary:
Serial verbs are very common in Papuan languages, but the passage argues that no single cross-linguistic definition works well, so they should be defined within specific typological and genealogical groupings. In Mauwake, serial verbs consist of one finite or medial verb plus one or more bare verb roots, with shared arguments, negation, and obliques, which shows that they form a nuclear-level verbal complex.

Semantically, Mauwake serial verbs are mainly of two types: a productive motion/direction type in which a motion verb follows another verb, and a less productive lexical type in which two verbs combine more loosely. The language does not use serial verbs for benefactive, aspect, or instrument marking, since those functions are expressed by morphology, auxiliary constructions, switch-reference, or adverbial phrases.

text:
Distinguishing serial verbs from compound verbs on the one hand and medial clauses on the other is not a problem for Mauwake only, as serial verbs can behave very much like either. Crowley suggests the following continuum of gradually loosening syntactic juncture: verbal compounds nuclear serial verbs core serial verbs clause chains subordinate clauses coordinate clauses (ibid. 18). In the following I will briefly discuss the relationship of serial verbs to adjunct plus verb constructions, to verbal groups consisting of a main verb plus auxiliary, and to medial clauses in Mauwake.

The serial verbs in Mauwake show the following characteristics of compounding (cf. regarding Papuan languages). The first verb appears as a mere root (or as a stem, if it has undergone derivation); secondly, the verbs obligatorily share the same arguments; thirdly, the meaning of the whole may differ from the combined meanings of the parts. Furthermore, the stress and intonation contour of a serial verb is that of a single word rather than that of a phrase or a clause. There are two main reasons for calling them serial verbs. The first one is that especially the first type is productive. I also want to link them to a typologically widespread phenomenon instead of looking at them from a strictly language-specific point of view. In this I follow, who maintains that ``the term `compound' does not by definition contradict an analysis as serialization''. A similar position is also strongly defended by and by.

Because of the tight restriction of ``root only'' for the first element in a serial verb in Mauwake, the main verb plus auxiliary combinations are left outside the group by definition. Another reason for this differential treatment is the fact that different processes seem to be going on in the two groups: grammaticalization in the main verb + aux group, lexicalization in the true serial verbs. In some other languages main verb + aux constructions are included among serial verbs (e.g.; ). notes the ``staging'' aspects of the two constructions: in medial verbs the temporal relationship of the two verbs may be specified, but as ``the verbal constituents of svc s [serial verb constructions] do not specify temporal borders or overlapping relationships, the events they represent can blend into a unit and present the svc is a complex but integrated event''.

In Mauwake the clause chaining is structurally midway between serialization and main clause coordination, and may consequently be used instead of either in some cases. The instrumental may in Mauwake be expressed by a `take-instrument-do' structure ex:3:x387 which in many serializing languages is a serial verb construction; but in Mauwake there is no good reason to call the structure anything other than a combination of a medial and final clause. This shows more clearly in example ex:3:x388, which does not pass the rule for verbal groups: ``no non-verbal elements between the parts''.

Fura aaw-ep puuk-a-m. \\
knife take- ss. seq cut- pa -1s \\
`I took a knife and cut it.' Or: `I cut it with a knife.'

Burir aaw-ep nomokowa unowa war-e-mik. \\
axe take- ss. seq tree many fell- pa -1/3p \\
`We took an axe and felled many trees.' Or: `We felled many trees with an axe.'

For Mauwake, I propose the following continuum where the syntactic juncture gradually loosens: serial verb verb + aux group subordinate + main clause clause chain coordinate main clauses.

The borderline between serial verbs and medial verbs on the one hand, and between verb + aux groups and medial verbs on the other is not absolutely clear-cut. In ex:3:x389 the medial verb structure is used instead of a serial verb, even though the two actions are simultaneous, not sequential as indicated by the form of the medial verb. Mauwake does not allow same subject simultaneous forms following each other except in a strictly coordinate structure where the verbs do not so much indicate simultaneity with each other as with the final verb.

Wi Malala=ke muf-ep ekap-emi \\
3p. unm Malala= tp pull- ss. seq come- ss. sim \\
`The Malala people came pulling it and '

Likewise, the four verbs in ex:3:x390 describe one protracted action in spite of the sequential form in the medial verbs:

Ifa nain murar-ep wiok-ap ekap-ep ekap-ep owowa kerer-ek.\\
snake that1 follow- ss. seq follow.them- ss. seq come- ss. seq come- ss. seq village arrive- pa -3s\\
`The snake kept following them and arrived in the village.'

The main verb in verb plus aux combinations has to be in medial form. The only exception found is the continuous aspect form of the verb wiaw- `move around'. The mere root of this verb is used when it is the second verb in a serial structure which then takes an aspectual auxiliary ex:3:x391:

Ifara mufe- wiaw-ik-ok \\
vine pull-move.around-be- ss \\
`As he was pulling the vine around '
summary: The passage argues that Mauwake shows a continuum from tighter to looser syntactic combinations, with serial verbs, verb-plus-auxiliary groups, medial clauses, clause chains, and coordination shading into one another. Mauwake serial verbs have compounding-like properties, but they are treated as serial verbs because they are productive and typologically comparable to serialization; by contrast, main verb + auxiliary constructions are excluded because they involve grammaticalization rather than lexicalization. The text also notes that clause chaining and medial verb forms can sometimes function instead of serial verbs, but the boundaries among these constructions are not always clear-cut.

text:
Papuan languages typically enlarge their verb inventories through adjunct plus verb combinations. Foley only discusses nominal adjuncts, but adverbial adjuncts are commonly used in these structures as well.

Mauwake is not nearly as productive in the use of the adjunct plus verb construction as many other Papuan languages. Some of them use almost exclusively generic verbs (;; ), whereas others employ a larger set of verbs in these constructions. Farr divides the nominals in these constructions into `complements' an `adjuncts'. Korafe does not seem to use adverbial adjuncts in these structures.

Nominal adjunct plus verb

The nominal adjuncts look like object nps, and the origin of at least some of them probably is in object nps, but currently there are syntactic and semantic differences between the two. An object np may be separated from the verb by the negator adverb me or by an accusative or a dative pronoun, but a nominal adjunct must immediately precede the verb ex:3:x450. The meaning of the nominal adjunct plus verb construction often cannot be derived from the meanings of its constituent parts.

Meta yia miim-ap yia miira puuk-ekap-e-mik. \\
fame 1p. acc hear- ss. seq 1p. acc face cut-come- pa -1/3p\\
`They heard about us and came to greet us.'

An object np only occurs with a transitive verb, but a nominal adjunct can also occur with an intransitive verb ex:3:x451:

Uura or-op arua karu-e-mik. \\
night descend- ss. seq torch run- pa -1/3p\\
`At night we went down to sea and fished with a torch.'

Those nominal adjunct plus verb structures where the verb is transitive look like two-object clauses, and in a few cases behave like them syntactically. In ex:3:x452 the nominal adjunct kema `liver' is in its normal adjunct position, but in ex:3:x453 it is in object np position. The basic meanings of the two sentences are the same, but with a different prominence: ex:3:x452 encodes marked negative focus and ex:3:x453 verb focus. The clause ex:3:x1874 with an initial theme pronoun yo `I' is pragmatically more neutral than the others except in cases where the initial pronoun receives extra stress. Note the intervening negator also in ex:3:x1489 below.

Me efa kema suuw-a-k. \\
not 1s. acc liver push- pa -3s\\
`He did not think of me.'

Kema me efa suuw-a-k. \\
liver not 1s. acc push- pa -3s\\
`He didn't think of me.'

Yo me efa kema suuw-a-k. \\
1s. unm not 1s. acc liver push- pa -3s\\
`He didn't think of me.'

In cases where the adjunct only occurs with a certain verb it is difficult to give it a specified meaning apart from the verb ex:3:x454. The same is true for verbs that do not occur independently, only with an adjunct ex:3:x455.

Naruw ir-a-mik. \\? ascend- pa -1/3p\\
`They acted silly.'

Naap kema tuup-am-ika-i-ya. \\
thus liver?- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.3s\\
`He is hoping so.'

Most of the verbs in Mauwake indicating physiological or psychological states and cognition are nominal adjunct plus verb constructions. The verb takes the person marking from the experiencer. tab:3:nominaladjunctplusverbconstruction gives only a small sample of these constructions, where the most common nominal is kema `liver'. A good list of these is in, where she has described a large number of body image concepts formed with kema from semantic point of view. For that study the syntactic characteristics of the structures were not relevant. The second column provides a literal translation. A few more examples of these constructions are in the sentences ex:3:x1490- ex:3:x1489.

Uura uroma ikiw-e-m. \\
night stomach go- pa -1s\\
`Last night I had diarrhea.'

Kema samor-ar-ep maa me enim-i-yem. \\
liver spoil- inch - ss. seq food not eat-Np- pr.1s\\
`I am sad and don't eat.'...oko emina urur - ep soomar-ikiw-i-kuan. \\...other occiput drop- ss. seq walk-go-Np- fu.3p\\
` lest they feel ashamed and walk away.'

Muuka gelemuta akena kema me puk - e - mik. \\
son small very liver not burst- pa -1/3p\\
`Little boys/children do not think well (yet).'

Adverbial adjunct plus verb

Adverbial adjuncts also have to precede the verb without any intervening words ex:3:x456, ex:3:x457.

Maamuma efar ikum aaw-e-mik. \\
money 1s. dat illicitly get- pa -1/3p\\
`They stole money from me.'

Maa me efa pepek er-a-k. \\
food not 1s. acc enough go- pa -3s\\
`The food wasn't enough for me.'

Some of the adverbial adjuncts, like ikum `illicitly' ex:3:x456 and pepek `enough' ex:3:x457, also function as independent adverbs, shown by an intervening pronoun ex:3:x458 and/or negator ex:3:x459.

Yo oram ikum efa wu-a-n. \\
1s. unm for.nothing illicitly 1s. acc put- pa -2s\\
`You accused me for theft without grounds.'

No pepek me ma-e-n. \\
2s. unm enough not say- pa -2s\\
`You didn't say right.'

Other adjuncts like ane `together' ex:3:x460 and anu `apart' ex:3:x461, only combine with verbs to form verbal groups, and it is hard to give them an exact meaning; the glosses below are just approximations.

Apura ane suuw-am-ika-iwkin pok-ap ik-ok om-o-k.\\
widow together push- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds sit.down- ss. seq be-SS cry- pa -3s\\
`They were supporting the widow (sitting against her back) and she sat and wailed.'

Opora anu fien-owa me pepek. \\
talk apart/aside brush.off- nmz not enough \\
`He wasn't able to disregard the talk.'

It was mentioned above that the meanings of the adjunct plus verb combinations are often idiomatic rather than analytically derivable from the meanings of the parts. But this is a somewhat dangerous statement for one to make who comes from outside the speech community. For example, how literally kema `liver', which figures very strongly in the adjunct plus verb constructions, is understood to be really involved in the emotional and cognitive processes would need to be established in a separate study.
summary: Papuan languages commonly expand their verb systems through adjunct-plus-verb combinations, but Mauwake is less productive in this pattern than many others. In Mauwake, nominal and adverbial adjuncts must immediately precede the verb, and the resulting meanings are often idiomatic; nominal adjuncts frequently resemble objects but differ syntactically and semantically, while many expressions of physiological, psychological, and cognitive states use the nominal adjunct kema “liver.”

text:
Adverbs in Mauwake are a heterogeneous class morphologically, syntactically and semantically. definition of adverbs as words functioning ``as modifiers of constituents other than nouns'' is quite usable for Mauwake. Functionally the adverbs can be divided into four groups. The material adverbs Ahlman used the term in classifying adverbs in Finnish, and I find it useful in describing the adverbs in Mauwake as well, since the temporal, locative and manner adverbs share some characteristics which differentiate them from the other adverbs. form the largest group, which contains the subgroups of locative, temporal and manner adverbs. The second group, that of intensity adverbs, In some grammars these form a class of their own, called ``intensifiers''. But that name is somewhat misleading as it may contain words like somewhat or hardly which do not intensify the meaning of the adjacent adjective or adverb. consists of a small group of adverbs that function on phrase level and modify an adjective or adverb. Sentential (or modal) adverbs modify a whole sentence. The last group consists of the two free adverbs pun `also' and muutiw `only'.

A material adverb may function as the head of an adverbial phrase. In this respect, however, adverbs differ from most other word classes: whereas the head of a noun phrase is usually a noun, that of a verb phrase a verb, and an adjective phrase an adjective, an adverbial phrase typically either consists of an adverb only, or does not contain an adverb word at all ( sec:4.6 ).

The position of adverbs within a clause is also discussed under adverbial phrase ( sec:4.6 ).
summary: Mauwake adverbs are a heterogeneous class in morphological, syntactic, and semantic terms, but they can be usefully defined as words that modify constituents other than nouns. Functionally, they are divided into four groups: material adverbs, which include locative, temporal, and manner adverbs and form the largest group; intensity adverbs, which modify adjectives or adverbs at the phrase level; sentential or modal adverbs, which modify an entire sentence; and the two free adverbs *pun* ‘also’ and *muutiw* ‘only’.

text: The material adverbs function as peripherals in a clause. They are divided into locative, temporal, and manner adverbs. The temporal and manner adverbs may be subdivided into deictic and non-deictic adverbs, and the locative adverbs are practically all deictic; in this they differ from the intensity and modal adverbs, which cannot be deictic.
summary: Material adverbs function as clause peripherals and are divided into locative, temporal, and manner adverbs. Temporal and manner adverbs may be either deictic or non-deictic, while locative adverbs are mostly deictic; this contrasts with intensity and modal adverbs, which cannot be deictic.

text:
All the non-controversial locative adverbs are deictic ex:3:x1933, ex:3:x1934, and they were discussed above in section on spatial deictics ( sec:3.6.3 ).

mokoma kuisow naap fan yiam=iya ik-e-mik. \\
year one thus here 1p. refl = com be- pa -1/3p\\
` for about a year they were here with us.'

mua owawiya neeke ik-ok uruf-ap kiiriw ep-i-kuan. \\
man with there. cf be-SS see- ss. seq again come-Np- fu.3p\\
` having been with her husband there and seeing [her father] they will come (back) again.'

The words that are formed with a noun plus the locative clitic - pa are treated as (adverbial) locative phrases, since they are expandable.

The words epasia Epasia has probably developed from epa asia `wild place'. `far (away)' ex:3:x467 and mamaiya `near, close' ex:3:x469, ex:3:x1856 are actually locative nouns, but may be in the process of becoming adverbs. They optionally take the locative clitic - pa, but its presence or absence causes no semantic difference. Tiil `edgewise, close' ex:3:x470 cannot take the locative clitic. Its use is quite restricted, and it might be more accurately classified as a manner adverb.

Epasia ikiw-em-ik-omkun yia far-e-k. \\
far go- ss. sim -be-1s/p. ds 1p. acc call- pa -3s\\
`As we were (still) walking at a distance, he called us.'

Fikera mamaiya=pa nan pok-ap \\
kunai.grass near= loc there sit- ss. seq \\
`Having sat there near the kunai grass '

Mua oko=ke mamaiya pok-a-k. \\
man other= cf near sit- pa -3s\\
`Another man slept with her (lit: sat near).'

Saapipia baliwep me wu-a-m, tiil wu-a-m. \\
trap well not put- pa -1s on.edge put- pa -1s\\
`I didn't put the trap well, I put it right on the edge (of the reef).'

Locative expressions that in some other languages would be expressed through pre- or postpositions or adverbs are formed with locative phrases containing locative relational nouns in Mauwake ex:3:x468.

koor kuenuma =pa \\
house underside= loc \\
`underneath (lit: in/on the underside of) the house'
summary:
The passage explains that the non-controversial locative adverbs in Mauwake are deictic and were already discussed as spatial deictics. It also notes that some forms built from a noun plus the locative clitic **-pa** are treated as expandable locative phrases, while words like **epasia** and **mamaiya** are locative nouns that may be becoming adverbs, and **tiil** is a restricted form that may actually be a manner adverb.

It further states that some locative expressions that other languages would express with prepositions or postpositions are instead formed with locative phrases containing locative relational nouns, such as **koor kuenuma=pa** ‘underneath the house.’

text:
The temporal adverbs can be classified semantically as deictic or non-deictic. The meaning of the former is tied to the time of the utterance, whereas the meaning of the latter is independent of it. Both the deictic and non-deictic temporal adverbs are either specific or non-specific. This grouping is relevant on the syntactic level, as it influences the ordering of multiple temporal adverbials within a clause ( sec:4.6.2 ).

Deictic specific temporal adverbs refer to a certain day in relation to the time of the utterance ex:3:x471, ex:3:x472. The only exception to this in the data is uurika, which in the forms uurik ona (lit: `tomorrow place') and uurika naap nain (lit: `tomorrow thus that') means `the following day' and takes the time of the event as the deictic centre. They are given in tab:3:deicticsepecifictemporaladverbs.

Unan nainiw yiam fiirim-e-mik. \\
Yesterday again 1p. refl gather- pa -1/3p\\
`Yesterday we met again.'

Uurika emeria manina ikiw-ep en-owa nop-ap or-eka.\\
tomorrow woman garden go- ss. seq eat- nmz fetch- ss. seq descend- imp.2p\\
`You women, go to the garden tomorrow and fetch food (and come) down.'

The deictic non-specific temporals ( tab:3:deicticnonspecifictemporals ) refer to a time that is related to the time of the utterance (or in some cases to the time of the event), but is not restricted to a certain day ex:3:x473-- ex:3:x474.

Aria, no aakisa maa enim-e. \\
alright 2s. unm now thing/food eat- imp.2s\\
`Alright, eat now.'

Eewuar, eka me saanar-owa ik-ua. \\
not.yet water not dry- nmz be- pa.3s\\
`Not yet, the water hadn't dried.'

No emeria iiriw sesek-a-mik. \\
2s. unm woman already send- pa -1/3p\\
`We already sent your wife (away).'

Both ikoka and wiimar mean `later', and they can occasionally be used interchangeably. Ikoka is the more common of the two, and has to be used when referring to a later time the same day ex:3:x476. Wiimar always refers to a less specific time somewhere in the future, but the use of ikoka is spreading to cover that too. The sentence ex:3:x477 is from a wedding speech, and it was unlikely that the young couple would be fighting later the very same day.

Wiimar ikiw-i-yan, ikoka weetak. \\
later go-Np- fu.1p later no\\
`We'll go some other time, not later today.'

No ikoka mua ikos irak-ep me efar kerer-e. \\
2s. unm later man with fight- ss. seq not 1s. dat arrive- imp.2s\\
`Later when you fight with your husband, don't come to me.'

Aakisa `now' can be modified to further specify the meaning, as the exact present moment is so short that a word referring to it only is practically useless. Aakisa kuisow (lit: `now one') refers to something that will take place `just now', in a moment ex:3:x478, aakisa fan (lit: `now here') refers to something that has happened just now ex:3:x479 and aakisa fain (lit: `now this') compares the present situation with earlier times ex:3:x480.

Aakisa kuisow on-e, ikoka weetak. \\
now one do- imp.2s later no\\
`Do it right now, not later.'

Muuna kirip-owa ma-e-mik nain aakisa fan kirip-a-mik. \\
debt return- nmz say- pa -1/3p that1 now here return- pa -1/3p\\
`They (only) just now returned the debt they have talked about returning.'

Iiriw miiw-aasa marew, aakisa fain miiw-aasa nepik akena. \\
earlier land-canoe none now this land-canoe crowd real\\
`Earlier there were no cars, now(adays) there are lots of cars.'

The non-deictic specific temporals ex:3:x698, ex:3:x699 refer to a specific time, but their interpretation is not tied to the time of the utterance ( tab:3:nondeicticspecifictemporal ).

Amirika ama kekan-eya uurar-i-mik. \\
day sun strong-2/3. ds rest-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`During the day (or: at noon) when the sun is strong, we take a rest.'

Yaapan=ke uura ifera=pa nan pok-om-ow-a-mik. \\
Japan= cf evening/night sea= loc there sit- ben - caus - pa -1/3p\\
`In the evening the Japanese made him sit in the sea.'

The temporal adverbs in tab:3:nondeicticnonspecifictemp are both non-deictic and non-specific ex:3:x502, ex:3:x504.

Yo anane naap mauw-am-ika-i-yem. \\
I always thus work- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.1p\\
`I always work like that.'

Irak-owa maneka ewur me imen-ar-e-k. \\
fight- nmz big quickly not find- inch - pa -3s\\
`The big fight/war didn't start quickly.'

Nainiw ex:3:x697 and kiiriw ex:3:x1762 both mean `again', and they can be used interchangeably when referring to repeated action.

Ne nainiw sande uura yiam fiirim-e-mik. \\
add again Sunday evening 1p. refl gather- pa -1/3p\\
`And again on Sunday evening we gathered together.'

Ne kiiriw enuma on-am-ik-e-mik. \\
add again new make- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`And again they kept making a new one.'

When some action or event results in a state that is the same or similar as before, even if the action itself is not repeated, only kiiriw can be used. Thus, only kiiriw is possible in ex:3:x503. Kiiriw indicates that Jesus is alive again, as he had been before, whereas nainiw would indicate that he had risen from the dead earlier too.

Yeesus kiiriw iikir-a-k. \\
Jesus again rise- pa -3s\\
`Jesus rose again (= rose from the dead).'

Also, if the action is the same but the situation changes, kiiriw is used. The example ex:3:x1761 describes a situation where a grandmother first sent her younger grandchild, a girl, to listen to a sound. Later she sent the grandson for the same errand; the act of sending was repeated but the person who was sent changed:

Kiiriw morena iperowa nain sesek-a-k. \\
again male older that1 send- pa -3s\\
`Again she sent the elder male (grandchild).'

Occasionally, kiiriw and nainiw can be used together ex:3:x700:

Ar-ep ik-eya aria kiiriw mua nain nainiw urup-o-k.\\
become- ss. seq be-2/3s. ds alright again man that1 again ascend- pa -3s\\
`When she had become like that, alright the man came up again.'
summary:
The passage classifies temporal adverbs as deictic or non-deictic, depending on whether their meaning is tied to the time of utterance, and as specific or non-specific, with this distinction affecting the ordering of temporal adverbials in the clause. It then illustrates several sets of temporal adverbs: deictic specific forms like `yesterday` and `tomorrow`, deictic non-specific forms like `now`, `already`, and `not yet`, and non-deictic forms such as `daytime` or `evening`, which refer to specific times without being anchored to utterance time.

It also distinguishes two words for `later` (`ikoka` and `wiimar`), noting that `ikoka` is more common and can refer to later the same day, while `wiimar` refers more generally to the future. Finally, it contrasts `nainiw` and `kiiriw`, both meaning `again`, showing that

text:
The manner adverbial phrase is often manifested by just an adverb word rather than a longer phrase. The same distinction between deictic and non-deictic adverbs that was made with the other material adverbs can be made with the manner adverbs as well. The description of the deictic manner adverbs ex:3:x1935, ex:3:x1936 is in sec:3.6.4....maa oposia pun naap sesek-a-mik. \\
thing meat also thus sell- pa -1/3p\\
` like that they also sold meat.'

Soo nain feenap: era erup ik-ua. \\
fishtrap that1 like.this way two be- pa.3s\\
`The fishtrap (custom) is like this: there are two ways.'

Most of the non-deictic manner adverbs are non-derived ex:3:x704-- ex:3:x507, but a few have been derived from adjectives by the deletion of word-final < a> ex:3:x506. This process is not productive. tab:3:nondeicticmanneradverbs gives a list of some of the more common non-deictic manner adverbs.

Naap yia ma-i-kuan na-ep yo ariman nefa maak-i-yem.\\
thus 1p. acc say-Np- fu.3p say/think- ss. seq 1s. unm openly 2s. acc tell-Np- pr.1s\\
`I am telling you this openly, thinking that they will say like that about us.'

Opaimika baliwep me wiar amis-ar-e-m. \\
talk well not 3. dat knowledge- inch - pa -1s\\
`I don't/didn't know their language well.'

Fikera ikum kuum-e-mik nain ma-i-yem. \\
kunai.grass illicitly burn- pa -1/3p that1 say-Np- pr.1s\\
`I tell about that when the kunai grass was burned by arson.'

Samor akena aruf-a-mik. \\
badly very hit- pa -1/3p\\
`They beat him very badly.'
summary:
Manner adverbial phrases are often expressed by a single adverb word rather than a fuller phrase, and they can be divided into deictic and non-deictic forms just like other material adverbs. Most non-deictic manner adverbs are underived, though a small number are formed from adjectives by deleting final *-a*, a process that is not productive.

Examples show meanings such as “thus/like this,” “openly,” “well,” “illicitly,” and “badly,” illustrating the range of manner adverbs in the language.

text:
Intensity adverbs are a small and heterogeneous group of adverbs that modify a verb, an adjective, a quantifier or another adverb ex:3:x508, ex:3:x510. Some of them ( akena, maneka) are also adjectives, some others ( lawisiw, iiwawun, wenup) are non-numeral quantifiers ( sec:3.4.2 ) with a second function as intensity adverbs. The distribution is different for each of the intensity adverbs ( tab:3:intensityadverbs ).

Moma fain eliw(a) oram. \\
taro this good just/very \\
`This taro is very good.'

Koora nain maala pepek. \\
house that long enough\\
`That house is long enough.'

Akena `really, truly' is more flexible than the other intensity adverbs in that it can modify a word belonging to almost any word class ex:3:x706-- ex:3:x1875.

Eka mamaiya akena i yoowa me aaw-i-yen \\
river near very 1p. unm hot not get-Np- fu.1p\\
`Very near the river we'll not get hot.'

Iikamin akena=ko imen-ar-i-non? \\
when really= nf find- inch -Np- fu.3s\\
`Exactly when is it going to appear?'

Sira samora piipu-eka akena. \\
habit bad leave- imp.2p really\\
`You (pl) must really leave (your) bad habits.'

Yiena ikos akena iw-u. \\
1p. gen two.together really go- imp.1d\\
`Lets's go just the two of us together.'

Weetak akena, i=ko me kuum-e-mik. \\
no really, 1p. unm = nf not burn- pa -1/3p\\
` Really no, we did not burn it.'

Lawisiw `somewhat' is different from the rest in that it precedes the expression it modifies, rather than following it ex:3:x703.

Uuw-owa nain lawisiw yoowa. \\
work- nmz that1 somewhat hot/hard\\
`That work is somewhat hard.'

As an adjective maneka `big' is very common, but as an intensity adverb `very' it is very restricted in its distribution. Maneka cannot modify a verb, but it can intensify some non-numeral quantifiers like unowa `many' and iiwawun `altogether', as well as the temporal adverb anane `always' ex:3:x509.

Yo anane maneka naap mauw-am-ika-i-yem. \\
I always very thus work- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.1s\\
`I always keep working like that.'
summary: Intensity adverbs form a small, heterogeneous set that can modify verbs, adjectives, quantifiers, or other adverbs, and several of them also belong to other word classes. Their distribution varies by item: *akena* is the most flexible and can modify almost any word class, *lawisiw* precedes the expression it modifies, and *maneka* is common as an adjective but very restricted as an intensity adverb, unable to modify verbs and limited to certain quantifiers and the temporal adverb *anane* “always.”

text:
The two modal adverbs in Mauwake differ from each other not only semantically, but morphologically and syntactically as well. Modality of a predication is discussed in sec:6.1.

Eliw `all right, well' The manner adverb `well' is baliwep ( sec:3.9.1.3 ). is a deontic adverb and expresses permission or desirability: `it is all right/good that '. It can often be translated with the auxiliary `may' in English. It follows the subject, if there is any, but precedes the other clause constituents ex:3:x514. It may also be in the tail position after the clause, either following a clause that already has eliw in it ex:3:x515, or by itself ex:3:x516.

Wie wi eliw wiar op-i-kuan. \\
3s/p.uncle 3p. unm well 3. dat hold-Np- fu.3p\\
`Her uncles may get (lit: hold) them (=clay pots) from her.'

Eliw Kululu ma-e-man, eliw. \\
well Kululu say- pa -2p well\\
`It is all right that you mentioned Kululu, that is OK.'

Nomokowa, nie owowa=pa fan pok-a-n, eliw. \\
2s/p.brother 2s/p.uncle village= loc here sit- pa -2s well\\
`It is good/OK that you settled here in your brother's and uncle's village.'

An epistemic modal adverb is the clitic - yon (with an alternative form - nion), expressing hesitation or non-committal assumption: `perhaps', `maybe', `I suppose'. It is attached to the predicate, which usually is a verb ex:3:x517, ex:3:x518, but can also be non-verbal ex:3:x519. The question word kamenion `or what' is related to the modal adverb - yon ( sec:3.9.3 ).

Maa me wu-om-a-mik= yon. \\
thing/food not put- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p-perhaps\\
`Perhaps they didn't put food (aside) for him.'

Yo me efa ma-e-n= yon aa? \\
1s. unm not 1s. acc say- pa -2s-perhaps aa\\
`I suppose you weren't saying it about me?'

Ni kema puk-owa marewa=ke= yon! \\
2p. unm liver burst- nmz none= cf -perhaps\\
`You must be crazy!' (Lit: `I suppose your liver hasn't burst (yet).')
summary: Mauwake has two modal adverbs that differ semantically, morphologically, and syntactically. **Eliw** is a deontic adverb meaning “all right/good that,” expressing permission or desirability and typically following the subject but preceding other clause constituents, while the epistemic clitic **-yon** (also **-nion**) means “perhaps/maybe/I suppose” and attaches to the predicate, which can be verbal or non-verbal.

text:
The adverbs muut(a )/ muutiw `just/only' and pun `also, too' are called free adverbs, as they can move around quite freely and attach themselves to various elements in a clause. Muutiw is a combination of muut(a) and the limiter clitic - iw, and it restricts the scope of a preceding noun phrase or adverbial phrase ex:3:x747-- ex:3:x807. Muut(a) is used almost exclusively with noun phrases ex:3:x1820, ex:3:x1821.

Aaya muutiw en-em-ika-i-mik. \\
sugarcane only eat- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`They are only eating sugarcane.'

Ofa sepa muutiw (if-o-k). \\
paint black only paint- pa -3s\\
`He painted with only black paint.'

Ewar wuun-i-ya nain muutiw miim-i-nan. \\
wind blow-Np- pr.3s that only hear-Np- fu.2s\\
`You will hear only the wind blowing.'

Lotu koora Ulingan=pa muutiw ik-ua=i? \\
worship house Ulingan= loc only be- pa.3s= qm \\
`Is there a church only at Ulingan?'

Aakisa muutiw niir-i-mik. \\
today only play-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`They play only today.'

Eliw muutiw. \\
well only\\
`It's just all right.'

Yo opora muut naap. \\
1s. unm talk only thus\\
`That's my talk.'

Uf-owa erup muuta naap uf-e-mik. \\
dance- nmz two only thus dance- pa -1/3p\\
`We only danced two dances like that.'

Pun `also' has even wider distribution than muutiw: it can occur following almost any element in a clause ex:3:x749-- ex:3:x808. Pun may be in the process of developing into a clitic. As a one-syllable word it it often has a weak stress, and some speakers also write it attached to the preceding word with a hyphen, the way clitics are written in the Mauwake orthography.

Ne waaya nain pun afila marew, waaya asia pun. \\
and pig that1 also grease no(ne) pig wild also\\
`And that pig also didn't have fat, (as) it was a wild pig too.'

Yos pun wie opora nainiw ma-i-yem. \\
1s. fc too 3s/p.uncle talk again say-Np- pr.1s\\
`I, too, will again give ``uncle-talk'' (=cultural instruction).'

Ne pun aakisa iperowa korokor or-owa sira iiriw wafur-a-mik.\\
and also now middle.aged initiation descend- nmz custom earlier throw- pa -1/3p\\
`Also, now the middle-aged people have already rejected the initiation custom.'

Iiriw pun miiwa muuta nain irak-owa marew. \\
earlier also ground because.of that1 fight- nmz no(ne)\\
`Earlier there were also no fights over ground' (or: `Earlier, too, there were no fights over ground.')

Teeria maneka wadol opora mik-a-mik pun naap, \\
group big lie talk hit- pa -1/3p also thus\\
`(When) the big group lied it was also like that, '
summary:
The adverbs *muut(a)/muutiw* ‘just/only’ and *pun* ‘also, too’ are described as free adverbs because they can move relatively freely and attach to different clause elements. *Muutiw* combines *muut(a)* with the limiter clitic *-iw* and restricts the scope of a preceding noun phrase or adverbial phrase, while *muut(a)* occurs almost exclusively with noun phrases.  

*Pun* has an even wider distribution than *muutiw*, appearing after almost any element in a clause, and it may be developing into a clitic, as shown by its weak stress and occasional hyphenated writing in the orthography.

text:
Mauwake has four negators: weetak, wia, me and marew. They are morphologically free and syntactically heterogeneous, each one having its specific position. Of the four negators me is positioned before the negated element ex:3:x654, ex:3:x1112, while marew follows the negated element ex:3:x655. Weetak and wia either form a complete utterance by themselves, or they are sentence-initial when used as negative interjections ex:3:x707 but clause-final when functioning as non-verbal predicates ex:3:x1212, and when replacing full clauses they take the position of the clause they replace ex:3:x705, ex:3:x1111.

Maamuma me tuun-owa ik-e-mik. \\
money not count- nmz be- pa -1/3p\\
`They haven't counted the money (yet).'

Mukuna me op-a, nefa kuum-i-non! \\
fire not touch- imp.2s 2s. acc burn-Np- fu.3s\\
`Don't touch the fire, it will burn you!'

I muuka marew. \\
1p. unm son no(ne).\\
`We have no son.'

Wia, me kookal-i-yem. \\
No not like-Np- pr.1s \\
`No, I don't like it.'

Yo uuw-owa oko weetak. \\
1s. unm work- nmz other no\\
`I have no other work.'

Wafur-a-k na weetak, ufer-a-k. \\
throw- pa -3s but no, miss- pa -3s\\
`He threw it (a spear), but no (=he didn't succeed), he missed (the pig).'

Akup-a-mik, akup-a-mik, wia. \\
search- pa -1/3p search- pa -1/3p no\\
`We searched and searched, but no (=we did not find it).'

According to a rough generalization, the most frequent negator me is basically a clause and constituent negator. It is also used to negate imperatives. Weetak and wia are negative interjections or predicates in verbless clauses, and marew can negate non-verbal predicates and occasionally noun phrase constituents. Marew often has the meaning `none at all' ex:3:x652.

Weetak ex:3:x1875, wia and occasionally marew ex:3:x652, may be intensified by a postposed intensity adverb akena `truly, very'. Me can only be intensified as a verbal negator, in which case akena comes after the verb rather than after the negator ex:3:x653.

Ni niam erup kema marew akena! \\
2p. unm 2p. refl two liver no(ne) really\\
`The two of you have really no sense at all!'

Me on-a-m akena. \\
not do- pa -1s really\\
`I really didn't do it.'

A fuller treatment of the negators is in sec:6.2, where negation as a functional category is discussed. gives a somewhat more comprehensive treatment of negation in Mauwake, but some of the analysis has changed since the writing of the article.
summary:
Mauwake has four morphologically free negators—me, marew, weetak, and wia—that differ in syntactic position and function. Me is the most common and serves mainly as a clause and constituent negator, including imperatives; marew follows the negated element and is used for non-verbal predicates and sometimes noun phrases, often with the sense ‘none at all’; and weetak and wia can stand alone, occur sentence-initial as negative interjections, or appear clause-final as predicates or replacements for full clauses.

These negators can sometimes be intensified by the postposed adverb akena ‘truly, very’. With me, however, intensification is only possible when it functions as a verbal negator, in which case akena follows the verb rather than the negator.

text:
The inventory of connectives in Mauwake is small. They are called connectives rather than conjunctions, because conjunctions are normally understood as a class of words, but in Mauwake a connective may be a word or a phrase. The term conjunction is reserved for the conjunctive coordination construction ( sec:8.1.1 ). Many of the connectives also have another primary function.

The main division is into pragmatic and semantic connectives; all of them are coordinate. Subordination is discussed in sec:8.3. The connectives mostly operate on sentence level, joining clauses ( sec:8.1 ). Almost all of the coordinators also conjoin sentences. Only the pragmatic connectives and the disjunctive connective e `or' are able to conjoin elements on the word and phrase levels as well.

The most typical way of combining clauses is clause chaining through medial verbs, with no connective words at all ( sec:8.2 ). When there are connectives, they are always placed between the two clauses.
summary: Mauwake has a small set of connectives, a term used because these forms may be words or phrases rather than a single word class; “conjunction” is reserved for the conjunctive coordination construction, and many connectives also have another main function. They are divided into pragmatic and semantic connectives, all coordinate, and they mainly join clauses at the sentence level, though pragmatic connectives and the disjunctive *e* ‘or’ can also join words or phrases. The most common way to combine clauses is clause chaining with medial verbs and no connective, and when connectives are used, they occur between the two clauses.

text:
Instead of clearly specifying the semantic relationship between the units they connect, like semantic connectives do, the pragmatic connectives signal a pragmatic relationship between them. For this distinction on pragmatic and semantic connectives I am indebted to Stephen Levinsohn. In terms they are `medial [and] prepositive', meaning that they occur between the items they conjoin, and are linked more closely to the following constituent rather than the preceding one.

The connective ne `additive' only indicates that something is added to what has just been said. It can connect word and phrase level units ( sec:4.1.2 ), but is mostly used between clauses ( sec:8.1 ) and even sentences. It is semantically neutral. When it conjoins words ex:3:x711 or phrases ex:3:x1359, and often when it coordinates clauses ex:3:x713 or sentences ex:3:x714, it can be translated into English with `and'.

kumin, wutkekela ne mera... \\
hermit.crab calamari add fish\\
`hermit crabs, calamari and fish '

Inawera sira unowa, ne kemena unowa. \\
dream custom many add inside many\\
`There are many kinds of dreams, and (they have) many meanings.'

Ne yo aakisa tep=pa ma-i-yem. \\
add 1s. unm now tape.recorder= loc say-Np- pr.1s\\
`And now I say it to a tape recorder.'

Words or phrases in lists are most commonly joined by juxtaposition only. If a connective is used, ne usually joins the last two ex:3:x1359 coordinands. It is also possible to place the connective(s) closer to the beginning of the list.

Sesa nain waaya erup arow ne maamuma kuuma erepam ikur ne manar kuisow, waa eneka, naap muuka sesenar-i-nen.\\
price that1 pig two three add money stick four five add forehead.ornament one pig tooth thus son buy-Np- fu.1s\\
`(As for) the price, I will buy my son with two-three pigs and forty-fifty kina and a forehead ornament (and) pig's tusk(s), like that.'

There is no emphatic coordinate connective of the type `both and' in Mauwake.

If the propositions connected by ne contrast with each other in some way, it may be interpreted as adversative and translated into English with `but' ex:3:x715, ex:3:x716. Many Papuan languages have a connective that is glossed `and/but'. I suggest it is an additive connective like ne, interpreted as either `and' or `but' according to the content of the clauses conjoined. In these cases it is always a ``weak'' adversative in contrast to the demonstrative nain used in ``strong'' adversative clauses ( sec:8.1.3 ).

Maa en-owa iw-e-mik, ne rais weetak. \\
thing eat- nmz give.him- pa -1/3p add rice no\\
`They gave him food, but not rice.'

Wi me kuum-e-mik, ne wi murar-owa=pa mukuna nain kerer-e-k. \\
3p. unm not burn- pa -1/3p add 3p. unm follow- nmz = loc fire that appear- pa -3s\\
`They didn't burn it, but the fire started after them.'

In a number of cases either neutral additive or contrastive interpretation is possible ex:3:x1361:

Wiam erup irak-ep puk-e-mik, aalbok=ke ifera or-o-k ne osaiwa=ke soor(a) asia ikiw-o-k.\\
3p. refl two fight- ss. seq disperse- pa -1/3p black.cuckoo-shrike= cf sea descend- pa -3s add bird.of.paradise= cf forest wild go- pa -3s\\
`The two of them fought and went their separate ways, the black cuckoo-shrike went down to the coast and/but the bird of paradise went to the wild (rain)forest.'

There are two discourse-marking pragmatic connectives, aria and ne aria. They both mark discontinuity in the text.

Aria `alright' The translation reflects the Tok Pisin word orait, which sometimes has a similar discourse function. Aria occurs in many Madang languages, and the speakers of those languages tend to use aria in Tok Pisin too. usually comes sentence-initially, but can also or occur sentence-medially. Its main function is to indicate a break in the topic chain. In ex:3:x717 the topic changes from the snake to the man, and in ex:3:x718 from a health extension officer to a group of men:

Keraw-eya aria nomokowa gelemuta puuk-ap ifa nain ifakim-o-k.\\
bite-2/3s. ds alright tree small cut- ss. seq snake that kill- pa -3s\\
`It (=the snake) bit him, and he cut a small tree and killed the snake.'

miim-o-k. Aria wi kiiriw neeke \\
3s. unm precede- pa -3s. Alright 3p. unm again there. cf...\\
` he went ahead. (When) they were there again '

It often signals the beginning of a turn in a conversation ex:3:x721, or beginning of a speech ex:3:x720, again indicating a break with the preceding text.

Aria wiipa, i yia uruf-e. \\
alright daughter, 1p. unm 1p. acc see- imp.2s\\
`Daughter, look at us.'

Aria, i owowa=ko urup-u. \\
alright, 1p. unm village= nf ascend- imp.1d\\
`Alright, let's go back to the village.'

Even if the topic stays the same, aria can be used, especially when there is a contrast between alternatives ex:3:x719, or sometimes when an expected sequence of events is broken ex:3:x722.

Mua maneka maamuma erup, aria wi suule takira maamuma kuisow, naap omopora sesenar-e-mik.\\
man big money two alright 3p. unm school child money one thus door buy- pa -1/3p\\
`The grown men paid two coins (=20 toea) for entrance, the schoolchildren one coin.'

Wiawi onak urera maa uup-e-mik, aria maa me wu-om-a-mik=yon.\\
3s/p.father 3s/p.mother evening food cook- pa -1/3p alright food not put- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p-perhaps\\
`In the evening his parents cooked food, (but) perhaps they didn't put any food for him.'

Ne aria `and alright' occurs less often than aria, and only sentence-initially ex:3:x723. It marks major points of development in the plot of a story. Sometimes it also signals return to foreground text (i.e. main story line) after some backgrounded material.

Naap wia maak-e-mik. Ne aria, ifa nain murar-ep \\
thus 3p. acc tell- pa -1/3p add alright snake that follow- ss. seq \\
`They told them like that. Now, the snake followed them and '
summary: The passage distinguishes pragmatic connectives from semantic ones: pragmatic connectives do not specify a clear semantic relation, but instead mark discourse relations, and they are medial and prepositive, linking more closely to the following constituent. In Mauwake, **ne** is a semantically neutral additive connective that usually means “and,” but it can also be interpreted as “but” when the clauses contrast, while **aria** and **ne aria** are discourse markers that signal discontinuity, topic breaks, turn beginnings, or major developments in a narrative.

text:
The semantic connectives specify the relationship between two propositions. The disjunctive connective e `or' can connect not only propositions but words or phrases as well. It is used both for standard ex:3:x724 and interrogative ex:3:x725 disjunction This terminology is from. (§§ sec:8.1.2, sec:7.2.2 ). When there are two alternatives, the connective occurs between them. It is also common to have the question marker - i cliticized to the end of the first alternative, especially in questions, but also elsewhere.

ama arow naap, e erepam naap, \\
sun three thus or four thus \\
`at about three o'clock, or at about four '

Emeria=ko efar uruf-a-man= i e weetak? \\
woman= nf 1s. dat see- pa -2p= qm or no\\
`Did you see my wife or not?'

When there are more alternatives than one and the question clitic is present, the connective may be left out altogether ex:3:x726, or it may occur between the first two alternatives ex:3:x727.

maa oposia=i moma, emera, naap \\
thing meat= qm taro, sago, thus\\
