`meat, or taro, or sago, (things) like that'

iwer eka=ki e mauwa=ki, a episowa=ki, ufia=ki \\
coconut water= cf. qm or what= cf. qm ah tobacco= cf. qm, betel.pepper= cf. qm \\
`coconut juice or - ummm - tobacco, or betel pepper '

The following consecutive connectives marking effect or result It is typical for Papuan languages to mark the effect/result clause rather than the cause/reason clause. For a Papuan language which has several connectives both for result and for reason, see. are used in sentences where the clauses have a consecutive, i.e. a cause-effect or reason-result relationship: naapeya/naeya, neemi, and naap nain. They can all be glossed with `therefore, (and) so'.

Naapeya/naeya is the most generic and frequently used of the four. Naapeya has developed from the manner adverb naap `thus' followed by the different-subject marker - eya ( sec:3.8.3.5.2 ); Actually this connective in the coastal villages is naapera, but because of the language committee's decision to use - eya for the 2/3s. ds marker, this form is used here too. the resulting meaning is `it being thus'. The origin of naeya is in the medial different-subject form of the verb na- `say, think'. The difference between the two is mainly dialectal, or areal: naapeya ex:3:x731, ex:3:x732 is used more on the coast, naeya ex:3:x735, ex:3:x1413 in the inland. They are used for marking the effect or result clause in a consecutive sentence.

I maamuma marew, naapeya ifera=ko me sesenar-e-mik. \\
1p. unm money no(ne), so salt= nf not buy- pa -1/3p\\
`We didn't have money, so we didn't buy salt.'

Ben uuw-owa piipu-a-k. Naapeya emina urur-ep me ekap-o-k.\\
Ben work- nmz left- pa -3s therefore occiput fall- ss. seq not come- pa -3s\\
`Ben has left the work. Therefore he was ashamed to come.'

Pika oona me kekan-ow-a-k. Naeya uura ewar=ke teek-a-k.\\
wall bone not strong- caus - pa -3s therefore night wind= cf tear- pa -3s\\
`He didn't strengthen the wall studs. So at night the wind tore it (the house) down.'

I miiw-aasa=pa ekap-e-mik, naeya o me yook-a-k.\\
1p. unm land-canoe= loc come- pa -1/3p therefore 3s. unm not follow.us- pa -3s\\
`We came in a car, so he didn't follow/come with us.'

The origin of naeya is so transparent that there are many cases where two different interpretations for naeya are acceptable ex:3:x734.

``Yo koka=pa ik-e-m.'' Na-eya Magerka=ke (ma-e-k) \\
1s. unm jungle= loc be- pa -1s say-2/3s. ds MacArthur (say- pa -3s)\\
` ``I was in the jungle.'' He said that, and (or: So) MacArthur said, '

But in ex:3:x733 naeya clearly means `therefore' and cannot be interpreted as a medial verb, as the correct verb form in this case would be plural naiwkin `they said and ', not singular naeya `you/(s)he said and '.

Iwera yia na-em-ik-e-mik. Naeya iwera wia uruk-am-ik-om-a-mik.\\
coconut 1s. acc say- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p So coconut 3p. acc drop- ss. sim -be- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p\\
`They kept asking us for coconuts. So we kept dropping coconuts for them.'

The originally dialectal difference may be developing into a semantic one. In the original text data from three decades ago there is no clear semantic distinction between the use of naapeya and naeya, but fairly recently when a group with members from different dialects, discussing language matters, produced consecutive clauses, nearly all of the sentences with naapeya were cases of cause-effect ex:3:x1414, and all of the sentences with naeya were cases of reason and result ex:3:x1415.

I fiirim-owa=pa ik-emkun ama or-o-k, naapeya epa kokom-ar-e-k.\\
1p. unm gather- nmz = loc be-1s/p. ds sun descend- pa -3s therefore place dark- inch - pa -3s\\
`When we were in the meeting the sun went down, so it became dark.'

I fiirim-owa=pa ik-emkun ama or-o-k, naeya maa me wiar en-owa ikiw-o-k.\\
1p. unm gather- nmz = loc be-1s/p. ds sun descend- pa -3s therefore food not 3. dat eat- nmz go- pa -3s\\
`When we were in the meeting the sun went down, so he went without eating the food.'

Naapeya can also co-occur with the conjunctive coordinators ne or aria. In argumentation, ne naapeya or aria naapeya has to be used, when the reason is not confined to one clause but extends to a longer stretch of the discourse ex:3:x1406.

Aria naapeya niena soomar-owa ne aakun-owa pun sira yi-e-k nain kaken=iw ook-ap soomar-eka.\\
alright therefore 2p. gen walk- nmz add talk- nmz also custom give.us- pa -3s that1 straight= lim follow- ss. seq walk- imp.2p\\
`So therefore, as concerns your walk and talk too, follow straight the behaviour that he gave us and walk that way.'

Neemi is used only in reasoning. It requires some point of similarity between the antecedent and the result clause ex:3:x736.

Teeria fain K10 wu-a-mik. Neemi wi teeria nain pun K10 wu-a-mik.\\
group this K10 put- pa -1/3p therefore 3p. unm group that1 too K10 put- pa -1/3p\\
`This group put down K10. Therefore that group put down K10, too.'
summary:
The passage describes the disjunctive connective **e** ‘or,’ which can join not only propositions but also words or phrases, and may appear with the question clitic **-i** especially in questions. With more than two alternatives, the connective may be omitted or used only between the first two items.

It then discusses consecutive connectives that mark effect or result clauses, especially **naapeya/naeya**, which both mean roughly ‘therefore/so’ and differ mainly by dialect, though a semantic distinction may be developing. Finally, it notes that **neemi** is used only in reasoning and requires a point of similarity between the antecedent and the result clause.

text:
Naap nain can be translated into English with `therefore', `in that case', `if so, then'. It is made up of the manner adverb naap `thus' and the distal demonstrative nain `that'. It is a strong connective, stressing the fact that the proposition following the connective is a logical conclusion from the preceding proposition ex:3:x737.

Ni moma uup-i-man=i? Naap nain yo saa uup-i-nen.\\
2p. unm taro cook-Np-2p= qm thus that 1s. unm rice cook-Np- fu.1s\\
`Are you cooking taro? In that case I'll cook rice.'

It is much less common in Mauwake to mark the reason clause than the result clause with a connective. When the reason clause is emphasized, it is marked with the connective moram ( wia) `because' and always follows the result clause rather than preceding it. The origin of the reason connective is in the question word moram `why?' and the negator wia `no(t)'. Moram as a reason connective is probably a calque on Tok Pisin bilong wanem `why, because'. The negator, which does not influence the meaning of the connective, may have been added in Mauwake to help distinguish the connective from the question word. The difference between moram wia and moram is that the former is mainly used across sentence boundary ex:3:x738, and the latter within a sentence ex:3:x739.

Maamuma senam aaw-e-mik. Moram wia, maa ele-eliwa sesek-a-mik. \\
money a.lot get- pa -1/3p why not thing rdp -good sell- pa -1/3\\
`They got a lot of money. (That's) because they sold good things/foods.'

Miiw-aasa muf-owa me ikiw-e-mik, moram os=ke naap ar-eya.\\
land-canoe pull- nmz not go- pa -1/3p why 3s. fc = cf thus become-2/3s. ds \\
`We didn't go to fetch a truck, because she had become like that (=died).'
summary: Naap nain is a strong connective meaning ‘therefore/in that case/if so,’ formed from *naap* ‘thus’ and the distal demonstrative *nain* ‘that,’ and it marks the following proposition as a logical conclusion from the previous one. Reason clauses are less commonly marked than result clauses; when emphasized, they follow the result clause and are introduced by *moram (wia)* ‘because,’ a form probably calqued on Tok Pisin *bilong wanem*, with *wia* apparently added to distinguish it from the question word *moram* ‘why?’.

text:
Since Mauwake is an sov language, it is natural that it has postpositions rather than prepositions. But their number is small: besides the comitative postpositions there are only two others, one for comparison and one indicating reason.

Unlike the postpositions, which are both phonological and grammatical words, clitics are grammatical words that together with the preceding word form one phonological word. The stress assignment rule does not affect them: they are always unstressed. If there are any derivational and inflectional suffixes in the host word, the clitics are added after all of them.

The nominal clitics associate with noun phrases and attach themselves phonologically to the last element of the noun phrase. They mark either the case role or the pragmatic function of the np. The only sentential clitic is the question marker - i. The modal clitic - yon `perhaps' was discussed above in sec:3.9.3.

The postpositions and clitics are discussed together because of their shared origin in some cases, causing similarity in form, and because some of them have similarities in function.
summary: Mauwake, as an SOV language, uses postpositions rather than prepositions, but it has only a small set: in addition to comitative forms, there are just two others, one for comparison and one for reason. The language also has clitics, which are grammatical words that attach to the end of a phonological host after any suffixes, remain unstressed, and can mark case or pragmatic function on noun phrases; the only sentential clitic is the question marker **-i**, while **-yon** means “perhaps.” The passage notes that postpositions and clitics are discussed together because some share a common origin and show similar forms or functions.

text:
Accompaniment, or a comitative relationship may be expressed by one clitic or by five different postpositions, three of which are formed with the clitic.

The comitative clitic is - iya `with, and, both and'. The clitic may be attached to either of the two related noun phrases ex:3:x775, ex:3:x776, or to both ex:3:x777.

Nan pok-ap-ik-e-mik, mua=iya emeria. \\
there sit- ss. seq -be- pa -1/3p man= com woman.\\
`They were sitting there, (both) husband and wife.'

Muuka wiip=iya kerer-e-mik. \\
son daughter= com appear- pa -1/3p\\
`(Both) a son and a daughter appeared.'

Bom=iya kateres=iya, bom=iya kateres=iya (fuurk-a-mik). \\
bomb= com cartridge= com bomb= com cartridge= com drop- pa -1/3p\\
`They dropped (both) bombs and cartridges, (both) bombs and cartridges.'

It combines with pronouns to form comitative pronouns ( sec:3.5.9 ), and the word for `all', unowiya, is made up of unowa `many' plus the comitative clitic.

Occasionally the clitic can also be used to indicate instrument ex:3:x778.

Mauwa ar-e-n, amia=iya nenar-e-mik=i? \\
what become- pa -2s bow= com shoot.you- pa -1/3p= qm \\
`What happened to you, did they shoot you with a gun?'

Owawiya /owawik `with, together with' is used only for humans; it can refer to two or more people ex:3:x821. It can also occur by itself ex:3:x822. The origin of the first part owaw- is unknown. The second part is either the comitative clitic - iya or the root of the existential verb ik - `be', a reflection of an earlier construction owawiya ik - `be together' ex:3:x1817.

Yoli onak owawiya efa amukar-e-mik. \\
Yoli 3s/p.mother with 1s. acc scold- pa -1/3p\\
`Yoli and his mother scolded me.'

Owawiya feeke pok-ap ik-ok soomar-ek-eka. \\
with here. cf sit- ss. seq be-SS walk-go- imp.2p\\
`(First) sit here with us and (then) go.'

Iikir-ami onak owawik soomar-e-mik. \\
get.up- ss. sim 3s/p.mother with walk- pa -1/3p\\
`He got up and walked with his mother.'

The postposition onaiya/onaria /onaiyik may be based on the third person singular genitive pronoun ona and the clitic - iya; onaiyik also includes the root of the verb ik - `be'. This postposition is more generic and can be used with noun phrases referring to people ex:3:x754 but is also common when referring to things ex:3:x755. When the relationship between the two noun phrases is unequal, onaiya may used, like in ex:3:x823, where the other people carried the sick man. The subject marking on the verb is influenced by how active part the referents of the comitative noun phrase take in the action. When all the participants are active, the subject marking on the verb is plural. The speech in ex:3:x1819 was directed towards the villagers who were instructed to stay away from the Japanese troops.

Mua unowa onaiya ikiw-e-mik. \\
man many with go- pa -1/3p\\
`We went with many people.'

Urom(a) onaiya ik-ua. \\
stomach with be- pa.3s\\
`She is/was pregnant.'

Mua napuma onaiya Medebur ek-a-mik. \\
man sick with Medebur go- pa -1/3p\\
`They went to Medebur with the sick man.'

No ara sepa ara kia onaiyik bilik ar-i-nan=na \\
2s. unm trunk black trunk white together mixed become-Np- fu.2s= tp \\
`If you, a black person, are together with the white people mixed with them '

Another comitative postposition that mainly refers to things is feekiya `with' ex:3:x824-- ex:3:x1818. It originates from the combination of feeke `here' and - iya `comitative', but the meaning does not reflect the deictic origin of the initial part. In those rare cases when it is attached to a [+human] noun phrase, the referent of this np is subordinate to the referent of the other np and not in control, but still influencing the subject marking of the verb ex:3:x825.

Mokok urupa kaik-i-man nain feekiya baurar-eka. \\
eye cup tie-Np- pr.2p that1 with flee- imp.2p\\
`Flee with your ``eye cups'' (a singsing decoration) still on.'

Wiamun gelemuta pun aaw-ep feekiya ikiw-e-mik. \\
3s/p.brother small also take- ss. seq with go- pa -1/3p\\
`He took his little brother too, and went with him.'

Maa eliw akena nain aaw-ep feekiya ikiw-o-k. \\
thing good very that1 take- ss. seq with go- pa -3s\\
`He took the very good thing and went with it.'

The dual comitative ikos `with, together (with)' can only be used when two human participants are referred to ex:3:x752. It can also occur alone, without a preceding noun phrase, when the participants are known from the person/number suffix in the verb, or from the context ex:3:x753. The parties are considered equally active, so the verb is always in the plural.

Wekera ikos irak-e-mik. \\
3s/p.sister with fight- pa -1/3p\\
`He fought with his sister.'

Ikos ikiw-i-yen. \\
with go-Np- fu.1p\\
`Let's go together (just the two of us).'

Associative ame `with others' is different from the comitative postpositions above in that only one of the parties is specified. The identity of `the others' is left unspecified ex:3:x826, ex:3:x827.

Auwa ame wia maak-eya res aaw-ep merena puuk-a-mik.\\
1s/p.father assoc 3p. acc tell-2/3s. ds razor take- ss. seq leg cut- pa -1/3p\\
`He told my father and the others, and they took a razor and made a cut on his leg.'

Kuuten ame=ke miim-e-mik. \\
Kuuten assoc = cf precede- pa -1/3p\\
`Kuuten with (some) others went ahead of them.'

Reason postposition muuta (nain)

Muuta (nain) `because of, for' gives a reason for an action, when the reason is expressed in a noun phrase rather than a full clause. It has developed from the adverb muuta `a little, only', and in some cases the meaning `only' is retained with the new function as well ex:3:x756, ex:3:x1876. The distal-1 demonstrative nain `that' is optional, and is left out especially when there is another demonstrative nain preceding muuta ex:3:x759.

Iiriw miiwa muuta nain irak-owa marew, oram momor mauw-am-ik-e-mik.\\
earlier land for that1 fight- nmz no(ne) just indiscriminately work- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`Earlier there was no fighting for land, they just worked indiscriminately (on any land).'
summary:
The passage describes several ways to express comitative relations, including the clitic **-iya** and postpositions such as **owawiya/owawik**, **onaiya/onaria/onaiyik**, **feekiya**, and **ikos**. These forms differ in what kinds of noun phrases they can accompany, whether they are mainly used with humans or things, and whether the participants are treated as equally active; some also affect verb agreement, with plural marking used when all participants are active.

It also notes the associative form **ame** ‘with others,’ where only one participant is specified and the others remain implicit. Finally, **muuta (nain)** is presented as a reason postposition meaning ‘because of, for,’ used when the cause is expressed by a noun phrase rather than a clause.

text:
Yia amukar-owa muuta nain nan iiriw ifakim-e-mik. \\
1p. acc scold- nmz for that1 there earlier kill- pa -1/3p\\
`We killed her earlier (only) because she scolded us (lit: for her scolding of us).'

Opora ara nain muuta ifakim-u na-ep on-a-mik. \\
Talk section that1 for kill- imp.1d say- ss. seq do- pa -1/3p\\
`(Only) because of that talk they tried to kill him.'

Comparison postposition saarik

Saarik `like' occurs with noun phrases ex:3:x760 and with nominalized clauses ex:3:x761. It indicates a point of similarity between two essentially different things.

Mua eliwa saarik aakun-e-k. \\
man good like speak- pa -3s\\
`He spoke like a good man.'

No sia on-owa saarik magimal puuk-a-n. \\
2s. unm netbag make- nmz like vine.sp. cut- pa -2s\\
`You cut magimal vine as if you were going to make a netbag.'

For the functional category of comparison, see sec:6.5.

Locative clitic - pa

The locative clitic - pa mainly marks locative in noun phrases ex:3:x762. The most common verb that it collocates with is ik- `be' ex:3:x1880. When it occurs with the directional verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.5 ), it often indicates source ex:3:x1877, but it can also be used for path ex:3:x770, or for instrument in cases where it has a strong locative meaning as well ex:3:x771. It is rarely used for goal ex:3:x1879; this is possible in cases where the goal is the location for an event taking place immediately.

Pon piipa unowa= pa soomar-em-ik-eya mik-a-m. \\
turtle seaweed many= loc walk- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds spear- pa -1s\\
`The turtle was walking among the seaweeds and I speared it.'

Ona owowa= pa ik-eya epa wiim-o-k. \\
3s. gen village= loc be-2/3s. ds place dawn- pa -3s\\
`When he was in his village it dawned.'

Ifa maneka=ke iinan= pa or-o-k. \\
snake big= cf on.top= loc descend- pa -3s\\
`A big snake dropped from above.'

Saa= pa ir-am-ika-i-mik. \\
sand= loc come/go- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`They are coming on/along the beach.'

Miiw aasa= pa ikiw-e-mik. \\
land canoe= loc go- pa -1/3p\\
`We went by car/in a car.'

Mua nain... eka kapa =pa ir-ap eka nain up-o-k.\\
man that1... river top= loc come/go- ss. seq river that1 block- pa -3s\\
`The man went to the top/source of the river and blocked the river.'

As temporal phrases locate an event in time, they also use the same locative clitic ex:3:x763.

Fraide= pa maapora puk-o-k, urera. \\
Friday= loc celebration burst- pa -3s, afternoon.\\
`On Friday the celebration started, in the afternoon.'

It can also be used with an essive meaning, when referring to people's jobs ex:3:x765:

Yena mua owowa ekap-o-k, amia mua= pa ik-ok. \\
1s. gen man village come- pa -3s bow man= loc be-SS \\
`My husband came back to the village, having been a policeman.'

The locative clitic has its origin in the word epa `place'; the transition vowel [e] can sometimes be heard between the clitic and its host, when the host word ends in a consonant ex:3:x764.

Ne Sarak ikos Gawar=( e) pa ik-emkun yia maak-e-mik \\
add Sarak with Gawar= loc be-1s/p. ds 1p. acc tell- pa -1/3p\\
`And as Sarak and I were in Gawar, they told us, '

Instrumental clitic - iw

The instrumental clitic - iw is used both for concrete ex:3:x766 and abstract ex:3:x768 instruments. A less emphasized way to add an instrument is to use the chaining structure: `take instrument do something' ex:3:x387, ex:3:x388.

Nomokowa galua-galua nain= iw biiris on-am-ik-e-mik \\
tree soft-soft that1= inst bridge make- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`They kept making bridges with soft timber.'...wiena opaimik= iw yia maak-em-ik-e-mik. \\
3p. gen mouth= inst 1p. acc tell- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`They talked to us in their language.'

It is also used for path and has the meaning `along'; the verb indicates action that continues for some time ex:3:x767.

Saa= iw ir-am-ika-i-mik,... \\
sand= inst ascend- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.3p\\
`They are coming along the beach '

The difference between ex:3:x767 and ex:3:x770 above is that in ex:3:x770 the people were coming along the beach at least some of the way, and more specifically at the time of the speaking; whereas ex:3:x767 indicates that they travelled along the beach more or less the whole way.

The instrumental may also be utilized to indicate manner ex:3:x1881-- ex:3:x774:

Uurik ona naap= iw iw-ap poka aaw-e-mik. \\
tomorrow place thus= inst go- ss. seq housepost get- pa -1/3p\\
`The following day they went in the same way and got houseposts.'

Karu-(o)w= iw ekap-o-k. \\
run- nmz = inst come- pa -3s\\
`He came running.'

Ne ikoka maa marew eliw manek= iw ika-i-nan. \\
add later thing none well big= inst be-Np- fu.2s\\
`And later you will have no problems, you will just be very well.'

Waaya=ke anane wiar en-ow= iw ika-i-ya. \\
pig= cf always 3. dat eat- nmz = inst be-Np- pr.3s\\
`A pig stays eating their (taro) all the time.'

Another usage is in those temporal phrases that refer to something taking place repeatedly at the same time ex:3:x1882:

I amirik= iw... Gawar wiar ikiw-e-mik. \\
1p. unm daytime= inst Gawar 3. dat go- pa -1/3p\\
`In the daytime we always went to Gawar '

Limiter - iw

The limiter clitic - iw `only, just' is homophonous with the instrumental. The two probably are of common origin, but synchronically their meanings and positions in the word are distinct ( sec:3.12.9 ). The limiter does not mark a case but restricts the applicability of the predication to the element that it is attached to ex:3:x769, ex:3:x772.

Maa eka NP = iw en-ep en-ep lebum-ar-i-nan. \\
food water= lim eat- ss. seq eat- ss. seq lazy- inch -Np- fu.2s\\
`When you keep eating only food cooked with water you become tired of it.'

Mua= iw pok-aka. \\
man= lim sit- imp.2p\\
`Sit just among the men.'

The limiter clitic may attach itself to genitive and focal pronouns, resulting in restrictive pronouns ( sec:3.5.7 ).
summary:
The passage explains several postpositions and clitics in the language. The comparison postposition **saarik** means “like” and can occur with noun phrases or nominalized clauses, while the locative clitic **-pa** mainly marks location but can also express source, path, limited instrument, goal in restricted contexts, temporal location, and even essive meaning; it derives from the word *epa* “place.”  

It also describes the instrumental clitic **-iw**, which marks concrete or abstract instruments, can indicate path, manner, and repeated temporal settings, and is homophonous with a separate limiter **-iw** meaning “only, just.” The limiter does not mark case; instead, it restricts the scope of the predication to the attached element.

text: The free adverb muutiw `only' is a combination of muut(a) `only' and the limiter clitic - iw ( sec:3.9.4 ).
summary: The free adverb **muutiw** ‘only’ is analyzed as a combination of **muut(a)** ‘only’ and the limiter clitic **-iw**. This shows that the form is morphologically complex rather than simple.

text: The topic and focus markers indicate the discourse function of the noun phrases that they are attached to.
summary: Topic and focus markers show the discourse role of the noun phrases they attach to. In other words, they indicate whether those noun phrases are functioning as topics or as focus in the sentence.

text:
Of the two topic markers ena is fairly low in frequency, and the description given here is only tentative. It seems that ena as an independent word originally had a topic marking function, but later the topic clitic -(e)na developed from it and is now used for highlighted topic ( sec:9.2.4 ) in main clauses. Ena still marks a topic, but mainly in relative clauses. It often has a specifying function as well: `the/that (particular one)' ex:3:x1681.

Mua ena ma-e-k nain makena yos. \\
man spec say- pa -3s that1 true 1s. fc \\
`The man that he talked about is I.'

In long relative clauses, where it is attached to the relnp, it helps to distinguish it from all the other nps in the clause ex:3:x1815, ex:3:x1683.

Mua papako ena Australia=ke wia aaw-ep wiena feekiya yiaw-e-mik nain me epa fan irak-owa uruf-a-mik \\
man other spec Australia= cf 3p. acc take- ss. seq 3p. gen with walk.around- pa -1/3p that1 not place here fight- nmz see- pa -1/3p\\
`Those other (particular) men whom the Australians took and with whom they walked around did not see the war here in this place '

I mua owowa=pa ik-ok ena irakowa uruf-a-mik nain nanar nain yo fan ma-i-yem.\\
1p. unm man village= loc be-SS spec fight- nmz see- pa -1/3p that1 story that1 1s. unm here say-Np- pr.1s\\
`I am telling the story of us (particular) people who stayed in the village and saw the fighting.'

If the head noun of the np is is recoverable from the context, it may be deleted, leaving behind only ena. In ex:3:x1682 the head noun epira `bowl(s)' has been omitted.

Aakisa fan ena maneka wu-a-mik nain eliw, wie wi eliw wiar op-i-kuan.\\
now here spec big put- pa -1/3p that1 well 3s/p.uncle 3p. unm well 3. dat grab-Np- fu.3p\\
`Those big (bowls) that we put just now, all right, the uncles may take those from them.'

The example ex:3:x1816, taken from Bible translation, has a highlighted topic marker - na on the sentence-initial topic np, which is part of the main clause, and ena inside the relative clause:

Ni Samaria=na o ena me baliwep amis-ar-e-man nain RC lotu on-i-man.\\
2p. unm Samaria= tp 3s. unm spec not well knowledge- inch that1 worship do-Np- pr.2p\\
`You Samaritans worship [the one that you do not know well].'

Without ena in the relative clause the sentence would mean `You Samaritans do not know him well but (still) worship him.'

The more common topic clitic -(e)na The clitic has mostly lost the phoneme /e/, but it can sometimes be heard when the host word ends in a voiceless consonant. is used to highlight a changed topic, to which attention is drawn. The topic may have been introduced in the immediately preceding clause. The use of this device is infrequent in texts. It can often be glossed with `as for X'. Highlighted topics are discussed in sec:9.2.4.

Example ex:3:x779 is from a traditional story, where a man has gone hunting and the spirit of his lover comes to his home. When the wife sees her, she knows what the spirit woman has come to look for and comments:

Nena mua= na urema osarena ikiw-o-k. \\
2s. gen man= tp bandicoot path go- pa -3s\\
`(As for) your husband, he went to catch bandicoots.'

In ex:3:x1751 the answer to the question reveals the identity of the person asked about; the topic marker may be used even in a short exchange like this but especially if the text continues to tell more about the topic.

Mua nain naareke? Mua nain= na owow saria maneka=ke. \\
Man that1 who. cf man that1= tp village headman big= cf \\
`Who is that man? -That man is the big village headman.'

In ex:3:x780 the speaker changes the topic to the addressee after a discussion on something else:

Nos= na? \\
2s. fc = tp \\
`(So,) what about you?'

An important function for the topic marker - na is to mark conditional clauses ex:3:x744, ex:3:x745 ( sec:8.3.5 ). This is a common function for topic markers in Papuan languages (;, Reesink1987; ).

Opora wiar ika-i-ya= na eliw urup-ep wia maak-uk.\\
talk 3. dat be-Np- pr.3s= tp well ascend- ss. seq 3p. acc tell- imp.3p\\
`If they have something to say, they can get up and tell them.'

O emeria aaw-owa kookal-ek-a-k= na iw-ek-a-mik.\\
3s. unm woman get- nmz like- cntf - pa -3s= tp give.him- cntf - pa -1/3p\\
`If he had liked to get a wife, they would have given him one.'

It is also used in adversative subordinate clauses ( sec:8.3.4 ) when the main clause expresses a frustrated effort or a cancelled expectation ex:3:x1399, or surprise.

Ikiw-ep mukuna nain umuk-a-mik= na me pepek. \\
go- ss. seq fire that1 extinguish- pa -1/3p= tp not enough/able\\
`We went and (tried to) extinguish the fire, but couldn't.'
summary: The passage describes two topic markers: the lower-frequency **ena**, which likely originated as an independent topic marker and now appears mainly in relative clauses with a specifying meaning like “the/that particular one,” and the more common clitic **-(e)na**, which marks highlighted or changed topics in main clauses. **Ena** can help identify a noun phrase in long relative clauses or even stand alone when the head noun is recoverable from context, while **-(e)na** is used for topic shifts, contrastive focus, and also commonly marks conditional and adversative subordinate clauses.

text:
There are two focus clitics, the contrastive focus marker -( e) ke and the neutral focus marker - ko, which has developed from the indefinite oko `a certain, other'. Most of this section is based on J\"arvinen (1988b:81--96). The main candidate for the contrastive focus marker is the subject of a noun phrase ex:3:x781. When the object is fronted as a theme ( sec:9.1 ), the subject usually gets the contrastive focus marking to distinguish it from the object ex:3:x782.

Iiriw ifa marasin= ke kekan-e-k. \\
earlier snake poison= cf be.strong- pa -3s\\
`The snake poison had already taken effect.'

Episowa ifa nain atua= ke en-e-k. \\
tobacco leaf that1 worm= cf eat- pa -3s\\
`The tobacco leaves were eaten by worms.'

Another possible host is the non-verbal predicate of a verbless clause ex:3:x783 ( sec:5.6 ).

Iperuma nain me enim-eka, inasin mua= ke. \\
eel that1 not eat- imp.2p spirit man= cf \\
`Do not eat that eel, it is a spirit man.'

There are a few isolated cases where it occurs on some other contrasted element of a clause ex:3:x784.

Amirika= ke eliw ika-i-yem, uura= ke napum-ar-i-yem. \\
noon= cf well be-Np- pr.1s night= cf sickness- inch -Np- pr.1s\\
`At noon I'm well, at night I am sick.'

Contrastive focus as a pragmatic device in a text is discussed in sec:9.3.1.

The neutral focus clitic -ko mostly occurs in irrealis-type clauses: Because of this, it was called Irrealis focus clitic in J\"arvinen (1988b). questions ex:3:x785, commands ex:3:x786, negative clauses ex:3:x787, or those with future tense ex:3:x788. Unlike the contrastive focus marker, the neutral focus marker can be attached to almost any element of a clause except the final verb. Neutral focus as a textual device is discussed further in sec:9.3.2.

Mukuna= ko op-a-man=i? \\
fire= nf hold- pa -2p= qm \\
`Did you hold any fire?'

Mua nain= ko onak-e! \\
man that1= nf give.to.eat- imp.2s\\
`Give it to that man to eat!'

Oposia en-e-man nain yo= ko me uruf-a-m. \\
meat eat- pa -2p that1 1s. unm = nf not see- pa -1s\\
`I didn't (even) see the meat that you ate.'

Akim-ap= ko uruf-i-yen. \\
try- ss. seq = nf see-Np- fu.1p\\
`We'll try and see.'
summary:
The passage describes two focus clitics: the contrastive focus marker **-(e)ke** and the neutral focus marker **-ko**, which developed from an indefinite form. Contrastive **-(e)ke** most often marks the subject of a noun phrase, especially when the object is fronted as a theme, and can also appear on non-verbal predicates or other contrasted elements.

The neutral **-ko** occurs mainly in irrealis-type clauses such as questions, commands, negative clauses, and future clauses. Unlike the contrastive marker, it can attach to almost any clause element except the final verb.

text:
The question marker - i is a sentential clitic, used to form polar questions, and it attaches itself to the clause-final verb ex:3:x789 or another clause-final element ex:3:x790. Its relationship to the alternative connective e `or' ( sec:3.11.2 ) is unclear; it is possible that i was originally an alternative connective but was also employed as a question marker and became so established in this function that a new alternative connective e developed. It is not uncommon in TNG Madang languages that the question marker and the alternative connective are either the same or closely related. In Usan and Amele the alternative connector and the question marker are the same (, ). Maia has -i `QM' and e `or' like Mauwake. Bargam has borrowed the Tok Pisin o as an alternative connector but has retained the clitic -e as the question marker. Kobon may use the alternative interrogative connector aka `or' sentence-finally in leading polar questions, where the speaker expects the addressee to agree with the proposition.

Sira nain piipua-i-nan= i? \\
habit that1 leave-Np- fu.2s= qm \\
`Will you give up that habit?'

Nobonob ikiw-e-man nain, owowa eliwa= i? \\
Nobonob go- pa -2p that1 village good= qm \\
`You went to Nobonob, is it a good village?'

The question marker can also be used in statements, when two or more alternatives are given ex:3:x791:

Mua kuisow manina erup= i (e) arow= i (e) naap. \\
man one garden two= qm (or) three= qm (or) thus\\
`A man can have two gardens, or three, like that.'
summary:
The clitic **-i** is a sentential question marker used to form polar questions, attaching to the clause-final verb or another clause-final element. Its relation to the alternative connective **e** “or” is uncertain, but the text suggests they may historically be connected; similar patterns are found in several TNG Madang languages, where question markers and alternative connectives are identical or closely related.

The marker can also appear in statements when alternatives are listed. In some contexts, especially leading polar questions, a related alternative interrogative connective may be used sentence-finally when the speaker expects agreement.

text:
It is possible to have two or more clitics attached to the same word; only the topic marker does not allow other clitics with it. A case marking clitic, forming a constituent with the preceding noun phrase, is placed first. Next comes the focus clitic ex:3:x792, with the scope over a phrase but not forming a constituent. The limiter - iw may have a phrase with the focus marking in its scope, so it follows the focus marker. When the limiter follows another clitic, there is a transition consonant <r>between the clitics ex:3:x795, ex:3:x796. The modal clitic - yon `perhaps' ( sec:3.9.3 ) may have a scope over a whole predication, so its position is after the limiter ex:3:x793. The sentential clitic, with a scope over the whole sentence, comes last. When the contrastive focus marker - ke and the question marker - i are adjacent, they become a portmanteau clitic - ki ex:3:x794.

Fura= iw= ko me puuk-a-mik. \\
knife= inst = nf not cut- pa -1/3p\\
`They didn't cut it with a knife.'

Fikera= pa-r= iw fiirim-eka. \\
kunai.grass= loc - = lim gather- imp.2p\\
`Gather them right at the kunai grass.'

Os= ke-r= iw maa en-emi ewur-ar-e-k. \\
3s. fc = cf - = lim food eat- ss. sim haste- inch - pa -3s\\
`Only he rushed with his food.'

Wi anim onoma pun o makena Krais=ke na-i-mik= yon= i?\\
3p. unm blade basis also 3s. unm truly Christ= cf say-Np- pr.1/3p=perhaps= qm \\
`Are also the authorities perhaps saying that he truly is Christ?'

Mua fain Saror muuka= ki? \\
man this Saror son= cf.QM\\
`Is this man Saror's son?'
summary: A word can host multiple clitics in a fixed order: case-marking clitics come first, then the focus clitic, the limiter, the modal clitic, and finally the sentential clitic. The topic marker is the only clitic that cannot co-occur with others, and when the contrastive focus marker and question marker appear together, they fuse into the portmanteau clitic -ki.

text:
There are a lot of interjections in Mauwake; the following tab:3:interjections is not even nearly exhaustive. The pronunciation of interjections may differ from that of other words: intonational variations are greater, and lengthening, even extreme lengthening, of the final vowel is common. Interjections are not part of the normal clause structure, and they usually occur either sentence-initially or finally ex:3:x797-- ex:3:x800. Some can also be placed between clauses in a coordinate sentence ex:3:x801. The glosses given in tab:3:interjections for the interjections are just rough approximations.

Aa, kema=ko kir-ek-a-n aa! \\
oh liver= nf turn- cntf - pa -2s oh\\
`Oh, if only you had changed your ways (lit: turned your liver)!'

Arika, takira, yo yook-eka. \\
let's.go boy 1s. unm follow.me- imp.2p\\
`Alright boys, follow me (and will get going).'

Laman tapala wu-a-k, aiyoo! \\
Laman hat put- pa -3s intj \\
`My goodness, Laman put a hat on (and exposed himself and us to the fighter pilots)!'

Emawa, nena niawi um-o-k. \\
sorry 2s. gen 2s/p.father die- pa -3s\\
`Sorry, your father is dead.'

Naap ma-emi om-em-ika-i-nan, na. \\
thus say- ss. sim cry- ss. sim -be-Np- fu.2s intj \\
`You must cry saying like that.'

Yo damol-al-e-m oo, fiker fufa iw-a-m oo. \\
1s. unm bad- inch - pa -1s oh kunai.grass old.grass enter- pa -1s oh\\
` Oh, I'm in a bad way, I am hiding among the grass.'

Ni kaaneke ik-e-man oo, ni ekap-omak-eka oh\\
2p. unm where be- pa -2p oh 2p. unm come- distr / pl - imp.2p oo!\\
`O where are you? -- come!'

Yii, ifa=ke yee! \\
Eek snake= cf intj \\
`Eek, that's a snake oh!
summary: Mauwake has many interjections, and the list given is not exhaustive. They are pronounced with greater intonational variation than other words, often with final-vowel lengthening, and they do not belong to normal clause structure, usually appearing at the beginning or end of a sentence, though some can occur between clauses in coordinated sentences. The glosses for these forms are only rough approximations.

text: The noun phrase in Mauwake functions as subject, object or non-verbal predicate in a clause. It can also function as a head in an adverbial phrase, or as a possessor, qualifier or post-modifier in another noun phrase.
summary: In Mauwake, the noun phrase can serve as a subject, object, or non-verbal predicate in a clause. It can also function as the head of an adverbial phrase, or as a possessor, qualifier, or post-modifier within another noun phrase.

text:
The most common noun phrase structure consists of the head noun only. That is slightly more frequent than a head noun plus one or more attributive elements. The head noun may have either pre- or postmodifiers, or both. The relative order of the np constituents is as follows: The superscript n indicates that it is possible to have more than one of these constituents within a single NP.

Unmarked/Genitive pronoun -- Temporal phrase -- Possessive np -- Genitive pronoun -- Qualifying np -- head noun -- Modifying np -- Adjective phrase n -- Quantifier phrase n / Indefinite -- Demonstrative -- Dative pronoun

The relative clause, in which the head noun is modified by an entire clause, is discussed in sec:8.3.1.

The order of np constituents following the head noun agrees with a cross-linguistic generalization of sov languages: noun-adjective-numeral-demonstrative.

Theoretically it is possible, and grammatically correct, to have a np like the one in ex:4:x392, but natural language data seldom has any nps with more than two modifiers. Example ex:4:x393 is one of those.

auwa ona mera sia maala erup nain \\
1s/p.father 3s. gen fish net long two that1\\
possnp genpr qualnp hn ap qp dem \\
`my father's two long fish nets' / `the/those two long fish nets of my father'

iiriw Naawura miiw-aasa awona nain \\
earlier Naawura land-canoe old that1 \\
tmpp possnp hn ap dem \\
`the/that earlier truck of Naawura's'

yiena iiriw kae sira nain \\
1p. gen earlier 1s/p.grandfather custom that1 \\
`that traditional custom of ours'

The only modifier in a noun phrase is most typically either a possessor ex:4:x395, a deictic ex:4:x396 or a qualifying noun or noun phrase. The qualifying noun in ex:4:x397 is a compound noun.

ona siowa \\
3s. gen dog \\
`his/her dog'

ifa nain \\
snake that1 \\
`the/that snake'

owow(a) maneka mua \\
village big man \\
`townsman'

In the following, each np position is discussed in turn, starting with the leftmost one.

An unmarked third person plural pronoun is used as an optional plural marking for humans and other human-like beings in ex:4:x398 and ex:4:x1831.

Wi sawur=ke kuura puuk-a-mik. \\
3p. unm spirit= cf fly change.into- pa -1/3p \\
`The spirits changed into flies.'

Ne nan wi owow mua wia maak-e-mik, \\
add there 3p. acc village man 3p. acc tell- pa -1/3p \\
`And there they told the village men, '

The plural-marking pronoun differs from the appositive use ex:4:x399 of the unmarked pronoun in that the former is unstressed, whereas the latter is stressed. Furthermore, the appositive use is not restricted to the third person plural pronoun. (For appositional nps, see sec:4.1.4.)

' Yo nena niawi=ke nefa maak-i-yem. \\
1s. unm 2s. gen 2s/p.father= cf 2s. acc tell-Np- pr.1s \\
`I, your father, tell you...'

A special case of the plural-marking unmarked pronoun is its occurrence in connection with a place name to refer to the people of that place ex:4:x400. The head noun mua `men, people' or emeria mua `people' is not needed. It may be used, but is usually left out.

Wi Lasen=ke ekap-e--mik. \\
1p. unm Lasen= cf come- pa -1/3p \\
`The Lasen (village) people came.'

A temporal phrase is rare as a np constituent. It is mainly the temporal words aakis 'present-day' from aakisa 'now, today' ex:4:x401 and iiriw 'earlier' ex:4:x1883 that are used. A temporal phrase is also allowed but uncommon.

ni aakis takira \\
2p. unm present-day young.person \\
`you young people of today'

wi iiriw akena mua \\
3p. unm earlier truly man \\
`the people of long ago'

The structure of the two pre-modifying nps, possessive np and qualifying np, is similar to that of the basic np. It is because of their position and function inside another np that they are named differently here.

The head noun of a
possessive np can only be [+human], with `human' including spirits ex:4:x402 and sometimes some domestic animals like dogs or pigs ex:4:x403. The humanness of the possnp is stressed by the fact that it may be followed by a pronoun copy in the genitive ex:4:x402.

sawur emeria ona onak wiawi \\
spirit woman 3s. gen 3s/p.mother 3s/p.father \\
`the spirit woman's parents'

siowa wiawi \\
dog 3s/p.father \\
`the dog's owner'

The head noun of the possnp may itself be possessed ex:4:x404, ex:4:x405:

yiena kae sira \\
1p. gen 1s/p.grandfather custom \\
`our ancestors' (lit: grandfathers') custom'

i emeria apura yiena mua weria emeria nain=ke \\
1p. unm woman widow 1p. gen man planting.stick woman that1= cf \\
[Poss NP [Poss NP [HN]\,]\,] Dem \\
`the wives of the ``weria-men'' The weria -men are relatives responsible for a person's burial. For more information see sec:1.3.6. of us widows'

The semantic relation of the ``possessor'' to the ``possessed'' may be that of real ownership, paraphrasable with `have' ex:4:x406, a human relationship ex:4:x402, origin ex:4:x404 or subjecthood ex:4:x407.

ona koora \\
3s. gen house \\
`his house'

takira niir-owa \\
youth play- nmz \\
`young people's play(ing)'

Either an unmarked pronoun or a genitive pronoun may be used as a possessive pronoun ex:4:x409. Often the two can be used interchangeably, but the following rules and tendencies have been observed. First, when the pronoun is a pronoun copy of a preceding possessive np, it must be in the genitive ex:4:x410.

Ona apura maa oposia me enim-i-non. \\
3s. gen widow thing meat not eat-Np- fu.3s \\
`His widow will not eat meat.'

sawur emeria ona onak wiawi \\
spirit woman 3s. gen 3s/p.mother 3s/p.father \\
`the spirit woman's parents'

Second, an unmarked pronoun is used especially with things that are closely related to a person ex:4:x1315, whereas the genitive pronoun tends to be used more when the ownership is emphasized ex:4:x1314.

Oo, no emeria iiriw sesek-a-mik. \\
Oh 2s. unm woman already send- pa -1/3p \\
`Oh, we already sent your wife away.'
summary:
The passage describes noun phrase structure, noting that the most common NP consists only of a head noun, though it may also include pre- and postmodifiers. It gives the relative order of NP constituents and observes that, although longer NPs are grammatically possible, natural data usually contains no more than two modifiers, with possessor, deictic, or qualifying nouns being the most common single modifiers.

It then discusses specific leftward NP positions, including unmarked third-person plural pronouns used as plural markers, rare temporal phrases, and possessive NPs whose head nouns are typically [+human]. The passage also explains that possessive relations can express ownership, kinship, origin, or subjecthood, and that unmarked and genitive pronouns are often interchangeable, though the genitive is required for pronoun copies and tends to be used when ownership is more strongly emphasized.

text:
Nep(a) opaimika me amis(a)-ar-ep wiena opaimik(a) =iw yia maak-em-ik-e-mik.\\
bird talk not knowledge- inch - ss. seq 3p. gen talk= inst 1p. acc tell- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`They did not know Tok Pisin and talked to us in their (own) language.'

Third, an unmarked pronoun used possessively often receives extra stress in speech ex:4:x408.

Nain 'i sira=ke. \\
that1 1p. unm custom= cf \\
`That is our custom.'

In recursive genitive structures like ex:4:x405, more than one possessive pronoun may occur as a pronoun copy, so ex:4:x411 is a possible alternative for ex:4:x405:

i emeria apura yiena mua weria wiena emeria nain=ke\\
1p. unm woman widow 1p. gen man planting.stick 3p. gen woman that1= cf \\
`the wives of the ``weria-relatives'' of us widows'

A qualifying noun phrase usually consists of the head noun only ex:4:x413-- ex:4:x1832. If it has other elements, the structure is that of the basic noun phrase. The distinction between a qualifying np and a possessive np on the one hand, and between a qualifying np and a n+n compound on the other, is often hard to make. (See sec:3.2.5 for a discussion on the distinction between compound nouns and nps.) Unlike a possessive np, a qualifying np may not take a genitive pronoun copy.

Fiker(a) epia nain aw-i-non. \\
kunai.grass fire that1 burn-Np- fu.3s \\
`The grass fire will burn.'

Mua takira unowa ne emeria wiip-takira=ke me unowa akena.\\
man youth many add woman daughter-youth= cf not many very \\
`There are many young boys but not very many young girls.'

Epa kokom-ar-eya urera siowa mua ookinon. \\
place dark- inch -2/3s. ds afternoon dog man follow-Np- fu.3s \\
`When it gets dark in the afternoon he will follow the ``dog man'' (a certain nominated person in the singsing traditions).'

A place name may be a qualifier for a locative noun functioning as head noun ex:4:x834, ex:4:x833.

Bogia era \\
Bogia road \\
`the Bogia road'

Malala owowa \\
Malala village \\
`Malala village'

The qualifying np can also be a nominalized clause. This is most common when the head noun is an abstract noun like sira `custom' ex:4:x414 or opora `talk, story'.

garanga oko muuka wiar aaw-owa NP sira \\
family other son 3. dat get- nmz custom \\
`adoption custom (lit: the custom of getting a son from another family)'

The head noun is either a single or a compound noun. If the head noun is replaced by a pronoun, it can only take post-modifiers ex:4:x415:

wi(am) arow nain \\
3p. unm ( refl ) three that1 \\
`the three of them / those three'

A post-modifying noun phrase often expresses qualities that in many European languages would be expressed by true adjectives ex:4:x416, or via adjectivalized ex:4:x417 or comitative expressions ex:4:x418.

labuel(a) mua \\
pawpaw man \\
`male pawpaw'

takira emin(a) kekanowa \\
boy occiput strong \\
`pig-headed boy'

mua bug maala nain \\
man wind long that1 \\
`the man with good lungs'

A noun phrase can have one or more adjective phrases as modifiers. The adjective phrase typically consists of an adjective only. If there are more ap s than one, the order is as follows: colour - physical property or human propensity - size/age - value ex:4:x419.

Waa(ya) muuka kia gelemuta op-a-m. \\
pig son white small catch- pa -1s \\
`I caught a small white piglet.'

In recorded texts the maximum number of adjective phrases per np is two, but the speakers have no difficulty producing nps with more ap s ex:4:x420:

Emer(a) itita enum(a) eliwa nain enak-e. \\
sago soft new good that1 feed.me- imp.2s \\
`Give me the good new soft sago/bread to eat.'

The position of either a quantifier phrase or an indefinite is after the adjective phrase ex:4:x804.

Siowa morena oko aruf-a-k. \\
dog male another hit- pa -3s \\
`He hit another male dog.'

The last regular post-modifier in a noun phrase is a demonstrative. Especially the distal demonstrative nain `that' is very common ex:4:x805, and in many cases it is no more than a marker for given information.

koora erepam nain \\
house four that1 \\
`the/those four houses' or `the fourth house'

The dative pronoun ( sec:3.5.5 ) is unusual as a modifier. Semantically, it belongs to the noun phrase, marking a possessive relationship, but syntactically it still reflects its origin as a [+human] locative adverbial ( sec:4.6.1 ) of the verb. It is often non-contiguous with the rest of the np, which can be fronted for a theme while the dative pronoun needs to stay in its pre-verbal position ex:4:x1811. Other elements that can separate the dative pronoun from the rest of the np are me `not' ex:4:x1812, and the free adverbs muutiw `only' and pun `also' ex:4:x1938.

Owow emeria mua unowa sira eliwa wiar uruf-ap \\
village woman man many custom good 3. dat see- ss. seq... \\
`The many villagers saw his good manners and '

Pina gelemuta eliw owowa=pa nefar kaken-ami welaw-i-kuan.\\
guilt small well village= loc 2s. dat straighten- ss. sim finish-Np- fu.3p \\
`Your small guilt they can well straighten and finish in the village.'

Amina fain me wiar op-aka. \\
pot this not 3. dat hold- imp.2p \\
`Don't hold/touch these pots of hers.'

Yo miira me uruf-a-m, afifa muutiw wiar uruf-a-m. \\
1s. unm face not see- pa -1s hair only 3. dat see- pa -1s \\
`I didn't see the face, I only saw his hair.'
summary:
The passage describes several kinds of noun phrase modification. Possessive pronouns may appear with extra stress, and in recursive genitive constructions more than one possessive pronoun can occur as a pronoun copy; by contrast, qualifying noun phrases usually consist of just the head noun, may include modifiers such as nominalized clauses or place names, and cannot take a genitive pronoun copy.

It also explains the order and types of post-modifiers in noun phrases: adjective phrases can stack in a fixed order, quantifiers and indefinites follow them, and demonstratives come last, with distal *nain* often marking given information. Finally, the dative pronoun is a special modifier that semantically marks possession but syntactically remains pre-verbal and may be separated from the rest of the noun phrase by elements like negation or certain adverbs.

text:
Joining noun phrases into a coordinate noun phrase can be done either by simple juxtaposition or with connectives. Juxtaposition is the default strategy ex:4:x810, ex:4:x811. In spoken texts the juxtaposed noun phrases are separated by a longer pause, in written texts by a comma.

Amina, wiowa, eka napia koor miira=pa iimar-ow-a-mik. \\
pot spear, water bamboo house face= loc stand- caus - pa -1/3p \\
`We placed the pots, spears and water bamboos in front of the house.'

I mua unowa, emeria papako ikiw-e-mik. \\
1s. unm man many woman some go- pa -1/3p \\
`Many men (including the narrator) and some women went.'

The pragmatic connective ne `additive' ( sec:3.11.1 ) is used rather infrequently to connect the parts of a coordinate noun phrase ex:4:x812. When it is used, and when there are more than two noun phrases to connect, it is usually placed between the last two noun phrases ex:4:x814, but other positions are possible too, see (3. ex:3:x1359 ).

Nie ne neke nomokow fiira=ke. \\
2s/p.maternal.uncle add 2s/p.grandfather tree root= cf \\
`Your maternal uncle and your grandfather are the most important relatives.'

Mera kas, mulamul ne popotimaw aaw-i-mik. \\
fish mackerel trevally.sp add trevally.sp get-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`We catch mackerel, mulamul trevally and popotimaw trevally.'

A focus clitic ex:4:x893 or a case marking clitic ex:4:x894 is only added to the last noun phrase in a coordinate noun phrase.

Manin koora nain koka ne ifara=ke wakesim-o-k. \\
garden house that1 jungle add vine= cf cover- pa -3s \\
`The garden house was covered by jungle and vines.'

Wiena merena ne wapen=iw era akup-a-mik. \\
3p. gen foot add hand= inst road search- pa -1/3p \\
`They felt (lit: searched) for the road with their feet and hands.'

The pragmatic connective aria `alright', too, can occasionally join the elements of a coordinate noun phrase ex:4:x815, ex:4:x816. As a sentential or clausal connective it indicates a break in the discourse, but when it joins two noun phrases there does not seem to be a significant difference between that and ne `additive.' It may be that aria draws more attention to the separate noun phrases being joined than either juxtaposition or ne does.

Yos, yena auwa, aria wi emer en-ow(a) mua kuisow ikiw-e-mik.\\
1s. fc 1s. gen 1s/p.father alright 3p. unm sago eat- nmz man one go- pa -1/3p\\
`I, my father, and one Sepik man went.'

Moma, aria emera naap lawisiw eeyar-e-k. \\
taro, alright sago thus rather last- pa -3s \\
`Taro, and sago, lasted a little (longer).'

The disjunctive connective e `or' ex:4:x817 ( sec:3.11.2 ), and/or the question marker - i ex:4:x818 is used in a coordinate noun phrase if the noun phrases are presented as alternatives.

Mera aaw-owa sira e era ikur okaiwi=pa kuisow ik-ua. \\
fish get- nmz custom or way five other.side= loc one be- pa.3s \\
`There are six means, or ways, of catching fish.'

Maa oposia =i moma, emera, naap sesek-a-mik. \\
thing meat= qm taro sago thus sell- pa -1/3p \\
`They sold meat, or taro, (or) sago, (things) like that.'
summary: Coordinate noun phrases in this language are formed either by simple juxtaposition, which is the default and is marked in speech by a pause and in writing by a comma, or by connectives. The additive connective *ne* and occasionally *aria* can join noun phrases, while focus or case clitics attach only to the final noun phrase in the coordinate structure. Alternatives are expressed with the disjunctive *e* ‘or’ and/or the question marker *-i*.

text:
A comitative noun phrase is made up of one or two basic noun phrases plus a comitative postposition or clitic ( sec:3.12.1 ). A comitative pronoun ( sec:3.5.9 ) can also form a comitative phrase either by itself or attached to a np ex:4:x828-- ex:4:x830. When there is only one overt noun phrase and if it is unmarked for number, the plurality is shown both by the comitative marking and in the verb person marking ex:4:x819. The choice of the comitative marker and the number marking in the verb, when relevant, reflect whether the noun phrases in the comitative relationship are co-subjects/co-objects of the same verb ex:4:x832, or whether one is a dominant member ex:4:x831.

Ikoka mua owawiya irak-ep me efar kerer-e. \\
later man with fight- ss. seq not 1s. dat appear- imp.2s \\
`Later when you fight with your husband, do not come to me.'

Wi Yaapan oos onaiya Madang ikiw-e-mik. \\
3p. unm Japan horse with Madang go- pa -1/3p \\
`The Japanese went with horses to Madang.'

Parosifa siisim-ep muuka feekiya sesek-i-nen. \\
letter write- ss. seq son with send-Np- fu.1s \\
`I will write a letter and send it with my son.'

Ona siowa ikos manina ikiw-e-mik,... \\
3s. gen dog with garden go- pa -1/3p \\
`He went to the garden with his dog, ' or: `He and his dog went to the garden, '

Rabaul kemena=pa naap pok-ap ik-e-mik, mua=iya emeria. \\
Rabaul bay= loc thus sit- ss. seq be- pa -1/3p man= com woman \\
`They are now sitting in the Rabaul bay, the husband and/with the wife.'

Wiamiya irak-owa na-ep ikiw-e-mik. \\
3p. com fight- nmz say- ss. seq go- pa -1/3p \\
`We went to fight with them.'

With the dual comitative postposition ikos there may be an additive connective ne between the two noun phrases ex:4:x820. It seems to be more common with younger speakers.

Osaiwa ne aalbok ikos womar wiam op-a-mik. \\
bird.of.paradise add black.cuckoo.shrike with 3s/p.friend 3p. refl hold- pa -1/3p \\
`The bird of paradise and/with the black cuckoo-shrike were friends.'
summary:
A comitative phrase consists of one or two basic noun phrases plus a comitative postposition or clitic, and a comitative pronoun may form such a phrase on its own or attached to a noun phrase. If only one noun phrase is overt and it is unmarked for number, plurality is indicated both by the comitative marking and by verb person marking; the form of the comitative marker and verbal number marking also depends on whether the noun phrases are co-subjects/co-objects or whether one member is dominant.

With the dual comitative postposition *ikos*, an additive connective *ne* may appear between the two noun phrases, and this seems more common among younger speakers.

text:
An appositional noun phrase consists of two noun phrases which have identical or similar reference. Very commonly, the first noun phrase is either a personal pronoun ex:4:x835 or a kinship term ex:4:x836, ex:4:x839, the second one a proper name, but there are other possibilities as well ex:4:x837, ex:4:x838.

Yo nena nie=ke nefa maak-i-yem. \\
1s. unm 2s. gen 2s/p.uncle 2s. acc tell-Np- pr.1s \\
`I, your uncle, am telling you this.'

Yena yaiya Tup ifa=ke keraw-a-k. \\
1s. gen 1s/p.uncle Tup snake= cf bite- pa -3s \\
`My Uncle Tup was bitten by a snake.'

Inasina Rubaruba nain=ke ona emeria aaw-ep p-ikiw-o-k.\\
spirit Rubaruba that1= cf 3s. gen woman take- ss. seq bpx -go- pa -3s \\
`The spirit Rubaruba took his wife and went.'

Manina gelemuta, esewa, nena kookal-owa=pa perek-i-nan.\\
garden small esewa 2s. gen like- nmz = loc pull.out-Np- fu.2s \\
`You may harvest the little garden, ``esewa'', at your desire.'

Wokome=ke wiimasip oko, suwina gelemuta nain maak-e-k \\
3s/p.grandmother= cf 3s/p.grandchild other female small that tell- pa -3s \\
`The grandmother told her other grandchild, the little girl '
summary: An appositional noun phrase consists of two noun phrases with identical or similar reference. The first noun phrase is often a personal pronoun or kinship term and the second a proper name, though other combinations also occur.

text:
The head of an adjective phrase ( ap ) is an adjective. Most commonly it occurs alone, but it can be intensified by an intensity adverb either preceding or following it, or both ex:4:x841. The negator marew `none, no' when following the adjective, negates its quality, thus creating its opposite ex:4:x842.

Owowa nain lawiliw manek(a) akena. \\
village that1 rather big very \\
`The village is rather big'

Koora eliw(a) marew nan ik-e-mik. \\
house good none there be- pa -1/3p \\
`They live in the bad (lit: no-good) house.'

When the adjective masia `bitter' takes a nominalized verb as its modifier, the meaning of the adjective changes to indicate that one is doing a lot of some action ex:4:x840.

Mua manin(a) mauw-ow(a) masia nain emeria wi-i-mik. \\
man garden work- nmz compulsive that1 woman give.him-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`We give a wife to a hard-working man.'

The adjective phrase functions as a post-modifier in a noun phrase ex:4:x842, or as a non-verbal predicate ex:4:x841.

A coordinate adjective phrase is also possible ex:4:x891. The additive ne is used instead of juxtaposition.

Oka keraw-a-k nain efefa ne eliwa akena. \\
hand.drum carve- pa -3s that1 light add good very \\
`The hand drum that he carved is light and very good.'

The pragmatic function of adjectives in discourse For the function of adjectives in English and Mandarin Chinese spoken text see and. The former claims their main function is to predicate the property of an established discourse referent; attributive function, or modification, is secondary and used almost exclusively for new participants. Croft, however, considers modification the main discourse function of the adjectives. As for Papuan languages, Roberts reports that in Amele the adjective normally functions as a modifying (lit: attributive) element in a NP ( Roberts1987). seems to vary according to the language. In Mauwake, the modification of a new participant is the main function of adjective phrases. In the text data nearly half of the occurrences (48%) of adjectives were in attributive positions where the adjective modified a new participant. Also, a known participant is modified by an adjective especially in cases where the adjective is needed for contrast: manin( a) maneka `big garden' and manin( a) gelemuta `small garden', referring to two different types of garden (also called ekina and esewa, respectively), were repeated several times in a text describing garden work.
summary:
An adjective phrase in this language has an adjective as its head and may appear alone or be intensified by an adverb before or after it. The negator *marew* following the adjective reverses its meaning, and an adjective can also change meaning when modified by a nominalized verb; adjective phrases may function as noun-phrase postmodifiers, non-verbal predicates, or coordinate phrases joined by *ne*.

The passage also discusses discourse use of adjectives, noting that in Mauwake their main function is to modify new participants, with nearly half of the text examples occurring in attributive position. Known participants are also modified when contrast is needed, such as to distinguish different kinds of gardens.

text:
A quantifier phrase ( qp ) usually only consists of a quantifier head ex:4:x845 ( sec:3.4 ), but it can be modified by a few intensity adverbs ex:4:x844 ( sec:3.9.2 ).

I koora kuisow yiar aw-o-k. \\
1p. unm house one 1p. dat burn- pa -3s \\
`One of our houses burned.'

Koora arow akena ku-a-mik. \\
house three truly build- pa -1/3p \\
`We built exactly three houses.'

A quantifier phrase most commonly functions as a post-modifier in a noun phrase ex:4:x846, but it can also be used as a non-verbal predicate ex:4:x843.

Maamuma unowa akena aaw-e-mik. \\
money much truly/very get- pa -1/3p \\
`They got very much money.'

Yo muuka arow. \\
1s. unm son three. \\
`I have three sons.' (Lit: `My sons are three.)

Quantifier phrases may also be coordinated. The most plausible coordination semantically is disjunction ex:4:x1360:

Waaya maneka wiowa erup-i e arow naap mik-iwkin um-i-ya.\\
pig big spear two= qm or three thus spear-2/3p. ds die-Np- pr.3s \\
`They spear a big pig with two or three spears and it dies.'
summary: A quantifier phrase usually consists of just a quantifier head, though it can be modified by a few intensity adverbs. It most often functions as a post-modifier in a noun phrase, but it can also serve as a non-verbal predicate, as in expressions of possession or quantity. Quantifier phrases may also be coordinated, with disjunction being the most natural semantic interpretation.

text:
The possessive phrase Not to be confused with the Possessive NP. is a very specific and rare structure ex:4:x847. It consists of an unmarked or genitive pronoun, followed by the long form of the dative pronoun ( sec:3.5.5 ), which has developed from the dative pronoun and the verb ik- `be'. The verb has lost all inflection and only retains the root, which has merged into the dative pronoun. The possessive phrase only functions as a non-verbal predicate. It is always without a head noun. A co-referential noun or pronoun is encoded in an earlier np in the same clause.

Auwa maa unowa nain pun yo/yena efarik. \\
father thing many that1 also 1s. unm /1s. gen 1s. dat \\
`My father's possessions, too, are mine.'
summary: The possessive phrase is a rare construction made up of an unmarked or genitive pronoun followed by the long form of the dative pronoun, which has developed from the dative pronoun plus the verb *ik-* ‘be’. In this structure, the verb has lost all inflection and survives only as a root merged into the dative pronoun. It functions only as a non-verbal predicate, always lacks a head noun, and refers back to a co-referential noun or pronoun mentioned earlier in the same clause.

text:
There is no justification in Mauwake for a verb phrase as it is understood in the generative sense, i.e. as a constituent including almost everything else than the subject of the sentence. The verb phrases in the traditional sense of the word, a group of verbs functioning as one unit, are treated under verbal clusters ( sec:3.8.5 ). But there is one structure that can be called a verb phrase: an accusative pronoun plus a verb. In this structure, nothing can come between the two elements, not even a verbal negation, which is usually placed immediately before the verb.

Every transitive verb requires an accusative pronoun for a [+human] object, regardless of whether there is an object noun phrase or not ex:4:x848-- ex:4:x850. The accusative pronoun is also required, when the verb is in benefactive form and the beneficiary is plural ex:4:x851.

Nan wi owow mua wia maak-e-mik, \\
there 3p. unm village man 3p. acc tell- pa -1/3p \\
`There they told the village men,... '

Nefa war-iwkin naap ma-e. \\
2s. acc shoot-2/3p. ds thus say- imp.2s \\
`When they shoot you, say like that.'

Mua me wia imen-a-mik. \\
man not 3p. acc find- pa -1/3p \\
`We did not find the men.'

Yaapan=ke i emeria yia aaw-urum-i-kuan. \\
Japan= cf 1p. unm woman 1p. acc take- distr / a -Np- fu.3p \\
`Japan will take all of us women.'

Takira enow gelemuta wia on-om-a-mik. \\
child meal small 3p. acc make- ben - bnfy 2- pa -1/3p \\
`We made a feast for the children.'
summary:
Mauwake does not justify a verb phrase in the generative sense, but it does have a tighter structure consisting of an accusative pronoun plus a verb. Nothing may intervene between these two elements, not even verbal negation, which normally comes immediately before the verb.  

A transitive verb requires an accusative pronoun for a [+human] object whether or not an object noun phrase is present, and the pronoun is also required with benefactive verbs when the beneficiary is plural.

text:
An adverbial phrase may consist of an adverb word alone, or it may be modified by an intensity adverb, a noun phrase plus a clitic or a postposition, or a dative pronoun functioning as a [+human] locative phrase.

The main function of an adverbial phrase is to modify the verb. An advp is an optional constituent in a clause, not an obligatory argument.

The default position of the adverbial phrase depends on the semantic type of the advp. Recursion is possible, and is more common in the case of locative and temporal phrases than the others.
summary: An adverbial phrase may consist of a single adverb or be expanded by an intensity adverb, a noun phrase with a clitic or postposition, or a dative pronoun used as a [+human] locative phrase. Its main function is to modify the verb, and it is an optional clause constituent rather than an obligatory argument. The default position of an adverbial phrase depends on its semantic type, and recursive adverbial phrases are possible, especially with locative and temporal phrases.

text:
The number of locative adverbs is small ( sec:3.6.3 ). Most locative phrases are made up of a noun phrase plus a clitic if they indicate a location, source or path, and of a noun phrase only if they indicate a goal. distinguishes between the locative adverbials and the locative objects of certain verbs. The former have the whole clause in their scope, the latter only the verb. While there is this scope difference between the two, they are syntactically similar in Mauwake.

The locative adverbs ( sec:3.6.3 ), all of which are deictic, occur by themselves, without modifiers ex:4:x870-- ex:4:x1833. The same form can be used for location, source, or goal, depending on the verb.

Miiw-aasa nan ik-eya mua nain nabena suuw-a-mik. \\
land-canoe there be-2/3s. ds man that1 carrying.pole push- pa -1/3p \\
`The car stayed there, and they carried the man on their shoulders.'

Fura op-ap ik-o-n nain feeke wu-e. \\
knife hold- ss. seq be- pa -2s that1 here. cf put- imp.2s \\
`Put here the knife that you are holding.'

Manin(a) onoma maa en-owa nan aaw-i-ya. \\
garden basis thing eat- nmz there get-Np- pr.3s \\
`An owner of a garden (lit: the garden basis) gets his food from there.'

When the locative phrase is based on a noun phrase, one form is used both for a location where something takes place and a source, but a goal is marked differently. The phrases indicating a location are formed by adding the locative clitic - pa to a noun phrase ex:4:x856-- ex:4:x865.

Pon sisina=pa ik-eya mik-a-m. \\
turtle shallow.water= loc be-2/3s. ds spear- pa -1s \\
`The turtle was in shallow water and I speared it.'

Sapara=pa nan suusa iw-e-mik. \\
Sapara= loc there needle give.him- pa -1/3p \\
`There in Sapara he was given an injection.'

Nomokowa unowa serer-iw-ap Takora=pa nan or-o-mik.\\
tree many hang-go- ss. seq Takora= loc there descend- pa -1/3p \\
`They went hanging to many trees, and at Takora they got down.'

Source is also marked as a location, with the clitic - pa ex:4:x858-- ex:4:x864. In some cases there is possible ambiguity as to the interpretation, but the context usually provides a clue.

Parosifa siisim-ep iinan aasa=pa wafur-a-mik. \\
paper write- ss. seq sky canoe= loc throw- pa -1/3p \\
`They wrote papers and threw them from airplanes.'

Aite=ke manina=pa yia aaw-om-iwkin enim-i-mik. \\
1s/p.mother= cf garden= loc 1p. acc get- ben -1s/p. ds eat-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`Our mothers get (it) from the garden for us and we eat (it).'

Me fan Madang kame=pa ekap-e-mik. \\
not here Madang side= loc come- pa -1/3p \\
`They didn't come here from the Madang side.'

The noun phrase indicating a goal normally does not take the locative clitic or any other marking. The directional verbs are the most common ones used with goal ex:4:x860, ex:4:x861, but other verbs of motion can be used as well ex:4:x862, ex:4:x863.

Ae, o fiker gone urup-o-k. \\
yes 3s. unm kunai.grass middle ascend- pa -3s \\
`Yes, he went up to the middle of the kunai grass area.'

Manina=pa nan Source koka Goal iw-a-mik. \\
garden= loc there jungle go- pa -1/3p \\
`From the garden there the day they went into the jungle.'

Medebur karu-eka, baurar-eka. \\
Medebur run- imp.2p flee- imp.2p \\
`Run to Medebur, flee!'

Ulingan nan bom fu-fuurk-ikiw-e-mik. \\
Ulingan there bomb rdp -throw-go- pa -1/3p \\
`They went throwing bombs to Ulingan.'

It is possible to mark the goal with the locative clitic if the goal is mainly important as the location of the following verb. The frequency of this usage for the clitic is low. Example (3. ex:3:x1878 ) is repeated below as ex:4:x1884:

Ne soran-emi epia mukuna=pa or-omi aw-o-k.
\\
add get.startled firewood fire= loc descend- ss. sim burn- pa -3s \\
`And he got startled and fell on the fire and burned himself.'

When the locative phrase is [+human], the dative pronoun ( sec:3.5.5 ) must be used ex:4:x1061, ex:4:x1939.

Mua oko=ke waaya nain mik-ap nefar aaw-i-non. \\
man other= cf pig that1 spear- ss. seq 2s. dat take-Np- fu.3s \\
`Another man will spear the pig and take it from you.'

Feeke wiar ik-ok kiiriw mua wiar urup-e. \\
here. cf 3. dat be- ss again man 3. dat ascend- imp.2s \\
`Stay here with him and (then) go (back) to your husband again.'

The dative pronoun is also commonly added when the location is a village or a larger area, which is seen mainly as a setting for the people. In both ex:4:x862 and ex:4:x863 above it is the location which is in focus, in the former as the closest village to flee to, and in the latter as an object of bombing, so the dative pronoun is not used. In ex:4:x1801 a certain culturally important place referred to is in the area of the Koran village people and considered their property:

Koran epa=pa wiar ik-ua. \\
Koran place= loc 3. dat be- pa.3s \\
`It is in Koran area.'

The noun phrase indicating a path is marked with the instrumental clitic - iw ex:4:x866, ex:4:x867, or occasionally with the locative clitic - pa (3. ex:3:x770 ).

Iinan=iw iinan=iw wu-ami feenap ikiw-o-k. \\
on.top= inst on.top= inst put ss. sim like.this go- pa -3s \\
`They (airplanes) flew (lit: put) high up, high up, and went like this '

Saa =iw ir-am-ika-i-mik, oos ono-onaiya. \\
sand= inst ascend- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.1/3p, horse rdp -with \\
`They are coming along the beach, with horses.'
summary:
The passage explains that Mauwake has a small set of locative adverbs, all deictic, which occur alone and can refer to location, source, or goal depending on the verb. It contrasts these with locative phrases built from noun phrases: locations and sources are typically marked with the locative clitic -pa, goals are usually unmarked, and paths are marked with the instrumental clitic -iw, though -pa may occasionally mark a goal or path.  

It also notes that when the locative phrase is [+human], a dative pronoun must be used, and that dative marking is often added with villages or larger areas when these are treated as the setting belonging to people.

text:
When a clause has more locative phrases than one, the following rules apply. If the phrases have a different function, source is placed before goal ex:4:x861. When they have the same function and a deictic locative adverb strengthens another locative phrase, the adverb follows the other locative ex:4:x857, ex:4:x863. But the dative pronoun, when used locatively, has to be placed even after the locative adverb ex:4:x1939. When both of the phrases have an independent meaning, the phrase indicating the more general location comes first, and the one marking the more specific location follows ex:4:x868, ex:4:x869.

Mia aka nain aaw-ep p-ikiw-ep manina=pa upuna =pa wu-a-k.\\
body blood that1 take- ss. seq bpx -go- ss. seq garden= loc row= loc put- pa -3s \\
`She took the menstrual blood with her and put it in a (plant) row in a garden.'

Ikiw-ep eeneke wiena owowa=pa uruf-a-mik, \\
go- ss. seq there 3p. gen village= loc see- pa -1/3p \\
`They went and there, in their village, they saw, '
summary: When a clause contains more than one locative phrase, their order depends on their functions and meanings. A source phrase comes before a goal phrase, while a deictic locative adverb follows the locative phrase it modifies; a locative dative pronoun follows even the locative adverb. If both phrases are independent, the more general location precedes the more specific one.

text:
Temporals mark location in time, so it is natural that temporal phrases behave very similarly to locative phrases. They can consist of a temporal adverb ( sec:3.9.1.2 ), possibly modified by an intensity adverb ( sec:3.9.2 ) or of a noun phrase ( sec:4.1 ) with a head noun indicating time ex:4:x872, plus a locative clitic with some nouns ex:4:x873 ( sec:3.12.4 ).

Uuriw akena mukuna nain kerer-e-k. \\
morning truly/very fire that1 appear- pa -3s \\
`The fire started early in the morning.'

Ne fraide=pa maapora puk-o-k, urera. \\
add Friday= loc feast burst- pa -3s afternoon \\
`And on Friday the feast started, in the afternoon.'

Recursion of temporal phrases is possible and quite common. When there are two or more temporal phrases in the same clause, the order is determined by whether the temporals are deictic and/or specific ex:4:x874-- ex:4:x876 ( sec:3.9.1.2 ). Their default order relative to each other is as follows:

(non-deictic non-specific) deictic non-specific deictic specific TempNP (day) non-deictic specific TempNP (time of day) (non-deictic non-specific)

The position of the non-deictic non-specific temporal is either as the first ex:4:x874 or the last element ex:4:x876 of the group of temporals.

Ne nainiw sande uura yiam fiirim-e-mik. \\
add again Sunday night 1p. refl gather- pa -1/3p \\
`And we gathered again on Sunday night.'

Uurika mande uuriw amia mua feeke kerer-i-non. \\
tomorrow Monday morning bow man here. cf appear-Np- fu.3s \\
`Tomorrow Monday a policeman will come here in the morning.'

Unan urera ama ikur naap on-a-mik. \\
yesterday afternoon sun five thus do- pa -1/3p \\
`We did it yesterday afternoon around five o'clock.'

Ikoka trinde =pa nainiw aakun-i-yen. \\
later Wednesday= loc again talk-Np- fu.1p \\
`We'll talk again later on Wednesday.'

When a noun phrase acts as a temporal phrase, the locative clitic - pa is attached to it ex:4:x876, unless it is followed by another temporal phrase specifying it further or it includes a demonstrative ex:4:x875. If there are several of these temporal noun phrases, their relative order is from the larger time unit to the smaller one ex:4:x878.

Mokoma fain siiwa Mas =pa weeser-i-non. \\
year this month March= loc finish-Np- fu.3s \\
`It will finish in March this year.'

A temporal phrase may be formed with the instrumental clitic - iw ( sec:3.12.5 ) when something takes place repeatedly at the same time of the day. The example (3. ex:3:x1882 ) is here repeated as ex:4:x1907:

I amirik= iw... Gawar wiar ikiw-e-mik. \\
1p. unm daytime= inst Gawar 3. dat go- pa -1/3p \\
`In the daytime we (always) went to Gawar '
summary:
Temporal phrases behave much like locative phrases and may be formed either by a temporal adverb, optionally modified by an intensity adverb, or by a noun phrase with a time-denoting head noun. When temporal noun phrases are used, the locative clitic **-pa** is usually attached, unless the phrase is further specified by another temporal phrase or contains a demonstrative.

The passage also notes that multiple temporal phrases can occur in one clause, with their order determined by deictic and specificity distinctions, and that when several temporal noun phrases are present, they are ordered from larger time units to smaller ones. Finally, a temporal phrase can take the instrumental clitic **-iw** to express repeated events at the same time of day.

text:
An adverbial phrase indicating manner most often consists of just a manner adverb ex:4:x880 ( sec:3.9.1.3 ). That is occasionally intensified by an intensity adverb ex:4:x879, ex:4:x881( sec:3.9.2 ).

Iwera nainiw kaken iimar-e-k. \\
coconut again straight stand.up- pa -3s \\
`The coconut palm stood up straight again.'

Koran wiena balisow akena epa nain amis-ar-e-mik.\\
Koran 3p. gen well truly/very place that1 knowledge- inch - pa -1/3p\\
`The Koran people themselves know that place very well.'

O iiwawun samor aaw-o-k. \\
3p. unm altogether badly get- pa -3s \\
`He got it really bad (= he got into a very bad condition).'

A manner phrase can also be formed by a noun phrase plus a clitic, either instrumental - iw ex:4:x882 or, less frequently, with locative - pa ex:4:x884.

Siowa wiawi=ke siowa aluowa miim-ap karu-(o)w(a)=iw ekap-o-k.\\
dog 3s/p.father dog noise hear- ss. seq run- nmz = inst come- pa -3s \\
`The dog's master heard its noise and came running.'

Yiena kae sira=pa mauw-owa ik-ua. \\
1p. gen grandfather custom= loc work- nmz be- pa.3s \\
`We have to work according to the custom of our grandfathers.'

If there are more manner phrases than one, one of them is usually deictic naap `thus, like that' ex:4:x883, or feenap `like this' either preceding or following the other manner phrase(s).

Wi Yaapan naap kuisow=iw ekap-em-ik-e-mik. \\
3p. unm Japan thus one= inst come- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
`The Japanese came like that one by one.'

When comparison is indicated in the manner phrase, the postposition saarik `like, as' follows the noun phrase ex:4:x885.

Wie, wiawi nain ifa saarik in-urum-ep-ik-e-mik.\\
3s/p.uncle 3s/p.father that1 snake like sleep- distr / a - ss. seq -be- pa -1/3s \\
`His uncles and fathers were all sleeping like snakes.'
