One type of a manner phrase is one that indicates instrument. It is always formed with a noun phrase plus one of three clitics: instrumental - iw ( sec:3.12.5 ), locative - pa ( sec:3.12.4 ) or comitative - iya ( sec:3.12.1 ). The instrumental clitic is the most common ex:4:x886, ex:4:x889.

Ifa mia nain fura=iw lalat-em-ik-om-a-mik. \\
snake skin that1 knife= inst sweep- ss. sim -be- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p \\
`They kept scraping the snake skin off her with a knife.'... wiena opaimik=iw yia maak-em-ik-e-mik. \\
3p. gen mouth/language= inst 1p. acc tell- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
` they kept telling us in their language.'

When a coordinate noun phrase is made into an instrumental manner phrase, the instrumental clitic only follows the last noun phrase ex:4:x892.

Wiena merena ne wapen=iw era akup-amik. \\
3p. gen foot add hand= inst way search- pa -1/3p \\
`With their feet and hands they felt (lit: searched) for the road.'

The use of locative clitic is restricted almost exclusively to those cases where the instrument is a vehicle ex:4:x887, so they could also be understood as locatives. In other cases it is used rarely ex:4:x888.

Yo iiriw iinan aasa=pa karu-owa erup ar-ep me keker op-a-m. \\
1s. unm earlier sky canoe= loc run- nmz two become- ss. seq not fear hold- pa -1s \\
`I had already travelled by plane twice, and was not afraid.'

Sureka =pa owora nain teek-ap aaw-e-mik. \\
harvesting.stick= loc betelnut that1 pluck- ss. seq get- pa -1/3p \\
`They picked the betelnuts with a harvesting stick.'

The comitative clitic is also possible but infrequent in instrumental manner phrases ex:4:x890. Its use in this function may be influenced by Tok Pisin, where wantaim `together (with)' is used not only for accompaniment, but for instruments as well.

Mauwa ar-e-n, amia=iya nenar-e-mik=i? \\
what become- pa -2s bow/gun= com shoot.you- pa -1/3p= qm \\
`What happened to you, did they shoot you with a gun?'

In Mauwake texts, manner phrases are much less frequent than either locative or temporal phrases.
summary: Manner phrases in Mauwake are usually simple adverbial phrases headed by a manner adverb, sometimes intensified by an additional adverb, and they may also be formed from a noun phrase plus a clitic. When comparison is involved, the postposition *saarik* ‘like, as’ follows the noun phrase, and instrumental manner phrases are most often marked with *-iw*, with *-pa* and *-iya* used less often; coordinated noun phrases take the instrumental clitic only on the last noun. The passage also notes that locative clitic use is mainly restricted to vehicles, and that manner phrases are less frequent than locative or temporal phrases in Mauwake texts.

text:
A clause, I use the separate terms clause and sentence to avoid confusion. A simple sentence consists of just one clause, but most of the sentences in Mauwake have more than one clause in either coordinate, chaining or subordinate relationship. or simple sentence, typically expresses one predication and is a minimal utterance that can stand alone.

In Mauwake the predicate is the only obligatory element in those clauses that have a verbal predicate. Verbless clauses need to have both an overt subject and a predicate. The different clause types are discussed in sec:5.3 -- sec:5.6.

Instead of the common two-way distinction between main and subordinate clauses, in Trans New Guinea languages it is practical to talk about main, medial and subordinate clauses. Main clauses have a finite verb, and most commonly it is the last element in a sentence. Medial clauses ( sec:8.2.1 ) are coordinate with the main clauses but dependent on them, and the verbs are in medial form ( sec:3.8.3.5 ). The default position for a medial clause is non-final, but for pragmatic purposes it may be postposed to follow the main clause. Also a subordinate clause ( sec:8.3 ) usually precedes the main clause.
summary:
A simple sentence in Mauwake consists of one clause and typically expresses one predication, while most sentences contain multiple clauses in coordinate, chaining, or subordinate relations. In clauses with a verbal predicate, the predicate is the only obligatory element, but verbless clauses require both an overt subject and a predicate.  

Rather than a two-way main/subordinate distinction, Trans New Guinea languages are better described as having main, medial, and subordinate clauses: main clauses have finite verbs and are usually final, medial clauses are coordinate yet dependent and usually non-final, and subordinate clauses typically precede the main clause.

text:
Two seemingly conflicting statements about the clausal constituent order in Papuan languages have been given by and. maintains that they have a rigid sov order; claims that the order in most Papuan languages is relatively free, and therefore he prefers to call them just verb-final (ibid. 10). But it seems that the two linguists are talking about somewhat different things, and both of them are correct in what they say. The default constituent order in neutral sentences is sov, as Wurm claims, but Foley is right in that the interpretation of the arguments of a verb as subject or object does not rely heavily on the constituent order. Especially in languages with extensive verb morphology marking the syntactic roles on the verb itself the order of the nominals can be relatively free, and is mainly constrained by pragmatic factors.

The basic constituent order in Mauwake clauses is quite rigid sov, even if the verb morphology cross-references the syntactic roles to some extent. Although only a fraction of the clauses in the text corpus -- less than 10% -- have an overt subject and object np it is possible to establish the dominant order. About nine out of ten of those clauses that do have an overt subject and object np manifest sov order. SOV: 210 clauses, OSV: 22 clauses They are also pragmatically neutral ex:5:x896, whereas the other possible order, osv, only occurs when the object is fronted as a theme ex:5:x897.

Owow mua S kau kuisow O aaw-e-mik. \\
village man cow one get- pa -1/3p \\
`The village men got one cow.'

Yena aamun O ariwa=ke S aaw-o-k. \\
1s. poss 1s/p.younger.sibling arrow= cf get- pa -3s \\
`My younger brother was killed by an arrow.'

As was described in sec:1.4.2.2, Mauwake exhibits many typological characteristics associated with sov languages.

The basic constituent order is always based on the structure of a transitive clause. Intransitive clauses ( sec:5.4 ) do not have objects, but otherwise the structure is the same as that in the transitive clauses. The structure of other types of clause is described in the relevant sections.

The constituent order in an extended predication is harder to establish, because a clause typically has very few constituents, the average being only 1.2 non-verb constituents per clause; because any non-verbal element can be fronted as topic; and because the subject is often shown only by a verbal suffix and the object by an accusative pronoun in the VP. A clause formula for a maximally extended predication is hypothetical, and mainly shows the order of the constituents on the basis of their attested orders in relation to each other:

S X 1 O 1 X 2 O 2 X 3 V

There are two object positions The two objects are discussed further in the next sections sec:5.2 and sec:5.3 and three X-positions for adverbial phrases. Depending on the grammatical model, the adverbial phrases may be called peripherals, obliques, satellites or adjuncts. I call them peripherals and reserve the term adjunct for the non-verb part of an adjunct plus verb construction. If a clause has only one object, it occupies the O 2 position immediately preceding the verb regardless of whether the semantic function is that of a patient, a recipient or a beneficiary. When there are two objects, their position is dictated mainly by their relative topicality. A [+human] argument tends to be more topical than a [ -human] one, so an object that is semantically a recipient ex:5:x928, ex:5:x933, or a beneficiary ex:5:x916, typically occupies the first object position, and the other object, typically a [ -human] patient, fills the second object position.

Muuka O1 sira O2 iw-i-mik. \\
son custom give.him-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`They teach the right behaviour to the son.'

Sarak=ke wi takira O1 inglis O2 wia O1 ofakow-i-ya. \\
Sarak= cf 3p. unm child English 3p. acc teach-Np- pr.3s \\
`Sarak teaches the children English.'

Compare this with: Sarak=ke inglis wia ofakowiya `Sarak teaches (them) English' and Sarak=ke wi takira wia ofakowiya `Sarak teaches the children.' Both the recipient and the patient are coded in the same way as an object.

Ni auwa O1 maa O2 p-ikiw-om-aka. \\
2p. unm 1s/p.father food bpx -go- ben - bnfy 2. imp.2p \\
`Take food to/for father.'

If a [-human] patient object is more topical than a [+human] object, it can occupy the first object position. A more topical [+human] object in ex:5:x917 would have an unmarked third person plural pronoun before the [-human] object. More examples of can be found in sec:5.3.2.

Onak=ke aaya O1 wia O2 aaw-om-aya enim-or-om-ik-e-mik. \\
3s/p.mother sugarcane 3p. acc get- ben - bnfy 2.2/3s eat-descend- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
`Their mother got sugarcane for them and they went down eating it.'

If both the objects are [-human], the one that is more clearly the patient, i.e. more profoundly affected by the action, occupies the O 2 position ex:5:x927. Usually the object in O 1 position has a more locative-type meaning ex:5:x934.

Epira O1 lolom O2 if-e-mik. \\
plate mud smear- pa -1/3p \\
`They smeared the plate with mud' or: `They smeared mud on the plate.'

Wut makena nain O1 ona O2 puuk-a-m. \\
Derris.root.tree seed that1 hole cut- pa -1s \\
`I cut a hole in the seed of a derris root tree.'

The normal position of the peripherals is between the subject and the object np, if any ex:5:x895, or between the first and second object ex:5:x913.

Yo uura arua isim-ap... \\
1s. unm night torch light- ss. seq \\
`I lighted a torch in the night and...'

Wiipa nain O1 samapora iinan=pa AdvP epia O2 ururum-om-ap \\
daughter that floor top= loc fire light- ben - bnfy 2. ss. seq \\
`They lighted a fire for the daughter on top of the floor, and...'

A locative adverbial can also come between an object np and a verb. A deictic locative phrase ex:5:x914 or another short locative phrase ex:5:x931 is common in this position.
summary:
The passage argues that Papuan languages can be both “rigid SOV” in neutral clause order and relatively free in how verb arguments are interpreted, especially where verbal morphology marks syntactic roles. In Mauwake, the default clause order is strongly SOV: most clauses with overt subject and object noun phrases show SOV, while other orders are pragmatically marked, such as OSV when the object is fronted as a theme.

It also explains that extended clauses can contain multiple object positions and peripheral elements between subject, objects, and verb. When there are two objects, their order is mainly determined by topicality: more topical or more human arguments tend to appear earlier, while the more patient-like or less topical object appears closer to the verb.

text:
Emer en-ow(a) mua=ko emeria O fan AdvP aaw-o-k. \\
sago eat- nmz man= nf woman here get- pa -3s \\
`A Sepik man got a wife here.'

Yo maa unowa O koora=pa AdvP wu-a-m. \\
1s. unm thing many house= loc put- pa -1s \\
`I put (the) many things in the house.'

The position immediately before the verb is also the only possible place for a [+human] locative adverbial, manifested by a dative pronoun ( sec:3.5.5 ). In both ex:5:x854 and ex:5:x855 there are two locative adverbials, a [-human] and a [+human] one. The [+human] locative adverbial refers to the people of the location. If it is left out, the other locative refers to the location but not the people.

Ni koka-pa AdvP wiar AdvP in-em-ik-e-man nain rc kerer-omak-eka. \\
2p. unm jungle= loc 3. dat sleep- ss. sim -be- pa -2p that1 appear- distr / pl - imp.2p \\
`You(pl.) who have slept in the jungle (villages), come!'

I amirk=iw Gawar AdvP wiar AdvP urup-e-mik. \\
1p. unm day= inst Gawar 3. dat ascend- pa -1/3p \\
`During the day we went to Gawar.'

If there are more adverbial phrases than one, a temporal phrase normally precedes any others ex:5:x915. The relative order of the other adverbial phrases is syntactically quite free and depends on their relative topicality ex:5:x915, ex:5:x918.

I amirika owowa ewur me ekap-em-ik-e-mik. \\
1p. unm day village quickly not come- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
`In the daytime we didn't come quickly to the village.'

Niena ikoka oram neeke ika-i-non. \\
2s/p.mother later for.nothing there. cf be-Np- fu.3s \\
`Your mother will later just be there (without you).'

Mokoma kuisow naap fan yiam=iya ik-e-mik. \\
year one thus here 1p. refl = com be- pa -1/3p \\
`They were here with us for about a year.'

Both transitive ex:5:x981 and intransitive clauses ex:5:x1057 are negated with the verbal negator me `not' placed immediately before the verb phrase. For the placement of me as a constituent negator, see sec:6.2.2.

I me wia amukar-e-mik. \\
1p. unm not 3. acc scold- pa -1/3p \\
`We didn't scold them.'

Nain yo me baurar-em-ik-e-m. \\
but 1s. unm not run.away- ss. sim -be- pa -1s \\
`But I didn't keep running away.'

As was mentioned above, pragmatic factors influence the constituent order. A constituent that is fronted as a theme to the beginning of the clause is still part of the constituent structure of the clause ex:5:x930 (for theme, see sec:9.1 ). In Amele the pre-verbal position is a focus position, but in Mauwake this does not seem to be the case. Focus is indicated by a heavier stress and sometimes by focus markers.

Oposia gelemuta O1 wiam erup fain wia O2 wu-om-a-m. \\
meat little 3p. refl two this 3p. acc put- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1s \\
`A bit of the meat I put (aside) for these two.'

A left-dislocated theme ( sec:9.1 ) and an afterthought are outside the clause proper. A left-dislocated theme ex:5:x935 is separated from the clause by a short pause and a comma intonation, slightly rising pitch at the end of the utterance. An afterthought ex:5:x929, right-dislocated, is also separated from the rest of the clause by a short pause.

Irak-owa fa, opora unowa akena. \\
fight- nmz intj talk much very \\
`The war, now - there is much to talk about.'

Inasin opaimika eliwa me yia maak-e-mik, wi Yaapan=ke. \\
spirit talk good not 1p. acc tell- pa -1/3p 3p. unm Japan= cf \\
`They didn't speak good Pidgin to us, the Japanese (didn't).'
summary: The passage explains that clause-internal constituent order in Mauwake is flexible and influenced by pragmatic factors such as topicality, with temporal adverbials typically preceding other adverbials and the relative order of other adverbials being freer. It also notes that the position immediately before the verb is reserved for negation with *me* and for a [+human] locative adverbial, while focus is not marked by pre-verbal position but by stress and sometimes focus markers. Left-dislocated themes and right-dislocated afterthoughts lie outside the clause proper and are set off by pauses and intonation.

text:
Syntactic arguments together with the verb form the core of a clause. They differ from the peripherals in that they have a grammatical relation to the verb, and therefore have to do with the valence of the clause. The basic syntactic structure is influenced by the arguments but not by the peripherals. In Mauwake the only syntactic arguments are subject and object.

Since Mauwake is very clearly a nominative-accusative type language, the grammatical role of subject and the semantic role of agent or actor normally converge on the same constituent, which usually, but not always, also has the pragmatic role of topic. Another semantic role the subject may have is that of experiencer, and in verbless clauses that of `` theme''. This semantic role ``theme'' is different from the pragmatic function ( sec:9.1 ) and refers to the participant which is said to be in some state, or located in some place. Because of a possible confusion with the pragmatic role of theme, the term for the semantic role is written inside double quotes.

The syntactic coding of the subject includes both the clausal constituent order and cross-referencing on the verb ex:5:x936. In pragmatically neutral clauses the subject is the first of two argument noun phrases. It is also obligatorily marked on the person/number suffix of the verb. The same distinctions are made in the subject marking of the verb as in the personal pronouns: first, second or third person and singular or plural number.

Komori emeria wu-a-k. \\
Komori woman put- pa -3s \\
`Komori buried his wife.'

The subject governs reflexivization. A noun phrase itself is marked as subject only when the subject np is a pronoun: then it has to be unmarked ex:5:x920 ( sec:3.5.2.1 ) or in the genitive case ( sec:3.5.4 ).

Tirinde uura i nainiw yiam fiirim-e- mik. \\
Wednesday evening 1p. unm again 1p. refl gather- pa -1/3p \\
`On Wednesday evening we gathered again.'

The switch-reference system ( sec:8.2.3 ) basically tracks the subject ex:5:x921. Roberts maintains that in Amele and most other Papuan languages the switch reference system tracks the thematic notion of topic across clauses ( Roberts1988b, Roberts1997). But his definition of topic ( Roberts1988b) is such that in Mauwake it practically excludes all other clause constituents except the subject.

imen- ap maak- iwkin o miim-o-k. \\
find- ss. seq tell-2/3p. ds 3s. unm precede- pa -3s \\
` when they found him and told him, he went ahead.'

In ex:5:x922, the object/topic/theme of the first clause is the Australians; in the second clause they become the subject.

Wi Australia Amerika=ke wia asip- iwkin irak-owa nomak-e-mik. \\
3p. unm Australia America= cf 3p. acc help-2/3p. ds fight- nmz win- pa -1/3p \\
`Australians were helped by Americans and won the war.'

Syntactic operations like passivization and dative shift do not apply to Mauwake and consequently cannot be used to define either the subject or other syntactic arguments.

Although the prototypical subject is a [+human] agent, also an instrument that is unable to initiate an action can become a metaphorical agent, thus the subject. This is very common in expressions describing cases where one involuntarily hurts oneself with some instrument ex:5:x958. (In the following example, there is also possessor raising ( sec:5.3.2.3 ) resulting in two objects.)

Fura=ke S merena O1 efa O2 puuk-a-k. \\
knife= cf leg 1s. acc cut- pa -3s \\
`I cut my leg / myself in the leg.' (Lit: `A knife cut my leg.')

Because the subject is so often marked by only a verbal suffix, it would be possible to treat the subject marking on the verb as the real subject, as suggest for those languages that mark the core arguments on the verb. Although this approach would have some advantages, The main advantage would be having an overt subject in every clause, regardless of the presence of a separate subject NP. I choose the more traditional way of treating the np as the subject, both because 1) an object is not marked in the verb inflection but requires either a separate np or an accusative pronoun outside the verb proper, The small group of object cross-referencing verbs ( sec:3.8.4.2.4 ) are an exception. and because 2) the constituent order, based on the position of the subject and object nps, has many interconnections with various parts of the syntax.

The object as a syntactic role is not coded on the verb word except in the few object cross-referencing verbs ( sec:3.8.4.2.4 ). A [+human] object must be referenced by an accusative pronoun ( sec:3.5.3 ) preceding the verb in the verb phrase ( sec:4.5 ), even if the object is also expressed by a full noun phrase earlier in the clause ex:5:x923. The position of the object np in the argument structure of the clause is between the subject and the verb ex:5:x924, but this syntactic definition is not very useful, as subject and object do not co-occur very often, and sometimes when they do, the object is fronted to the clause-initial theme position ex:5:x925.

Emeria naap wia aruf-i-nen na-ep on-a-k. \\
woman thus 3p. acc hit-Np- fu.1s say- ss. seq do- pa -3s \\
`He tried to hit women that way.'

Amia mua=ke wiam erup nain wia nokar-e-k. \\
bow man= cf 3p. refl two that1 3p. acc ask- pa -3s \\
`The policeman asked those two.'

Mua emeria muuka wiipa eka=ke wia mu-o-k. \\
man woman son daughter river= cf 3p. acc swallow- pa -3s \\
`A man and his wife and children were drowned by the river.'
summary:
The passage explains that in Mauwake the core syntactic arguments of a clause are subject and object, with the subject marked by word order and obligatory verb agreement, while the object is generally not cross-referenced on the verb. Mauwake is nominative-accusative: the subject typically aligns with the semantic role of agent/actor, though it can also be an experiencer, a “theme” in verbless clauses, or even a metaphorical agent such as an instrument.  

The author argues for treating the noun phrase, not just verbal agreement, as the true subject because subject position affects syntax, reflexivization, and switch-reference, whereas object marking is much more limited. Syntactic operations like passivization and dative shift are absent, and objects may be expressed by a full noun phrase or an accusative pronoun, sometimes fronted to clause-initial topic position.

text:
There is not enough basis in Mauwake for positing a separate syntactic category indirect object. In many languages the most typical verb requiring an indirect object for the semantic role of recipient is `give'. But in Mauwake the verbs `give' and `feed/give to eat' are among the few object cross-referencing verbs ( sec:3.8.4.2.4 ), which change their stem according to the patient or recipient object. The verb `send', another cross-linguistically typical verb taking an indirect object, in Mauwake requires the benefactive suffix on the verb ( sec:3.8.4.3.2 ), rather than a marking on the np. In ex:5:x932 the verb maak- `tell' has two objects, the patient object moma `taro' and the recipient object yia `us', which is marked by an accusative pronoun in the vp in the same way as a [+human] undergoer/patient.

Wi moma O yia O maak-i-mik. \\
3p. unm taro 1p. acc tell-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`They are telling us (to get them) taro.'

This is consistent with survey results showing that ``a large number of [Papuan] languages... do not differentiate between Patient and Recipient''. Rather, there are verbs that are capable of taking two objects (ibid. 52). Usan behaves in the same way as Mauwake. Amele is one of those Papuan languages that clearly have indirect object as a syntactic category.

It could be argued that a locative adverbial is an argument rather than a peripheral clause constituent with the directional verbs For Usan, where motion verbs have either the goal or locative as a nuclear argument, see. ( sec:3.8.4.4.5 ) and with the verb ik- `be/live (somewhere)' ( sec:3.8.4.4.1 ), as these verbs so often co-occur with a locative. But these verbs also occur without a locative so often that it would be both unnatural to interpret all of those instances as elliptical constructions and sometimes difficult to posit the ``deleted'' locative ex:5:x1456, ex:5:x1457.

Maak-e-mik, ``No ikiw-e, irak-owa maneka fan-e-k a.'' \\
tell- pa -1/3p 2s. unm go- imp.2s fight- nmz big here- pa -3s intj \\
`They told him, ``Go, the war is here.'' '

Iwera uruk-am-ika-iwkin wi ikiw-emi aaw-em-ik-e-mik...\\
coconut drop- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds 3p. unm go- ss. sim get- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`When they i kept dropping coconuts, they j kept going and getting them '

The verb ik- `be' seldom occurs alone ex:5:x1458. This is probably due to its very neutral semantic character. When it denotes being or living somewhere, it is accompanied by a locative adverbial phrase ex:5:x1459. Another very common adverbial phrase accompanying the verb is a manner phrase, especially the adverb naap `thus' ex:5:x1460. Rather than positing separate clause types with adverbials as arguments it seems reasonable to subsume clauses like these under intransitive clauses.

Ika-i-nen. \\
be-Np- fu.1s \\
`I will just be like this.'

Siiwa erepam naap nan ik-ok napuma sariar-e-k. \\
moon four thus there be- ss sickness heal- pa -3s \\
`He was there about four months and his sickness was healed.'

Komor(a) muuka nain memel-am-ik-emkun naap ik - ok iir oko uura baurar-e-k. \\
cuscus son that1 tame- ss. sim -be-1s/p. ds thus be- ss time other night escape- pa -3s \\
`I was taming the cuscus and it was like that and then one night it escaped.'
summary:
The passage argues that Mauwake does not provide enough evidence for a separate syntactic category of indirect object, since verbs like *give*, *feed*, and *send* handle recipient meanings through verb cross-referencing or benefactive marking rather than a distinct NP role. It notes that in sentences with two objects, the recipient can be marked like a patient, and this pattern matches survey findings for many Papuan languages, though not all languages such as Amele.

It also suggests that locative phrases with directional verbs or with *ik-* “be/live” should not be treated as arguments in a special clause type, because these verbs often occur without locatives and their meaning is often too neutral to require one. Instead, such clauses are better analyzed as ordinary intransitive clauses, with locative or manner phrases as optional adverbials.

text:
Transitivity is an important characteristic of both a verb and a clause; which of these is primary has been an object of a great deal of discussion. In transformational grammar ( est ) verbs had to be subcategorized in the lexicon according to whether they allowed a NP-object or not. Also consider transitivity essentially a characteristic of a verb, distinguishing between the semantic, syntactic and macrorole transitivity of each verb., and, among others, maintain that transitivity is primarily a characteristic of a whole clause. Taking still another angle, Hopper and claim that transitivity is very closely bound with discourse features, namely background and foreground. This may be language-specific. In languages like English where an intransitive verb like sneeze can be made transitive in a construction He sneezed the napkin off the table, it makes sense to say that the verb combines with a transitive argument structure construction. But in Mauwake it can be claimed that the transitivity of the verb is primary. The claim is supported by the clear distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs and the fact that transitive verbs often require a dummy object when there is no real object available.

Clauses are here looked at from the point of view of syntactic transitivity: clauses that have an overt object are treated as transitive clauses, regardless of the semantic role of the object.

Linguistically the most interesting transitive clauses are those that have two or possibly even three objects. These can be divided into three different groups: clauses where a transitive verb can take more than one object without requiring any morphological or syntactic operation ( sec:5.3.2.1 ) and those where an object has been added by a valence-increasing operation ( sec:5.3.2.2 ) or by possessor raising ( sec:5.3.2.3 ).
summary:
The passage discusses whether transitivity is primarily a property of the verb or of the clause, noting that different frameworks have treated it both ways and that its status may vary by language. Here, transitivity is defined syntactically: any clause with an overt object is transitive, regardless of the object’s semantic role.  

It then notes that especially interesting transitive clauses are those with two or three objects, which fall into three types: those where a transitive verb takes multiple objects directly, those where an object is added by a valence-increasing operation, and those where an object is added through possessor raising.

text:
Monotransitive clauses have a transitive verb and one object, which is prototypically a patient ex:5:x937, ex:5:x939.

Sawur emeria nain=ke S ona soma mua nain O ifakim-o-k. \\
spirit woman that1= cf 3s. gen lover man that1 kill- pa -3s \\
`The spirit woman killed her lover.'

Amirika i S maa eneka fain O uup-ep enim-i-yen. \\
noon 1p. unm thing tooth this cook- ss. seq eat-Np- fu.1p \\
`At noon we'll cook and eat this (edible) animal.'

If there is only one np argument in a transitive clause, it is usually the object rather than subject ex:5:x941, unless marked with the contrastive focus marker - ke ex:5:x938.

Wiawi O kuum-eya aw-ep eka iw-a-k=na wia. \\
3s/p.father burn-2/3. ds burn- ss. seq river go- pa -3s= tp no \\
`(It) burned their father and when he burned he went into the river but it didn't help.'

Ufer-iwkin urup-em-ik-eya yos=ke S mik-a-m. \\
miss-2/3p. ds ascend- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds 1s. fc = cf shoot- pa -1s \\
`When they missed and it was going up, I shot it.'

But in ex:5:x940 the contrastive focus marker is not needed to disambiguate the subject from the object: wiam arow `the three of them' has to be the subject. If it were the object, it would require the third person plural accusative pronoun wia in the np.

Ne wiam arow S miim-ap \\
and 3p. refl three hear- ss. seq \\
`And the three of them heard it, and '

Clauses with an impersonal experience verb ( sec:3.8.4.4.7 ) as the predicate are also transitive. The subject is inanimate, usually a body part where the pain is felt, and the human experiencer is the object ex:5:x1012, ex:5:x1015. The possibility of adding the contrastive focus clitic to the noun indicating a body part shows that it is the subject rather than a second object ex:5:x1012.

Uuw-ap uuw-ap oona=ke S efa O sirir-i-ya. \\
work- ss. seq work- ss. seq bone= cf 1s. acc hurt-Np-3s \\
`I have worked and worked, and my bones hurt (me).'

Yo uroma S efa O op-am-ik-eya yo haussik me ikiw-e-m. \\
1s. unm stomach 1s. acc hold- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds 1s. unm aidpost not go- pa -1s \\
`I was having birth pains (lit: My stomach was holding/grabbing me) but I did not go to the aidpost.'
summary: Monotransitive clauses contain a transitive verb and one object, typically a patient, and when only one noun phrase is overtly present in such clauses, it is usually the object rather than the subject unless the subject is marked with contrastive focus. The passage also notes that clauses with impersonal experience verbs are transitive, with an inanimate body-part subject and a human experiencer object; the contrastive focus clitic can attach to the body-part noun, confirming it is the subject.

text:
A number of ditransitive clauses ex:5:x928-- ex:5:x917 were already listed under sec:5.1. They belong to the three different groups below.

Inherent ditransitivity

Some ditransitive clauses are called inherently ditransitive, because they do not require a morphological or syntactic process to make them ditransitive. The most common verbs in ditransitive clauses of this type are the object cross-referencing verbs and the utterance verb maak- `tell', and the verb ofakow- `show, teach'.

The (recipient) object is marked in the verb root of the object cross-referencing verbs denoting giving and feeding ( sec:3.8.4.2.4 ), but it may appear as a separate np as well ex:5:x950:

Mua yiar ekap-e-mik nain O pura kui-kuisow O wi-e-mik. \\
man 1p. dat come- pa -1/3p that bunch rdp -one give.them- pa -1/3p \\
`We gave a bunch each to the men who came to us.'

The section on utterance verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.6 ) describes in some detail how these verbs behave in clauses. Maak- `tell' requires the addressee/recipient to be a [+human] obligatory object, and as a second object it often has a np denoting the speech itself ex:5:x1839 or the contents of that speech ex:5:x955.

I opora muut nain O nefa O maak-u na-ep ep-a-mik. \\
1p. unm talk only thus 2s. acc tell- imp.2d say- ss. seq come- pa -1/3p \\
`We came wanting to tell you just that (talk).'

Wi moma O yia O maak-i-mik, moma=ko wi-i-yan. \\
3p. unm taro 1p. acc tell-Np- pr.1/3p taro= nf give.them-Np- fu.1p \\
`They tell us (to get them) taro, (so) we'll give them taro.'

Na- `say, speak, call, think' most commonly has the quotation as a speech complement, but it may also have up to two nominal objects instead ex:5:x956.

Waaya O yia O na-iwkin waaya wienak-em-ik-e-mik. \\
pig 1p. acc say-2/3p. ds pig feed.them- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
`They spoke about pigs to us and we kept giving them pigs to eat.'

There are a few verbs that are ordinary transitive verbs but which can take semantically different objects. It is also possible to have one of each kind in the same clause. The verb if- `paint, spread' can have a patient or goal object; the sentence in example ex:5:x944 includes both. Another such verb is mik - `spear, hit' ex:5:x953.

Yena aasa O ofa O if-e-m. \\
1s. gen canoe colour paint- pa -1s \\
`I painted my canoe with paint.' Or: `I spread paint on my canoe.'

Derived ditransitivity

When the transitivity is increased by one of the valence-increasing strategies ( sec:3.8.4.3 ), a recipient or beneficiary ex:5:x947, ex:5:x1840 becomes a second object. The linear order of the two objects depends on their relative topicality.

Moma pura oko O Kuuten O amap-urup-om-a-mik. \\
taro bunch other Kuuten bpx -ascend- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p \\
`They took another bunch of taro up for Kuuten.'

Ne mua nain O waaya O mik-om-a-mik. \\
add man that1 pig spear- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p \\
`And they speared that man a pig.'

Possessor raising

There are also cases with two patient-type objects, either one of which could be the single patient of the same verb. One of these objects has resulted from possessor raising: the possessor of the initial object np, which has to be a semantic patient, has been ``raised'' to become a second object (; ). Especially when something is done to a body part ex:5:x951 or name ex:5:x952, or something closely identified with a person ex:5:x957-- ex:5:x949, both the person and the other noun occur as objects.

Merena O efa O keraw-a-k. \\
leg 1s. acc bite- pa -3s \\
`It bit me in the leg.' Or: `It bit my leg.'

No unuma O nefa O faker-i-kuan. \\
2s. unm name 2s. acc raise-Np- fu.3p \\
`They will praise (lit: raise) your name.'

Opaimika O efa O fien-a-man. \\
talk 1s. acc push.aside- pa -2p \\
`You disregarded/disobeyed my talk.'

Era=pa ekera wiam erup O1 kukusa O2 wia O1 aaw-o-k. \\
way= loc 1s/p.sister 3p. refl erup picture 3p. acc take- pa -3s \\
`On the way he took a picture of my two sisters.'

Mua papako=ke irak-owa O wia O puuk-a-mik. \\
man some= cf fight- nmz 3p. acc cut- pa -1/3p \\
`Some men i stopped their j fight.'

Even three objects are allowed, but this is rare ex:5:x953: the verb mik- `spear, hit' itself allows two different objects, and the third one is added via possessor raising. The objects have to be in this order. Note that in the English translation, only one direct object is allowed, and the other two phrases have to be either possessive or oblique.

[ Keema-muuna, umakuna] O meta O yia O mik-i-mik. \\
knee-joint neck ritual.paste 1p. acc hit-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`They stick the meta paste on our knees and necks' or: `They mark our knees and necks with the meta paste.'

As the preferred clause structure in Mauwake is short and because it is harder to process a verb with many arguments, a common strategy is to divide the arguments between more than one clause, so that each clause has only one or two arguments ex:5:x967.

I dabuela aaw-ep Yaapan wi-em-ik-e-mik. \\
1p. unm pawpaw take- ss. seq Japan give.them- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
`We took pawpaws and gave them to the Japanese' or: `We gave pawpaws to the Japanese.'

Even if having more than one np in non-subject argument or peripheral positions in the same clause is not preferred, it is still reasonably common. But having more than one pronoun as arguments or peripherals is unusual. In the rare case that that does happen, the accusative pronoun occupies the position closest to the verb ex:5:x1574, ex:5:x1577, next the dative pronoun ex:5:x1575, then the others. The first two of the following three examples have been elicited.

Mua nain teeria muutiw wame wia ofakow-a-k. \\
man that group only 3s. refl 3p. acc show- pa -3s \\
`He only showed himself to that man's group.'
summary:
The passage distinguishes three kinds of ditransitive clauses in Mauwake: inherently ditransitive verbs, ditransitivity derived by valence-increasing strategies, and cases of possessor raising. Inherently ditransitive verbs include object cross-referencing giving/feeding verbs, utterance verbs like *maak-* ‘tell’ and *na-* ‘say/speak,’ and some ordinary transitive verbs that can take two semantically different objects.  

Derived ditransitives add a recipient or beneficiary as a second object, with object order determined by topicality, while possessor raising creates clauses with two patient-like objects, often involving body parts, names, or closely associated entities. The text notes that even three-object clauses are possible but rare, and speakers often avoid heavy argument structures by splitting them into multiple clauses.

text:
O wiar nefa sesek-i-yem. \\
3s. unm 3. dat 2s. acc send-Np- pr.1s \\
`I am sending you to him.'

Emeria ikoka Yaapan wiena niar aaw-i-kuan \\
woman later Japan 3p. gen 2p. dat take-Np- fu.3p \\
`Later the Japanese will take your wives as their own.'
summary: The examples show a verb marked with a nonpast stem plus person agreement, used to express present or future time. In the first sentence, the form means “I am sending you to him,” and in the second it means “Later the Japanese will take your wives as their own,” illustrating that the same verbal construction can have present or future reference.

text:
An intransitive clause in Mauwake is a verbal clause that does not have an object. It normally indicates an event of some kind (action or process), or a state. This differs from the definition used for typological studies of an intransitive predication consisting of ``a one-place predicate and its argument'' in that in Mauwake those predications that indicate some property or quality, or designate a class, are not treated as intransitive but as verbless clauses ( sec:5.6 ). Any of the intransitive verbs ( sec:3.8.4.2.1 ) can be the predicate in an intransitive clause, whereas a verbless clause characteristically has no verb. The only negation strategy for clauses with a verbal predicate is the negator me `not', whereas verbless clauses have more negator options.

The following clauses ex:5:x961-- ex:5:x968 are typical intransitive clauses:

Epa wiim-eya mua karer-omak-e-mik. \\
place dawn-2/3s. ds man gather- distr / pl - pa -1/3p \\
`When it got light a lot of people gathered.'

O koora=pa naap ik-ok um-o-k. \\
3s. unm house= loc thus be- ss die- pa -3s \\
`She was in the house like that and died.'

Uuriw akena mukuna nain kerer-e-k. \\
morning truly fire that1 appear- pa -3s \\
`The fire started early in the morning.'

Iiwawun iwera pun wiar aw-omak-e-k. \\
altogether coconut also 3. dat burn- distr / pl - pa -3s \\
`His many coconut trees too burned altogether.'

I Sarak ikos owowa ekap-em-ik-e-mik. \\
1p. unm Sarak with village come- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p \\
`Sarak and I kept coming back to the village.'

Fikera mamaiya=pa nan pok-ap ik-e-mik. \\
kunai.grass close= loc there sit- ss. seq be- pa -1/3p \\
`We were sitting near the kunai grass.'

Ne kiiriw miiw-aasa nan ik-eya \\
and again land-canoe there be-2/3s. ds \\
`And again the car was/stayed there, and '

Many climate expressions ex:5:x1020-- ex:5:x1021 are normal intransitive clauses.

Moram ewar pun wuun-e-k ne \\
why west.wind too blow- pa -3s and \\
`Because wind blew too, and ' Or: `Because it was windy too, and '

Ipia or-om-ik-eya owora aaw-ep up-o-k. \\
rain descend- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds betelnut take- ss. seq plant- pa -3s \\
`When it was raining he took betelnuts and planted them.'

Epa kokom-ar-eya in-e-mik. \\
place dark- inch -2/3s. ds sleep- pa -1/3p \\
`It became dark and we slept.'

The resultative verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.4 ) require a nominal argument, i.e., a noun ex:5:x966 or an adjective ex:5:x963, expressing the result of change:

Mua eneka, woosa kia kir-em-ik-ua. \\
man tooth head white turn- ss. sim -be- pa.3s \\
`The people's teeth and skulls were turning white.'

Arim-emi emeria ar-e-k. \\
grow- ss. sim woman become- pa -3s \\
`She grew and became a woman.'

A few intransitive verbs can occur with a syntactic object or object-like element whose semantic role is not a patient. These differ from true patient objects in that the range of possible ``objects'' for those verbs is very restricted, they cannot be substituted with an accusative pronoun, and the verb cannot occur with the dummy object maa `thing'. The first type can be called a ``content object'' ex:5:x308:

Wis pun wiisa uf-e-mik. \\
3p. fc too wiisa dance- pa -1/3p \\
`They, too, danced ``wiisa''.'

The second type is an object-like adverbial, as it functions in the same way as an adverbial phrase ex:5:x307.

Era maala soomar-e-mik. \\
way long walk- pa -1/3p \\
`We walked a long way.'
summary:
Mauwake intransitive clauses are verbal clauses without an object, typically expressing events, processes, or states. Unlike typological definitions of intransitivity, Mauwake treats property- or class-denoting predications as verbless clauses, and verbal predicates in intransitive clauses have the negator *me* `not`, while verbless clauses allow other negators.  

The passage gives typical examples, including climate expressions and clauses with resultative verbs, which require a nominal argument expressing the result of change. It also notes that some intransitive verbs may take restricted object-like elements that are not true patient objects, either as a “content object” or as an adverbial-like element.

text: Existential clauses and possessive clauses are distinguished from the intransitive clauses. Only the verb ik- `be' is used as the predicate in both of them.
summary: Existential clauses and possessive clauses are set apart from intransitive clauses. In both types, the only predicate used is the verb **ik-** “be.”

text:
Existential clauses are not very common in Mauwake. names these clauses as one of the main devices for introducing a new topic into a discourse, but in Mauwake they are not used very much in that function ( sec:9.2.1 ). Existential clauses use the verb ik- `be' as their predicate, and they often contain a locative phrase ex:5:x970, but it is not necessary ex:5:x971, ex:5:x1067.

Aaya=ko feeke ik-eya nefa aaw-ep enim-i-yen. \\
sugarcane= nf here. cf be-2/3s. ds 2s. acc take- ss. seq eat-Np- fu.1p \\
`If there is (any) sugarcane here, we'll take and eat you (the sugarcane).'

Aakisa Malala suule ik-ua, \\
now Malala school be- pa.3s \\
`Now there is the Malala school, '

Both the past ex:5:x1068 and future tense forms ex:5:x1067 can be used; the past tense may be used for both present and past meaning.

Kuisow owowa=pa=ko me ik-ua. \\
one village= loc = nf not be- pa.3s \\
`There was/is not even one in the village.'

Waaya ika-i-non-(na) waaya uup-i-nan. \\
pig be-Np- fu.3s-( tp ) pig cook-Np- fu.2s \\
`If there is a pig, you will cook a pig.'

When an existential clause of this type is negated with a negator other than me, it becomes a verbless clause ( sec:5.6.3 ).

A special type of existential clause has one of the two location verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.3 ) as the predicate. These verbs are only used in the past tense, even with the present tense meaning ex:5:x1154, ex:5:x1155.

Nomokowa unowa fan-e-mik, aakisa wia uruf-i-n. \\
2s/p.brother many here- pa -1/3p now 3p. acc see-Np- pr.2s \\
`Many of your brothers are here, now you see them.'

No niawi akena nan-e-k, no fain me nena niawi akena=ke. \\
2s. unm 2s/p.father real there- pa -3s 2s. unm this not 2s. gen 2s/p.father real= cf \\
`Your real father is there, this isn't your real father.'
summary: Existential clauses are not very common in Mauwake and are not often used to introduce new topics, unlike in some other languages. They typically use the verb *ik-* ‘be’ and often include a locative phrase, though this is not required; both past and future forms occur, and the past tense can have present or past meaning. A special existential construction uses one of the location verbs as predicate, but these appear only in the past tense even when referring to present situations.

text:
Possessive clauses, or so-called `have' clauses, are formed with a dative pronoun and the verb ik- `be' ex:5:x595. This is a grammaticalization from [+human] locative constructions with the semantic function of goal or locative, as was already mentioned in sec:3.5.5.

The possessee is the patient-of-state subject, which is shown by the fact that it may take the contrastive focus clitic - ke ex:5:x1065 and it determines the person inflection on the verb as well ex:5:x1323. The possessor is a habitive adverbial, like a corresponding construction in Finnish is called. Giv\'on calls it a dative object ( Givon1984), but I prefer to keep the term ``object'' for those arguments in a transitive clause that can take an accusative form when they are [+human]. calls the initial argument position copula subject (CS) and the second one copula complement (CC), regardless of whether the position is filled by the possessor or the possessee.

Aaya efar ikua, ifera wia. \\
sugar 1s. dat be- pa.3s salt no \\
`I have sugar, but no(t) salt.'

Apu maa epira marok maneka=ke wiar ik-ua. \\
Apu food plate prawn big= cf 3. dat be- pa.3s \\
`Apu has/had big prawns on his food plate.' (Lit: `Apu's food plate Theme he has/had big prawns.')

Woos(a) mua yiar ik-e-mik, wis=ke eliw nia kaken-i-kuan. \\
head man 1p. dat be- pa -1/3p 3p. fc = cf well 2p. acc straight-Np- fu.3p \\
`We have leaders, they can straighten you out.'

Because the possessee is typically inanimate and often indefinite whereas the possessor is human and definite, this causes a violation to the universal discourse-pragmatic principle, according to which animate/human and definite participants tend to precede inanimate and indefinite participants. In order to follow the principle, Mauwake often makes the possessor a theme by moving the possessor noun phrase to sentence-initial position. Only the dative pronoun keeps its position immediately preceding the verb ex:5:x972. If there is no other possessor np, an unmarked pronoun is used as a theme ex:5:x973. In these two sentences, moving part of the np to the theme position causes the np to be non-contiguous. In the example ex:5:x595 the possessee subject aaya `sugar' is also the theme, and in ex:5:x1323 the possessee is animate/human, so in those clauses there is less pressure to make the possessor into the theme.

I Theme sira naap me yiar ik-ua. \\
1p. unm custom thus not 1p. dat be- pa.3s \\
`We do not have a custom like that.'

Mua oko Theme ona koor miira=pa nan waaya unowa wiar ik-ua. \\
man other 3s. gen house face= loc there pig many 3. dat be- pa.3s \\
`Another man has many pigs there in front of his house.'

Clauses like the example ex:5:x1321, where the possessed noun is [+human] and [+plural], triggering the plural form of the verb, are quite rare, and it seems that the singular verb form is also becoming possible in these cases:

Mua nain pun muuka wiipa wiar ik-ua. \\
man that1 also son daughter 3. dat ik- pa.3s \\
`That man also has children/son(s) and daughter(s).'

All the tenses are possible. The past tense form normally covers both present and past meaning.

Naap on-i-non=na pina wiar ika-i-non. \\
thus do-Np- fu.3s= tp guilt 3. dat be-Np- fu.3s \\
`If he does like that he will have guilt.'

When the present tense form is used, it indicates a more transitory possession ex:5:x1201:

Wis pun maa eliwa=ko wiar ika-i-ya=na iw-i-mik. \\
3p. unm too thing good= nf 3. dat be-Np- pr.3s= tp give.him-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`They too, if they (happen to) have good things, give to him.'

A possessive clause may be elliptical, with the verb deleted, in cases where the possessed np has at least one post-modifier, which most commonly is a quantifier ex:5:x1322.

Yo muuka arow, wiipa kuisow muuta. \\
1s. unm son three, daughter one only \\
`I have three sons, (and/but) only one daughter.'

When the possessor is not human, the possessive clause is made with the existential verb ik- `be' plus a comitative construction rather than the dative pronoun, and the possessor always precedes the possessee ex:5:x1807, ex:5:x1810. These are cross-linguistically typical features for the grammaticalization strategy that uses a comitative phrase for a possessive predication. As was noted in sec:3.5.4, in this case the third person singular genitive pronoun ona is used for a non-human possessor.

Parina ona wakesim-owa onaiya ika-i-ya. \\
lamp 3s. gen cover- nmz with be-Np- pr.3s \\
`The lamp has a cover.'

Miiwa ona mua onaiya ik-ua. \\
land 3s. gen man with be- pa.3s \\
`The land has its men.' (Each piece of ground ``has'' men whose responsibility it is to see how the land is allocated for gardens.)

Possessive clauses are similar to existential clauses in that when a possessive clause is negated with a negator other than me, it becomes a verbless clause ( sec:5.6.3 and sec:6.2.1 ).
summary:
Possessive or “have” clauses in Mauwake are formed with a dative pronoun plus the verb *ik-* ‘be’, reflecting a grammaticalization from locative constructions; the possessee functions as the subject, while the possessor is treated as a habitive adverbial. Because the possessee is usually inanimate and indefinite while the possessor is human and definite, the language often fronted the possessor as the theme to match discourse-pragmatic ordering, though the possessor remains immediately before the verb.  

The pattern differs when the possessor is non-human: then Mauwake uses *ik-* with a comitative construction and the possessor precedes the possessee, with the genitive pronoun *ona* used. The passage also notes that all tenses are possible, some possessive clauses may be verbless when the possessed noun has a post-modifier, and negated possessive clauses can likewise be verbless.

text:
The predicate of a verbless clause belongs to some other phrase class than the verbs. The two subtypes below, equative ex:5:x1036 and descriptive clauses ex:5:x1037, are very similar syntactically; their differences are mainly in the semantics of the predicates. Their negation strategies are also slightly different from each other.

Mua nain yena kae panewowa=ke. \\
man that1 1s. gen 1s/p.grandfather old= cf \\
`That man is my old grandfather.'

Waaya nain me maneka, muuka kia gelemuta. \\
pig that1 not big son white small \\
`The pig wasn't big, it was a small white piglet.'

In certain cases the verb ik- `be' is required as a copula. This happens mainly in the future ex:5:x986 or sometimes in the past tense, or when the clause requires a medial form to indicate that it is a medial clause ex:5:x987.

Ikoka mua eliwa ne mua oona ika-i-nan. \\
later man good and man bone be-Np- fu.2p \\
`Later you will be a good and strong man.'

No gelemuta ik-eya \\
2s. unm little be-2/3s. ds \\
`When you were little, '
summary: Verbless clauses have predicates that are not verbs, and their main subtypes—equative and descriptive clauses—are syntactically very similar, differing mostly in the meaning of the predicate and in slightly different negation patterns. In some cases, however, the verb *ik-* ‘be’ is required as a copula, especially in future contexts, sometimes in the past tense, or when a medial form is needed to mark a medial clause.

text:
Syntactically equative and classifying clauses are identical. The non-verbal predicate typically has contrastive focus marking - ke, even though it is not absolutely necessary.

In an equative clause the subject and the non-verbal predicate have the same reference, so their order can be reversed with the basic meaning staying the same ex:5:x975, ex:5:x976.

Dogimaw yiena owow saria=ke. \\
Dogimaw 1p. gen village headman= cf \\
`Dogimaw is our village headman.'

Yiena owow saria Dogimaw(=ke). \\
Our village headman Dogimaw(= cf ) \\
`Our village headman is Dogimaw.'

An equative clause is only negated with the verbal negator me ex:5:x1752:

Dogimaw me yiena owow saria=ke. \\
Dogimaw not 1p. gen village headman= cf \\
`Dogimaw is not our village headman.'

In classifying clauses, calls them ``clauses with a true nominal predicate''. the reference of the subject is not identical with the reference of the predicate ex:5:x977, ex:5:x978.

Yo inasin mua=ke. \\
1s. unm spirit man= cf \\
`I am a spirit man.'

Oo Kululu takira=ke, o me amis-ar-e-k. \\
oh Kululu young.person= cf 3s. unm not knowledge- inch - pa -3s \\
`Oh, Kululu is a youth (compared to us), he doesn't know.'

The classifying clauses are negated with the verbal negator me ex:5:x980 or with a clause-final negator weetak/wia ex:5:x984. also gives marew `no(ne)' as a possible negator for equative clauses, but actually the equative clauses do not use it, only the descriptive clauses.

Nain me inasin mua=ke, iperuma=ke. \\
that1 not spirit man= cf eel= cf \\
`That is not a spirit man, it is an eel.'

O somek mua weetak/wia. \\
he song man no \\
`He is not a teacher (lit: song man).'

The predicates of both these clauses are more time-stable compared both with verbal predicates and those in the descriptive clauses (; ).
summary:
Syntactically, equative and classifying clauses are treated as identical, and their non-verbal predicates often take contrastive focus marking **-ke**, though this is optional. In equative clauses, subject and predicate refer to the same entity and can be reversed without changing the basic meaning; they are negated only with the verbal negator **me**.  

In classifying clauses, by contrast, the subject and predicate do not have identical reference, and these clauses can be negated either with **me** or with a clause-final negator such as **weetak/wia**. The passage also notes that the predicates in both clause types are more time-stable than verbal predicates and those in descriptive clauses.

text:
A descriptive clause is very much like an equative clause, but the predicate is an adjective phrase ex:5:x974, a noun phrase with an adjective ex:5:x988, or less frequently a numeral ex:5:x979 or an adverbial phrase ex:5:x985. On the time-stability scale these predicates are in between verbal and nominal predicates.

Irak-owa nain kekanowa akena. \\
fight- nmz that1 strong very \\
`The fighting was very fierce.'

Yiena miiwa kuisow. \\
1p. gen land one \\
`Our land is one.'

Nain pun sira naap=iw, mua me kerer-e-mik. \\
that1 too custom thus= inst man not appear- pa -1/3p \\
`That, too, was like that: people didn't arrive.'

A descriptive clause can use any of the negation strategies available in Mauwake ex:5:x990-- ex:5:x989 ( sec:3.10, sec:6.2 ).

Biiris me eliwa, damo-damola=ko. \\
bridge not good rdp -bad= nf \\
`The bridges were not good, they were bad.'

Yo (mua) maala marew. \\
1s. unm (man) long no(ne) \\
`I am not (a) tall (man).'

Awuliak nain eliwa weetak/wia. \\
sweet.potato that1 good no \\
`That sweet potato is not good.'
summary:
Descriptive clauses are similar to equative clauses, but their predicates are adjective phrases, noun phrases with adjectives, or less often numerals or adverbial phrases. These predicates fall between verbal and nominal predicates on the time-stability scale.  

Such clauses can use any of the negation strategies available in Mauwake, as shown by examples meaning that something was not good, not tall, or not good enough.

text:
The existential ( sec:5.5.1 ) and possessive clauses ( sec:5.5.2 ) are different from the other verbal clauses with regard to negation. Besides the standard verbal negation they can use all the other negators as well ex:5:x982 ex:5:x983 ( sec:6.2.1 ). The verb ik- `be' is retained only with the verbal negator me. With all the other negators the negator itself replaces the verb, and the clause becomes a verbless clause:

Iiriw miiwa muuta nain irak-owa marew. \\
earlier land for that1 fight- nmz no(ne) \\
`Earlier there was no fighting for land.'

I urupa weetak, i soomia wia, i epira marew. \\
1p. unm cup no 1p. unm spoon no 1p. unm plate no(ne) \\
`We had no cups, no spoons, no plates.'
summary: Existential and possessive clauses differ from other verbal clauses in that they can take not only the standard verbal negation but also the other negators. The verb *ik-* ‘be’ is kept only with the verbal negator *me*; with the other negators, the negator replaces the verb and the clause becomes verbless.

text:
Lexical nominalization, where an action nominal is a regular noun, was discussed in sec:3.2.6.1; in this section nominalization as an operation on the whole clause is described.

Action nominals and infinitives are usually assumed to be two separate non-finite categories. discusses the similarities and differences between various non-finite verb forms and presents insightful definitions based mainly on their syntactic functions. Many of the details are not relevant to Mauwake, however, as there are no verb forms that would easily fit under the categories of converbs or participles in Mauwake, and because it seems that infinitives and action nominals may be collapsible into one category. Cross-linguistically, the two often tend to be identical in form, and there is apparently a separate tendency for their functions to look rather similar as well (ibid. 196--197). It seems that the origin of the infinitive in many languages is in a nominalized verb.

In Mauwake there is just one form, and rather than positing two homonymous forms with different functions, I maintain that action nominals function both like prototypical nouns or adjectives and in functions typically associated with infinitives: as complements Ylikoski widens the definition of complement to cover ``obligatory and argumental adverbials as well'' ( Ylikoski2003). of certain verbs, in goal/purpose and deontic structures among others.

Structurally there are two kinds of nominalized clauses in Mauwake. They may occur as complements of the same verbs, with somewhat different semantics. The first type is what the term nominal ized clause most commonly refers to: the verbal predicate of a clause is nominalized, and consequently the whole clause becomes a noun phrase. The second type retains the form of a verbal clause, but the distal deictic nain `that' after the finite verb nominalizes it. The first type has a wider distribution.
summary:
The passage explains that, in Mauwake, nominalization is treated as an operation on an entire clause rather than just as lexical nominalization of action nouns. Although action nominals and infinitives are usually considered separate non-finite categories, Mauwake appears to have a single form that functions both like a noun/adjective and like an infinitive, occurring in complements and in goal/purpose and deontic constructions.

It also distinguishes two structural types of nominalized clauses in Mauwake: one in which the verbal predicate is nominalized and the whole clause becomes a noun phrase, and another in which the clause remains verbal but is nominalized by the distal deictic nain “that” after the finite verb. The first type is said to have the broader distribution.

text:
When verbs are nominalized, the action or event referred to still keeps some of its verbal characteristics. Languages differ as to how verbal or nominal in character their nominalized verbs are, and also within one language the outcomes of different nominalization strategies may vary in regard to this. In this respect Mauwake is a very verbal language: the nominalized verbs retain a number of their verbal characteristics.

Neutralization of tense or aspect distinctions, as well as the loss of other than just one argument are common features associated with nominalization. In Mauwake the nominalized verb forms may keep all of the derivational suffixes but not the inflectional ones, which include tense and person/number marking ex:5:x1226.

Aakisa=ko me kerer-em-ika-i-ya, wia bala op-aw-ap wia wiim-om-owa nain. \\
now= nf not appear- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.3s 3p. acc decoration hold- caus - ss. seq 3p. acc escort- ben - nmz that1 \\
`Now it doesn't take place (any more), decorating them and escorting them for them (i.e. escorting girls to their prospective husbands).'

The long subject np consisting of a nominalized clause has been right-dislocated.

Verbal groups showing aspect may be nominalized as well, so the aspectual distinction is retained ex:5:x1841:

Mua papako maa ik-em-ik-owa nain kawus wiar uruf-i-kuan. \\
man some food roast- ss. sim -be- nmz that1 smoke 3. dat see-Np- fu.3p \\
`They will see the smoke from some men's roasting of food.'

The nominalized verb in itself is neutral in regard to modality, even if it often gets deontic interpretation. But it can be, and frequently is, used in cases where modality is intentionally left unspecified. In ex:5:x1257 the reason for not coming may be that one is not allowed, or able, or willing, to come.

Yo ekap-owa wia. \\
1s. unm come- nmz no \\
`I won't come.'

But note ex:5:x1238 where the contrastive focus marker added to the nominalized verb forces a deontic interpretation. See also sec:6.1.2.

The nominalized verb can keep all the arguments and peripherals that a corresponding finite verb would have. This sometimes results in very long noun phrases. In ex:5:x1234 there is lexical nominalization of the verb kookal- `like' as well, besides the clausal nominalization.

Manin(a) maneka, ekina, naisow nena kookal-owa =pa perek-owa weetak. \\
garden big ekina 2s. isol 2s. gen like- nmz = loc pull.out- nmz no \\
`You are not allowed to harvest the big garden, called ekina, at your own liking.'

In ex:5:x1235 and ex:5:x1236 only the nominalized verb is within the scope of the negation. The nominalized clauses are in brackets.

Maa eneka me en-owa maa marew. \\
thing tooth not eat- nmz thing none \\
`Not eating meat is all right / is not an issue.'

Wi mua naap me on-owa nain=ko ik-e-mik=i? \\
3p. unm man thus not do- nmz that1= nf be- pa -1/3p= qm \\
`Are there people who wouldn't do / keep doing like that?'

Any of the four negators ( sec:6.2.1 ) may be used to negate the nominalized clause ex:5:x1257-- ex:5:x1236.

Cross-linguistically nominalized clauses also vary as to whether they retain a manner adverbial of the corresponding verbal clause or change it into an adjective. Mauwake keeps the adverbial ex:5:x1237.

Wiena teeria baliwep wia kakalt-owa sira nain wia maak-e-k. \\
3p. gen family well 3p. acc look.after- nmz custom that1 3p. acc tell- pa -3s \\
`He talked to them about the custom of looking after their families well.'

One common feature in nominalized clauses is that the arguments, instead of taking the morphology they would have in a finite clause, tend to follow typical np morphology in their marking. This is perhaps clearest with the subject, which in many languages gets possessive/genitive marking in a nominalized clause. In Mauwake this criterion is not very helpful. The pronominal subject of this first type of nominalized clause, if present, is often genitive ex:5:x1228, but may be nominative as well. But also the subject of a finite clause can be nominative or genitive in form, depending on whether it is neutral or emphatic; and if the subject of a nominalized clause is also the theme, it is nominative rather than genitive ex:5:x1257. A pronominal object in a nominalized clause is in the accusative ex:5:x1237.

Yiena owow maneka ikiw-owa nain ma-i-yem. \\
1p. gen village big go- nmz that1 say-Np- pr.1s \\
`I am talking about our going to town.'

The nominalized verb may take an adjective as a modifier ex:5:x1240:

Kema suuw-owa eliwa aaw-ep kekan-e-k. \\
liver push- nmz good get- ss. seq get.strong- pa -3s \\
`He got good thinking and became strong.'

Another structural indicator of the nominal status of a nominalized clause is the focus marking, which can be attached to the verb ex:5:x1238.

I uuw-owa yi-iwkin baliwep uuw-owa=ke ik-ua. \\
1p. unm work- nmz give.us-2/3p. ds well work- nmz = cf be- pa.3s \\
`When they give us work, working well is our duty.'

Nominalized clauses, like other noun phrases, use the far deictic nain `that' as a determiner ex:5:x1842, ex:5:x1843.

Ona epa maneka or-owa nain fofa=pa... unow-iya taan-e-mik. \\
3s. gen place big descend- nmz that1 day= loc many= com fill- pa -1/3p \\
`On the day of his coming down to the big place all of them filled (the place).'

Niena waaya mik-owa nain on-ami kuep-i-man, niena maa=ke, niena wiowa=ke. \\
2p. gen pig spear- nmz that1 do- ss. sim break-Np- pr.2p 2p. gen thing= cf 2p. gen spear= cf \\
`If you break (the spears) (while) doing your pig-hunting (lit: pig-spearing), that is your business, they are your spears.'

An interesting structure, and not much described in Papuan languages, is one where a same-subject medial clause is in the scope of the nominalization. In Mauwake this tends to happen when the medial verb shares an object with the following verb and there is no, or very little, intervening material between the verbs ex:5:x1885, ex:5:x1845.
summary: Mauwake nominalized verbs remain notably verbal: they can retain derivational suffixes, aspect distinctions, full argument structure, adverbials, and even focus marking, while losing inflectional marking such as tense and person/number. Although nominalized clauses show some nominal properties like determiners and sometimes genitive subject marking, these are variable in Mauwake, and the language also allows same-subject medial clauses to fall within the scope of nominalization.

text:
Dabe wiawi maa ik-ep en-owa na-ep manin(a) koora iw-a-k. \\
Dabe 3s/p.father food roast- ss. seq eat- nmz say- ss. seq garden house go- pa -3s \\
`Dabe's father wanted to roast and eat food and went to the garden house.'

Toiyan iiriw maak-ep-pu-a-mik, uuriw yia aaw-ep Madang ikiw-owa nain. \\
Toiyan already tell- ss. seq - cmpl - pa -1/3p morning 1p. acc take- ss. seq Madang go- nmz that1 \\
`We already told Toiyan about taking us in the morning and going to Madang.'

Medial clauses preceding nominalized clauses do not automatically fall within the scope of the nominalization. Just looking at the linguistic form it would be possible to analyse the following examples so that the medial clause is outside the nominalization. In that case the free translation of ex:5:x1227 would be `Having worked on the garden alone it is not acceptable to leave it there', and ex:5:x1239 `Hold the planting stick and keep practising the making of planting holes'. But culturally these alternative interpretations are not valid. Even starting to work on a big garden without previous negotiations and proper rituals is not acceptable, and the holding of the planting stick and making planting holes form a cultural `expectancy chain' and belong together conceptually.

Manina waisow mauw-ap neeke wafur-ap-pu-owa nain weetak. \\
garden 3s. isol work- ss. seq there. cf throw- ss. seq - cmpl - nmz that1 no \\
`Working on the garden alone and leaving it there (=without proper rituals) is not (acceptable/customary).'

[ Weria op-ap wiinar-owa] nain akim-am-ik-e. \\
planting.stick hold- ss. seq make.planting.holes- nmz that1 try- ss. sim -be- imp.2s \\
`Keep practising the making of planting holes with the planting stick.'

In ex:5:x1844 the medial clause has to be within the scope of the nominalization for the sentences to make sense. The speaker had seen a possum in a tree and would have liked to shoot it, but since he had not taken his bow and arrows with him, he did not climb up the tree either.

Nomokowa ir-ap mik-owa nain yena amia me aaw-e-m. \\
tree climb- ss. seq shoot- nmz that 1s. gen bow not take- pa -1s \\
`(For) climbing the tree and shooting (an animal), I hadn't taken my bow (and arrows).'

An intervening overt object may block a same-subject medial clause from being within the scope of a following nominalized verb ex:5:x1886. A different-subject medial clause does not fall within the scope of a nominalized verb.

Irak-ep luuwa niir-owa piipu-a-mik. \\
fight- ss. seq ball play- nmz leave- pa -1/3p \\
`We fought and stopped (lit: left) playing football.'

The nominalized clause has several different functions. Like any other noun phrase, it may function as an argument ex:5:x1230 or in the periphery of a clause ex:5:x1241, or in another noun phrase ex:5:x1229.

Epia wilin-owa O uruf-ap bom yia wafur-om-i-kuan na-e-mik. \\
firewood shine- nmz see- ss. seq bomb 1p. acc throw- ben -Np- fu.3p say- pa -1/3p \\
`They i /we said that when they j see the light (lit: shining) of the fire they j will throw bombs at us.'

Wiena oram niir-emi wiam kookal - owa=pa Advl nan wiam aaw-i-mik. \\
3p. gen just play- ss. seq 3p. refl like- nmz = loc there 3p. refl take-Np- pr.3s \\
`They just play together and (on the basis of) liking each other they marry each other.'

garanga oko muuka wiar aaw-owa NP sira NP \\
family other son/child 3. dat get- nmz custom \\
`the adoption custom' (Lit: the custom of getting a child from another family')

The following functions are often associated with infinitives in languages that distinguish between infinitives and nominalizations.

Expressions of obligation ( sec:6.1.2 ) use the nominalized form of the main verb. It is followed by the contrastive focus clitic, when it is either a non-verbal predicate ex:5:x1242, ex:5:x1244 or the subject of the verb ikua `is' ex:5:x1243.

Yo uurika owow maneka ikiw-owa=ke. \\
1s. unm tomorrow village big go- nmz = cf \\
`I have to go to town tomorrow.'

Wi iperowa ekima wia op-ap baliwep ik-owa=ke ik-ua. \\
3p. unm middle-aged forehead 3p. acc hold- ss. seq well be- nmz = cf be- pa.3s \\
`One has to respect The verbal expression for respecting someone is ekima opowa `holding someone's forehead'. the middle-aged/elderly and behave well.'

Inasina wia patir-a-mik nain me wiar en-owa=ke. \\
bush.spirit 3p. acc sacrifice- pa -1/3p that1 not 3. dat eat- nmz = cf \\
`One must not eat what has been sacrificed to the bush spirits.'

Directional verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.5 ) may take a nominalized clause as the goal. In many of these cases it is hard to distinguish between goal and purpose, which can be expressed via nominalization as well ex:5:x1245.

Yo emeria aaw-owa urup-e-m. \\
1s. unm woman take- nmz ascend- pa -1s \\
`I came up to take my wife.'

Nominalized clauses are used as complements of various complement-taking verbs ex:5:x1246, ex:5:x1248 ( sec:8.3.2 ).

Miiw-aasa muf-owa ikiw-owa na-em-ik-omkun o ar-e-k. \\
land-canoe pull- nmz go- nmz say- ss. sim -be-1s/p. ds 3s. unm die- pa -3s \\
`As we were talking about going to get a vehicle, she died.'

Maa uup-owa paayar-ep ep-a-n. \\
food cook- nmz know- ss. seq come- pa -2s \\
`You know cooking and you came.'

A nominalized clause is sometimes used to express habituality. It indicates a more deliberate and permanent habit than that expressed by the continuous aspect, which is the default marking for the habitual ex:5:x1249, ex:5:x1250 ( sec:3.8.5.1.1 ).

Wi mua naap me onowa nain=ko ik-e-mik=i? \\
3p. unm man thus not do- nmz that1= nf be- pa -1/3p= qm \\
`Are there people who wouldn't keep doing like that?'

Mua papako opor(a) makena me ookowa, sira samora on-am-ika-i-mik. \\
man other talk true not follow- nmz custom bad do- ss - sim -be-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`Some people (as a rule) do not follow the true talk (but) keep doing bad things.'
summary: The passage explains that medial clauses may or may not fall within the scope of a following nominalized clause, and that although some structures could be analyzed either way, cultural interpretation determines the correct reading. It also shows that nominalized clauses function in several ways: as arguments or peripheral constituents, and in expressions of obligation, directional or purposive complements, complements of certain verbs, and in more deliberate habitual meanings.

text:
Mauwake verbs may take a causative suffix, which often indicates causation ( sec:3.8.4.3.1 ). When the causation is less mechanical and requires the cooperation of the object of the causation, the verb suuw- `push' is used together with a nominalized clause ex:5:x1252:

Mua naareke naap on-owa nefa suuw-a-k? \\
man who. cf thus do- nmz 2s. acc push- pa -3s \\
`Who made you do like that?'

Ability is expressed via a nominalized clause followed by the intensity adverb pepek `enough, able' ex:5:x1251.

Ariwa perek-owa me pepek. \\
arrow pull.out- nmz not enough/able \\
`(He was) not able to pull out the arrow.'

One strategy for purposives is to use the nominalized form of the main verb followed by the same-subject sequential form naep of the verb `say/think'. This strategy is used especially when the purpose is understood to be somewhat generic ex:5:x1253 or when the purpose clause is right-dislocated ex:5:x1255. For purpose clauses, see sec:8.3.2.1.4.

Weniwa=pa en-owa na-ep uuw-i-mik. \\
hunger.time= loc eat- nmz say- ss. seq plant-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`We/they work in order to eat during the time of hunger.'

Ona siowa ikos manina ikiw-e-mik, pika on - owa na - ep.
\\
3s. gen dog together.with garden go- pa -1/3p fence make- nmz say- ss. seq \\
`He went together with his dog to the garden (in order) to make a fence.'

Mauwake has an idiosyncratic clausal structure for the expression `not yet'. The negated verb is nominalized, and it is followed by an appropriate form of the verb ik- `be' ex:5:x1254. The presence of the negative temporal adverb eewuar `not yet' indicates expectation that what hasn't happened yet will, or should, take place in not too distant future ex:5:x1256.

Aakisa baliwep me amis-ar-owa ik-e-mik. \\
now well not knowledge- inch - nmz be- pa -1/3p \\
`Now we do not yet know it well.'

Iwera popoka wafur-am-ika-iwkin or-op `bulak', eewuar, eka me saan-ar-owa ik-ua. \\
coconut unripe throw- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds descend- ss. seq plop not.yet water not dry- inch - nmz be- pa.3s \\
`They i kept throwing unripe coconuts j and when they j dropped they j said `plop' (so they i knew:) not yet, the water had not dried yet.'

Unlike many other languages, in Mauwake a nominalized clause does not function as a complement of an adjective. Rather, the nominalized clause functions as the subject and it takes the adjective as a non-verbal predicate ex:5:x1258, ex:5:x1259:

Maa wiar ikum aaw-owa eliwa=ki? \\
thing 3. dat illicitly take- nmz good= cf. qm \\
`Is it good to steal?'

Galasim-owa lawisiw yoowa. \\
spear.fish- nmz rather hot/hard \\
`Spearing fish is rather hard.' Or: `It is rather hard to spear fish.'

The verb for spear-fishing is a loan from Tok Pisin, which refers to the goggles used when diving to spear fish.
summary:
Mauwake uses nominalized clauses in several constructions: causatives can be formed with a causative suffix or with *suuw-* ‘push’ plus a nominalized clause, ability is expressed by a nominalized clause followed by *pepek* ‘enough, able’, and purposives may use a nominalized main verb followed by the same-subject sequential form of ‘say/think’. It also has a special structure for ‘not yet’, where the negated verb is nominalized and followed by a form of *ik-* ‘be’, often with the adverb *eewuar* indicating expected future occurrence.  

In addition, nominalized clauses do not serve as complements of adjectives in Mauwake; instead, they function as subjects with the adjective as a non-verbal predicate, as in examples meaning ‘Is it good to steal?’ and ‘Spearing fish is rather hard.’

text:
The second strategy for nominalizing a clause is to end an ordinary verbal clause with the far demonstrative nain `that' used as a determiner. The demonstrative is the only element marking the clause as nominalized. call this type ``clausal nominalization'' (2007:376--377). suggests that there may be a correlation ``between the degree of nounhood of a nominalized expression and its ability to take determiners''. In Mauwake this is clearly not the case, as the demonstrative is obligatory in this second type of nominalized clause but only optional in the first type, which is otherwise more like a noun phrase.

The distribution of finite clauses nominalized only with a demonstrative is more restricted than that of clauses with a nominalized verb. They function as complement clauses ex:5:x1260 ( sec:8.3.2 ), relative clauses ex:5:x1261 ( sec:8.3.1 ), or temporal clauses ex:5:x1940 ( sec:8.3.3.1 ), but not in the many other specific functions where the other type can occur. Forming complement clauses and relative clauses by adding a demonstrative pronoun after a finite verb is a common strategy in Papuan languages (; Reesink1987;; ).

Takira en-ow( a) gelemuta wia on-om-a-mik
nain CC ma-i-yem.
\\
child eat- nmz small 3p. acc make- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p that1 say-Np- pr.1s \\
`I tell about our making/having made a feast for the children.'

Akia ik-e-k nain rc me en-e-k. \\
banana roast- pa -3s that1 not eat- pa -3s \\
`He did not eat the bananas that he roasted.'

Koora ikiw - i - mik nain TempC mera eka me enim-i-mik. \\
house go-Np- pr.1/3p that1 fish water not eat-Np- pr.1/3p \\
`When/After we go into the house, we do not eat fish soup.'
summary:
The passage describes a second way of nominalizing a clause in Mauwake: an ordinary finite verbal clause can be marked as nominalized simply by adding the far demonstrative **nain** “that,” which is the only nominalizing element. Unlike the first nominalization type, this demonstrative is obligatory here, and the author notes that Mauwake does not support the proposed correlation between “nounhood” and the ability to take determiners.

Clauses nominalized in this way are more restricted in function than those with a nominalized verb: they can serve as complement, relative, or temporal clauses, but not the wider range of uses available to the other type. The passage also notes that forming complement and relative clauses by adding a demonstrative after a finite verb is a common strategy in Papuan languages.

text: This chapter describes various functional systems that affect the clause or the sentence as a whole. Most of them are touched upon in various other parts of the grammar where they are relevant, but here they are treated in a more systematic manner.
summary: The chapter presents a range of functional systems that operate on the clause or sentence as a whole. Although these systems are discussed elsewhere in the grammar when relevant, this chapter treats them in a more systematic way.

text:
Modality, or mode -- expressing the speaker's attitude to a situation -- relates not just to the verb but to the whole proposition. Because of this it is typically not expressed via verbal inflection. In Mauwake the counterfactual modality is manifested by a suffix on the verb
sec:3.8.3.2; more often the modality is conveyed via various other strategies outlined below.

Many Papuan languages make a distinction between realis and irrealis mode, calls it status. and tense. estimates that, on the whole, tense is more prominent than mode, but there are also languages like Hua and Maia which do not have tense as a verbal category at all, only mode. But in Mauwake the realis-irrealis dichotomy is not grammatically relevant.
summary: Modality expresses the speaker’s attitude toward an entire proposition, so it is usually not marked by verbal inflection; in Mauwake, counterfactual modality is an exception, marked by a verbal suffix, though modality is more often expressed by other strategies.
