The passage also notes that many Papuan languages distinguish realis and irrealis mode, sometimes called status, but Mauwake does not grammatically distinguish realis and irrealis.

text:
Epistemic modality has to do with certainty, probability and possibility: it ``relates to the speaker's commitment to the probability that the situation is true''.

The default and unmarked mood in statements is indicative, when something is stated as a fact. If the speaker wants to strengthen the proposition more, the intensity adverb akena `truly, very' is added to the end of the statement ex:6:x1050, ex:6:x1051.

Wi owow oko oko pun wia maake-miaw-i-yem akena. \\
3p. unm place other other also 3p. acc tell-wander- nps - pr.1s truly\\
`I really walk around telling people in many other places too.'

Wi o ook-owa nain me pepek akena. \\
3p. unm 3s. unm follow.him- nmz that1 not able truly\\
`They really are not able to follow him.'

When the proposition is considered less than certain, either probable or just possible, the modal adverb clitic - yon `probably/perhaps/I think' ( sec:3.9.3 ) is attached to the last word in the statement, usually either a verb ex:6:x1052 or non-verbal predicate ex:6:x1053. An interjection can still follow the word with - yon ex:6:x1071.

Mua Maneka=ke lawisiw wia amukar-e-k= yon. \\
man big= cf somewhat 3p. acc scold- pa -3s-perhaps\\
`Perhaps God reproached/punished them a little.'

Nis pun kema puk-owa marewa=ke= yon aa! \\
2p. unm also liver burst- nmz none= cf -perhaps intj \\
`Ah, I think you don't have any sense at all (lit: your liver hasn't burst)!'

Naap= yon. \\
thus-perhaps\\
`I think/suppose it is like that.'

The counterfactual form of the verb ( sec:3.8.3.2 ) is used in speculative statements where the situation mentioned in the proposition did not happen, although it could have ex:6:x1054-- ex:6:x1056.

Lawisiw akena um- ek-a-m. \\
somewhat very die- cntf - pa -1s\\
`I very nearly fell (but in reality didn't).'

Yena kookal-owa=pa uuw- ek-a-m=na sesa na-ek-a-m. \\
1s. gen like- nmz = loc work- cntf - pa -1s= tp price say- cntf - pa -1s\\
`If I had worked on my own will, I would have required payment.'

Naap wiar amis-ar- ek-a-mik oo! \\
thus 3. dat knowledge- inch - cntf - pa -1/3p intj \\
`Oh, if only we had known that about him/them!'

Abilitative is expressed by the adverb pepek `enough, correctly, able' as a non-verbal predicate. In affirmative statements the verb that the adverb refers to often occurs in the following clause ex:6:x1089:

No pepek, eliw on-i-nan. \\
2s. unm able well do-Np- fu.2s\\
`You are able, you can do it.'

The verb may also be in the same clause but in the nominalized form; this is more common in negative statements ex:6:x1088:

mukuna nain umuk-owa me pepek. \\
fire that1 extinguish- nmz not able\\
` (we were) not able to extinguish the fire.'

Evidentials are an important feature in some Papuan languages, but Mauwake does not have them as a grammatical category.
summary:
The passage describes Mauwake expressions for epistemic modality, including certainty, probability, possibility, and counterfactual speculation. Indicative statements are the default for facts, while stronger certainty can be marked with *akena* “truly, very,” weaker certainty with the clitic *-yon* “probably/perhaps/I think,” and speculative or unreal situations with the counterfactual verb form.

It also explains abilitative meaning, which is expressed by *pepek* “enough, correctly, able,” either as a non-verbal predicate or with a nominalized verb. Finally, it notes that although evidentials are important in some Papuan languages, Mauwake does not have them as a grammatical category.

text:
The deontic modality indicates obligation or permission. Deontic expressions can vary from a statement of a strong obligation to a polite request or to expressions of permission or denying permission.

The syntactic strategy for expressing strong obligation is to use the nominalized form of the verb followed by the contrastive focus clitic, and optionally an appropriate form of the verb `be' ex:6:x1077.

Yo uurika owow maneka ikiw-owa=ke (ik-ua). \\
1s. unm tomorrow village big go- nmz = cf be- pa.3s\\
`I have to go to town tomorrow.'

A nominalized clause structure may may be interpreted to express obligation even without the contrastive focus clitic, and in a medial clause. A dative pronoun is added if clarification is needed to state who is obligated to do something ex:6:x1079.

Ekap-owa efar ika-eya ekap-e-m. \\
come- nmz 1s. dat be-2/3s. ds come- pa -1s\\
`I had to come, so I came.'

A polite request can also take the form of a question ex:6:x1163.

No maa nain=ko eliw yi-i-nan=i? \\
2s. unm thing that= nf well give.me-Np- fu.2s= qm \\
`Will/would you give that to me (please)?'

Permission is indicated by the adverb eliw `well/all right' placed before the verb, which is in the future form ex:6:x1085, ex:6:x1086.

Yiena miiwa kuisow, eliw feeke soop-i-yen. \\
1p. gen land one well here. cf bury-Np- fu.1p\\
`Our land is one, we may bury him here.'

Eliw ek-ap fook-i-nan, fook-ap ep-i-nan. \\
well come- ss. seq split-Np- fu.2s split- ss. seq go-Np- fu.2s\\
`You may come and split (coconuts), and having split them, go.'

Prohibition or denial of permission is done with a negated nominalized form of a verb ex:6:x1087, ex:6:x1078.

Manin maneka na-isow nena kookal-owa=pa perek-owa weetak. \\
garden big 2s. isol 2s. gen like- nmz = loc harvest- nmz no\\
`You are not allowed to harvest the big garden by yourself when your like.'

I me sira samora on-owa=ke, weetak.\\
1p. unm not custom bad do- nmz = cf no\\
`We must not do bad things.'

In sentences expressing disobedience to a prohibition, it is particularly common to have the prohibition in a relative clause where the nominalized verb is negated with the verbal negator me ex:6:x1887, ex:6:x1888. Here the contrastive focus clitic is not used.

Maa=ko me on-owa nain nis=ke on-i-man. \\
thing= nf not do- nmz that1 2p. fc = cf do-Np- pr.2p\\
`You do things that must not be done.'

Sabat fofa=pa me uuw-owa nain emeria nain saliw-a-k. \\
sabbath day= loc not work- nmz that1 woman that1 heal- pa -3s\\
`He healed the woman on a Sabbath day when it was forbidden to work.'
summary: The passage describes deontic modality as expressing obligation, permission, polite requests, and prohibition. Strong obligation is typically marked by a nominalized verb, often with a contrastive focus clitic, while permission is expressed with the adverb *eliw* before a future verb and polite requests can be phrased as questions. Prohibition or lack of permission is shown with negated nominalized forms, often in relative clauses with the verbal negator *me* and without the contrastive focus clitic.

text:
Mauwake has more variety in negation than many other Papuan languages. The contents of this sec:6.2 is mostly based on.

There are four negators in Mauwake instead of only one or two: me, weetak, wia and marew, which have somewhat overlapping functions ( sec:3.10 ). Negation can also express frustration or be used as a verb root with certain suffixes; its scope can vary from one constituent to a whole sentence; and it may be emphasized. Double negation results in cancellation of the negation rather than emphasizing it.
summary: Mauwake has a relatively rich negation system compared with many other Papuan languages. It has four negators—me, weetak, wia, and marew—with overlapping functions, and negation can also express frustration, function as a verb root with certain suffixes, vary in scope from a constituent to a whole sentence, and be emphasized. In Mauwake, double negation cancels negation rather than reinforcing it.

text:
Verbal clauses are negated with the negator me `not', placed before the verb ex:6:x1090, verbal group ex:6:x1091 or verb phrase ex:6:x1092.

This type of negation, also called standard negation, is symmetric in Mauwake: the negative clause is similar to the corresponding affirmative clause apart from the presence of the negator. The negation strategy is the same for transitive and intransitive, independent and dependent clauses, and for imperatives ex:6:x1113 as well.

I iinan aasa me kuuf-a-mik. \\
1p. unm sky canoe not see- pa -1/3p\\
`We did not see the airplanes.'

Yo me keker op-a-m, Kedem=ke makena. \\
1s. unm not fear hold- pa -1s, Kedem= cf true\\
`I was not afraid, true, Kedem was.'

Mua me wia kuuf-a-mik, me wia furew-a-mik, ne me wia imen-a-mik.\\
man not 3p. acc see- pa -1/3p not 3p. acc sense- pa -1/3p and not 3p. acc find- pa -1/3p\\
`We did not see, sense, or find the men.'

Ni uf-ep=na maadara me iirar-eka. \\
2p. unm dance- ss. seq = nf forehead.ornament not remove- imp.2p\\
`If/when you have danced, do not remove your forehead ornaments.'

The non-verbal predicate in equative ex:6:x1093 and descriptive clauses ex:6:x1095 can be negated with any of the four negators.

O somek mua weetak/wia. \\
3s. unm song man no\\
`He is not a teacher.'

O me somek mua=ke. \\
3s. unm not song man= cf \\
`He is not a teacher.'

However, marew is possible in these clauses only if the predicate contains an adjective ex:6:x1096.

Awuliak fain afila weetak/wia/marew. \\
sweet.potato this sweet no\\
`This sweet potato is not sweet.'

Awuliak fain me afila(=ke). \\
sweet.potato this not sweet= cf \\
`This sweet potato is not sweet.'

When the possessive and existential clauses are negated with the verbal negator me, they are like other verbal clauses ex:6:x1098, ex:6:x1099. But if any of the other negators is used, the negator replaces the verb and becomes a non-verbal predicate, so these clauses become verbless clauses ex:6:x1094, ex:6:x1100 ( sec:5.6.3 ).

I sira naap me yiar ik-ua. \\
1p. unm custom thus not 1p. dat be- pa.3s\\
`We do not have a custom like that.'

Wi Yaapan emeria weetak, mua manek=iw. \\
3p. unm Japan woman no, man big= lim \\
`The Japanese had no women/wives, (they were) only men.'

Iiriw miiwa muuta nain irak-owa me ik-ua. \\
earlier land for that1 fight- nmz not be- pa.3s\\
`Earlier there was no fighting for land.'

Iiriw miiwa muuta nain irak-owa marew, \\
earlier land for that1 fight- nmz no(ne)\\
`Earlier there was no fighting for land,...'

With so many possible alternatives, the speaker has a choice of repeating the same negator ex:6:x1128 or using different ones ex:6:x1127 when several items are negated. Either strategy is used by good language users.

I muuka marew a, i wiipa marew a. \\
1p. unm son no(ne) oh 1p. unm daughter no(ne) oh\\
`We have no son, and we have no daughter.'

I urupa weetak, i soomia wia, i epira marew.\\
1p. unm cup no 1p. unm spoon no 1p. unm plate no(ne)\\
`We had no cups, we had no spoons, we had no plates.'

In a few cases the choice of a negator indicates a difference in meaning. The example ex:6:x1130 is the Mauwake equivalent for the common Tok Pisin idiom nogat tok `I do not have anything against it'.

Yo opora weetak/wia. \\
1p. unm talk no\\
`I have no talk. (= I do not have anything to say.)'

Yo opora marew. \\
1p. unm talk no(ne)\\
`I have no talk. (= It is OK / I do not have anything against it.)'

The predicate function of the negators weetak and marew is also shown in the fact that they take a medial different-subject suffix, when the verbless negative possessive or existential-presentative clauses occur sentence-medially in a chaining structure ex:6:x1101. Wia cannot be suffixed with the medial verb suffix.

Maa pela marew-eya / weetak-eya fofa er-a-m. \\
thing leaf no(ne)-2/3s. ds / no-2/3s. ds market go- pa -1s\\
`I had no greens and went to the market.'
summary:
Verbal clauses in Mauwake are negated with the preverbal negator **me**, and this standard negation is symmetric: it applies in the same way to transitive and intransitive clauses, independent and dependent clauses, and imperatives. Non-verbal equative and descriptive clauses can be negated by any of four negators, though **marew** is restricted to predicates containing an adjective, and in possessive/existential clauses the choice of negator can determine whether the clause remains verbal or becomes verbless.

When several items are negated, speakers may repeat the same negator or use different ones, and both are acceptable. In a few cases, the choice between negators changes meaning, as in a possessive/existential expression where different negators correspond to different interpretations.

text:
Papuan languages typically do not have lexicalized constituent negation of the type `nothing', `nobody' etc., and even syntactic constituent negation may be lacking. But in Mauwake it is possible to negate various constituents within a clause, and, although very rarely, even inside a noun phrase. The basic constituent negator is me `not'. It precedes the negated element, which receives extra stress. Position of the negator, stress, and sometimes the neutral focus clitic all interact in constituent negation ex:6:x1102-- ex:6:x1105.

Me napuma=ke ifakim-o-k. \\
not sickness kill- pa -3s\\
`It wasn't sickness that killed him.'

Maa oposia me ewur enim-i-mik. \\
thing meat not soon eat-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`Meat we will not eat soon (after spouse's death).'

Me epa fan irak-owa uruf-a-mik. \\
not place here fight- nmz see- pa -1/3p\\
`It was not here that they saw the fighting.'

Nepa opaimika me baliwep miim-a-mik. \\
bird talk not well hear- pa -1/3p\\
`They did not hear (understand) Tok Pisin well.'

Me nomokowa eliwa aaw-e - mik. \\
not tree good take- pa -1/3p\\
`It wasn't good trees that they took.'

In clauses with quantifiers, constituent negation has an important function disambiguating the meaning. If the subject or object noun phrase has a quantifier, the negation is done in different ways depending on whether the quantifier is in the scope of the negation or not. In ex:6:x1142 the noun phrase with the particular quantifier kuisow `one' is not in the scope of the negation, but in ex:6:x1143 it is. The neutral focus clitic is required to clarify the meaning; it can even be attached to some other constituent between the quantifier and the negator ex:6:x1147.

Mua kuisow me ekap-o-k. \\
man one not come- pa -3s\\
`One (particular) man did not come.'

Mua kuisow= ko me ekap-o-k. \\
man one= nf not come- pa -3s\\
`Not (even) one man came.'

Mua kuisow owowa=pa= ko me ik-ua. \\
man one village= loc = nf not be- pa.3s\\
`Not (even) one man stayed in the village.'

The example ex:6:x1145 is ambiguous as to whether only one man did not go down or whether it is negated that only one man went. The first alternative is the more likely meaning, and if one wants to make sure to give the second meaning, the standard strategy for constituent negation ex:6:x1144 is used.

Mua kuisow muuta me ekap-o-k. \\
man one only not come- pa -3s\\
`Only one man did not come.' Or: `Not only one man came (but more).'

Me mua kuisow (muuta) ekap-o-k. \\
not man one (only) come- pa -3s\\
`Not only one man came.'

Similarly, with the universal quantifier unowiya `all', the scope of the negation may be ambiguous. The preferred interpretation for ex:6:x1148 is that the statement about not following God's talk refers to all people, thus no one follows it; but it may also be understood that even if all the people do not follow it, some do.

Emeria mua unowiya Mua Maneka opora me ook-i-mik. \\
woman man all Man Big talk not follow-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`All the people do not follow God's talk.'

If the negator is in the constituent negation position, the statement is unambiguous ex:6:x1149. In this respect Mauwake behaves differently from Usan, which does not allow a constituent negation structure.

Nain me mua unowiya opora wiar op-i-mik. \\
but not man all talk 3. dat hold-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`But not all men/people believe in him (= some do).'

Stress may also be employed to give a constituent negation interpretation to a negated clause. When the clausal stress is on the negator, the whole clause is negated ex:6:x669. In order to negate the universal quantifier rather than the verb, the main stress needs to be on the quantifier ex:6:x671. This type of negation is used in Usan as well (ibid. 277).

Mua unow=iya 'me ikiw-e-mik. \\
man many= com not go- pa -1/3p\\
`All the men didn't go (=none of them went).'

Mua 'unow=iya me ikiw-e-mik. \\
man many= com not go- pa -1/3p\\
` All the men didn't go (=only some went).'

When a clause with the universal quantifier unow onaiya `all' is negated, it tends to be interpreted as a constituent negation of the quantifier, possibly because unow onaiya is a heavier structure than unowiya and as such more prominent ex:6:x668.

Unow onaiya me ikiw-e-mik. \\
many with not go- pa -1/3p\\
`Not all of them went (= only some went)'

The example ex:6:x1150 is not a case of unowa negated separately inside a np; instead, mua `man' is fronted as a theme ( sec:9.1 ):

Mua me unowa ekap-e-mik. \\
man not many come- pa -1/3p\\
`There were not many men that came.' Or: `As for men, not many came.'

Eliwa `good' may be the only adjective that can be negated by itself inside a noun phrase. These structures are very rare and would need a more careful study ex:6:x1106, ex:6:x1107. ex:6:x1106 may also be a combination of a non-verbal clause and a transitive clause where the object np only retains the adjective; the noun is deleted because it occurs in the previous clause.

Maa en-owa eliw(a) marew p-or-o-mik. \\
thing eat- nmz good no(ne) bpx -descend- pa -1/3p\\
`They brought down not-good food.'

Biiris me eliwa, damo-damola=ko on-a-mik. \\
bridge not good rdp -bad= nf make- pa -1/3p\\
`They did not make good bridges (but) bad ones.' (Or: The bridges were not good, they made bad ones.)

The example ex:6:x1114 looks like a constituent negation attached to the noun mokoka `eye(s)', but actually me here is a clausal negator negating the whole idiomatic sentence of `keeping one's eyes shut' (i.e. being ignorant).

Me mokoka op-ar-ep ik-e. \\
not eye(s) closed- caus - ss. seq be- imp.2s\\
`Do not have your eyes closed.'

Those cases of constituent negation where me precedes a verb can be distinguished from clausal negation only in spoken language on the basis of extra stress on the verb ex:6:x1110.
summary:
Mauwake allows constituent negation with the basic negator **me** “not,” which precedes the negated constituent and is accompanied by extra stress; although rare, this can occur even inside noun phrases. The passage shows that constituent negation is especially important with quantifiers such as **kuisow** “one” and **unowiya/unow onaiya** “all,” where stress and the neutral focus clitic help determine scope and avoid ambiguity.

It also notes that Mauwake can negate an adjective inside a noun phrase in rare cases, while some apparent constituent negations are actually clausal negation, distinguishable in speech by stress. Overall, Mauwake differs from some related languages such as Usan in allowing clearer constituent negation structures.

text:
Ni iperuma fain me e nim-eka, wafur-eka! \\
2p. unm eel this not eat- imp.2p throw- imp.2p\\
` Don't eat this eel, throw it away!'
summary: The passage gives an example of an imperative prohibition in which the speaker tells the addressee not to eat a eel and instead to throw it away. The form uses the negative marker *me* with the verb *eat* and an imperative form of *throw* addressed to the second person plural.

text:
A negative interjection is used as a one-word reply to a question or a statement. It stands as a complete sentence by itself or is preposed and syntactically independent of the rest of the sentence. Two of the negators are used as negative interjections: weetak and wia ex:6:x1115, ex:6:x1116. They are synonymous and usually interchangeable, but in a few environments one or the other is preferred. For the use of weetak/wia as an answer to a negative question, see sec:7.2.7.

No aaya sesenar-e-n=i? - Weetak/wia (me sesenar-e-m). \\
2s. unm sugar buy- pa -2s= qm -no (not buy- pa -1s)\\
`Did you buy sugar?' --`No (I didn't).'

Yomar owora efar aaw-o-k. - Weetak/wia, me os=ke aaw-o-k.\\
1s/p.cousin betelnut 1s. dat take- pa -3s -no not 3s. fc = cf take- pa -3s\\
`My cousin took my betelnut. --No, it wasn't he who took it.'
summary: Negative interjections are one-word replies to questions or statements and can function as complete sentences on their own or as independent preposed elements. In this language, the negators *weetak* and *wia* are used this way; they are synonymous and usually interchangeable, though one may be preferred in certain contexts, including as answers to negative questions.

text:
When an affirmative clause is followed by a negative one, and the two only differ by the contrasted element, the whole clause apart from the contrasted element is replaced by weetak or wia ex:6:x1119, ex:6:x1120. A full clause is possible instead of weetak/ wia, but it is not as common.

Mua bug maala nain=ke mera unowa isak-i-non, mua bug iiwa nain weetak/wia.\\
man wind long that1= cf fish many spear-Np- fu.3s man wind short that1 no.\\
`A man with long breath (=big lungs) will spear many fish, a man with short breath will not.'

Mera papako unowa, papako weetak/wia. \\
fish some many some no\\
`Some fish there are many, some not.'

Also when an affirmative question is followed by a negative alternative, weetak or wia is used ex:6:x1121, ex:6:x1122.

Sira nain piipua-i-nan=i e weetak? \\
habit that leave-Np- fu.2s= qm or no\\
`Will you stop that habit or not?'

Yo emeria=ko efar uruf-a-man=i e weetak? \\
1s. unm woman= nf 1s. dat see- pa -2p= qm or no\\
`Have you seen my wife or not?'

If an action fails to have the expected result, again one of the two negative interjections is used either by itself ex:6:x1124, ex:6:x1126 or followed by a full clause ex:6:x1123.

Marasin wu-om-a-mik=na weetak. \\
medicine put- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p= tp no\\
`They put medicine in him but no (=with no result).'

Naap ik-ok uruf-am-ika-iwkin wia. \\
thus be- ss see- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds no\\
`They were thus watching him (but) no (he did not revive).'

I unan maa en-e-mik en-e-mik wia, ipoka taan-ep enakiwa wu-a-mik. \\
1p. unm yesterday food eat- pa -1/3p eat- pa -1/3p no stomach become.full- ss. seq half put- pa -1/3p\\
`Yesterday we ate and ate, (but) no (=we could not finish the food), our stomachs were full and we put half of it aside.'

When the clause expressing frustration of an effort starts a new sentence and begins with the additive connective ne `and/but', the negator is always wia, and an explanatory clause follows ex:6:x1125.

Ne wia, papako=ke ma-e-mik, ``Weetak, moram owowa p-ikiw-i-yan?'' \\
add no other= cf say- pa -1/3p no why village bpx -go-Np- fu.1p\\
`But no, others said, ``Why take him to the village?'' '

Mauwake has two different kinds of double negation. In both cases the negation is cancelled and the result is affirmative, but not an emphatic affirmative. A negated verb ex:6:x1131 or an inherently negative verb ex:6:x1132 may occur with the clausal negator me `not':

Ona muuka me sesek-owa=ke me ma-e-k. \\
3s. gen son not send- nmz = cf not say- pa -3s\\
`He did not say that he wouldn't send (lit: say about not sending) his son.'

Maamuma me marew-ar-e-mik. \\
money not no(ne)- inch - pa -1/3p\\
`We/They did not lack money.'

In the second type of double negation a speaker's negative statement is challenged by another speaker. In this case a different negator is used to challenge the original negation ex:6:x1133.

Yo episowa weetak. - Weetak wia. \\
1s. unm tobacco no. -no no\\
`I have no tobacco.' `Don't say you don't have any.'

The negation can be emphasized with the intensity adverb akena `very' ex:6:x1134, ex:6:x1135:

Weetak akena, i me kuum-e-mik. \\
no very 1p. unm not burn- pa -1/3s\\
` No, we did not burn it.'

I me kuum-e-mik akena. \\
1p. unm not burn- pa -1/3p very\\
`We did not burn it.'

Another possible strategy for emphasizing a negative statement or command is to attach the neutral focus clitic - ko to the verbal negator me `not' ex:6:x1152-- ex:6:x1137. In ex:6:x1136 the neutral focus clitic appears twice, as the speaker wants both to emphasise the negation and to distance himself from the situation (without implying that someone else did see what he did not).

I me=ko miim-a-mik. \\
1p. unm not= nf hear- pa -1/3p\\
`We did not hear it.'

Yo=ko me=ko uruf-a-m. \\
1s. unm = nf not= nf see- pa -1s\\
` I did not see it.'

Me =ko niir-e sa, kae napum-ar-e-k. \\
not= nf laugh- imp.2s intj grandfather sick- inch - pa -3s\\
`Do not laugh, grandfather is sick.'

Negative spreading is fairly common in languages that have a medial verb system. The negation can spread forwards or backwards, or both, depending on the language. In Mauwake both forward ex:6:x1138 and backward ex:6:x1140 spreading is possible across medial clause boundaries, but only with the same-subject medial verbs. In Usan, the negation of a final clause can spread backwards even with a different subject medial verb, but Hua, like Mauwake, requires a same subject medial verb. The spreading is not common, but it is more acceptable if the verbs form a logical sequence, an ``expectancy chain''.

Nain yo me ep-ap nefa aaw-e-m. \\
but 1s. unm not come- ss. seq 2s. acc get- pa -1s\\
`But I did not come and get you.'

Nainiw ekap-ep maa me sesek-a-mik. \\
again come- ss. seq food not sell- pa -1/3p\\
`They did not come back and sell food again.'

But negative spreading is not automatic; even with a same-subject medial verb two clauses can have different polarity ex:6:x1156, ex:6:x1763. If the speaker wants to avoid ambiguity, finite clauses can be used when the polarity is different ex:6:x1153.

Nepa opaimika me baliwep amis-ar-ep wiena opaimik=iw yia maak-em-ik-e-mik.\\
bird talk not well knowledge- inch - ss. seq 3p. gen talk= inst 1p. acc tell- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`They did not know Tok Pisin well and talked to us in their own language.'

Mua lebuma me arim-ep takira ik-ok emeria wia aaw-i-mik.\\
man lazy not grow- ss. seq young be- ss. sim woman 3s. acc take-Np- pr.1/3p\\
`Lazy men, not having grown and (still) being young, take wives.'

Nainiw ekap-e-mik, nain maa me sesek-a-mik. \\
again come- pa -1/3p that1 food not sell- pa -1/3p\\
`They came back again, but did not sell any food.'
summary:
The passage describes several uses of the negative interjections **weetak/wia** in Mauwake. They can stand in for a repeated clause in contrastive affirmatives and negatives, appear in affirmative questions with a negative alternative, and express that an expected result did not occur; **wia** is especially used when a new sentence begins with the connective **ne**.

It also distinguishes two kinds of double negation: one where negation is canceled within a clause or with inherently negative verbs, and another where a speaker challenges someone else’s negative statement. Negation can be emphasized with **akena** or with the focus clitic **-ko**, and it may spread across medial clauses forward or backward, though this is limited and depends on clause type and the logical relation between events.

text:
If the context is not clear enough, the negator can be repeated for each negated verb in a medial verb construction. In ex:6:x1139, if only the first verb is negated, the sentence could mean that many people do not know the person but follow him nevertheless; whereas if only the second verb is negated, the sentence might be taken to mean that many people do know the person but do not follow him.

Mua unowa o me amis-ar-ep me ook-i-mik.\\
man many 3s. unm not knowledge- inch - ss. seq not follow-Np- pr.3p\\
`Many people do not know him and do not follow him.'

Different-subject marking blocks negative spreading in both directions. Thus in ex:6:x1141 the polarity changes with each new clause:

Soomar-em-ika-iwkin me wia far-eya nefa ma-i-kuan, \\
walk- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds not 3p. acc call-2/3s. ds 2s. acc say-Np- fu.3p\\
`When they walk past, and you do not call them, they will say about you that '

Negative transportation from a complement clause to a main clause does not take place in Mauwake. This is true of Amele as well, but Usan allows it.
summary: In medial verb constructions, if the context is ambiguous, the negator may be repeated on each negated verb to avoid different interpretations about which action is negated. Different-subject marking blocks negative spread in both directions, so each clause keeps its own polarity. Negative transportation from a complement clause to a main clause does not occur in Mauwake, and this is also true in Amele, though Usan permits it.

text: Different parts in the grammar interact to produce the deictic system, the spatio-temporal and personal orientation related to the speech situation or another situation specified in the text. The default deictic centre is the speaker, the speaker's location and the present time.
summary: The grammar’s different components work together to create a deictic system that organizes reference around a speech situation or another context specified in the text. By default, this deictic centre is the speaker, along with the speaker’s location and the present time.

text:
Only the first and second person are inherently deictic, as they get their whole meaning, apart from the number, from the speech situation. The person marking is done by pronouns ( sec:3.5 ) and by person/number suffixes on the verbs ( sec:3.8.3.4, sec:3.8.3.5 ). The special status of the first person as against both the second and third persons shows in the imperative and the switch-reference marking. In the imperative the dual number is only possible in the first person ex:6:x1262 ( sec:3.8.3.3.2 ):

Aria, i owowa=ko urup- u. Auwa aite wia karu-i-yan, owowa=pa wia uruf- u.\\
alright 1p. unm village= nf ascend- imp.1d 1s/p.father 1s/p.mother 3p. acc visit-Np- fu.1p village= loc 3p. acc see- imp.1d\\
`Alright, let's (dl) go up to the village. We'll visit father and mother, let's (dl) see them in the village.'

In the different-subject medial verbs the first person singular and plural share the same suffix, whereas the second and third persons are grouped together and the distinction is made according to number, between singular and plural ex:6:x1263 ( sec:3.8.3.5.2 ).

I ikoka urup-ep nia maak-omkun ora-iwkin, aria owawiya feeke pok-ap ik-ok \\
1p. unm later ascend- ss. seq 2p. acc tell-1s/p. ds descend-2/3p. ds alright together here. cf sit- ss. seq be- ss \\
`Later when we come up and tell you and (then) you come down and we sit down together here and '

Even though the first and second person pronouns are already deictic in themselves, their unmarked plural forms can both co-occur with the proximate demonstrative fain 'this', ex:6:x1269

and the second person also with the distal demonstrative nain `that'. As only one of the people referred to by these plural forms typically is a speech act participant and the others may or may not be present, the addition of the demonstrative makes it clear that all the people referred to are present in the situation:

Ikoka Yaapan=ke ekap-emi ni emeria unowa fain nia aaw-urum-i-kuan.\\
later Japan= cf come- ss. sim 2p. unm woman many this 2p. acc take- distr / a -Np- fu.3p\\
`Later the Japanese will come and take all of you many women [here in this village].'

Mauwake has no separate system of social deixis, as there are no honorifics, nor are there special pronouns used for particular kin or social groups or the like.

Emotional deixis, associating the speaker with the topic of conversation or distancing him from it, is a possible use for demonstratives in Papuan languages and worldwide (, ). In Mauwake that possibility is not utilized: the demonstratives are neutral in this respect.
summary: Only first and second person are inherently deictic in Mauwake, and person is marked by pronouns and by person/number suffixes on verbs. The first person has special behavior in the imperative and switch-reference system, while plural first- and second-person pronouns can co-occur with demonstratives to show that all referents are present in the speech situation. Mauwake lacks social deixis and does not use demonstratives for emotional deixis; in this language, demonstratives are neutral.

text:
Locative deixis, which relates the location to the speech act participants, utilizes several different word classes. The proximate demonstrative fain `this' ex:6:x1273 ( sec:3.6.2 ) and the corresponding locative adverb fan `here' ex:6:x1274 ( sec:3.6.3 ) are truly deictic, as their meaning is based on the location of the speaker. The distal-1 demonstrative nain `that' and the adverb nan `there' are more neutral, and the less common distal-2 and -3 deictics have other defining features besides the distance to the speaker.

Ep-ap owora fain aaw-ep enim-eka, iwer(a) eka fain enim-eka. \\
come- ss. seq betelnut this take- ss. seq eat- imp.2p coconut water this eat- imp.2p\\
`Come and take this betelnut and eat it, (and) drink this coconut water.'

Yo wia wiim-urup-ep fan wia wu-ap kiiriw iw-a-m.\\
1s. unm 3p. acc escort-ascend- ss. seq here 3p. acc put- ss. seq again go- pa -1s\\
`I escorted them up here and went (back) again.'

In the location verbs fan- `arrive/be here' ex:6:x1275 and nan- `arrive/be there' ( sec:3.8.4.4.3 ) the deictic goal forms the verb root.

Auwa afura fan-e-k a, no=ko wiar akim-ap=ko uruf-e.\\
1s/p.father lime here- pa -3s intj 2s. unm = nf 3. dat try- ss. seq = nf see- imp.2s\\
`Ah, father's lime is here, you try it and see.'

In the directional verbs ex:6:x1278 ( sec:3.8.4.4.5 ) as well as the related bring-verbs ex:6:x1279 ( sec:3.8.2.4.2 ) the verb root gives indication as to the direction of the movement. Only those directional verbs where the direction is clearly related to the speaker are deictic. The second person is not a possible alternative deictic centre for the verb ekap- `come'.

Uurika nefar ikiw-i-nen. \\
tomorrow 2s. dat go-Np- fu.1s \\
`Tomorrow I'll come to you.' (Lit: ` I'll go (from my present place)...')

Mua imen-ap=na feeke wia p-ekap-eka. \\
man find- ss. seq = tp here. cf 3p. acc bpx -come- imp.2p\\
`If you find the men, bring them here.'

Although the prototypical deictic centre is close proximity to the speaker, it may be extended to quite a large area. In ex:6:x1892 where the coming of the Japanese troops is described, it covers the whole North Coast of the New Guinea island:

Ne ekap-ep Numbia=pa nan urup-e-mik. \\
add come- ss. seq Numbia= loc there ascend- pa -1/3p\\
`And they came and landed at Numbia.'

In narratives it is more typical that the verbs ekap- `come' and ikiw- `go', as well as the related verbs for `bring' and `take', get their deictic centre from the main character ex:6:x1277, not the narrator, since the narrator often is not even a participant in the story.

Sawur emeria nain ikiw-eya o iikir-ami owowa ekap-o-k. \\
spirit woman that go-2/3s. ds 3s. unm get.up- ss. sim village come- pa -3s\\
`When the spirit woman went (away), he came to the/his village.'
summary:
Locative deixis in the language is expressed through several word classes, including demonstratives, locative adverbs, and certain verbs. The proximate forms fain `this` and fan `here` are directly speaker-based, while distal forms such as nain `that` and nan `there` are less strictly deictic, and some more distant forms have additional features beyond distance.

Deictic meaning also appears in location and motion verbs, where the verb root itself can encode a goal or direction. In narratives, the deictic center often shifts from the narrator to the main character, and in some contexts the speaker’s deictic area can extend over a large region.

text:
Temporal deixis relates time to the speech act, or alternatively to the time of a specific event. Tense marking ( sec:3.8.3.4 ) is the most important device for this in Mauwake, as tense is an obligatory category in verbs. In some Papuan languages tense markers and demonstratives are morphologically related (Cindi Farr, p.c.), but this is not the case in Mauwake. The present tense marks the default deictic centre, the past tense refers to the time before that point, and the future tense to the time after it. The example (3. ex:3:x1029 )

is repeated here as ex:6:x1893:

Unan aakun-e-mik, aakisa aakun-i-mik ne uurika nainiw aakun-i-yen.\\
yesterday talk- pa -1/3p now/today talk-Np- pr.1/3p add tomorrow again talk-Np- fu.1p\\
`Yesterday we talked, now/today we talk and tomorrow we'll talk again.'

Papuan languages in general favour presenting a narrative in strictly chronological order, so a relative tense, where the deictic centre is shifted either to the past or to the future, is not utilized widely. This is true of Mauwake as well. When a shift to the past is needed, it can be done by right-dislocating a medial clause after a past-tense marked final clause ex:6:x1268:

Wilkar wia muf-em-ik-om-a-mik, mua kui-kuisow wia maak-iwkin.\\
cart 3p. acc pull- ss. sim -be- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p man rdp -one 3p. acc tell-2/3p. ds \\
`They 1 pulled carts for them 2, after they 2 had told the men 1 one by one.'

The same-subject sequential forms of the directional verbs ekap- `come' and ikiw- `go' also have temporal deictic use, the former referring to time extending to the present moment, the latter mainly to time from the present moment onward. The examples (3. ex:3:x290 ) and (3. ex:3:x437 )

are repeated below as ex:6:x1941 and ex:6:x1942.

Naap on-am-ik-e-mik, ekap-ep aakisa. \\
thus do- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p come- ss. seq now\\
`We have been doing like that (all the time) up until now.'

No naap ik-ok iki(w-e)p mokoma enuma iiwawun aakun-i-nan.\\
2s. unm thus be- ss go- ss. seq year new altogether talk-Np- fu.2s\\
`You will be like that (long time) but next year you will talk.'

The two groups of deictic temporal adverbs ( sec:3.9.1.2 ) behave differently as to what the deictic centre is. The specific temporal adverbs, which refer to a certain day in relation to the utterance, always take the time of the speech act as their deictic centre ex:6:x1889.

i uurika ora-i-yan, ifera un-owa ora-i-yan.\\
1p. unm tomorrow descend-Np- fu.1p sea(water) fetch- nmz descend-Np- fu.1p\\
` we will go down tomorrow, we will go down to fetch sea water.'

The non-specific temporals normally do this too ex:6:x1890:

Nain iiriw me kerer-e-k, aakisa fan. \\
that1 earlier not appear now here \\
`That didn't appear ealier/long ago but just now (lit: now here).'

But their time reference may also be relative, with the time of the event taken as the deictic centre. This is especially true of aakisa `now', which is used for perspectivization. The `` was-now paradox'' occurs in ``free indirect style'' when ``[t]he deictic centre of the utterance is the writer/narrator, but certain deictic elements are relativized to give the impression of direct access to the character's mental states: these include temporal and spatial expressions such as now, here, today but not tense or person.''. In the following two examples, the temporal adverbs aakisa `now' and aakisa fan `just now', do not refer externally to the time close to the speech event; instead, they are text-internal perspectivization devices to highlight the importance of the event to the main characters in the text. ex:6:x475 is from an old traditional story and ex:6:x1891 tells about events that took place over four decades before the recording.

Nain or-op ``buu'' (na-e-k), aakisa eka saanar- e-k. \\
that1 fall- ss. seq buu say- pa -3s now water dry- pa -3s\\
`It fell with a thud (and they knew that) now the water had dried up.'

Ekap-ep, ekap-ep, aakisa fan unowa Wewak=pa nan urup- e-mik.\\
come- ss. seq come- ss. seq now here many Wewak= loc there ascend- pa -1/3p \\
`They came and came, and just now many came up there in Wewak.'

For the deictic shift that takes place in indirect speech, see sec:8.3.2.1.2.
summary:
Temporal deixis in Mauwake is mainly expressed through obligatory verbal tense, with present as the default deictic center, past marking time before it, and future marking time after it. The language generally prefers strictly chronological narration, so relative tense and shifted deictic centers are not widely used, though a past shift can be created by certain clause structures and by the directional verbs *ekap-* ‘come’ and *ikiw-* ‘go’ in temporal uses.

Temporal adverbs also differ in how they set the deictic center: specific adverbs normally refer to a time relative to the speech act, while non-specific adverbs usually do as well but can also be interpreted relative to the event time. In particular, *aakisa* ‘now’ and *aakisa fan* ‘just now’ can function as perspectivization devices in text-internal narration rather than referring directly to the time of speaking.

text:
Nouns are not inflected for number in Mauwake, and in the whole noun phrase the number may be left unspecified ex:6:x1284. The verbs are marked for either singular or plural, but the plural form can be used also for unspecified number ex:6:x1285. The pronouns must be either singular or plural. Besides these two obligatory number marking devices the language has several other means for quantification.

Waaya kiikir=iw uruf-i-mik, owowa=pa. \\
pig first= inst see-Np- pr.1/3p village= loc \\
`First they look at the pig(s) in the village.'

Nain pun sira naap=iw, mua=ko me kerer-e-mik. \\
that1 too custom thus= inst man= nf not appear- pa -1/3p\\
`That was like that too, the (guilty) person/people did not appear.'
summary: In Mauwake, nouns are not inflected for number, and number can remain unspecified throughout the noun phrase. Verbs are marked for singular or plural, though the plural form may also indicate unspecified number, while pronouns must be overtly singular or plural. Beyond these obligatory number-marking devices, the language also has additional means of quantification.

text:
Numerals ( sec:3.4.1 ) are used when the exact number is relevant ex:6:x1286, ex:6:x1308, non-numeral quantifiers ( sec:3.4.2 ) are used elsewhere ex:6:x1287.

Masin erup nainiw wu-owa epa ik-ua. \\
engine two again put- nmz place be- pa.3s\\
`There is a place for putting two more engines.'

Waa muuka arow ekap-o-k. \\
pig son three come- pa -1s\\
`Three piglets came.'

Emeria unow=iya ikiw-ep eka nain imar-e-mik. \\
woman many= com go- ss. seq river that1 catch.fish- pa -1/3p\\
`All the women went and fished at the river.'

The third person plural unmarked pronoun functions as a pluraliser both in an ordinary non phrase ex:6:x1288 and with place names when the population of the place is referred to ex:6:x1289 ( sec:4.1.1 ).

Nain wi mua sira=ke, emeria soop-owa sira. \\
that1 3p. unm man custom= cf woman bury- nmz custom\\
`That is the men's custom, the custom of burying wife/wives.'

Irak-owa weeser-eya aria wi Simbine baurar-e-mik.\\
fight- nmz finish-2/3s. ds alright 3p. unm Simbine flee- pa -1/3p\\
`When the fighting was finished, alright the Simbine people fled.'

Even without the pluralizing pronoun, the word for, or a name of, a village may occasionally, as a subject of a clause, refer to the population and thus be interpreted as plural. In ex:6:x1307 this shows in the plural marking in the verb.

Ne owowa oko nain=ke maak-e-mik, \\
add village other that1= cf tell- pa -1/3p\\
`And (the people of) that other village told him, ''

Reduplication is another pluralizing device used in the noun phrase. Only a small group of nouns can undergo reduplication ex:6:x1290 ( sec:3.2.6.2 ), but in adjectives it is somewhat more common ex:6:x1291 ( sec:3.3 ).

Waaya pa-ep kio-kiowa naap uup-e-mik. \\
pig butcher- ss. seq rdp -piece thus cook- pa -1/3p\\
`We butchered the pig and cooked the pieces like that.'

Owow(a) saria=ke kiikir perek-i-mik, mua or-oram fain weetak.\\
village headman= cf first pull.out-Np- pr.1/3p man rdp -insignificant this no\\
`The village headmen harvest it first, not common people like this/us.'

Comitative noun phrases ( sec:4.1.3 ) are used to indicate duality ex:6:x1292, ex:6:x1293 or plurality ex:6:x1294, ex:6:x1295.

(Yo/I) auwa ikos fan ik-e-mik. \\
1s/1p. unm 1s/p.father together.with here be- pa -1/3p\\
`I and my father are here.'

No ikoka mua owawiya irak-ep me efar kerer-e.\\
2s. unm later man with fight- ss. seq not 1s. dat appear- imp.2s\\
`Later when you and your husband fight, don't come to me.'

Ne bom=iya kateres=iya bom=iya kateres=iya. \\
and bomb= com cartridge= com bomb= com cartridge= com \\
`And bombs and cartridges, bombs and cartridges (kept dropping).'

Pauli ame era=pa wia uruf-ap \\
Pauli assoc road= loc 3p. acc see- ss. seq \\
`I saw Pauli and the others on the road, and '

Personal pronouns have to mark the number, Except for third person dative pronoun, which is wiar for both singular and plural. but in cases where the number is unknown or unspecified, the plural is used ex:6:x1309.

Ikiw-ep mua wia uruf-a-k na weetak, mua=ko me wia furew-a-k. \\
go- ss. seq man 3p. acc see- pa -3s but no man= nf not 3p. acc sense- pa -3s\\
`She went and looked for anyone/people but no, she did not sense (there was) anyone (there).'
summary:
The passage describes several ways number and plurality are expressed in the language. Numerals are used when exact quantity matters, while non-numeral quantifiers are used otherwise; plurality can also be marked by the third-person plural pronoun, reduplication in some nouns and adjectives, and comitative noun phrases for dual or plural reference.

It also notes that personal pronouns normally mark number, except for the third-person dative pronoun *wiar*, which is used for both singular and plural. When number is unknown or unspecified, the plural form is used.

text:
The person/number suffix in the finite verbs ( sec:3.8.3.4 ) is the most frequently used device to indicate quantification: it shows whether the subject is singular or plural. Often the person/number suffix in the verb is the only element in a clause overtly showing number ex:6:x1296.

Mauw-am-ik-ok ik-ok mauw-owa weeser-eya urera ekap-e- mik.\\
work- ss. sim -be- ss be- ss work- nmz finish-2/3s. ds afternoon come- pa -1/3p\\
`They came and landed there at Numbia.'

But if the subject noun is [-human], even the person/number suffix may not indicate the number, since plural marking is only used for humans and occasionally for large animals, and only very rarely for inanimates. In ex:6:x1283, the verbs in both sentences refer to airplanes, but because the action in the first sentence is attributed to the soldiers inside the planes, the finite verb is in plural form.

Amerika irak-ow(a) iinan aasa ekap-ep Ulingan nan bom fu-fuurk-ikiw-e-mik. Iinan=iw iinan=iw wu-ami feenap Wewak kame naap ikiw-o-k.\\
America fight- nmz sky canoe come- ss. seq Ulingan there bomb rdp -drop-go- pa -1/3p sky= inst sky= inst put- ss. sim like.this Wewak side thus go- pa -3s\\
`American fighter planes came and went on dropping bombs there in Ulingan. They were really high up and went like this to Wewak.'

Reduplication is more common in verbs than in nouns or adjectives ( sec:3.8.2.4.1 ). In transitive verbs the reduplication indicates plurality of the resulting object ex:6:x1298, ex:6:x1297.

Kau nain pa-ep, gele-gelemuti-tik pu-puuk - ap uup-e-mik.\\
cow that1 butcher- ss. seq rdp -small- rdp rdp -cut- ss. seq cook- pa -1/3\\
`They butchered the cow and cut it into small pieces and cooked it/them.'

Aruf-irapar-emi meren(a) suuw-owa wiar pere-perek-a-mik.\\
hit-to.and.fro- ss. sim leg pull- nmz 3. dat rdp -tear- pa -1/3p\\
`They hit him all over and tore his trousers to pieces.'

Both the distributive suffixes ( sec:3.8.2.3.2 ) mark plurality; the argument that the marking pluralizes depends on the type of verb ex:6:x1300-- ex:6:x1302.

Iinan aasa fan or-om-ik-omak-i-ya. \\
sky canoe here descend- ss. sim -be- distr / pl -Np- pr.3s\\
`Many planes are descending here.'

Koora pun ariwa=ke kuum-eya aw-omak-e-k. \\
house also arrow= cf burn-2/3s. ds burn- distr / pl - pa -3s\\
`Also many houses burned down when the ammunition burned them.'

Owowa wia wi-urum-e-p naap ikiw-i-kuan. \\
village 3p. acc give.them- distr / a - ss. seq thus go-Np- fu.3p\\
`They give villages to all of them and then they go like that.' (Certain villages are designated for certain people to go to.)

O iiriw maa bala wiar aaw-urum-ep ona mia=pa-r=iw wu-a-k.\\
3s. unm earlier thing ornament 3. acc get- distr / a - ss. seq 3s. gen body= loc - = lim put- pa -3s\\
`Earlier he had received ornaments from all of them and (now) he put them on his own body only.'

In the object cross-referencing verbs ( sec:3.8.4.2.4 ) the root shows singularity ex:6:x1304 or plurality ex:6:x1303 of the object that is cross-referenced.

Iperowa opora wiok-i-yan. \\
middle.aged talk follow.them-Np- fu.1p\\
`We'll follow/obey the talk of the middle-aged men.'

Maa eneka kes mane-maneka oram iw-e-mik. \\
thing tooth case rdp -big just give.him- pa -1/3p\\
`They gave him big meat (tin) cases for free.'

When a numeral follows a nominalized verb form and precedes the resultative verb ar- `become' ( sec:3.8.4.4.4 ), that indicates how many times an action was performed ex:6:x1305, ex:6:x1306.

Ewar maneka muf-owa erup ar-e. \\
wind big pull- nmz two become- imp.2s\\
`Breathe deeply twice.'

Kiikir iinan=pa akim-owa arow ar-e-mik. \\
first top= loc try- nmz three become- pa -1/3p\\
`First they tried it three times on top.'
summary:
The passage describes several ways the language marks plurality or repeated action. Finite verb person/number suffixes are the most common plural markers, though with nonhuman subjects they may not reliably indicate number; reduplication and distributive suffixes also mark plurality, with their exact effect depending on the verb type.

It also notes that in object cross-referencing verbs, the root itself can show whether the referenced object is singular or plural. Finally, a numeral placed between a nominalized verb and the resultative verb *ar-* ‘become’ indicates how many times an action occurred.

text:
As the inventory of adjectives is typically small in Papuan languages (,, ), it is no surprise that regular morphological or syntactic forms to express comparative and superlative are rare, or even non-existent. In Mauwake comparison can be expressed in various ways, but there are no specific forms that could be called comparative or superlative. Since the overall frequency of comparative constructions is very low, it is not possible here to call any of them the preferred strategy.

One way to express comparison is to conjoin two structurally similar clauses, where the adjective in the first one functioning as the non-verbal predicate is not intensified, but in the second clause it has an intensifier. The first clause contains the standard of comparison ex:6:x1336.

Poka fain maala, ne oko maala akena. \\
stilt this long add other long very\\
`This stilt is long but the other one is longer (lit: very long).'

Although the clauses usually are descriptive, as above, they do not have to be. In the following example the locative noun iinan `top', functioning like an adjective here, modifies the head noun in both the clauses ex:6:x1324.

Ema iinan urup-e-m, ne no ema iinan akena urup-o-n.\\
mountain top ascend- pa -1s add 2s. unm mountain top very ascend- pa -2s\\
`I climbed a high mountain, but you climbed a higher (lit: very high) mountain.'

Another way is to use adjectives that are antonymous ex:6:x1325. As a comparative structure this is problematic in that it is arbitrary to call the subject of one clause the standard and the subject of the other the object of comparison.

Waaya nain gelemuta, oko nain maneka. \\
pig that1 small other that1 big\\
`That pig is smaller than the other one.' Or: `That other pig is bigger than that one.' (Lit: That pig is small, the other one is big.)'

The same caveat applies to the following structure, where the adjective is negated for comparison ex:6:x1326:

Auwa uuw-owa eliwa, mua oko fain wia. \\
1s/p.father work- nmz good man other this no\\
`My father's work is better than this other man's. (Lit: My father's work is good, this other man's is not.) '

According to this Conjoined Comparative strategy, exemplified above, is prevalent in Australia and New Guinea. But the sample of New Guinean languages used for the generalization is very small (and includes both Austronesian and Papuan languages), and I suggest that at least for tng languages the Exceed Comparative, the strategy represented in that sample only by Amele, is a possible alternative and may actually be as common as, or more common than, the Conjoined Comparative strategy. My opinion is mainly based on the experience of working with national translators. When searching for translation equivalents for comparison forms, they often start with the Conjoined Comparative pattern, but very soon after realising that they do not have to stay within the limits of stative clauses only or stick to the adjective class, many actually tend to prefer the Exceed Comparative as the more natural and accurate expression for comparison. mentions both of these mechanisms for Usan. There are two clauses in this pattern too: one may be equative and contain an adjective, the other is a transitive clause containing the verb nomak- `exceed/surpass' as the predicate and the standard of comparison as the object ex:6:x1327-- ex:6:x1333. The order of the two clauses is free.

Maa mane-maneka, maa fain nomak-ep ik-ua. \\
thing rdp -big thing this surpass- ss. seq be- pa.3s\\
`They are big things, greater than these.'

No yiena nembesir nomak-ep maneka ar-ek-a-m na-ep=i?\\
2s. unm 1p. gen ancestor surpass- ss. seq big become- cntf - pa -1s say- ss. seq = qm \\
`Do you want to become greater than our ancestors?'

Nomokowa kakawa fain iiwa, oko nomak-ep puuk-a-m. \\
tree strip this short other surpass- ss. seq cut- pa -1s.\\
`This piece of timber is short, I cut the other one longer.'

A transitive clause with nomak- is also used, when a noun rather than an adjective describes the characteristic under comparison ex:6:x1329, ex:6:x1894.

O kekan-owa=ke yo kekan-owa efar nomak-e-k.\\
3s. unm be.strong- nmz = cf 1s. unm be.strong- nmz 1s. dat surpass- pa -3s\\
`He is stronger than I. (Lit: His strength surpasses my strength.)'

Mua oko=ke ikiwosa/amisa efar nomak-e-k. \\
man other= cf head/knowledge 1s. dat surpass- pa -3s\\
`Someone else is more intelligent than I. (Lit: surpasses my head/knowledge.)'

In ex:6:x1895, nomak- is employed to compare arrival times:...wia nomak-ep me miim-ep... urup-i-yen, weetak.\\
3p. acc surpass- ss. seq not precede- ss. seq ascend-Np- fu.1p no\\
` we'll not go up earlier than they, no.'

For superlatives, the quantifier unowiya `all' may be used in the object np ex:6:x1330.

No unuma nain mua unow=iya wia nomakek. \\
2s. unm name that1 man many= com 3p. acc surpass- pa -3s\\
`You are the most important of all people.' (Lit: `Your name surpasses all people.')

In ex:6:x1337, the two comparison strategies are employed in the same sentence, and the intensifier akena `very' indicates superlative:

Poka fain maala, nain nomak-e-k, ne oko nain maala akena.\\
stilt this long that1 surpass- pa -3s add other that1 long very\\
`This stilt is longer than that one, and/but that other one is the longest.'

When there is a difference between things that are compared, but the difference is not graded, the phrase sira oko 'different (lit: another kind)' is used to modify the noun ex:6:x1334, ex:6:x1335.

Iwakara sira oko miim-ap baurar-e-mik. \\
neck kind other hear- ss. seq flee- pa -1/3p\\
`They heard a different voice and ran away.'

Takira opor(a) sira oko=ko me wia maak-e. \\
youngster talk kind other= nf not 3p. acc tell- imp.2s\\
`Don't tell different things to the youngsters (from what you are supposed to tell them).'
summary:
Mauwake has no dedicated comparative or superlative morphological forms; instead, comparison is expressed through several clause-based strategies. These include conjoined clauses with intensification or antonymic/negative contrasts, and an “exceed” construction using the verb *nomak-* ‘surpass,’ which can compare adjectives, nouns, and even arrival time; superlatives may be formed with *unowiya* ‘all’ or with the intensifier *akena* ‘very’ in a comparison context.  

The passage also notes that the conjoined comparative is widespread in Australia and New Guinea, but argues that in Trans-New Guinea languages the exceed strategy may be equally or more common. For non-graded differences, Mauwake uses *sira oko* ‘different, another kind’ to modify nouns.

text:
A possible outcome of comparison is that the compared items, or actions, are identical or similar rather than different. Mauwake has several equative constructions, The term ``equative construction'' is not to be confused with equative clauses discussed in sec:5.6.1 ways of expressing similarity.

For an equivalent of `as adj as' structure, the intensity adverb pepek 'enough' is used, often together with another intensifier ex:6:x1331, ex:6:x1332.

No merena maneka yo merena iiwawun pepek. \\
2s. unm foot big 1s. unm foot altogether enough\\
`Your feet are big, just as big as my feet.' Or: `Your big feet are just as big as mine.'

Urauwa maala Moro owowa maala pepek akena. \\
hole long Moro village long enough very\\
`The hole (is) as deep as Moro village is long.'

The two most common words used in equative constructions are the deictic manner adverb naap `thus, like that' ( sec:3.9.1.3 ) and the postposition saarik `like' ( sec:3.12.3 ). Naap is used to compare things that are essentially the same, even identical ex:6:x1338-- ex:6:x1348.

Auwa mia maneka, muuka pun naap. \\
1s/p.father body big son also like.that\\
`The father is big, (and) the son is like that too.'

Muuka nain (ona) wiawi naap. \\
boy that1 3s/p. gen father like.that\\
`The boy/son is like his father.'

I maa en-owa naap nain yienak-e. \\
1p. unm food eat- nmz like.that that1 feed.us- imp.2s\\
`Give us food like that.'

Also the corresponding proximal manner adverb feenap 'like this' is used occasionally ex:6:x1347:

Uura feenap nain, wi wilkar nain muf-e-mik. \\
night like.this that1 3p. unm cart that1 pull- pa -1/3p\\
`On nights like this they pulled the carts.'

The postposition saarik `like' expresses some similarity between two essentially different things. The actual point of similarity may be expressed explicitly ex:6:x1341 or left implied ex:6:x1340.

Pon oposia eliwa, aara oposia saarik. \\
turtle meat good chicken meat like\\
`Turtle meat is good, like chicken meat.'

Mera iperuma ifa saarik. \\
fish eel snake like\\
`An eel is like a snake.'

The similarity may not be a particular quality, expressible with an adjective. In ex:6:x1342 it is the number of different things that is compared.

Ulingan fa=na iinan aasa nepa saarik, unow(a) akena. \\
Ulingan intj = tp sky canoe bird like many very\\
`Ulingan -- wow -- the airplanes were like birds, there were lots of them.'

When saarik is postposed after a nominalized verb, it indicates pretension. This is a case of a similarity of action, but not ``the real thing'' ex:6:x1343, ex:6:x1344.

Moram era paayar-owa saarik fan yia p-or-o-n?\\
why road understand- nmz like here 1p. acc bpx -descend- pa -2s\\
`Why did you bring us down here as if you knew the road?'

O Menamura or-owa saarik iwera fook-a-k. \\
3s. unm Manam descend- nmz like coconut split- pa -3s\\
`He split coconuts (for copra), as if he were going to Manam.'

In other cases it may not indicate pretension but a false or ungrounded expectation ex:6:x1345:

Yo efa sesenar-owa saarik oram maneka uuw-owa yoowa on-a-m. \\
1s. unm 1s. acc buy- nmz like for.nothing big work- nmz hot do- pa -1s\\
`I worked hard for nothing, as if they would pay me for it (lit: buy me).'

The phrase nainiw akena `exactly like' is reserved for the cases of striking similarity ex:6:x1346.

Wiipa nain onak miikapura nainiw akena. \\
girl that1 3s/p.mother face again very\\
`The girl's face is exactly like her mother's.'
summary:
Mauwake expresses equative comparison in several ways. For “as adj as” structures it uses the intensifier pepek ‘enough’, while the deictic adverb naap ‘thus, like that’ is used for things that are essentially the same or identical, and the postposition saarik ‘like’ for similarity between different things.

The proximal form feenap ‘like this’ is also sometimes used. When saarik follows a nominalized verb, it can express pretension or an ungrounded expectation, and the phrase nainiw akena ‘exactly like’ is reserved for striking similarity.

text: The basic speech acts are mostly expressed by the functional sentence types typical of them: a statement by a declarative sentence, a question by an interrogative sentence and a command by an imperative sentence.
summary: The passage states that basic speech acts are generally expressed by typical functional sentence types. Statements use declarative sentences, questions use interrogative sentences, and commands use imperative sentences.

text: The declarative sentence, used to make a statement/assertion, is the unmarked sentence type, default in narrative, descriptive and procedural texts and common in other text types as well. The final verb has full tense and person/number marking. The intonation pattern in declarative sentences is falling ( sec:2.1.3.2 ).
summary: Declarative sentences are the unmarked sentence type used to make statements or assertions, and they are the default form in narrative, descriptive, and procedural texts, as well as being common in other text types. In these sentences, the final verb carries full tense and person/number marking, and the intonation pattern falls.

text: The basic function of questions, or interrogative sentences, is to request either information or some action from the addressee(s). Rhetorical questions have other functions as well. Structurally the two basic types are non-polar, or content, questions and polar, or yes-no, questions. Echo questions and confirmation questions are modifications of these.
summary: Questions, or interrogative sentences, are used primarily to request information or action from the addressee, though rhetorical questions may serve other functions. Structurally, the main types are non-polar (content) questions and polar (yes-no) questions, with echo questions and confirmation questions as modifications of these basic forms.

text:
Non-polar questions, or content questions, require the use of question words ( sec:3.7.1 ). There is no question-word fronting: a question word occupies the same position that the questioned element would have in a statement. This is typical of Papuan sov languages. The intonation is falling like in a statement, but the stressed syllable of the question word has a slightly higher pitch than the words before and/or after it ( sec:2.1.3.2 ).

Any argument or peripheral in a clause can be questioned, as well as its constituents ex:7:x1167-- ex:7:x1174.

( Mua) naareke koora ku-am-ika-i-ya? \\
(man) who. cf house build- ss. sim -be-Np-3s \\
`Who is building a house?'

Muuka nain maa mauwa enim-i-non? \\
son that1 thing what eat-Np- fu.3s \\
`What will the son eat?'

No muuka wiipa kamin (nefar ik-ua)? \\
2s. unm son daughter how.many (2s. dat be- pa.3s)\\
`How many children (lit. son daughter) do you have?'

Mua napuma moram owowa p-ikiw-i-yan? \\
man sick/body why village bpx -go-Np- fu.1p \\
`Why should we take the body to the village?'

Mukuna aw-o-k nain kamenap umuk-i-yen? \\
fire burn- pa -3s that1 how extinguish-Np- fu.1p \\
`How could we extinguish the fire that was burning?'

Maa nain epa kain=pa imenar-i-non? \\
thing that1 place which= loc appear-Np- fu.3s \\
`Where (lit: in which place) will that thing appear?'

Wi kaakew mua=ke uf-e-mik? \\
3p. unm which.village man= cf dance- pa -1/3p \\
`The men of which village danced?'

The kind of ambiguity between a subject and an object that Usan has, which arises from the fronting of a topicalized element A theme in my terminology here., is not possible in Mauwake. This is because the question words take the contrastive focus marker - ke when functioning as a subject. Because of elision, and the merging of the contrastive focus marker with the question word, the word for `who' in Mauwake actually has a contrasted/nominative ex:7:x1167, ex:7:x1171 and an accusative form ex:7:x1170. The object is fronted in ex:7:x1171 as a theme; in ex:7:x1172 the object is not fronted.

Mua nain S naarew O aruf-a-k? \\
man that1 who( acc ) hit- pa -3s \\
`Who did that man hit?'

Mua nain O naareke S aruf-a-k? \\
man that1 who. cf hit- pa -3s \\
`Who hit that man?'

(Mua) naareke S mua nain O aruf-a-k? \\
(man) who. cf man that1 hit- pa -3s \\
`Who hit that man?'

It is most common to have the question in a main clause, but medial clauses also easily allow non-polar questions. The scope of the question word only extends to the clause which contains it. In ex:7:x1168 the fact that the people ran away is not questioned.

Mua naareke wia aruf-eya baurar-e-mik? \\
man who. cf 3p. acc hit-2/3s. ds run.away- pa -1/3p \\
`Who hit them (so that) they ran away?'

A constituent in a complement clause (with a nominalized verb) can be questioned ex:7:x1175, but not in a relative clause ex:7:x1176.

Ama kamin ikiw-owa ma-e-mik? \\
sun/time how.much go- nmz say- pa -1/3p \\
`At what time did they say to go?'

*Wi iikamin ekap-e-mik nain wia uruf-a-n? \\
3p. unm when come- pa -1/3p that1 3p. acc see- pa -2s \\

Multiple constituents in the same clause can be questioned with a question word. This is not common, but the following elicited sentences are considered completely natural ex:7:x1177, ex:7:x1178.

Emeria naareke ama kamin=pa ekap-o-k? \\
woman who. cf sun/time how.much= loc come- pa -3s \\
`Who (woman) came at what time?'

Mua kain=ke emeria kain aaw-o-k? \\
man which= cf woman which take- pa -3s \\
`Which man took/married which woman?'

When there is a lot of hesitation in the question, the question clitic - i, which normally marks a polar question, is added to the end of the question ex:7:x1187. This is the same form that the echo questions have ( sec:7.2.3 ).

Auwa efa amukar-e-k nain yo kamenap ar-i-nen= i?\\
father 1s. acc scold- pa -3s that 1s. unm how become-Np- fu.1s= qm \\
`(I wonder) what will happen to me because father scolded me?'
summary:
Mauwake content questions use question words in the same clause position as the questioned element, with no question-word fronting; they also have falling intonation, though the question word carries slightly higher pitch. Any argument or peripheral can be questioned, and question words in subject position take the contrastive focus marker, which gives them distinct nominative versus accusative forms and prevents subject-object ambiguity found in Usan.  

Non-polar questions usually occur in main clauses, but they can also appear in medial clauses, with scope limited to the clause containing the question word; constituents in complement clauses can be questioned, but not those in relative clauses. Multiple constituents may be questioned in one clause, and in hesitant questions the polar-question clitic -i may be added at the end.

text:
Polar questions, also called nexus questions, or yes-no questions, expect either confirmation or negation of the questioned proposition. According to, a polar question in tng languages is often marked by an affix which is part of the verb complex. In Mauwake it is coded by the question clitic - i ( sec:3.12.8 ) and slightly rising intonation ( sec:2.1.3.2 ), both occurring sentence-finally. Because Mauwake is an sov language, the clitic most often attaches itself to a verb ex:7:x1179, but it can attach to another word class as well, when there is no final verb ex:7:x1180, ex:7:x1181:

Ni nain me=ko uruf-a-man =i? \\
2p. unm that1 not= nf see- pa -2p= qm \\
`Didn't you see that?'

Nos= i? \\
2s. fc = qm \\
`You?'

Maa nain eliwa= ki? \\
thing that1 good= cf. qm \\
`Is that thing good?'

When the polar question is in the negative, a one-word answer may be ambiguous. Traditionally the answer either affirmed or negated the affirmative or negative polarity of the question, but because of the influence of Tok Pisin and English, Mauwake is changing so that the answer tends to either affirm or negate the verb ( sec:6.2.4 ).

Alternative questions can be closed or open. calls only the former an alternative (or disjunctive) question, and the latter a question with standard disjunction. The former give two, or sometimes more, alternatives, one of which has to be chosen; the latter also allow the possibility that none of the alternatives is chosen. The two types differ in Mauwake as to the nature of the last alternative.

The non-final alternatives in a closed question take the question marker - i. The final alternative, usually preceded by the disjunctive coordinator e `or' ( sec:3.11.2 ), may be just a negation particle weetak or wia ex:7:x1182, a full statement ex:7:x1183, or an elliptical clause with only the questioned item ex:7:x1184.

Yo emeria=ko efar uruf-a-man= i e weetak? \\
1s. unm woman= nf 1s. dat see- pa -2p= qm or no \\
`Did you see my wife or not?'

Nain kema suuw-i-man= i e kema irin-ar-e-man? \\
that1 liver push-Np- pr.2p= qm or liver stuck- inch - pa -2p \\
`Do you remember (lit: push the liver) that, or have you forgotten (lit: liver is stuck) it?'

No Matukar ikiw-i-nan= i Dylup= i e Sarang? \\
2s. unm Matukar go-Np- fu.2s= qm Dylup= qm or Sarang \\
`Will you go to Matukar, Dylup, or Sarang?'

When the alternative question is open, the question marker - i marks not only the non-final alternatives but also the final one ex:7:x1185, ex:7:x1186.

Matukar ikiw-i-nan= i e Dylup ikiw-i-nan= i? \\
Matukar go-Np- fu.2s= qm or Dylup go-Np- fu.2s= qm \\
`Will you go to Matukar or Dylup (or perhaps neither)?'

Mukuna=ko wu-a-man= i e mua=ko wia uruf-a-man= i? \\
fire= nf put- pa -2p= qm or man= nf 3. acc see- pa -2p= qm \\
`Did you light a fire or did you feel (that there was) a man?'

An alternative question is left open also when the last alternative is replaced with the question word kamenion '(or) what?'/ `(or) how is it?' ex:7:x1350, ex:7:x1351.

Maa en-owa=ko p-ekap-e-mik= i kamenion? \\
food eat- nmz = nf bpx -come- pa -1/3p= qm or.what \\
`Did they bring food, or what?'

Beel(a)-al-i-non= i kamenion, naap uruf-am-ik-ua. \\
rotten- inch -Np- fu.3s= qm or.what thus see- ss. sim -be- pa.3s \\
`He was watching whether it would rot or what would happen.'

Leading questions are another subtype of polar questions. The person asking wants to guide the answer in a certain direction. This is done in Mauwake by adding the epistemic modal adverb clitic - yon `perhaps' to the predicate of the question clause. The slightly rising intonation in the question distinguishes it from a statement ex:7:x1349.

Me ikiw-o-k= yon? \\
not go- pa -3s-perhaps \\
`He didn't go, did he?'
summary:
Mauwake polar questions, or yes-no questions, ask for confirmation or negation of a proposition and are marked by the sentence-final clitic -i, often attached to the verb but able to attach elsewhere if there is no final verb; they also show slight rising intonation. In negative polar questions, short answers were traditionally interpreted according to the polarity of the whole question, though Tok Pisin and English influence is shifting this toward agreeing or disagreeing with the verb itself.  

The language also has alternative questions, which may be closed or open: in closed questions, only the non-final alternatives take -i and the final alternative may be a negation, a full clause, or an elliptical clause, while in open questions all alternatives, including the final one, take -i. A related subtype is the leading question, which is formed by adding the epistemic clitic -yon ‘perhaps’ and is distinguished from a statement by rising intonation.

text:
Echo questions are used when an original statement or question is questioned, either because it was not properly heard in the first place or because the addressee has some doubts about it. Structurally all echo questions are polar questions.

Echo question of a statement is like a normal polar question, except that the questioned element receives an extra stress ex:7:x1189.

A:Paapa Goroka ikiw-i-non. - B: Gor\'oka ikiw-i-non=i? \\
A:elder.sibling Goroka go-Np- fu.3p - B: Goroka go-Np- fu.3p= qm \\
`A: Big brother is going to Goroka. B: Is he going to Goroka?'

When the validity of a non-polar question ex:7:x1190 is questioned, the question clitic is attached directly to the end of the question already containing a question word ex:7:x1191.

A: Mua naarew wia maak-e-k? \\
A: man who 3. acc tell- pa -3s \\
`Who did he tell?'

B: Mua naarew wia maak-e-k= i? \\
B: man who 3. acc tell- pa -3s= qm \\
`Who did he tell???'

But if the addressee wants to check if (s)he heard correctly, the echoed question is made into a complement of a sentence-final utterance verb, to which a question clitic is attached ex:7:x1192.

B: Mua naarew wia maak-e-k na-i-n=i? \\
B: man who 3. acc tell- pa -3s say-Np- pr.2s= qm \\
`Are you asking who he told?'

Since polar questions already have a clause-final question clitic, an echo question cannot be formed by adding the same clitic a second time. Instead, the original question is made into a complement of the utterance verb ma- `say' or na- `say/think' ex:7:x1193.

A: Nain eliwa=ki? B: Nain eliwa-ki ma-e-n=i? \\
A: that1 good= cf. qm B: that1 good= cf. qm say- pa -2s= qm \\
`A: Is that good? B: Did you ask if that is good?'
summary: Echo questions are used to question a prior statement or question, either because it was not heard clearly or because the speaker is uncertain about it, and structurally they are always polar questions. For statements and for non-polar questions, the echo question is formed by repeating the original clause, with extra stress on the questioned element or with the question clitic attached to the end. If the original question is already a polar question with a clause-final question clitic, the echo is instead expressed as a complement of an utterance verb such as *say* or *think*, so the clitic is not doubled.

text:
Confirmation questions are mainly used in argumentation. The question word naap -i `(is it) like that?' is tagged to a statement, which may be preceded by another question ex:7:x1188.

Ni kema maneka naap efa wu-i-man=i, yo eliw nia saliw-i-nen, naap=i? \\
2p. unm liver big thus 1s. acc put-Np- pr.2p= qm 1s. unm well 2p. acc heal-Np- fu.1s thus= qm \\
`Do you believe about me that I can heal you, is that so?'
summary: Confirmation questions are mainly used in argumentation and are formed by attaching the question word **naap-i** ‘is it like that?’ to a statement. The statement may also be preceded by another question, as in the example where **naap=i** is added to confirm a previous claim.

text:
Indirect questions ex:7:x1203, ex:7:x1204 are a subgroup of complement clauses and are discussed under Indirect speech in sec:8.3.2.1.2.

Yo maa mauwa uruf-a-m efa na-e-k. \\
1s. unm thing what see- pa -1s 1s. acc say- pa -3s \\
`He asked me what I saw.'

Kamin wu-a-mik(-yon), yo me wiar amis-ar-e-m. \\
how.much put- pa -1/3p-perhaps 1s. unm not 3. dat knowledge- inch - pa -1s \\
`I don't know how much they put.'
summary: Indirect questions are treated as a subgroup of complement clauses and are discussed under indirect speech. The examples show embedded interrogative clauses used after verbs like “say” and “know,” as in “He asked me what I saw” and “I don’t know how much they put.”

text:
Traditionally the Mauwake speakers lived in a society where everyone more or less knew everybody's business and there was not much need for eliciting information by asking questions. Consequently, many questions in normal speech are rhetorical in nature. The question form may be used to emphasize the opposite of what is said ex:7:x1205, ex:7:x1206 or sometimes just to prompt the addressee to think more clearly, but very often rhetorical questions have an element of reproach or assigning blame as well ex:7:x1202, ex:7:x1207.

Maamuma kaaneke ika-eya ni-i-yan? \\
money where. cf be-2/3s. ds give.you-Np- fu.1p \\
`Where would we have that kind of money to give you? (=We do not have money to give you.)'

Yo anane niam=iya ika-i-nen=i? \\
1s. unm always 2p. refl = com be-Np- fu.1s= qm \\
`Will I be with you forever? (= I will not.)'

No moram naap om-em-ika-i-n? \\
2s. unm why thus cry- ss. sim -be-Np- pr.2s \\
`Why are you crying like that? (=You should not cry like that.)'

Mua naareke nia maak-eya ekap-e-man? \\
man who. cf 2p. acc say-2/3p. ds come- pa -2p \\
`Who told you to come? (=You shouldn't have come)'

Implied reproach or accusation is particularly common with questions including the word moram `why?' ex:7:x1208, but it is not limited to them. Especially accusations of theft are couched in neutral-looking questions ex:7:x1209.

Aa muuka, no moram naap yia on-a-n? \\
oh son 2s. unm why thus 1s. acc do- pa -2s \\
`Oh son, why did you do this to us?'

Yo seewa gelemuta uruma or-o-k nain uruf-a-man=i? \\
1s. unm rat small valley descend- pa -3s that1 see- pa -2p= qm \\
`Have you seen my ``little rat'' (pig) that went down to the valley? (implying: I have no doubt that you have stolen my pig.)'

Because questions are so easily understood as reproaches or accusations, real questions are often preceded by a preamble to prevent this interpretation ex:7:x1210-- ex:7:x1355.

Ama arow=pa mauw-owa weeser-eya maa mauwa on-a-man? \\
sun three= loc work- nmz finish-2/3s. ds thing what do- pa -2p \\
`After your work finished at three, what did you do?'

Yo oram nefa nokar-i-yem, soomia=ko efar uruf-a-n=i? \\
1s. unm just 2s. acc ask-Np- pr.1s spoon= nf 1s. dat see- pa -2s= qm \\
`I'm just asking: have you seen my spoon?'

Anane maneka ewur me urup-i-n nain moram? \\
always big quickly not ascend-Np- pr.2s that1 why \\
`What is the reason why you never come up quickly?'
summary:
In Mauwake, many ordinary questions are rhetorical because speakers traditionally lived in a close-knit society where little information had to be elicited directly. Such questions are often used to emphasize the opposite of what is said, prompt reflection, or, especially, to convey reproach or blame, with *moram* ‘why?’ frequently introducing accusations.

Because questions can easily be interpreted as reproaches, genuine information-seeking questions are often preceded by a preamble to avoid this reading. The passage illustrates this with examples of neutral-looking questions that still imply suspicion, including accusations of theft.

text:
Apart from rhetorical questions, a verbal answer is often expected. An affirmative answer to a polar question ex:7:x1216 may be just an affirmative interjection ex:7:x1217 or the verb from the question by itself or preceded by the interjection ex:7:x1218. A negative answer must have at least one negator ( sec:6.2 ), whether only a negative interjection ( sec:6.2.3 ), or any of the other negators, or both ex:7:x1220. Less commonly the answer may also be a full statement with or without a preceding affirmation ex:7:x1219 or negation.

No uurika owow maneka ikiw-i-nan=i? \\
2s. unm tomorrow village big go-Np- fu.2s= qm \\
`Are you going to town tomorrow?'

Ae/Oo. \\
yes \\
`Yes.'

(Ae,) ikiw-i-nen. \\
yes go-Np- fu.1s \\
`(Yes,) I am going.'

(Weetak,) me ikiw-i-nen. \\
no not go-Np- fu.1s \\
`(No,) I am not going.'

(Ae,) yo uurika owow maneka ikiw-i-nen. \\
yes 1s. unm tomorrow village big go-Np- fu.1s \\
`(Yes,) I'll go to town tomorrow.'

The reply to a non-polar question most typically includes an answer to the questioned item and often the verb of the original question too ex:7:x1221-- ex:7:x1222.

Maa sira kamenap nain en-em-ik-e-man? \\
thing/food kind how that1 eat- ss. sim -be- pa -2p \\
