`What kind of food did you eat?'

Wi mia kia en-owa nain (en-em-ik-e-mik). \\
3p. unm body white eat- nmz that1 (eat- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p) \\
`(We ate) the white people's food.'

If the speaker wants to negate the presupposition in the question ex:7:x1223, (s)he begins with a negator, and then goes on to answer the question itself ex:7:x1224.

Neremena kamenap nefa on-a-k? \\
2s/p.nephew how 2s. acc do- pa -3s \\
`What did your nephew do to you?'

Weetak, yo mauw-a-m ne o me efa uruf-a-k.\\
no 1s. unm work- pa -1s add 3s. unm not 1s. acc see- pa -3s \\
`I worked but he did not even look at me.' (Implying: Your presupposition is wrong; he did not do anything indecent to me.)

If the question or statement itself is negative, a one-word answer is ambiguous in present-day usage, and a full clause is needed to disambiguate it ex:7:x1151. Traditionally an answer to a question affirmed or negated the affirmative or negative polarity of the question or statement ex:7:x1117.

O aakun-owa marew=yon. - Wia, aakun-owa wiar ik-ua.\\
3s. unm talk- nmz no(ne)-perhaps -no talk- nmz 3. dat be- pa.3s \\
`Perhaps he doesn't have anything to say. --No, he does have something to say.'

Auwa me ekap-o-k=i? - Weetak (ekap-o-k). \\
1s/p.father not come- pa -3s= qm -no (come- pa -3s) \\
`Didn't father come? --Yes (he did).'

But Mauwake is changing to become more like English in that the negative answer stands for a negative statement regardless of the polarity of the question or statement that it is a reply to ex:7:x1118: A similar change is taking place in Tok Pisin, and it is likely that this is causing the development in Mauwake too.

Auwa me ekap-o-k=i? - Weetak (me ekap-o-k). \\
1s/p.father not come- pa -3s= qm -no (not come- pa -3s) \\
`Didn't father come? --No (he didn't).'
summary:
The passage explains that replies in Mauwake depend on the type and polarity of the question. Polar questions are typically answered with an interjection, the verb alone, or a fuller clause, while negative answers must include at least one negator; for non-polar questions, the answer usually states the requested information and often repeats the verb, and if the presupposition is rejected, the reply begins with a negator.  

It also notes that one-word answers to negative questions or statements are now ambiguous, so full clauses may be needed, and that Mauwake is changing so that a negative answer increasingly simply marks a negative statement regardless of the polarity of the original question, similar to English and Tok Pisin.

text:
The simple imperative is the default way of expressing a command in Mauwake. It shows in the verb inflection ex:7:x1072 ( sec:3.8.3.3.2 ). In a prohibition the verbal negator me `not' precedes the simple imperative ex:7:x1075.

Ni Medebur karu-eka, baurar-eka. \\
2p. unm Medebur run- imp.2p flee- imp.2p \\
`Run(pl.) to Medebur, flee.'

Momora, no naap me ma-e. \\
fool 2s. unm thus not say- imp.2s \\
`Fool, don't say like that.'

The simple imperative can be strengthened with the intensity adverb akena `very, truly' following the verb ex:7:x1073.

Ni sira samora piipu-eka akena.\\
2p. unm habit bad leave- imp.2p truly\\
`Really get rid of your bad habits.'

Another way to intensify it is with the clause-final interjection nom ` please!', which is only used when a person has already been told to do something at least once and has not complied ex:7:x1074.

Pootin-e, nom! \\
stop.crying- imp.2s please \\
`Stop crying, please!'

The imperative marking on verbs shows only in the finite forms. When a command or request is in a medial clause, and the final clause verb is in the indicative mood and future tense, there is nothing in the medial verb to indicate the mood ex:7:x1076.

No opaimika pon aaw-o-n nain ma-eya i miim-i-yen.\\
2s. unm talk turtle get- pa -3s that1 tell-2/3s. ds 1p. unm hear-Np- fu.1p \\
`Tell us about your catching a turtle, and we'll listen.' (Or: `You will tell us about your catching a turtle and we'll listen.')

This type of clause combination has given rise to a softer, less direct command, which is given with a medial different-subject form of a verb; the final clause is left out altogether ex:7:x1084. This fairly common use of a medial verb form in Papuan languages is probably the origin of the use of pastaim `first' in Tok Pisin commands, e.g. Kam pastaim `Come!' This form is particularly common when commands are given to children.

P-ekap- eya! \\
bpx -come-2/3s. ds \\
`Bring it!'

The imperative of the final clause may have an influence on the medial clause(s) so that they are also interpreted as belonging within the scope of the command. This happens very easily with same-subject medial verbs ex:7:x1082; it is also possible but much less likely when the subject changes ex:7:x1364. This example may also be interpreted to have two commands: a ``soft'' one, expressed with a medial verb, and a regular one. Example ex:7:x1846 is ambiguous: in the situation where it was said, the medial clause was not in the scope of the final clause imperative; in some other situation it could be. When the medial verb has a first person form, imperative interpretation is not possible ex:7:x1083.

Emeria manina ikiw-ep en-owa nop-ap or-eka. \\
woman garden go- ss. seq eat- nmz search- ss. seq descend- imp.2p \\
`Women, go to the garden, look for food and come down.'

Mua emeria wia maak-eya me efa enim-uk. \\
man woman 3p. acc tell-2/3s. ds not 2s. acc eat- imp.3p \\
`Tell the people and let them not eat me.'

Feeke wiar ik-ok kiiriw mua wiar urup-e. \\
here. cf 3. dat be- ss again man 3. dat ascend- imp.2s \\
`Having been here with him (=your brother), go up to your husband again.'

I or-op ununa anum-amkun ma-eka, `` '' \\
1p. unm descend slit.gong beat-1s/p. ds say- imp.2p \\
`When we go down and beat the slit gong, say, `` '' '

A special feature in Mauwake commands is that they occur with a pronominal subject more often than statements do (§ sec:3.5.2.1, sec:3.5.11 ).

Although a command is usually directed towards one or more people in the second person, it can also be directed towards the speaker as part of a group of two ex:7:x1157 or more ex:7:x1158, or towards a third person in singular ex:7:x1159 or plural ex:7:x1160.

Aria, i owowa=ko or-u. \\
alright 1p. unm village= nf descend- imp.1d \\
`Alright, let's go down to the village.'

Ikiw-ep=ko wia uruf-ikua. \\
go- ss. seq = nf 3p. acc see- imp.1p \\
`Let's go and see them.'

Womokowa me wia maak-inok. \\
3s/p.brother not 3p. acc tell- imp.3s \\
`Let her not talk to her brothers.'

Ona mua owawiya ek-ap uruf-am-ik-ok ep-am-ika-uk.\\
3s. gen man with go- ss. seq see- ss. sim -be- ss come- ss. sim -be- imp.3p \\
`Let her keep going with her husband, seeing him (= her father) and coming back.'

Imperatives cannot have tense distinctions, but aspectual distinctions are possible. The continuous aspect form is used for habitual aspect in ex:7:x1160 above, and for continuous aspect in ex:7:x1896. Completive aspect is used in ex:7:x1161 and stative aspect in ex:7:x1162.

Sira naap on-am-ik-eka. \\
custom thus do- ss. sim -be- imp.2p \\
`Keep doing like that.'

Aakisa naap on-ap-pu-e. \\
now thus do- ss. seq - cmpl - imp.2s \\
`Now do that.'

No me mokoka opar-ep-ik-e. \\
2s. unm not eye close- ss. seq -be- imp.2s \\
`Don't have/keep your eyes closed.'

The second person future tense form is also used for a command, but this is not very common. It is used in a specific situation, not for giving generic commands or rules. The sentence ex:7:x1080 was said to a person who was suspected of lying, and in ex:7:x1081 parents give instructions to their daughter how to mourn.

No me sail-i-nan! \\
2s. unm not lie-Np- fu.2s \\
`Don't lie!'

Naap ma-emi om-em-ika-i-nan na. \\
thus say- ss. sim cry- ss. sim -be-Np- fu.2s intj \\
`Say like that and wail.'
summary:
Mauwake normally expresses commands with the simple imperative, and prohibitions use the negator *me* before it. The imperative can be strengthened by adverbs like *akena* ‘very, truly’ or by the clause-final interjection *nom* ‘please,’ and although imperatives are usually second person, they can also be directed to first-person inclusive or third-person subjects; they may also show aspect but not tense distinctions.

Commands can also be expressed more softly through medial clause forms, sometimes with the final clause omitted, and imperative interpretation may extend to medial clauses when they occur in clause combinations. A second-person future form can occasionally be used as a command, but only in specific situations rather than for ordinary general directives.

text:
Some linguistic models, the mainstream generative grammar in particular, disregard the distinction between a clause and a sentence, but here the distinction is maintained. One of the main reasons is the medial clause system operating in Mauwake. A simple sentence in Mauwake consists of one clause, but if that is a verbal clause, it must be a finite clause, not a medial one, as medial clauses only function within a sentence in combination with other clauses. Their distribution is restricted to non-final position in a sentence -- they may occur sentence-finally only if they are dislocated or the final clause is ellipted. Medial clauses also add the chaining structure to the clause combination possibilities ( sec:8.2 ), besides regular coordination ( sec:8.1 ) and subordination ( sec:8.3 ).

A sentence has the following features. It consists of one or more clauses. The end of a sentence is marked in speech by a falling intonation, or by a slightly rising intonation in polar questions, and normally a pause. The sentence-final falling intonation is clear, and can be distinguished from a less noticeable fall at the end of a non-final finite clause. In writing the end of a sentence is marked by a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark.

A simple sentence is the same as a clause, and was discussed in chap:5. When two main clauses are joined in a coordinate sentence, they are independent of each other as to their functional sentence type. In ex:8:x1352 the first clause is declarative and the second one interrogative; in ex:8:x1358 the first clause is imperative and the second one declarative, but the order could also be reversed.

Yo owora=ko me aaw-e-m, no moram efa ma-i-n?\\
1s. unm betelnut= nf not take- pa -1s 2s. unm why 1s. acc say- Np - pr.2s\\
`I didn't take the betelnut, why do you accuse me?'

Ni uf-owa ikiw-eka, yo miatin-i-yem. \\
2p. unm dance- nmz go- imp.2p 1s. unm dislike- Np - pr.1s\\
`(You) go to dance, I don't want to.'

In clause chaining ( sec:8.2 ) and in complex clauses involving main and subordinate clauses ( sec:8.3 ), the situation is more complicated. Formally almost all of the subordinate and medial clauses are neutral/declarative. A subordinate clause typically lacks an illocutionary force of its own and conforms to the functional sentence type of the main clause. In the examples ex:8:x1357-- ex:8:x1898, the subordinate clauses are in brackets.

Ni ifa nia keraw-i-ya nain sira kamenap on-i-man?\\
2p. unm snake 2p. acc bite- Np - pr.3s that1 custom what.like do- Np - pr.2p\\
`When a snake bites you, what do you do?'

Ni yapen... wiar in-em-ik-e-man nain kerer-omak-eka!\\
2p. unm inland 3. dat sleep- ss. sim -be- pa -2p that1 arrive- distr/pl -2p. imp \\
`Those (many) of you, who have stayed inland, arrive (back in your villages)!'

Ni uf-ep-na ni maadara me iirar-eka.\\
2p. unm dance- ss. seq = tp 2p. unm forehead.ornament not remove-2p. imp \\
`If/when you have danced, do not remove your forehead ornaments.'

The non-polar questions are an exception, since the question word may also be in a subordinate clause ex:8:x1362. When a subordinate clause contains a question word, the illocutionary force of a question spreads to whole sentence.

No kaaneke ikiw-owa efa maak-i-n?\\
2s. unm where. cf go- nmz 1s. unm tell- Np - pr.2s\\
`You are telling me to go where?'

A medial clause is coordinate with the main clause but dependent on it ( sec:8.2 ). The imperative form is only possible in finite verbs, and the polar question marker only occurs sentence-finally. As an alternative marker, the qm is used in non-final clauses as well ( sec:3.12.8, sec:8.1.2 ). Because of these formal restrictions, it is impossible to have an imperative or interrogative medial clause coordinated with a declarative main clause. A medial clause commonly conforms to the illocutionary force of the final clause, but it does not need to do so. In the examples ex:8:x1899 and ex:8:x1900 the bracketed medial clause is questioned with the main clause, in ex:8:x1901 and ex:8:x1902 it is not.

Maamuma uruf-ap ma-i-n-i? \\
money see- ss. seq say- pa -2s= qm \\
`Have you seen the money and (so) ask?'

Yo pina on-amkun=ko efa uruf-a-man=i?\\
1s. unm guilt do-1s/p. ds = nf 2s. acc see- pa -2p= qm \\
`Did I do wrong and you saw me?'

Sande erup weeser-eya owowa ekap-e-man=i? \\
week two finish-2/3s. ds village come- pa -2p= qm \\
`When two weeks were finished, did you (then) come to the village?'...ikoka ekap-ep sira nain piipua-i-nan=i e weetak? \\
later come- ss. seq habit that1 leave- Np - fu.2s= qm or no\\
` later when you come, will you drop that habit or not?'

When a medial clause itself contains a question word, the illocutionary force spreads to the whole sentence ex:8:x1363, ex:8:x1903.

No maa mauwa uruf-ap soran-ep kirir-e-n?\\
2s. unm thing what see- ss. seq be.startled- ss. seq shout- pa -2s\\
`What did you see and (then) got startled and shouted?'

Naareke nia maak-eya ekap-e-man? \\
who. cf 2p. acc tell-2/3s. ds come- pa -2p\\
`Who told you to come?' (Lit: `Who told you and you came?')

When the final clause is in the imperative mood, the implication of a command often extends backwards to a medial verb marked for the same subject ex:8:x1365, but not so easily to one marked for a different subject. In (7. ex:7:x1364 ) above, the command /request extends to the medial clause, whereas in ex:8:x1356 it does not. For more examples, see (7. ex:7:x1082 )--(7. ex:7:x1083 ) above.

No nena maa fariar-ep muuka nain arim-ow-e.\\
2s. unm 2s. gen food abstain- ss. seq son that1 grow- caus - imp.2s\\
`Abstain from (certain) food(s) and bring up the son.'

Nefa war-iwkin naap ma-e. \\
2s. acc shoot-2/3p. ds thus say- imp.2s \\
`(If/when) they shoot you, (then) say like that.'
summary:
The passage distinguishes clauses from sentences in Mauwake, unlike some generative models, because medial clauses can only occur within larger sentences and are restricted to non-final position unless dislocated or the final clause is omitted. A sentence may contain one or more clauses and is marked by sentence-final intonation or punctuation, while simple sentences are just single clauses and coordinate sentences can combine clauses with different functional sentence types.

It also explains that subordinate and medial clauses are usually neutral/declarative and typically take their illocutionary force from the main or final clause, though question words can spread interrogative force across the whole sentence. Medial clauses are structurally dependent on main clauses, and because imperatives and polar question marking are limited to finite or sentence-final forms, certain imperative or interrogative medial clauses are impossible.

text:
Although it is impossible to have an imperative verb form in a medial clause, a ``soft'' command/request ( sec:7.3 ) may be used in medial clauses, as it takes the medial verb form. In ex:8:x1366, the first clause is a request, the second one a statement.

Aite, i aaya=ko yia aaw-om-aya enim-i-yan. \\
1s/p.mother 1p. unm sugarcane= nf 1p. acc get- ben - bnfy 2.2/3s. ds eat- Np - fu.1p\\
`Mother, get us sugarcane and we will eat it.'
summary: Imperative verb forms cannot occur in medial clauses, but a “soft” command or request can be used there because it takes the medial verb form. The example shows a first clause that is a request and a second clause that is a statement: “Mother, get us sugarcane and we will eat it.”

text:
Coordination links units of ``equivalent syntactic status''. Clausal coordination commonly refers to the coordination of main clauses, as that is much more frequent than the coordination of subordinate clauses. In the following, it is assumed that the discussion is about main clause coordination unless stated otherwise.

The main clauses joined by coordination are independent in the sense that they could stand alone as individual sentences. Examples ex:8:x1352 and ex:8:x1358 above show that they can even manifest different functional sentence types. But they are called clauses firstly because they are coordinated within one sentence, and secondly for the sake of consistency, since the coordinated medial ( sec:8.2.1 ) and subordinate clauses ( sec:8.3.7 ) could not be called sentences.

As points out, no clause in a text is truly independent from its context. Likewise, the coordination vs. subordination of clauses is in many languages a matter of degree rather than a clear-cut distinction.

Although the chaining of medial and final clauses ( sec:8.2 ) is the main strategy for combining clauses in Mauwake, coordination of main clauses is also common. It is used not only for the cross-linguistically typical cases of conjunction, disjunction, and adversative relations between clauses, but also for causal and consecutive relations.
summary: Coordination links units of equivalent syntactic status, and in clause coordination this usually means main clauses, which are more common than coordinated subordinate clauses. These main clauses can stand alone as sentences and may even differ in functional sentence type, but they are called clauses because they are coordinated within one sentence and because subordination is not always a clear-cut distinction. In Mauwake, although medial and final clause chaining is the main way to combine clauses, main-clause coordination is also common and expresses conjunction, disjunction, adversative, causal, and consecutive relations.

text: Conjunction is the most neutral form of coordination: two or more clauses are joined in a sentence, with or without a link between them. If there is a link, it is a pragmatic additive that does not specify the semantic relationship between the clauses. This sometimes allows different interpretations for the relationship, but usually the context constrains the interpretation considerably.
summary: Conjunction is presented as the most neutral type of coordination, in which two or more clauses are joined in a sentence either with no explicit link or with a pragmatic additive link. This link does not determine the semantic relationship between the clauses, so the relation can sometimes be interpreted in different ways, though context usually limits the possible interpretation.

text:
In juxtaposition Also called ``zero strategy'' by. two or more clauses are joined without any linking device at all. According to unwritten languages tend to lack their own coordinators and therefore use more juxtaposition and/or coordinators borrowed from other, more prestigious languages.

In Mauwake, juxtaposition is the most typical strategy for conjunction overall. Especially the coordination of verbless clauses is often symmetrical: the reversal of the conjuncts is possible without a change of meaning ex:8:x1367, ex:8:x1390.

Wi Yaapan emeria weetak, mua manek=iw. \\
3p. unm Japan woman no man big= lim \\
`The Japanese didn't have any wives, (they were) just the men.'

Kuuten wiawi iperowa, yo auwa kapa=ke. \\
Kuuten 3s/p.father firstborn 1s. unm 1s/p.father lastborn= cf \\
`Kuuten's father was the firstborn (son), my father was the lastborn.'

When one of the conjuncts is a verbless clause and another is a verbal one, symmetrical conjunction is quite common ex:8:x1391:

I uruwa miim-i-mik, ni sosora=ke.\\
1p. unm loincloth precede- Np - pr.1/3p 2p. unm grass.skirt= cf \\
`We father's side of the family (lit: loincloth) go first, you are mother's side (lit: grass skirt).'

Symmetrical conjunction of verbal clauses may be used, when there is parallelism between the clauses ex:8:x1368, ex:8:x1392:

Na-emi wi afa ar-omak-e-mik, osaiwa ar-e-mik, biri-birin-e-mik.\\
say- ss. sim 3p. unm flying.fox become- distr / pl - pa -1/3p bird.of.paradise become- pa -1/3p rdp -fly- pa -1/3p\\
`Saying so, they became many flying foxes, they became birds of paradise, they flew (away).'

Aria makera miirifa okaiwi soo=pa kaik-i-mik, okaiwi pia kaik-i-mik.\\
alright cane end other.side trap= loc tie- Np - pr.1/3p other.side bamboo tie- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`Alright we tie one end of the cane to the trap, the other to a (piece of) bamboo.'

In ex:8:x1851 the medial clause relates to both of the final clauses, not just to the first one:

Koora=pa efa uruf-am-ik-eya ikiw - i - nen ekap - i - nen.\\
house= loc 1s. acc see- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds go- Np - fu.1s come- Np - fu.1s\\
`You see me from the house and/as I will go and come.'

When the coordination is not symmetrical, the clause in the second conjunct is an example or an explanation of the first clause ex:8:x1370, or it follows the first one in a temporal sequence ex:8:x1369.

Auwa aite wia karu-i-yen, owowa=pa wia uruf-u.\\
1s/p.father 1s/p.mother 3p. acc visit- Np - fu.1p village= loc 3p. acc see-1d. imp \\
`We'll visit my parents, let's see them in the village.'

Miiw-aasa um-eya miiw-aasa nain on-am-ika-iwkin epa kokom(a)-ar-e-k, epa iimeka tuun-e-k.
\\
land-canoe die-2/3s. ds land-canoe that1 do- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds place dark- inch - pa -3s place ten count?- pa -3s\\
`The truck broke and while they were fixing the truck it became dark, (then) it was midnight.'

A fairly common structure is one where the first conjunct is not directly followed by another finite clause but by one or more medial clauses before the final clause ex:8:x1371:

Ikemika kaik-ow(a) mua nain nop-a-mik, imen-ap maak-iwkin o miim-o-k.\\
wound tie- nmz man that1 search- pa -1/3p find- ss. seq tell-2/3p. ds 3s. unm precede- pa -3s\\
`They looked for the medical orderly, and when they found him and told him, he went ahead of them.'

Juxtaposition in itself is neutral and only shows that the two or more clauses are somehow connected with each other, but it can be used when propositions joined by it have different semantic relationships with each other ex:8:x1404, ex:8:x1425.

Waaya maneka marew pun, mua unowa me wia pepek-er-a-k.\\
pig big no(ne) also man many not 3p. acc enough- inch - pa -3s\\
`Also, the pig was not big, (so) it was not enough for many people.'

Ni iperuma fain me enim-eka, inasin(a) mua=ke. \\
2p. unm eel this not eat- imp.2p spirit man= cf \\
`Don't eat this eel, (because) it is a spirit man.'
summary: The passage explains that juxtaposition, or “zero strategy,” joins clauses without any linking device, and is especially common in Mauwake, where it often appears in coordination of verbless clauses and can be symmetrical so that the conjuncts can be reversed without changing meaning. It also describes cases where coordination is asymmetrical, with the second clause serving as an explanation, example, or temporal sequence for the first, and notes that juxtaposition itself is neutral, merely indicating that clauses are connected even when their relationship is semantically different.

text:
Two of the three pragmatic connectives ( sec:3.11.1 ) are used as clausal coordinators: the additive ne and aria, `alright' which marks a break in the topic chain. Ne can be used in some of the contexts where mere juxtaposition is also used, but it is less frequent. If the second conjunct is an explanation or example of the first one, conjoining the clauses with ne is not allowed. Example ex:8:x1372 is a case of symmetrical coordination, but if the order of the two conjuncts were reversed, the adverbial pun `also', which has to be in the second conjunct, would not move to the first conjunct with the rest of the clause.

I mua=ko me wia furew-a-mik, ne yiena pun mukuna=ko me op-a-mik.\\
1p. unm man= nf not 3p. acc sense- pa -1/3p add 1p. gen also fire= nf not hold- pa -1/3p \\
`We didn't sense anyone there and we ourselves did not hold fire either.'

The example ex:8:x1373 is syntactically neutral, but semantically it is interpreted as both temporal and consecutive sequence....maa wiar fe-feef-omak-e-mik, ne wi ikiw-e-mik...\\
food 3. dat rdp -spill- distr / pl - pa -1/3p add 3p. unm go- pa -1/3p \\
` they i spilled their j food, and (so/then) they j went (away) '

When there are more than two coordinated clauses in a sentence without any intervening medial clauses, it is common to have ne joining the last two clauses ex:8:x1374:

Mua kuum-e-mik nain me wia kuuf-a-mik, me wia furew-a-mik, ne me wia imen-a-mik. \\
man burn- pa -1/3p that1 not 3p. acc see- pa -1/3p not 3p. acc sense- pa -1/3p add not 3p. acc find- pa -1/3p \\
`We didn't see the men who burned it, we didn't sense them and we didn't find them.'

The connective ne is also used in sentences where an adversative interpretation can be applied. Using terms, ne in the adversative function could be called an oppositive coordinator, as the second coordinand does not cancel an expectation like it does in adversative clauses formed with either the demonstrative nain or the topic marker - na ( sec:8.3.4 ). Example ex:8:x1375 describes a couple that stayed in the village during the war and placed some of their belongings outside their house to show that there were people living in the village, while many others ran away into the rainforest.

Amina, wiowa, eka napia koor(a) miira=pa iimar-aw-ikiw-e-mik, ne wi unowa baurar-e-mik. \\
pot spear water bamboo house front= loc stand- caus -go- pa -1/3p add 3p. unm many flee- pa -1/3p \\
`We placed the pots, spears and bamboo water containers in line in front of the house, but many ran away.'

The connective aria 'alright' may be used when there is a change of topic or an unexpected development within the sentence ex:8:x1376, ex:8:x1377.

Epa wii-wiim-ik-ua, aria wi sawur=ke ekap-ep takira nain samapora onaiya akua aaw-e-mik.\\
place rdp -dawn-be- pa.3s alright 3p. unm spirit= cf come- ss. seq boy that1 bed with shoulder take- pa -1/3p \\
`It was getting light, and spirits came and carried the boy with his bed (away) on their shoulders.'

Iiriw muuka oko wiawi onak urera maa uup-e-mik, aria maa me wu-om-a-mik yon \\
earlier boy other 3s/p.father 3s/p.mother afternoon food cook- pa -1/3p alright food not put- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p perhaps \\
`Long ago, the parents of a boy cooked food in the afternoon, (but) perhaps they did not put any food for him '

It is also the default coordinator when a non-verbal constituent in two or more otherwise very similar conjuncts are contrasted ex:8:x1379, or emphasized ex:8:x1380, in coordinated clauses.

Yo Malala mauw-owa nia asip-i-yem, aria yena owowa, Moro owowa wia asip-i-yem.\\
1s. unm Malala work- nmz 2p. acc help- Np - pr.1s alright 1s. gen village Moro village 3p. acc help- Np - pr.1s \\
`I help you Malala people with your work, and I help my village, Moro village.'

Eema pun ekap-ep yia maak-e-k, aria buburia ona pun ekap-ep yia maak-e-k. \\
Eema also come- ss. seq 1p. acc tell- pa -3s alright bald 3s. gen also come- ss. seq 1p. acc tell- pa -3s \\
`Eema came and told us, and the bald man himself too came and told us.'
summary:
The passage describes two pragmatic connectives used as clausal coordinators: **ne**, an additive coordinator, and **aria** “alright,” which signals a break in the topic chain or an unexpected development. **Ne** is less frequent than simple juxtaposition, cannot link a second conjunct that is an explanation or example of the first, and can also have an adversative or oppositive interpretation without fully canceling expectations.  

**Aria** is used when there is a topic change or unexpected turn, and it is the default coordinator when contrasted or emphasized non-verbal constituents appear in otherwise similar conjuncts. The examples show that it can coordinate clauses with contrastive meanings such as “but” or parallel emphasis.

text:
The speech of the Mauwake people tends to be rather concrete in the sense that they do not speculate much on different abstract alternatives. So disjunction of clauses, although possible, is not common. Disjunction is marked by the connective e `or' placed between the conjuncts ex:8:x1385 ( sec:3.11.2 ).

Nain=ke napum-ar-i-mik e um-i-mik, mua oko napum-ar-e-k nain erewar-e-n. \\
that1= cf sickness- inch - Np - pr.1/3p or die- Np - pr.1/3p man other sickness- inch - pa -3s that1 foresee- pa -2s \\
`That is about people becoming sick or dying, you foresaw (in a dream) that some man became sick.'

Sometimes the question marker - i replaces the connective ex:8:x1387.

Aria no ikoka mua owawiya irak-ep= i kamenap on-ap yo me efar kerer-e, no nomokowa Kululu fan-e-k a.\\
alright 2s. unm later man with fight- ss. seq = qm how do- ss. seq 1s. unm not 1s. dat arrive- imp.2s 2s. unm 2s/p.brother Kululu here- pa -3s intj \\
`Alright, later when you fight with your husband or do something like that, do not come to me, your brother Kululu is right here.'

Alternative questions ( sec:7.2.2 ) have the question marker - i cliticized to the end of the clause at least in the first conjunct. Closed alternative questions leave the question mark out of the last conjunct ex:8:x1386.

Ikoka ekap-ep feeke sira nain piipua-i-nan= i e weetak?\\
later come- ss. seq here. cf habit that1 leave- Np - fu.2s= qm or no\\
`Later when you come, will you here leave that habit or not?'

Open alternative questions have the question marker in all the conjuncts ex:8:x1384.

Mua oko miira inawera=pa uruf-ap ma-i-mik, mua oko=ke napuma aaw-o-k= i e um-o-k= i?\\
man other face dream= loc see- ss. seq say- Np - pr.1/3p man other= cf sickness get- pa -3s= qm or die- pa -3s= qm \\
`When we see some man's face in a dream we say, ``Has some other man become sick or died (or possibly neither)?'' '
summary: Mauwake speech is described as fairly concrete, so clause disjunction is possible but not common; when it occurs, the connective **e** ‘or’ is placed between the conjuncts. In alternative questions, the question marker **-i** may replace the connective, and in closed alternative questions it appears only in the first conjunct, whereas in open alternative questions it occurs in all conjuncts.

text:
There is no adversative coordinator in Mauwake. It was mentioned above ( sec:3.11.1, 8.1.1.2) that the pragmatic additive connective ne, which is semantically neutral, is possible when there is a relationship between clauses that may be interpreted as contrastive ex:8:x1388.

Iir nain Kedem manek akena keker op-a-k ne Yoli weetak.\\
time that Kedem big very fear hold- pa -3s add Yoli no \\
`That time Kedem was very scared but Yoli wasn't.'

There are two strategies that can be used when a strong adversative is needed. A `but'-protasis may be marked by either the distal demonstrative nain `that' ( sec:3.6.2 ), or the topic marker - na (§ sec:3.12.7.1, sec:8.3.4 ), added to a finite clause. Adversative clauses with the demonstrative nain differ from nominalized clauses functioning as complement clauses or relative clauses in the following respects. Intonationally, nain is the initial element in the second one of the contrasted clauses, rather than a final element in a subordinate clause, and it is often preceded by a short pause ex:8:x1395. The protasis may even be a separate sentence ex:8:x728.

Panewowa nain, wi iiriw eno-wa en-e-mik, nain me onak-e-mik.\\
old.person that1 3p. unm earlier eat- nmz eat- pa -1/3p that1 not give.3s- pa -1/3p\\
`As for the old woman, they (aready) ate the meal earlier but did not give (any of it) to her to eat.'

Yo bom koor miira=pa efar or-om-ik-ua. Nain yo me baurar-em-ik-e-m. \\
1s. unm bomb house face= loc 1s. dat fall- ss. sim -be- pa.3s that1 1s. unm not flee- ss. sim -be- pa -1s \\
`Bombs kept dropping in front of my house. But I didn't keep running away.'

The examples ex:8:x1389 and ex:8:x1394 are structurally very similar to sentences with relative clauses ( sec:8.3.1.2 ). But here the demonstrative nain is part of the adversative clause and is preceded by a pause.

Mera eka enim-i-mik, nain i mangala me enim-i-mik, waaya me enim-i-mik.\\
fish water eat- Np - pr.1/3p that1 1p. unm shellfish not eat- Np - pr.1/3p pig not eat- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`We eat fish soup, but we don't eat shellfish, (and) we don't eat pork.'

I nan soomar-e-mik, nain i mukuna=ko me op-a-mik.\\
1p. unm there walk- pa -1/3p that1 1p. unm fire= nf not hold- pa -1/3p \\
`We walked there, but we did not hold/have any fire.'

Compare ex:8:x1394 with the relative clause ex:8:x1396, where the demonstrative functions as a relative marker and comes at the end of the clause. This is shown by the slightly rising intonation on nain, as well as a pause following it in spoken text: This similarity creates a problem with written texts that do not have adequate punctuation. Sometimes either interpretation is acceptable.

I nan soomar-e-mik nain, i mukuna=ko me op-a-mik.\\
1p. unm there walk- pa -1/3p that1 1p. unm fire= nf not hold- pa -1/3p\\
`We who walked there didn't hold/have any fire.' (Or: `When we walked there, we didn't hold/have any fire.')

The adversative sentences formed with the topic marker - na are complex rather than coordinate sentences ( sec:8.3.4 ).
summary:
Mauwake has no dedicated adversative coordinator, but the additive connective *ne* can be used in contexts that are contrastive. For a stronger “but” relation, speakers use either the distal demonstrative *nain* at the start of the second contrasted clause or a topicalized finite clause marked with *-na*.

Clauses with initial *nain* are distinguished from relative or complement clauses by their intonation and by a pause before *nain*; in speech, the protasis may even stand as a separate sentence. However, in writing these constructions can be ambiguous because *nain* may also function as a relative marker at the end of a clause.

text:
Within a sentence, clauses are typically connected by one of the syntactically neutral strategies, which leave the semantic relationship implied. Some sentences using juxtaposition ex:8:x1425, the pragmatic additive ne ex:8:x1373 or clause chaining ex:8:x1412 can be interpreted as having a consecutive relationship between the clauses, although this does not show in the syntax. This section deals with the cases where the consecutive relationship is marked overtly.

Relationships of cause and effect, or reason and result, Reason-result relationship presupposes the presence of reasoning in the process, cause-effect relationship does not. are central in the discussion of causal and consecutive clauses. It seems that currently Mauwake may be developing a distinction between cause and reason on one hand, and between effect and result on the other. But the tendency, if there, is not very strong ( sec:3.11.2 ).

Both the clauses in a sentence expressing a cause-effect or reason-result relationship are main clauses and are in a coordinate relationship with each other. It is common for the two clauses to form separate sentences rather than be within the same sentence.

The tendency to present events in the same order that they occur, common to languages in general, is very strong in Papuan languages. Consequently, there is a strong preference to present a cause clause before an effect clause (,, ). In Mauwake consecutive coordination is the default, unmarked strategy for those sentences that express cause-effect or reason-result relationships overtly, because their structure follows this principle ex:8:x1400, whereas in causal coordination sentences the effect is stated before the cause.

Emar, nos=ke yo efa kemal-ep iripuma fain ifakim-o-n, naapeya iripuma fain ik-ep enim-e.\\
1s/p.friend 2s. cf = cf 1s. unm 1s. acc pity- ss. seq iguana this kill- pa -2s therefore iguana this roast- ss. seq eat- imp.2s\\
`Friend, it was you who pitied me and killed this iguana, therefore you roast and eat this iguana.'

Effect and result clauses use naapeya/naeya `therefore, (and) so' ( sec:3.11.2 ) as their connective ex:8:x1401-- ex:8:x1403.

Koora fuluwa unowa marew, naapeya in-i-mik nain dabela me senam furew-i-mik.\\
house hole many no(ne) therefore sleep- Np - pr.1/3p that1 cold not too.much sense- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`The houses do not have many windows, so those who sleep (there) do not sense/feel the cold too much.'

Pita weke wiar um-o-k, naapeya o suule me iw-a-k. \\
Pita 3s/p.grandfather 3. dat die- pa -3s therefore 3s. unm school not go- pa -3s\\
`Pita's grandfather died, so he (Pita) didn't go to school.'

pika oona me kekan-ow-a-k, naeya uura ewar maneka=ke kerer-emi koora nain wiar teek-a-k.\\...wall support not be.strong- caus - pa -3s therefore night wind big= cf appear- ss - sim house that1 3. dat tear- pa -3s\\
`He did not strengthen the wall supports, so at night a big wind arose and tore down his house.'

No nena pun pina sira naap nain on-i-n, naeya nos pun opora=pa ika-i-nan.\\
2s. unm 2s. gen also guilt custom thus that1 do- Np - pr.2s therefore 2s. fc also talk= loc be- Np - fu.2s\\
`You yourself do bad things like that too, therefore you too will be under accusation.'

Naapeya can also co-occur with the conjunctive coordinator ne ex:8:x1403.

Epa nan soomar-em-ik-ok or-o-mik, ne naapeya pina wi wiar korin-e-k. \\
place there walk- ss. sim -be- ss descend- pa -1/3p add therefore guilt 3p. unm 3. acc stick- pa -3s\\
`They were walking there in that place and came down, and so the guilt (for starting a forest fire) stuck to them.'

The use of naapeya and naeya is both external and internal, i.e., they connect events in a situation and ideas in a text. The internal use of ne naapeya and aria naapeya is restricted to intersentential use. They refer to a longer stretch in the preceding text as their protasis ex:8:x1407.

Aria naapeya wi inasina ook-i-mik sira nain me wiar ook-eka. \\
alright therefore 3p. unm spirit follow- Np - pr.1/3p custom that1 not 3. dat follow- imp.2p\\
`So therefore do not follow the behavior of those who follow/believe in spirits.'

As an internal connective naeya mainly connects full sentences ex:8:x1410, only seldom clauses within a sentence ex:8:x1411:

No mua woos reen-owa=ke, naeya no kema kir-owa miatin-i-n.\\
2s. unm man head dry- nmz = cf therefore 2s. unm liver turn- nmz dislike- Np - pr.2s\\
`You are hard-headed, therefore you do not like to change your (bad) ways.'

Ni sira-sira naap on-i-man. Naeya opora iiriw ma-e-k nain pepek akena nia ma-e-k.\\
2p. unm rdp -custom thus do- Np - pr.2p therefore talk earlier say- pa -3s that1 enough very 2p. acc say- pa -3s\\
`You do (bad) things like that. Therefore the talk that he already said about you is very accurate.'

Neemi is a consecutive coordinator that almost exclusively conjoins full sentences rather than clauses within a sentence: ex:8:x1409 is from translated text but considered natural. (3. ex:3:x736 ) is repeated here as ex:8:x1904. Neemi is an internal connective, only used in reasoning. It requires some point of similarity between the two conjuncts.

Teeria fain K10 wu-a-mik. Neemi wi teeria nain pun K10 wu-a-mik.\\
group this K10 put- pa -1/3p therefore 3p. unm group that1 too K10 put- pa -1/3p\\
`This group put down ten kina. Therefore that group put down ten kina, too.'

Krais sirir-owa aaw-omak-e-k, neemi is pun unowiya naap aaw-i-mik.\\
Christ hurt- nmz get- distr / pl - pa -3s therefore 1p. fc also all thus get- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`Christ received a lot of pain, so we all too get (pain) like that.'

The connective naap nain is used almost only inter-sententially ex:8:x1905. Between clauses in a sentence it is possible but rare ex:8:x1424:

Naeya nokar-e-mik, `` Naap nain no naareke?'' \\
therefore ask- pa -1/3p thus that1 2s. unm who. cf \\
`Therefore they asked, ``So then, who are you?'' '
summary:
The passage explains that Mauwake can express cause-effect or reason-result relations either implicitly, through juxtaposition or clause chaining, or overtly with specific consecutive connectives. In overt consecutive coordination, both clauses are main clauses and often occur as separate sentences, with a strong preference for cause clauses to precede effect clauses; the main connectives discussed are **naapeya/naeya**, **neemi**, and **naap nain**.

It also notes that **naapeya/naeya** can link both events in a situation and ideas across discourse, while internal uses such as **ne naapeya** and **aria naapeya** are restricted to intersentential connections. **Neemi** is used almost exclusively between full sentences in reasoning contexts and requires a point of similarity between conjuncts, and **naap nain** is used mostly between sentences, with clause-level use being rare.

text:
Wiam arow pepek nan urup-e-mik nain, naap nain yo moram urup-e-m. \\
3p. refl three enough there ascend- pa -1/3p that1 thus that1 1s. unm why/in.vain ascend- pa -1s \\
`(Since it is the case that) those three are enough and came up, so then why did I have to come up? (or: so then I came up in vain).'
summary: The passage gives an example of a clause expressing that “those three are enough and came up,” followed by a rhetorical question asking why the speaker also had to come up, or implying that the speaker came up in vain. It illustrates the use of this construction to express a consequence or justification and then question its necessity.

text:
The causal coordination is a very marked structure, which shows in the unusual ordering of the clauses: the causal clause follows rather than precedes the consequent clause. The causal clause in Mauwake begins with the connective moram `because' ( sec:3.11.2 ), which is originally the interrogative word for `why'. There are two possible origins for this untypical structure. It may be a recent calque on the Tok Pisin causal construction, which uses bilong wanem `why/because' as the connector and the same ordering of the two clauses. The ordering of the clauses shows that it may also have originated as an ``afterthought reason'', The term suggested by Ger Reesink. even though currently it is used when the cause or reason is emphasized ex:8:x1417, ex:8:x1420.

Owowa mamaiya soora weetak, moram iwera isak-omak-e-mik.\\
village near forest no because coconut plant- distr / pl - pa -1/3p\\
`There is no forest near the village, because we have planted a lot of coconut palms.'

Poh San uruf-ap kema ten-e-mik, moram i kema naap suuw-a-mik, napuma me sariar-owa ik-ua.\\
Poh San see- ss. seq liver fall- pa -1/3p because 1p. unm liver thus push- pa -1/3p sickness not heal- nmz be- pa.3s\\
`We saw Poh San and were relieved (lit: liver fell), because we had thought that (her) sickness hadn't healed yet (but it had).'

Moram wia is used almost exclusively between full sentences ex:8:x1906; the example ex:8:x1421 is the only intra-sentential instance of moram wia in the data. I have not noticed any semantic difference caused by the addition of the negator....maamuma senam aaw-e-mik. Moram wia, maa ele-eliwa sesek-a-mik.\\
money too/very.much get- pa -1/3p why not thing/food rdp -good sell- pa -1/3p\\
` they got a lot of money. (That's) because they sold good food.'

Iir nain yo owowa=pa=ko me mauw-a-m, moram wia yo Ukarumpa urup-owa=ke na-ep mauw-owa miatin-e-m.\\
time that1 1s. unm village= loc = nf not work- pa -1s because not 1s. unm Ukarumpa ascend- nmz = cf say- ss. seq work- nmz dislike- pa -1s\\
`That time I did not work in the village, because I thought that I was due to go up to Ukarumpa, and (so) I didn't like to work.'

Both a causative and a consecutive connective can co-occur in the same sentence. When that happens, the consecutive clause occurs twice: first without a connective and after the causal clause with a connective ex:8:x1422, ex:8:x1423. This underlines the strong preference to keep the cause-effect (or reason-result) order.

I epa unowa=ko me soomar-e-mik, moram owowa maneka, naapeya soomar-owa lebum(a)-ar-e-mik.\\
1p. unm place many= nf not walk- pa -1/3p because village big therefore walk- nmz lazy- inch - pa -1/3p\\
`We didn't walk in many places, because the village/town was big, therefore we didn't care to walk.'

Mua lebuma emeria me wi-i-mik, moram emeria muukar-eya muuka nain maa mauwa enim-i-non, naapeya mua lebuma emeria me wi-i-mik.\\
man lazy woman not give.them- Np - pr.1/3p because woman give.birth-2/3s. ds son that1 food what eat- Np - fu.3s therefore man lazy woman not give.them- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`We do not give wives to lazy men, because when the woman bears a child what would it eat, therefore we do not give wives to lazy men.'
summary:
The passage describes Mauwake causal coordination as a highly marked construction in which the causal clause follows the result clause, unlike the usual order. The causal connector is *moram* ‘because’, originally the interrogative ‘why’, and the structure may reflect either a recent calque from Tok Pisin or an “afterthought reason” construction; it is now used especially to emphasize the cause or reason.

It is used mainly between full sentences, with no clear semantic effect from adding the negator. When both causal and consecutive connectives appear, the consecutive clause is repeated, which reinforces the strong preference for cause-before-result interpretation even though the causal clause comes second.

text:
A less common clause type, that of apprehensive clauses, also called negative purpose clauses (, ), is perhaps more commonly subordinate than coordinate. But in Mauwake the apprehensive clauses are coordinated finite clauses ex:8:x1426, ex:8:x1427, originally separate sentences ex:8:x1428. The apprehension clause is introduced by the indefinite oko `other' ( sec:3.7.2 ), which has also developed the meaning `otherwise'.

Ni maa uru-uruf-ami ik-eka, oko mua oko=ke nia peeskim-i-kuan.\\
2p. unm thing rdp -see- ss. sim be- imp.2p other man other= cf 2p. acc cheat- Np - fu.3p\\
`Watch out, otherwise/lest you get cheated.'

Naap on-owa weetak, oko yiena sira puuk-i-yen. \\
thus do- nmz no other 1p. gen custom cut- nps - fu.1p\\
`We must not do like that, otherwise/lest we break our custom/law (or: lest we ourselves break the custom/law).'

Naap yo aakisa efa uruf-i-n. Oko neeke soomar-ekap-em-ik-omkun ma-i-nan, `` ``\\
thus 1s. unm now 1s. acc see- Np - pr.2s other there. cf walk-come- ss.sim -be-1s/p. ds say- Np - fu.2s\\
`So you see me now. Otherwise I'll be walking there and you will say, `` '''
summary: Apprehensive clauses in Mauwake, also known as negative purpose clauses, are usually subordinate in other languages but here are coordinated finite clauses, originally separate sentences. They are introduced by the indefinite *oko* ‘other,’ which has also come to mean ‘otherwise.’

text:
Clause chaining is a feature typical of Papuan languages, and of the Trans-New Guinea languages in particular. seems to consider clause chaining a genetic feature of the tng languages, but suggests that it is an areal feature., with the most data to date, suggests that there is a combination of both, but leaves the final decision open. A sentence may consist of several medial clauses The terms medial and final clauses are well established in Papuan linguistics. where the verbs have medial verb inflection ( sec:3.8.3.5 ), and a final clause where the verb has ``normal'' finite inflection ( sec:3.8.3.4 ). Clause chaining indicates either temporal sequence or simultaneity between adjacent clauses.

The division into just medial and final clauses is not adequate for describing the system. call the medial clauses marking clauses and the clauses following them reference clauses. and call them marked clauses and controlling clauses, respectively. Marking clause is simply another name for a medial clause and will not be used here. But a reference clause may be medial or finite I prefer the term finite to final clauses (and verbs), as it is the finiteness rather than the position in the sentence that is important in their relation with medial clauses. Subordinate clauses are the most typical non-final finite clauses, and they may also have medial clauses preceding them and relating to them. -- what is important is that both the temporal relationship of the medial verb, and the person reference, is stated in relation to the reference clause. When a reference clause for a preceding medial clause is also a medial clause, it again has its own reference clause following it.

The medial clauses linked by clause chaining are sometimes called cosubordinate (, This is cosubordination at the peripheral level; verb serialization is cosubordination at core or nuclear level. or coordinate- dependent, because they share features with both coordinate and subordinate clauses. Their relationship with each other and with the following finite clause is essentially coordinate, brings several syntactic arguments to show that basically switch reference is indeed coordination rather than subordination. But he also argues for a separate subordinate switch reference in Amele and some other languages. but the medial clauses are dependent on the finite clause both for their absolute tense, and, in the case of ``same subject'' forms, also for their person/number specification.

Another term commonly used for the chained clauses, switch-reference clauses ( sr ), Clause chaining and switch reference are two separate strategies, but in Papuan languages the two very often go together. is related to their other function as a reference-tracking device. They typically indicate whether their topic/subject is the same as, or different from, the topic/subject of the following clause. This is discussed below in sec:8.2.3. In this grammar the two terms are used interchangeably, as in Mauwake the medial verbs not only indicate a temporal relationship but are used for reference tracking as well.
summary:
Clause chaining is common in Papuan languages, especially Trans-New Guinea languages, and a sentence may contain multiple medial clauses followed by a finite clause. These medial clauses indicate temporal sequence or simultaneity and are dependent on the following reference clause for absolute tense and, in same-subject forms, person/number information.  

The passage argues that a simple medial/final distinction is insufficient: the relevant contrast is between marked clauses and reference clauses, with the latter sometimes also being medial or subordinate. It also notes that clause chaining and switch-reference are closely associated but distinct strategies, since switch-reference marks whether the subject/topic of a clause is the same as or different from that of the next clause.

text:
It is widely accepted that the relationship of medial clauses to their reference clauses is basically coordinate, but with some special features and exceptions. E.g.,,,. In Mauwake medial clauses are subordinate only if subordinated with the topic/conditional marker - na; otherwise they are coordinate.

Instead of giving background information like subordinate clauses do, medial clauses are predications that carry on the foreground story line ex:8:x2000. But they are also different from coordinate finite clauses. The similarities and differences are discussed in this section.

The pragmatic additives ne ex:8:x1485 and aria ex:8:x1486 ( sec:3.11.1 ) can occur between a medial clause and its reference clause, as between normal coordinate clauses. This is uncommon, however.

Wiawi ikiw-ep maak-eya, ne wiawi=ke maak-e-k \\
3s/p.father go- ss. seq tell-2/3s. ds add 3s/p.father= cf tell- pa -3s\\
`She went to her father and told him, and her father told her '... wiena en-emi, epira lolom if-emi ne owowa p-urup-em-ik-e-mik.\\... 3p. gen eat- ss. sim plate mud spread- ss. sim add village PBx -ascend- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`They ate it themselves, spread mud on the plates, and brought them up to the village.'

I ikoka yien=iw urup-ep nia maak-omkun ora-iwkin, aria owawiya feeke pok-ap ik-ok eka liiwa muuta en-ep aria ni soomar-ek-eka.\\
1p. unm later 1p. gen = lim ascend- ss. seq 2p. acc tell-1s/p. ds descend-2/3p. ds alright together here. cf sit- ss. seq be- ss water little only eat- ss. seq alright 2p. unm walk-go-2p. imp \\
`Later we (by) ourselves will come up and tell you (to come), and when you come down we will sit here together and eat a little bit of soup and then you can walk back.'

Coordinated main clauses are free in regard to their mood and, related to that, their functional sentence type. The medial clauses do not have any marking for mood. They usually conform to that of the finite clause, but this is a pragmatic matter, not a syntactic requirement.

When either the medial clause or the finite clause is a question, the whole sentence is interrogative, even if the other clause is a statement. In ex:8:x1449 the finite clause is a polar question, but the medial clause is not questioned. In the story that ex:8:x1452 is taken from, the killing is not questioned, only the manner. But since a medial clause cannot take the question marker, the verb in the finite clause has to carry the marking.

Sande erup weeser-eya owowa ekap-e-man=i? \\
week two finish-2/3s. ds village come- pa -2p= qm \\
`Two weeks were finished, and did you (then) come to the village?' Another possible translation is `When the two weeks were finished, did you (then) come to the village?' but this does not reflect the coordinate relationship of the clauses in the original.

Naap on-ap ifakim-i-nen=i?\\
thus do- ss. seq kill- Np - fu.1s= qm \\
`Shall I do like that and kill her?' (Or: `Is it in that way that I shall kill her?')

A non-polar question can be in either a medial ex:8:x1451 or in a finite clause ex:8:x1450.

No sira kamenap on-eya napuma fain nefar kerer-e-k?\\
2s. unm custom how do-2/3s. ds sickness this 2s. dat appear- pa -3s\\
`What did you do (so that) this sickness came to you?'

No karu-emi kame kaanek ikiw-o-n? \\
2s. unm run- ss. sim side where go- pa -2s\\
`You ran and where did you go?'

For more examples, see (7. ex:7:x1082 )--(7. ex:7:x1083 ) in sec:7.3 and the introductory section to chap:8.

In regard to the scope of negation, the same-subject medial clauses differ from all other clauses. Negative spreading ( sec:6.2.4 ) in both directions is allowed only between ss medial clauses and their reference clauses, and even there it is not very common. Backwards spreading is especially rare. In the following examples, negative spreading takes place in ex:8:x1443 and ex:8:x1447, but not in ex:8:x1446 and ex:8:x1448. Between other types of clauses negative spreading is not permitted at all.

Nainiw ekap-ep maa me sesenar-e-mik. \\
again come- ss. seq food not sell- pa -1/3p\\
`They did not come back and sell food.'

Ikiw-em-ik-ok me kir-ep uruf-e, no oram woolal-ikiw-em-ik-e.\\
go- ss. sim -be- ss not turn- ss. seq look- imp.2s 2s. unm just paddle-go- ss. sim -be- imp.2s\\
`While going, don't turn and look back, just keep paddling.'

Yaapan=ke urup-em-ika-iwkin wi Australia=ke wia uruf-ap baurar-emi me yia maak-e-mik.\\
Japan= cf ascend- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds 3p. unm Australia= cf 3p. acc see- ss. seq flee- ss. sim not 1p. acc tell- pa -1/3p\\
`When the Japanese were coming up the Australians saw them and ran away and/but did not tell us.'

Iiriw auwa=ke sira fain me paayar-ep muuka momor wiar aaw-em-ik-e-mik.\\
earlier 1s/p.father= cf custom this not understand- ss. seq son indiscriminately 3. dat get- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`Earlier our (fore)fathers didn't understand this custom, and (so) they adopted (lit: got/took) children indiscriminately.'

Like coordinated main clauses and unlike subordinate clauses, medial clauses are not embedded as constituents in other clauses. However, a medial clause may interrupt its reference clause and appear inside it, if the subject or object noun phrase of the reference clause is fronted as the theme and thus precedes the interrupting medial clause ex:8:x1464. For more examples, see (3. ex:3:x539 ) and (3. ex:3:x540 ). In the examples, the reference clause is bolded and the intervening medial clause is placed within square brackets.

Aria yena mua pun irak-owa kerer-owa epa weeser-em-ik-eya iirar-iwkin owowa ekap-o-k, o amia mua=pa ik-ok.\\
alright 1s. gen man too fight- nmz appear- nmz time finish- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds remove-2/3p. ds village come- pa -3s 3s. unm bow man= loc be- ss \\
`Alright, the war was getting close and they dismissed my husband and he came to the village, after he had been a soldier.'
summary:
Medial clauses in Mauwake are generally coordinate with their reference clauses rather than subordinate, though they become subordinate when marked with the topic/conditional suffix -na. They differ from subordinate clauses in that they continue the foreground storyline, and from ordinary coordinate clauses in that they do not carry mood marking of their own and usually conform pragmatically to the finite clause.

The passage also notes special interactions with questions, negation, and clause order: if either clause is interrogative, the whole sentence is interpreted as a question, and in same-subject medial clauses negative spreading can occur, though rarely and only between medial and reference clauses. Unlike subordinate clauses, medial clauses are not embedded constituents, but they may interrupt their reference clause when a fronted theme precedes them.

text:
In ex:8:x1465, both the object and the subject are fronted. After the first medial clause, the object of the finite clause is fronted as the theme of the remainder of the sentence, and it pulls with it the subject, marked with the contrastive focus marker. In the free translation, passive is used, because the object is fronted as a theme.

Sisina=pa wu-ap papako O mua=ke S mera saa urup-eya patopat=iw mik-i-mik. \\
shallow.water= loc put- ss. seq some man= cf fish sand ascend-2/3s. ds fishing.spear= inst spear- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`They drive (lit: put) them to the shallow water and the fish ascend to the beach and (then) some are speared by men with a fishing spear.'

The examples ex:8:x1466-- ex:8:x1468 show that some of the same-subject medial clauses interrupting the reference clause, especially those that have a directional verb or the verb aaw- `take, get', may be in the process of grammaticalizing into serial verbs:

I iwer(a) eka iki(w-e)p nop-a-mik. \\
1p. unm coconut water go- ss. seq fetch- pa -1/3p\\
`We went and fetched coconut water.'

Yo merena fura aaw-ep puuk-a-m. \\
1s. unm leg knife take- ss. seq cut- pa -1s\\
`I took a knife and cut (into) the leg. (Or: I cut into the leg with a knife.')

Um-eya merena ere-erup ifara aaw-ep kaik-ap nabena suuw-ap akua aaw-ep or-o-m.\\
die-2/3s. ds leg rdp -two rope take- ss. sim tie- ss. seq carrying.pole push- ss. seq shoulder take- ss. seq descend- pa -1s\\
`It (=a pig) died and I took a rope and tied its legs two and two together and pushed it to a carrying pole and carried it down on my shoulder.'

Right-dislocation of a medial clause is not unusual. One reason commonly given for right-dislocations is an afterthought: the speaker notices something that should be part of the sentence and adds it to the end ex:8:x1471. Another reason is giving prominence to the dislocated clause, since the end of a sentence is a focal position. The right-dislocation of same-subject sequential medial clauses in particular breaks the iconicity between the events and the sentence structure, and has this effect. Consequently, the right-dislocated ss sequential clauses, like the ones in examples ex:8:x1469 and ex:8:x1470, are much more prominent than medial clauses in their normal position.

Or-op naap wia uruf-a-mik, mua oona, eneka, woosa kia kir-em-ik-eya. \\
descend- ss. seq thus 3p. acc see- pa -1/3p man bone tooth head white turn- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds \\
`They went down and saw them like that, the people's bones, teeth and heads turning white.'

Aw-iki(w-e)m-ik-eya wiena mua unowa fiker(a) epia nain ook-i-kuan, wiowa aaw-ep.\\
burn-go- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds 3p. gen man many kunai.grass fire that1 follow- Np - fu.3p spear take- ss. seq \\
`It keeps burning and many men follow the kunai grass fire, having taken spears.'

Aaya muuna kuisow enim-i-mik, aite=ke manina=pa yia aaw-om-iwkin. \\
sugarcane joint one eat- Np - pr.1/3p 1s/p.mother= cf garden= loc 1p. acc get- ben -2/3p. ds \\
`We eat one joint of sugarcane, when/after our mothers have gotten it for us from the garden.'
summary: The passage describes cases where both object and subject are fronted, with the object serving as the theme of the rest of the sentence and the subject carried along with contrastive focus marking; in translation, this is often rendered with a passive because the object has been promoted. It also notes that some same-subject medial clauses, especially those with directional verbs or *aaw-* ‘take, get,’ may be developing into serial verbs. Finally, it explains that right-dislocated medial clauses are used either as afterthoughts or to give prominence, and that right-dislocated same-subject sequential clauses are especially prominent because they disrupt the normal event order-to-sentence order iconicity.

text:
Clause chaining in Mauwake distinguishes between sequential and simultaneous actions in the clauses joined by chaining, but only when the clauses have the same subject ( sec:3.8.3.5.1 ). The sequential action verb in ex:8:x1431 indicates that one action is finished before the next one starts.

No nainiw kir- ep ikiw- ep owow mua wia maak-eya urup- ep mukuna nain umuk-uk. \\
2s. unm again turn- ss. seq go- ss. seq village man 3p. acc tell-2/3s. ds ascend- ss. seq fire that1 extinguish- imp.3p\\
`Turn around, go and tell the village men and let them come up and extinguish the fire.'

When a clause has a simultaneous action medial verb ex:8:x1432, it indicates at least some overlap with the action in the following clause.

Or- omi yo koka koora=pa nan efa wu- ami ma-e-k, ``... '' \\
descend- ss. sim 1s. unm jungle house= loc there 1s. acc put- ss. sim say- pa -3s\\
`As he went down, he put me in the jungle house and said, ``... '' '

Simultaneity vs. sequentiality is not always a choice between absolutes; sometimes it is a relative matter. Example ex:8:x1433 refers to a situation where a man came back home from a period of labour elsewhere and got married upon arrival. In actual life, there may have been a time gap of at least a number of days, possibly longer, but because the two events were so closely linked in the speaker's mind, the simultaneous action form was used when the story was told decades after the events took place.

Ekap- emi yo efa aaw-o-k. \\
come- ss. sim 1s. unm 1s. acc take- pa -3s\\
`He came and married me.'

The simultaneous action form is less marked than the sequential action form: when the relative order of the actions or events is not relevant, the simultaneous action form is used. In example ex:8:x1437, the order of the preparations for a pighunt is not crucial, but the sequential action form on the last medial verb indicates that all the actions take place before leaving, rather than just at the time of leaving.

Maa en-ep-pu- ami top aaw- emi moma unukum- emi kapit, wiowa aaw- ep fikera iw-i-mik.\\
food eat- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. sim trap take- ss. sim taro wrap- ss. sim trap.frame spear take- ss. seq kunai.grass go- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`We eat, take the trap, wrap taro, take the the trap frame and spear(s) and go to the kunai grass area.'

A medial verb takes its temporal specification from the tense of the closest following finite clause ex:8:x1442-- ex:8:x1445, or in the case of a right-dislocated medial clause, from the preceding finite clause ex:8:x1471.

Nomokowa maala war-ep ekap-ep ifa nain ifakim- o-k.\\
tree long cut- ss. seq come- ss. seq snake that1 kill- pa -3s\\
`He cut a long stick, came and killed the snake.'

Mua=ke kais-ap neeke wu-ap miiw-aasa nop-ap miiw-aasa=ke iwer(a) ififa nain aaw-ep p-ekap-ep epia koora mamaiya=pa wu-eya fook- i-mik.\\
man= cf husk- ss. seq there. cf put- ss. seq land-canoe fetch- ss. seq land-canoe= cf coconut dry that1 take- ss. seq bp x -come- ss. seq fire house near= loc put-2/3s. ds split- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`Men husk them (coconuts) and put them there and fetch a truck, and the truck takes the dry coconuts and brings them close to the drying shed (lit: fire house), and we split them.'

Ikoka mua ar-ep emeria aaw-ep kamenap on- i-nan? \\

`Later when you become a man and take a wife, what will you do?'

The ds medial verbs ( sec:3.8.3.5.2 ) do not differentiate between sequential and simultaneous action. Sequential action ex:8:x1502 is the default interpretation for verbs other than ik- `be', which is interpreted as simultaneous with the verb in the reference clause ex:8:x1503. So in order to specify that two or more actions by different participants took place at the same time, the speaker needs to use the continuous aspect form ex:8:x1472:

Maa unowa ifer-aasa=ke p-urup -eya miiw-aasa=ke fan p-ir-am-ik-ua.\\

`The cargo was brought up (to the coast) by ship(s), and (then) trucks kept bringing it here.'

Wi yapen=pa ik-omak -iwkin Amerika kerer-e-mik.\\
3p. unm inland= loc be- distr / pl -2/3p. ds America appear- pa -1/3p\\
`Many people were inland and the Americans arrived.'

Ek-ap umuk-i-nen na-ep on-am -ik-eya ifa=ke keraw-a-k,...\\
go- ss. seq extinguish- Np - fu.1s say- ss. seq do- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds snake= cf bite- pa -3s\\
`He went and as he was trying to extinguish it (a fire), a snake bit him, '

Although the chaining structure itself only specifies the temporal relationship between the clauses and is otherwise neutral, it is open especially for causal/consecutive interpretation. notes this for different-subject medial verbs in Usan, and although not very common in Mauwake in general, it is more frequent with ds predicates ex:8:x1434, ex:8:x1412 than with ss verbs.

Yo maamuma marew -eya maak-e-m, Iir oko=pa ni-i-nen.''\\
1s. unm money no(ne)-2/3s. ds tell- pa -1s time other= loc give.you- Np - fu.1s\\
`I had no money and I told him (or: Because I had no money I told him), ``I'll give it to you another time.'' '

Iperowa=ke kekan- iwkin ma-e-mik, ``Aria,...'' \\
middle.aged= cf be.strong-2/3p. ds say- pa -1/3p alright\\
`The elders insisted, and (so) we said, ``All right, '' '

The causal/consecutive interpretation is most common when the object of a transitive medial clause becomes the subject in an intransitive reference clause: in example ex:8:x1504 `the son' is the object of the first two clauses and the subject of the final clause.

Muuka O p-or-op p-er-iwkin yak-i-ya. \\
son bpx -descend- ss. seq bpx -go-2/3p. ds bathe- Np - pr.3s\\
`They bring the son down (from the house) and take him (to the well) and (so) he bathes.'
summary: Mauwake clause chaining distinguishes sequential from simultaneous action in same-subject clauses: sequential forms signal that one event is completed before the next begins, while simultaneous forms indicate some overlap and are the less marked choice when relative order is not important. Medial verbs take their temporal reference from the nearest finite clause, and different-subject medial verbs do not contrast sequential and simultaneous in the same way; instead, they often allow causal or consecutive readings, especially when the object of the medial clause becomes the subject of the following clause.

text:
Cognition verbs and feeling or experiential verbs seem to be the only ones that allow a causal/consecutive interpretation when a medial clause has a ss verb ex:8:x1440-- ex:8:x1484:

Siiwa, epa maak-e-mik nain paayar-ep ma-e-k, ``Amerika aakisa irak-owa kerer-e-mik.''\\
moon place/time tell- pa -1/3p that1 understand- ss. seq say- pa -3s America now fight- nmz appear- pa -1/3p\\
`He understood the month and time/place that they (had) told him, and (so) he said, ``Now the Americans have come to fight.'' '... ne wi ikiw-e-mik, kerewar-ep ikiw-e-mik. \\... add 3p. unm go- pa -1/3p become.angry- ss. seq go- pa -1/3p\\
` and they went; they were angry and (so) they went.'

Mua oko=ko napum-ar- ep ikemika kaik-ow(a) mua wiar ikiw-o-k.\\
man other= cf sickness- inch - ss. seq wound tie- nmz man 3. dat go- pa -3s\\

summary: The passage says that cognition verbs and feeling/experiential verbs are the only verbs that allow a causal or consecutive reading when a medial clause contains an ss verb. The examples show that such clauses can express sequences like “he understood… and so he said,” “they were angry and so they went,” and “he got sick and so he went to a doctor.”

The switch-reference marking tracks the referents in a different way from the person/ number marking in finite verbs. The medial verb suffix indicates whether the clause has the same subject/topic as the reference clause that comes after it, and the ds suffixes also have some specification of the subject ( sec:3.8.5.2 ). In ex:8:x1436, the subjects are a man and his wife in the first two clauses and in the last one, and a spirit man in all the others:

Ikiw- ep i nan ika- iwkin i inasina mua j ifa puuk- ap j solon- ep j urup- ep j manina=pa waaya puuk- ap j moma wiar en-em-ik- eya j uruf-a-mik i.\\
go- ss. seq there be-2/3p. ds spirit man snake change.into- ss. seq crawl- ss. seq ascend- ss. seq garden= loc pig change.into- ss. seq taro 3. dat eat- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds see- pa -1/3s\\
`They went and were there, and a spirit man came and changed into a snake and crawled up and in the garden it changed into a pig and as it was eating their taro they saw it.'

Because the switch reference marking relates to the subject/topic in two different clauses at the same time, this sometimes causes ambiguities that need to be solved. If the subjects in adjacent clauses are partially same and partially different, a choice has to be made whether they are marked as ss or ds; only a few Papuan languages have a choice of marking both ss and ds on the same verb. Also, if the sr marking is considered to track the syntactic subject, there are a number of apparent irregularities in the marking. These have been discussed in particular by and with reference to Papuan languages. The next three subsections describe how Mauwake deals with these questions.
summary: Switch-reference marking differs from person/number marking because the medial verb suffix indicates whether the clause has the same subject/topic as the following reference clause, and the ds suffixes also include some subject specification. This system can create ambiguities when adjacent clauses share some but not all subjects, since a verb must be marked either ss or ds, and only a few Papuan languages allow both markings on the same verb. The passage notes that if switch-reference is analyzed as tracking syntactic subject, there are several apparent irregularities, which the next sections will address for Mauwake.

text:
When one of the subjects is plural and the other is singular included in the plural, this mismatch theoretically allows for a number of different choices in the switch-reference marking, but in practice each language limits this choice in a way peculiar to it. For a summary of how different Papuan languages treat this area of ambiguity, see, and. The following table tab:15:switchref shows this for Mauwake.

When a plural subject changes into a singular, the suffix is always the one used for same subject ex:8:x1438.

owowa urup-e-mik. Owowa urup- ep o koora ikiw-o-k.\\
village ascend- pa -1/3p village ascend- ss. seq 3s. unm house go- pa -3s\\
` We came up to the village. After we came up to the village he went into the house.'

When a singular subject changes into a plural there is more variation. First person singular changing into plural calls for same-subject marking ex:8:x1435, but second person singular switching into first person plural requires different-subject marking even when this second person singular is part of the group denoted by the first person plural ex:8:x1439.

Mik-ap, patot=iw mik-ap, aaw-ep, aasa=pa wu-ap, amap-urup-ep, yena koora=pa wu-ap, uuriw epa wiim-eya or-op, saa=pa pa- ep uup-e-mik.\\
spear- ss. seq fishing.spear= inst spear- ss. seq take- ss. seq canoe= loc put- ss. seq bp x -ascend- ss. seq 1s. gen house= loc put- ss. seq morning place get.light-2/3s. ds descend- ss. seq sand= loc butcher- ss. seq cook- pa -1/3p\\
`I speared it, I speared it with a fishing spear, and took it and put it in the canoe, brought it up and put it in my house, and in the morning when it was light I went down and butchered it on the beach, and we cooked it.'

Ekap- eya ikiw-i-yen.\\
come-2/3s. ds go- Np - fu.1p\\
`When you come we (including you) will go.'

When a second person plural switches into a first person plural (including the people indicated by the 2p), the marking has to be for different subject, but in the opposite case, the first person plural changing into the second person plural (again included in the 1p), the marking can be either for same or different subject. Both of these are exemplified in ex:8:x248. Here the switch from first person plural to second person plural is marked with the ss marking.

I ikoka yien=iw urup-ep nia maak-omkun ora- iwkin aria owawiya feeke pok-ap ik-ok eka liiwa muuta en- ep aria ni soomar-ek-eka. \\
1p. unm later 1p. gen = lim ascend- ss. seq 2p. acc tell-1s/p. ds descend-2/3p. ds alright together here. cf sit- ss. seq be- ss water a.little only eat- ss. seq alright 2p. unm walk-go- imp.2p\\
`Later we (by) ourselves will come up and tell you (to come), and when you come down we will sit here together and eat a bit of something and then you (can) walk back.'

With the rest, the speaker has a choice between the two forms. This choice is probably pragmatic and depends on whether the speaker wants to stress the change or the continuity of the referents.
summary: The passage explains that although mismatches in person and number can theoretically allow several switch-reference markings, individual Papuan languages restrict these possibilities in language-specific ways, as shown for Mauwake. In Mauwake, a plural-to-singular subject change always takes same-subject marking, while singular-to-plural changes show more variation: some cases require same-subject marking, others different-subject marking, and some allow either. The choice between the two forms is likely pragmatic, depending on whether the speaker wants to emphasize change or continuity of the participants.

subsubsection: Tracking a subject high in topicality
text:
claim that it is strictly the syntactic subject whose reference is tracked, but this statement has been challenged and modified by several others. and among others. If it is accepted as such, both Mauwake and other Papuan languages present a number of irregularities that have to be explained somehow.

suggests that the switch-reference system does monitor the subject co-referentiality in the medial clause and its reference clause, but topicality considerations cause apparent ``anomalies'' to the basic system. makes a well supported claim for Amele that in fact it is the topic that is tracked rather than the syntactic subject, or semantic agent, and he tentatively extends the claim to cover other Papuan languages as well. His later survey presents a more balanced view that sr can be either agent-oriented or topic-oriented, while maintaining that in most Papuan languages it is topic-oriented.

In a nominative-accusative language like Mauwake the syntactic subject, the semantic agent and the pragmatic topic coincide most of the time. The sr marking tracks the subject, but when there is competition between a more topical and less topical subject in clause chains, it is the more topical one that is tracked. An object, even if it is the topic, does not participate in the sr marking.

Competition between a more topical subject with a less topical one most commonly occurs when a clause with an inanimate subject intervenes between clauses where there is an animate/human subject. Even here the ``normal'' sr strategy is used, if the inanimate subject is topical enough to control the sr marking in the same way as animate subjects do. In the following examples, the drying of the soup ex:8:x1474 and the bending of the coconut palm ex:8:x1480 are important events in the development of the story and so the regular sr marking is maintained. In ex:8:x1480, the coconut palm can also be interpreted as a volitional participant, as it bends and straightens itself according to the needs of the people.

Uup-em-ika- iwkin maa eka saanar-em-ik- eya iki(w-e)p eka un-ep ekap-ep amina=pa feef-am-ik-e-mik.\\
cook- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds food water dry- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds go- ss. seq water draw- ss. seq come- ss. seq pot= loc pour- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`They were cooking it and the soup kept drying and they kept going and drawing water and coming and pouring it in the pot.'

Emeria panewowa nain wiimasip erup wia aaw-ep owow uruma or-op iimar-ep ika- iwkin iwera oko mekemkar-ep or- eya wi iwera ir- iwkin nainiw kaken iimar-e-k.\\
woman old that1 3s/p.grandchild two 3p. acc take- ss. seq village open.place descend- ss. seq stand.up- ss. seq be-2/3p. ds coconut other bend- ss. seq descend-2/3s. ds 3p. unm coconut climb-2/3p. ds again straight stand.up- pa -3s\\
`The old woman took the two grandchildren and they went down to the village square and were standing there, and a coconut palm bent down and they climbed up the coconut palm and it stood up straight again.'

When an inanimate subject is low in terms of topicality, the sr marking of the previous clause disregards it and indicates same-subject continuation, but the verb in the inanimate clause has to indicate a change of subject, if a more topical subject follows. This structure in many Papuan languages is typical of temporal and climate expressions and other impersonal predications (, ), which are often used for giving backgrounded calls this on-line background to distinguish it from the off-line background information of subordinate clauses. information. In examples ex:8:x1482 and ex:8:x1475 the verb in the initial medial clause predicating the action of human participants is marked with same subject following even when the following clause mentions the coming of darkness or dawn. Returning to the main line action requires different-subject marking. In the examples, the ``skipped'' medial clauses are in brackets.

Aria maa en-ep naap ik- ok kokom-ar- e y a in-e-mik.\\
alright food eat- ss. seq thus be- ss dark- inch -2/3s. ds sleep- pa -1/3p\\
`Alright we ate and stayed like that and (then) it became dark and we slept.'

In- ep epa wiim- eya onak maak-e-mik, `` ''\\
sleep- ss. seq place dawn-2/3s. ds 3s/p.mother tell- pa -1/3p\\
`They slept, and when it dawned they told their mother, `` '' '

If the impersonal predicate is important for the main story line, rather than providing backgrounded information, the impersonal verb itself is placed as a final verb, and the verb in the preceding medial clause is marked for different subject ex:8:x1492. notes a similar rule for Usan.

Kir-ep ekap-em-ika- iwkin epa wiim-o-k. \\
turn- ss. seq come- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds place dawn- pa -3s\\
`They turned and as they were coming, it dawned.'

In many Papuan languages, the impersonal predications include a number of experiential verbs (, ). In Mauwake, most of the experiential expressions are adjunct plus verb constructions ( sec:3.8.5.2.1 ), where the experiencer is a subject rather than an object; in chained clauses these behave in a regular manner. But those few experiential expressions that are impersonal do not trigger ds marking in the preceding medial clause, because the inanimate subject in the experiential clause is not topical enough to do it.
