In ex:8:x1491, the first person singular subject of the medial clauses becomes the object of the final clause, but the medial clause has same subject marking:

Uuw-ap uuw- ap oona=ke efa sirir-i-ya.\\
work- ss. seq work- ss. seq bone= qf 1s. acc hurt- Nc - pr.3s\\
`I worked and worked and my bones hurt.'

The verb weeser- `finish' is often used in chained clauses to indicate the finishing of an action. In this function, its low-topicality subject, the nominalized form of the preceding verb, is never mentioned overtly, and the preceding medial clause has ss marking ex:8:x1483:
summary:
The passage argues that in Mauwake switch-reference marking generally tracks the syntactic subject, but topicality can override this when two possible subjects compete, so the more topical subject is the one that is followed. It also reviews proposals that Papuan switch-reference systems may track topic rather than subject or agent, and notes that in Mauwake objects do not participate in switch-reference marking even if they are topical.  

The text further explains that low-topicality inanimate or impersonal clauses often behave as background information: a preceding medial clause may still show same-subject marking if the inanimate subject is not topical enough, but different-subject marking appears when the inanimate clause is prominent in the main story line. Experiential and “finish” constructions are also described as following these same topicality-based patterns.

subsubsection: Tracking a subject high in topicality
text:
Uup- ep weeser- eya aria oposia gelemuta wiam erup fain wia wu-om-a-m.\\
cook- ss. seq finish-2/3s. ds alright meat small 3p. refl two this 3p. acc put- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1s \\
`I cooked it and when it was finished, all right, I put (aside) a little of the meat for these two (women).'

In ex:8:x1476, there are two intervening clauses with different low-topicality inanimate subjects. The same-subject marking of the first clause ``jumps over'' these two clauses and refers to the subject in the last clause. The two clauses in between both have ds marking.

Maa uup- ep fofola urup- eya maa op- iya iiw-o-k.\\
food cook- ss. seq foam rise-2/3s. ds food be.done-2/3s. ds dish.out- pa -3s -1mm\\
`She cooked the food and when it boiled and was done she dished it out.'

Although human subjects are typically high on the topicality hierarchy, even a human subject may occasionally be so low in topicality that it gets overlooked in the sr marking ex:8:x1477, ex:8:x1478. gives similar examples from other Papuan languages. What is particularly striking with the example ex:8:x1477 is that the clause that is overlooked has a subject in first person singular, which is usually considered to be topically the highest possible subject. A plausible explanation is that politeness and hospitality requires the host of a big meal to downplay his own importance in this way.

Efa arew- ap maa eka liiwa muuta on- amkun en-ep-pu-ami soomar-ek-eka. \\
1s. acc wait- ss. seq food water little only make-1s/p. ds eat- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. sim walk-go- imp.2p\\
`Wait for me, and when I have made just a little soup you eat it and then you (may) go.'

Ikiw- ep mua nain urema osarena=pa iimar-ep ik- eya ona mua nain ifakim-o-k. \\
go- ss. seq man that1 bandicoot path= loc stand- ss. seq be-2/3s. ds 3s. gen man that1 kill- pa -3s\\
`She went and as the man was standing on the bandicoot path she killed that husband of hers.'

In process descriptions, the identity of people performing the actions is not important, and their topicality is low. In ex:8:x1481, the person watching the fire in the coconut drying shed is not mentioned in any way. This example is also like ex:8:x1476 above, in that there are two clauses with a different low-topicality subject, here one of them [+human], intervening between the second ss clause and the final clause, where the original subject is picked up.

Epia wu-ap ikiw- ep iwera kuuf-am-ik- eya iwera reen- eya iwer urupa anum-i-mik. \\
fire put- ss. seq go- ss. seq coconut watch- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds coconut dry-2/3s. ds coconut shell knock- Np - pr.1/3p \\
`We/they put them (the coconuts) on the fire and go, and (someone) keeps watching the coconuts and they dry and (then) we/they knock the shells away.'

Even an inanimate subject may override an animate/human one in sr marking, if its topicality is high enough. In ex:8:x1479 the subject/topic is kunai grass and the burning of the grass, which is such an important part of a pighunt that the hunt itself is called fiker(a) kuumowa `kunai-burning'. The grass is a continuing topic from the previous several sentences, so a noun phrase is not used for marking it.

Kuum- iwkin aw- emi mua unow maneka iiwawun fikera kuum-emi saawirin-ow- iwkin aria fiker epia aw-i-non.\\
burn-2/3p. ds burn- ss. sim man many very altogether kunai.grass burn- ss. sim round- caus -2/3p. ds alright kunai.grass fire burn- Np - fu.3s\\
`They burn it and it burns and all the men burn and surround the kunai grass, (and) alright the kunai fire will burn.'
summary: The passage explains that same-subject (ss) marking can “jump over” one or more intervening clauses and refer to a later clause’s subject if the intervening subjects have low topicality, even when those subjects are human. It notes that topicality can be low enough for a first-person singular subject to be overlooked, possibly for reasons of politeness, and that in process descriptions or other contexts, even inanimate subjects may control ss marking if they are the continuing topic.

text:
A medial verb with ds marking is used in two instances where it does not indicate a change of subject. Both types have two or more clauses with identical ds marking even though the subject is the same; only the last of those clauses really indicates a change of subject. One of them is recursion of a ds verb ex:8:x1493, indicating continuity; the identification of the subject is suspended until the repetition ends.

Wiawi kuum- eya kuum- eya kuum- eya aw-ep eka iw-a-k na wia, eka=ke saanar-e-k. \\
3s/p.father burn-2/3s. ds burn-2/3s. ds burn-2/3s. ds burn- ss. seq river enter- pa -3s but no river= cf dry- pa -3s\\
`It kept burning and burning their father and he burned and entered the river but no, the river dried.'

A medial clause that has the same subject as the following medial clause may have ds marking if both the medial clauses relate to the same finite clause as their reference clause, and the first of the medial clauses gets expanded or defined more closely in the second one. The ds verbs may be identical ex:8:x1494, but they do not need to be ex:8:x1495, ex:8:x1496.

Efa uruf-am-ik- eya, koora=pa efa uruf-am-ik- eya ikiw-i-nen ekap-i-nen.\\
1s. acc see- ss. sim -be-2/3. ds house= loc 1s. acc see- ss. sim -be-2/3. ds go- Np - fu.1s come- Np - fu.1s \\
`You will keep seeing me, you will keep seeing me from the house, and I will come and go.'...pon sisina=pa ik- eya, piipa unowa=pa soomar-em-ik- eya mik-a-m. \\
turtle shallow.water= loc be-2/3s. ds seaweed many= loc walk- ss. sim.be-2/3s. ds spear- pa -1s\\
` the turtle was in the shallow water, it was walking among a lot of seaweed and I speared it.'

No ikoka era=pa wia far- eya, owora wia maak- eya, aria mua=ke naap me nefa ma-i-nok, ``...'' \\
2s. unm later road= loc 3p. acc call-2/3s. ds betelnut 3p. acc tell-2/3s. ds alright man= cf thus not 2s. acc say- Np - fu.3s\\
`Later, when you see them on the road, when you ask them for betelnut, alright let your husband not say about you that '

The ss medial form of the verb `be' is used in the expression naap ikok `it is/was thus (and)', regardless of the following subject/topic ex:8:x1500, ex:8:x1501. The construction seems to have grammaticalized as an expression of an indefinite time span.

Naap ik-ok wi Saramun=ke wiisa uf-e-mik. \\
thus be- ss 3p. unm Saramun= cf dance.name dance- pa -1/3p \\
`It was like that and (then) the Saramun people danced wiisa.'...mua me wia imen-a-mik. Naap ik-ok sarere uura buburia ona amia mua wiar kerer-ep opaimika=pa yia wu-a-k.\\
man not 3p. acc find- pa -1/3p thus be- ss Saturday night bald 3s. gen bow man 3. dat appear- ss. seq talk= loc 1p. acc put- pa -3s\\
` we didn't find the men. It was like that, and on Saturday evening the bald man himself went to the police and accused us.'

Even when the final clause is verbless ex:8:x1497, ex:8:x1498, or missing completely because of ellipsis ex:8:x1499, a medial clause is still possible. In both cases, the sr marking is based on what the expected subject would be, if there were one.

Naap ik- ok uruf-am-ika- iwkin wia. \\
thus be- ss see- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds no\\
`He was like that and they were watching him, but no (he didn't get any better).'

Iinan aasa gurun-owa miim- ap eka=iw umuk-owa ewur. \\
sky canoe rumble- nmz hear- ss. seq water= inst extinguish- nmz quickly\\
`We heard the rumble of the airplane(s) and quickly extinguished (the fires) with water (lit: and the extinguishing with water quickly).'

The two sentences preceding the example sentence ex:8:x1499 mention American airplanes that flew over and dropped messages during the Second World War. The ``same subject'' needs to be picked from there -- as the story continues without another reference to the Americans for a while -- and the elliptical clause construed as something like naap onamik `and they did so'.

Wi Yaapan nan ik-e-mik nain wia uruf- ap. \\
3p. unm Japan there be- pa -1/3p that1 3p. acc see- ss. seq \\
`They had seen that the Japanese were there (and so they the Americans did so).'
summary:
The passage explains that ds marking on medial verbs can appear even when there is no real change of subject. One use is recursion, where repeated ds clauses indicate continuity and postpone identifying the subject until the repetition ends; another is when successive medial clauses share the same subject and both relate to the same finite clause, with the second clause elaborating or narrowing the first.  

It also notes that the ss form of ‘be’ is grammaticalized in the expression *naap ikok* ‘it is/was thus (and),’ which conveys an indefinite time span, and that medial clauses can still occur when the final clause is verbless or omitted by ellipsis, with subject marking based on the expected subject from context.

subsubsection: Medial clauses as a complementation strategy for perception verbs
text:
Perception verbs in Mauwake mostly use a medial clause as a complementation strategy, when the object of the perception verb is an activity ex:8:x1509-- ex:8:x1511. notes this for Usan too. Regular, nominalized complement clauses are only used with perception verbs when a fact is reported ( sec:8.3.2.2 ).

Moma wiar en-em-ik-eya uruf-a-mik. \\
taro 3. dat eat- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds see- pa -1/3p \\
`It was eating their taro, and they saw it.' (Or: `They saw that it was eating their taro.')

Aara muuk-ar-ep ik-eya uruf-a-mik.\\
hen son- inch - ss. seq be-2/3s. ds see- pa -1/3p\\
`The hen had laid an egg and we saw it.' (Or: `We saw that the hen had laid an egg.')

Yo me baliwep paayar-e-m, oram iperowa=ke nanar - iwkin miim-a-m.\\
1s. unm not well understand- pa -1s just middle.aged= cf tell.story-2/3p. ds hear- pa -1s \\
`I do not understand it well, I have just heard the older people tell stories about it.'
summary: In Mauwake, perception verbs usually take a medial clause as their complement when the perceived object is an activity. Regular nominalized complement clauses are used with perception verbs only when a reported fact is being expressed. The examples show both direct perception of an event and hearing a story about a state of affairs.

text:
Tail-head linkage is a typical feature especially in oral texts With the development of written style, this feature is becoming less prominent. in Papuan languages. It is an inter-sentential cohesive device and could be understood to belong outside ``syntax proper'', if syntax is defined very narrowly. It is mentioned here as it is an important linking device, and the chaining structure is used for it. In narratives and in descriptions of processes, tail-head linkage is utilized to tie sentences together within a thematic paragraph.

The tail-head link is formed when one sentence ends in a finite clause (``tail''), and the next sentence begins with a medial clause (``head'') that copies the verb but changes it into a medial one. The information in this medial clause is given rather than new, unlike in most other medial clauses. claims for Yimas, and assumes for the rest of Papuan languages, that these medial clauses are subordinate, but at least in Mauwake they are not -- they are coordinate like other medial clauses. In a narrative, the final verbs, which then get recapitulated in the next sentence, carry the core of the story line ex:8:x1505.

Wafur-a-k na weetak, ufer-a-k. Ufer-ap nainiw burir aaw-ep woosa=pa aruf-eya waaya nain in-e-k. In-eya yena ikiw-emi nainiw wiowa erup ar-ow-amkun iiwawun um-o-k. Um-eya merena ere-erup kaik-ap \\
throw- pa -3s but no miss- pa -3s miss- ss. seq again axe take- ss. seq head= loc hit-2/3s. ds pig that1 lie.down- pa -3s lie.down-2/3s. ds 1s. gen go- ss. sim again spear two become- caus -1s/p. ds altogether die- pa -3s die-2/3s. dn leg rdp -two tie- ss. seq \\
`He threw it (=a spear) but no, he missed. He missed it and again took an axe and hit it on the head and the pig fell down. It fell down and I myself went and speared it twice and it died completely. It died and I tied its legs two and two together and '

The repeated verb retains its arguments, but there is a choice in how overtly they and the peripherals are marked in the medial clause. Retaining them makes the medial clause more emphatic, and the first element becomes a theme for the new sentence ( sec:9.1 ). In ex:8:x1505 only the verbs are copied; ex:8:x1506 copies the subject as well, ex:8:x1507 the object and ex:8:x1508 the locative adverbial.

Miiw-aasa samor-ar-e-k. Miiw-aasa samor-ar-eya \\
land-canoe bad- inch - pa -3s land-canoe bad- inch -2/3s. ds \\
`The car broke. The car broke and '

Owowa or-op, wuailal-ep akia ik-e-k. Akia ik-ep en-em-ik-ok, \\
village descend- ss. seq be.hungry- ss. seq banana roast- pa -3s banana roast- ss. seq eat- ss. sim -be- ss \\
`He came down to the village, was hungry and roasted bananas. He roasted bananas and was eating them, and '

P-ikiw-ep Bogia=pa nan wu-a-mik. Bogia=pa nan wu-ap i kiiriw ekap-e-mik. \\
bpx -go- ss. seq Bogia= loc there put- pa -1/3p Bogia= loc there put- ss. seq 1p. unm again come- pa -1/3p \\
`We took it (=his body) and put/buried it in Bogia. We put it in Bogia and came back again.'

Most commonly the derivational morphology in the two verbs is identical, but sometimes the derivation in the finite verb is dropped from the medial verb ex:8:x1513, ex:8:x1514. In ex:8:x1513, there is a good reason for dropping the benefactive marking from the repeated verb: the spear was thrown for someone's benefit, but it missed, and consequently there was no benefit for anyone.

Olas=ke ekap-emi wiowa wafur-om-a-k. Wafur-a-k na weetak, ufer-a-k. \\
Olas= cf come- ss. sim spear throw- ben - bnfy 2. pa -3s throw- pa -3s but no miss- pa -3s \\
`Olas came and threw a spear for him. He threw it but no, he missed.'

Epa wiim-eya mua karer-omak-e-mik. Karer-a-p ma-e-mik, `` ''\\
place dawn-2/3s. ds man gather- distr / pl - pa -1/3p gather- ss. seq say- pa -1/3p\\
`It dawned and many men gathered. They gathered and said, `` '' '

Adding new derivation to the medial verb is possible, but rare: the example (3. ex:3:x237 ) is repeated below as ex:8:x1515.

Ikiwosa wiar pepekim-ep kaik-a-m. Kaik-om-ap \\
head 3. dat measure- ss. seq tie- pa -1s tie- ben - bnfy 2. ss. seq \\
`I measured her head and tied it (=headdress). I tied it for her and '

Similarly, aspect marking normally stays the same in both the verbs, but it is also possible to have aspect marking on the medial verb, although the finite verb is without any aspect marking ex:8:x1516, ex:8:x1517. When new information is added to the verb either by derivation or aspect marking, it is less clear if this still is a true case of tail-head linkage....nomokowa maala war-ep, ekap-ep ifa nain ifakim-o-k. Ifakim-em-ik-eya ifa nain=ke siowa wasirk-a-k.\\
tree long cut- ss. seq come- ss. seq snake that1 beat- pa -3s beat- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds snake that1= cf dog release- pa -3s\\
` he cut a long stick, came, and beat up the snake. As he was beating it, the snake released the dog.'

Moma manina mokomokoka nop - i - mik. Nop - ap-pu - ap nomokowa war-i-mik. \\
taro garden first clear- Np - pr.1/3p clear- ss. seq - cmpl - ss. seq tree cut- Np - pr.1/3p \\
`First we clear (the undergrowth for) taro garden. When we have cleared it we cut the trees.'

The tail-head linkage disregards right-dislocated items that come between the two verbs ex:8:x1518, ex:8:x1519.
summary:
Tail-head linkage is a common inter-sentential cohesive device in oral Papuan narratives and process descriptions, though it becomes less prominent in written styles. It links a sentence-final finite “tail” clause to the next sentence’s initial medial “head” clause, which repeats the verb and often earlier arguments; the repeated material is typically given information, and the core story line is carried by the finite verbs.

The passage notes that the amount of copied material can vary, from just the verb to the subject, object, or adverbial, and that derivational or aspect marking usually stays the same but may sometimes differ. It also observes that in Mauwake these medial clauses are coordinate rather than subordinate, and that right-dislocated material between the two verbs is ignored by the construction.

text:
Ne kiiriw nan Medebur ek-a-mik, mua napuma onaiya. Ek-ap Medebur=pa neeke \\
add again there Medebur go- pa -1/3p man sick with go- ss. seq Medebur= loc there. cf \\
`And again from there they went to Medebur, with the sick man. They went and there in Medebur '...pok-ap ika-iwkin mua wiar ekap-e-mik, wiinar-ep. Ekap-emi wia maak-e-mik, ``Maa iiw-eka.'' \\
sit.down- ss. seq be- ss. seq man 3. dat come- pa -1/3p make.planting.holes- ss. seq come- ss. sim 3p. acc tell- pa -1/3p food dish.out- imp.2p\\
` they were sitting and their husbands came, having made the planting holes. They came and told them, ``Dish out the food.'' '

A summary tail-head linkage with a generic verb ex:8:x1520, a common feature in many tng languages, is used very little in Mauwake.

Or-omi ma-em-ik-e-mik, ``Eka mamaiya akena i yoowa me aaw-i-yen.'' Naap on-am-ika-iwkin eka owowa kerer-ep \\
descend- ss. sim say- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p river near very 1p. unm hot not get- Np - fu.1p thus do- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds river village appear- ss. seq \\
`They went down and were saying, ``Very near the river we won't get hot.'' They were doing like that and (then) the river reached the village and '
summary: The passage notes that a summary tail-head linkage construction with a generic verb, which is common in many TNG languages, is used only rarely in Mauwake. It then gives an example of linked events in discourse, where successive actions are connected through chained verbs and reported speech.

text:
Subordinate clauses are a problematic area to define both cross-linguistically (, ) and even within one language. It seems that there is a continuum from fully independent to embedded clauses (, ).

Rather than treating subordinate clauses as one group, it is helpful to differentiate between embedding and hypotaxis. Embedded clauses have a function in the main clause: relative clauses as qualifiers within a np, complement clauses as objects or subjects, and adverbial clauses as adverbials. Hypotactic clauses are also dependent on the main clause, but they do not function as a constituent in it (, ). Even though subordination is ``a negative term which lumps together all deviations from some `main clause' norm'', the term still has limited usefulness, as there are some rules that affect both embedded and hypotactic clauses.

In Mauwake, subordinate clauses usually precede the main clauses, and they have a non-final intonation pattern. The initial position is related to the pragmatic function of topic that these clauses often have; but when the subordinate clause is right-dislocated, it does not have a topic function. For a discussion on the topic function of subordinate clauses see, e.g.,,,, and. The semantic function varies according to the type of subordinate clause.

Embedded clauses in Mauwake are nominalized clauses: relative clause nominalization ( rc) ( sec:8.3.1 ) is always done with the demonstrative nain `that' added to a finite clause, whereas complement clauses ( cc) ( sec:8.3.2 ) can use either one of the two nominalization strategies ( sec:5.7 ). The locative and temporal adverbial clauses ( sec:8.3.3 ), like the relative clauses, are Type 2 nominalized clauses ( sec:5.7.2 ). All of these clauses bear out claim that ``subordinate clauses, especially in sentence-initial position, are natural vehicles for the speaker's presuppositions''. ``Presuppositions'' here refer to pragmatic, not logical-semantic presuppositions. also suggests that the origin of the relative clause is in a paratactic construction. At least in Mauwake this seems to be true not only of the relative clause but of the complement clause ( sec:8.3.2 ) as well.

The hypotactic conditional and concessive clauses are dependent on their main clause, but not embedded in it.
summary:
The passage argues that subordinate clauses are hard to define because there is a continuum from independent to embedded clauses, so it is useful to distinguish embedding from hypotaxis. In Mauwake, embedded clauses are nominalized and serve functions such as relatives, complements, or adverbials, while hypotactic clauses are dependent on the main clause but do not function as constituents within it.  

It further notes that subordinate clauses in Mauwake usually occur before the main clause and have a non-final intonation, often reflecting a pragmatic topic function when sentence-initial. Relative, complement, and temporal/locative adverbial clauses all involve nominalization, and conditional and concessive clauses are described as hypotactic rather than embedded.

text:
I define a restrictive relative clause ( rc ), This definition only applies to restrictive relative clauses; non-restrictive rc s ( sec:8.3.1.4 ) are not real rc s although they are structurally similar to the real rc s. following, as a ``subordinate clause which delimits the reference of a np by specifying the role of the referent of that np in the situation described by the rc ''.

The relative clause is a statement about some noun phrase in the main clause. That np is here called the antecedent np ( antnp ), This is often called Head NP, but because it is not grammatically a ``head'' of anything, I prefer to call it antecedent np. The name ``antecedent'' is also somewhat of a misnomer, as in Mauwake it does not precede the relnp. since it is the unit that the the coreferential np in the relative clause derives its meaning from. The coreferential np in the rc is called the relative np ( relnp ). calls it a domain noun.

Often the referent of the antnp is assumed to be known to the hearer but not necessarily easily accessible, so the rc gives background information to help the hearer identify the referent.

The relative marker is the distal-1 demonstrative nain `that' ( sec:3.6.2 ) occurring clause-finally in the relative clause ex:8:x1527. It has a slightly rising non-final intonation indicating that the sentence continues; right-dislocated rc s have sentence-final falling intonation. Givenness is an essential part of the meaning of the demonstrative, which is also used in np s ex:8:x1528. The demonstrative in effect makes the rc into a noun phrase. The similarity of the two structures can be seen in the examples below.

Takira gelemuta nain NP uruf-a-m.\\
boy small that1 see- pa -1s \\
`I saw that/the small boy.'

Takira me arim-o-k nain rc uruf-a-m. \\
boy not grow- pa -3s that1 see- pa -1s \\
`I saw the boy that has not grown.'
summary:
A restrictive relative clause is defined as a subordinate clause that limits the reference of a noun phrase by specifying the role of that noun phrase’s referent in the situation described by the clause. The noun phrase in the main clause is called the antecedent NP, and the coreferential noun phrase inside the relative clause is called the relative NP; the relative clause typically provides background information to help identify a referent that is assumed to be known but not necessarily easily accessible.

In this language, the relative marker is the distal demonstrative *nain* ‘that’, which appears clause-finally in the relative clause and carries a slightly rising non-final intonation. This demonstrative emphasizes givenness and effectively turns the relative clause into a noun phrase, showing a structural similarity between relative clauses and ordinary noun phrases.

subsubsection: The type and position of the relative clause
text:
In typological terms, relative clauses in Mauwake are mostly replacive, also called internal ex:8:x1529-- ex:8:x1546. A normal finite clause is made into a noun phrase by the addition of the demonstrative nain, and the relnp inside the rc replaces the antnp. Pre-nominal rc s, where the rc precedes the antnp, are cross-linguistically more typical of ov languages than replacive ones, but the latter are also common in Papuan languages ( and,,, ). Often both pre-nominal and replacive rc s are possible, with one or the other being the dominant type.

Ni nomona unuf-a-man nain, aria iimeka kuisow na-e-man. \\
2p. unm stone call- pa -2p that1 alright ten one say- pa -2p \\
`The money that you mentioned, alright you said ten (kina).'

Ne eka opora biiris marew nain wiena on-am-ik-e-mik. \\
add river mouth bridge no(ne) that1 3p. gen do- ss. sim -be-1/3p\\
`And they themselves kept making bridges to river channels that didn't have them.'

Mua kuum-e-mik nain me wia kuuf-a-mik. \\
man burn- pa -1/3p that1 not 3p. acc see- pa -1/3p\\
`We/They did not see the men that burned it.'

Ne akia ik-e-k nain me en-e-k. \\
add banana roast- pa -3s that1 not eat- pa -3s\\
`And/but he did not eat the banana(s) that he roasted.'

It is possible to retain the antecedent np, in which case the relative clause is not replacive but pre-nominal. In Mauwake this is not common; it is used when the noun phrase that is relativized is given extra emphasis ex:8:x1532.

Fofa ikiw-e-mik nain, fofa nain yo me paayar-e-m. \\
day go- pa -1/3p that1 day that1 1s. unm not know- pa -1s\\
`The day that they went, I do not know the day/date.'

Even though the rc is usually embedded in the main clause, it can be right-dislocated. In that case the main clause contains the antecedent np, and the relative np is deleted from the rc. This way the first one of the coreferential np s is retained for easier processing. Reasons for right-dislocating a relative clause are firstly, a long rc, which would be hard to process sentence-medially ex:8:x1533, secondly, focusing on the rc, or thirdly, an afterthought: something that the speaker still wants to add ex:8:x1534.

Wi teeria papako o asip-a-mik, ona eka sesenar-ep wienak-e-k nain. \\
3p. unm group other 3s. unm help- pa -1/3p 3s. gen water buy- ss. seq feed.them- pa -3s that1\\
`Another group helped him, (those) that he had bought and given beer to.'

I mua yiam ikur, fikera ikiw-e-mik nain. \\
1p. unm man 1p. refl five kunai.grass go- pa -1/3p that1\\
`There were five of us men that went to the kunai grass (=pig-hunting).'

In a very rare case the antecedent np is deleted and the relative np is retained in the right-dislocated rc. What makes it possible in example ex:8:x1535 may be that the verb in the main clause can only have some food (or medicine/poison) as its object, so the object, although usually present, may also be left out.

Wi mua... ekap-iwkin wienak-e-mik, maa nop-a-mik nain.\\
3p. unm man... come-2/3p. ds feed.them- pa -1/3p food search- pa -1/3p that1\\
`The men came, and we gave it to them to eat, (that is,) the food that we had searched for.'

presents another typology based on how the role of the relative np is presented in the rc. Basically Mauwake is of the ``gap type'', which ``does not provide any overt indication of the role of the head within the relative clause''. Noun phrases get very little case marking for their clausal role, and this is reflected in the rc too. This results in ambiguous relative clauses when both a third person subject np and a third person object np are present in the rc and the context does not make the meaning clear enough ex:8:x1548:

Siowa kasi keraw-a-k nain um-o-k. \\
dog cat bite- pa -3s that1 die- pa -3s\\
`The dog that bit the cat died.' Or: `The dog that the cat bit died.'

The ambiguity can be avoided by adding the contrastive focus marker to the subject when the object is fronted to the theme position. For some reason this is done in relative clauses mainly with human subjects, although the contrastive focus marker can be added to non-human subjects as well. Although this is not case marking, it can function as such, because the subject is the best candidate for contrastive focus marking ex:8:x1549 ( sec:3.12.7.2 ).

Mua ona emeria=ke aruf-a-k nain uruf-a-m. \\
man 3s. gen woman= cf hit- pa -3s that1 see- pa -1s\\
`I saw the man whose wife hit him.'

``non-reduction type'' is exhibited in Mauwake by those few cases where the relative np keeps its oblique case marking. With overt case marking on the relnp, the antnp has to be retained ex:8:x1544:

[ Burir=iw nomokowa war-e-m nain,] burir nain duduw-ar-e-k.\\
axe= inst tree cut- pa -1s that1 axe that blunt- inch - pa -3s\\
`The axe with which I cut trees became blunt.'

But when the case marking does not appear in the rc, the antnp is not present in the main clause either, and the rc is a gapping-type relative clause ex:8:x1541:

Burir nomokowa war-e-m nain=ke duduw-ar-e-k. \\
axe tree cut- pa -1s that1= cf blunt- inch - pa -3s\\
`The axe with which I cut trees became blunt.'
summary:
Mauwake relative clauses are mostly replacive, or internal, with a demonstrative added to turn a finite clause into a noun phrase and replace the antecedent noun phrase inside the relative clause. Pre-nominal relatives, where the relative clause precedes the antecedent, are less common and are used for emphasis, while right-dislocated relatives may be used for long clauses, focus, or afterthoughts.  

The language is generally a “gap type,” with little overt marking of the head’s role inside the relative clause, which can create ambiguity when both subject and object are third person. A rare non-reduction type appears when the relative noun phrase retains oblique case marking, in which case the antecedent must also be retained.

subsubsection: The structure of the relative clause
text:
In Mauwake, the most typical relative clause is syntactically like a finite main clause, plus the distal-1 deictic nain functioning as a clause final relative marker. It was mentioned in sec:5.7.2 that this is one strategy for nominalizing clauses in Mauwake. The demonstrative as a possible origin of a relative marker is well attested cross-linguistically (e.g. ).

The verb of the relative clause is a fully inflected finite verb. But when a non-verbal clause is a relative clause, it has no verb and is structurally like other non-verbal clauses ex:8:x1943.

Ne eka opora biiris marew nain wiena on-am-ik-e-mik.\\
add river mouth bridge no(ne) that1 3p. gen do- ss. sim - pa -1/3p\\
`And they themselves kept making bridges to rivers that didn't have them.'

The relative np tends to be initial in the rc regardless of its syntactic function. This is because it often has the pragmatic function of theme, which takes the clause-initial position. The initial position is easy to have also because a typical clause in Mauwake has so few noun phrases: in many rc s the relnp is the only noun phrase ex:8:x1552.

Moma p-or-o-mik nain wiar sesenar-e-mik.\\
taro bpx -descend- pa -1/3p that1 3. dat buy- pa -1/3p \\
`They i bought from them j the taro that they j brought down.'

When a personal pronoun functions as a subject and the relative np in some other syntactic role, the pronoun tends to keep its initial position, thus maintaining the basic constituent order. The personal pronouns are high on the topicality hierarchy, so it is natural that they tend to keep the clause-initial and also sentence-initial position. Since the object sirirowa `pain' in ex:8:x1531 is not fronted, a temporal adverbial also keeps a place it would have in a neutral main clause.

The tense in the rc can be past ex:8:x1552 or present ex:8:x1559, but not future. For future meaning, the present tense form has to be used ex:8:x1531.

Yo ikoka sirir-owa aaw-i-yem nain, nis pun eliw aaw-owen=i?\\
1s. unm later hurt- nmz get- Np - pr.1s that1 2p. fc also well get- fu.2p= qm \\
`Is it all right that you will also get the pain that I (will) later get?'

As was mentioned above, the antecedent np only rarely occurs overtly. But a relative np can also be deleted if it is generic ex:8:x1561, or recoverable from situational ex:8:x1555 or textual context ex:8:x1559. In ex:8:x1555, the deleted relnp can either be generic `what/whatever' or it may be opora `talk'; in ex:8:x1559, the speaker is describing the process of making a fishtrap, which has already been mentioned in previous sentences.

Iinan aasa=pa or-omi kiikir furew-a-mik nain dabela. \\
sky canoe= loc descend- ss. sim first sense- pa -1/3p that1 cold\\
`What we first sensed/felt when we descended from the plane was the cold.'

Kululu ma-e-k nain kirip-i-yem. \\
Kululu say- pa -3s that1 turn/reply- Np - pr.1s\\
`I reply to what Kululu said.'

Aria malol=pa ifemak-i-mik nain aana puuk-i-mik.\\
alright deep.sea= loc press- Np - pr.1/3p that1 cane cut- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`Alright for those that we lower to the deep sea we cut cane.'

In ex:8:x1556, there is no other indication of the relative np than the person suffix of the verb. The group of women referred to were mentioned as a noun phrase only near the beginning of the story, whereas the example is from close to the end:

Domora=pa or-omi nan ik-e-mik, afa ar-e-mik nain. \\
Domora= loc descend- ss. sim there be-pa-1/3p flying.fox become- pa -1/3p that1\\
`They went down from Domora and were there, those (women) who became flying foxes.'

In the following two examples the rc s are identical, but they have a different relative np. The relnp of ex:8:x1557 is mukuruna `noise', but the relnp of ex:8:x1558, wi `they', only shows in the verbal suffix. The obligatory accusative pronoun in the main clause provides a key for the interpretation of ex:8:x1558.

Mukuruna wua-i-mik nain ikiw-ep miim-eka. \\
noise put- Np - pr.1/3p that1 go- ss. sim hear- imp.2p\\
`Go and listen to the noise that they are making.'

Mukuruna wua-i-mik nain ikiw-ep wia miim-eka.\\
noise put- Np - pr.1/3p that1 go- ss. seq 3p. acc hear- imp.2p\\
`Go and listen to those who are making the noise.'

The antecedent in most relative clauses has a specific reference. In Mauwake, when the reference is generic, a very generic noun is chosen as the head of the relativized np and is modified by a question word ex:8:x1562, ex:8:x1563. So-called free or condensed relative clauses, which usually replace the whole np with a generic or interrogative pronoun, are not used in Mauwake.

Maa mauwa maak-i-n nain me nefa miim-i-non.\\
thing what tell- Np - pr.2s that1 not 2s. acc hear- Np - fu.3s\\
`Whatever you tell him, he will not hear.'

Mua naareke kema enek-ar-i-ya nain eka dabela enim-i-nok.\\
man who. cf liver tooth- inch - Np - pr.3s that1 water cold eat- Np - imp.3s\\
`Whoever is thirsty must drink (cold) water.'

When the antecedent is generic and human, there are two more possibilities for the relnp: it may be mua `man, person' ex:8:x1564 or the third person singular pronoun, plus the specifier ena ex:8:x1565 ( sec:3.12.7.1 ).

Mua ena kema enek-ar-i-ya nain... \\
man spec liver tooth- inch - Np - pr.3s that1\\
`Whoever is thirsty '

O ena kema enek-ar-i-ya nain... \\
3s. unm spec liver tooth- inch - Np - pr.3s that1\\
`Whoever is thirsty '

Non-verbal descriptive clauses can be made into relative clauses, but it is only in the negative that they are recognizable as such. In the affirmative, they are exactly like noun phrases with a demonstrative ex:8:x1550, and because the meanings are so similar, it can be questioned whether there is such a thing as an affirmative non-verbal descriptive rc at all in Mauwake.

Mua eliwa nain kookal-i-yem.\\
man good that1 like- Np - pr.1s\\
`I like the good man.' Or `I like the man that is good.'
summary:
Mauwake relative clauses are typically formed like finite main clauses followed by the distal deictic *nain*, which functions as a clause-final relative marker; non-verbal clauses can also serve as relative clauses, though they are structurally identical to other non-verbal clauses. The relativized noun phrase usually appears clause-initially, but it may be omitted when recoverable from context, generic, or only indicated by verbal agreement, and future reference is expressed with present tense rather than future tense in the relative clause.

The language generally avoids free or condensed relative clauses, instead using a specific head noun or generic noun plus a question word for generic reference. Affirmative non-verbal descriptive relative clauses are especially hard to distinguish from noun phrases with demonstratives, and their status is therefore uncertain.

subsubsection: The structure of the relative clause
text:
In the negative, these clauses are different from the noun phrases because the negation is placed before the non-verbal predicate ex:8:x1551.

Koora me maneka nain uruf-a-m. \\
house not big that1 see- pa -1s\\
`I saw the house that is not big.'
summary: In negative clauses, these constructions differ from noun phrases because the negation comes before the non-verbal predicate. The example shows this pattern in a clause meaning “I saw the house that is not big,” where the negation precedes the adjective-like predicate.

text:
Several np functions can be relativized, and Mauwake conforms to Noun Phrase Accessibility Hierarchy: As Mauwake adjectives do not have comparative forms there can be no relativization for an object of comparison, which in Keenan and Comrie's hierarchy is the hardest to relativize. the higher up an np is in the hierarchy, the easier it is to relativize. Noun phrases with the following functions can be relativized: subject, object, recipient, beneficiary, instrument, comitative, object of genitive, temporal and locative.

Subject ex:8:x1537 and object ex:8:x1538 are the most frequent functions of the RelNP.

Mesa asia fiker(a) gone=pa ika-i-ya nain aaw-em-ik-e-m.\\
wingbean wild kunai.grass middle= loc be- Np - pr.3s that1 get- ss. sim -be- pa -1s\\
`I kept picking wild wingbeans that are/grow in the middle of the kunai grass.'

Muuka, yo opora nefa maak-i-yem nain miim-ap ook-e.\\
son 1s. unm talk 2s. acc tell- Np - pr.1s that1 hear- ss. seq follow- imp.2s\\
`Son, listen to and follow the talk that I am telling you.'

Recipient ex:8:x1539 and beneficiary ex:8:x1547 are possible to relativize, but in natural texts beneficiary is very infrequent.

Takira iwoka iw-e-m nain yena aamun=ke.\\
boy yam give.him- pa -1s that1 1s. gen 1s/p.younger.sibling= cf \\
`The boy that I gave yam to is my younger brother.'

Ne wi emeria papako iiriw sawur wia iirar-om-a-k nain \\
add 3p. unm woman some earlier bad.spirit 3p. acc remove- ben - bnfy 2. pa -3s that1\\
`And some women, from (lit: for) whom he had removed bad spirits, '

When an instrument is relativized, the relnp either takes the instrumental case marking ex:8:x1544 or has no case marking ex:8:x1553:

Aria maa unowa wakesim-e-mik nain sererk-a-mik.\\
alright thing many cover- pa -1/3p that1 distribute- pa -1/3p\\
`Alright they distributed the many things with which they had covered her (body).'

A comitative np ( sec:4.1.3 ) containing a comitative postposition may be relativized ex:8:x1542, but one formed with a comitative clitic may not.

Mua nain ikos ikiw-e-mik nain napum-ar-e-k. \\
man that1 with go- pa -1/3p that1 sick- inch - pa -3s\\
`That man with whom I went became sick.'

The object of genitive, or object of possessive as it should be called when describing Mauwake grammar, only uses the dative pronoun ( sec:3.5.5 ) when relativized ex:8:x1543, not the unmarked ( sec:3.5.2.1 ) or genitive ( sec:3.5.4 ) pronoun.

Mua emeria wiar um-o-k nain=ke baurar-ep owowa oko ikiw-o-k.\\
man woman 3. dat die- pa -3s that1= cf flee- ss. seq village other go- pa -3s\\
`The man whose wife died went away Moving to another village after some misfortune is quite common, and the verb `flee' is used in this context but here it does not have a strongly negative connotation; this is reflected in the free translation. to another village.'

Temporal ex:8:x1554 and locative ex:8:x1560 rc s are structurally identical to the other rc s when the relativized temporal or locative np does not have an adverbial function in the main clause.

Fofa ikiw-e-mik nain me paayar-e-m. \\
day go- pa -1/3p that1 not understand- pa -1s\\
`I don't know the day that they went.'

Koora maneka wiena opora siisim-i-mik nain uruf-a-mik. \\
house big 3p. gen talk write- Np -1/3p that1 see- pa -1/3p\\
`We saw the big house where they write their talk (=printshop).'

When the relativized temporal np is a temporal in the main clause as well, the relative marker can optionally be replaced by the locative deictic nan or neeke `there' ex:8:x1625.

[Aite uroma yaki-e-k fofa nain/nan/neeke] auwa Madang ikiw-o-k.\\
1s/p.mother stomach wash- pa -3s day that1/there/there. cf 1s/p.father Madang go- pa -3s\\
`The day that mother gave birth, father went to Madang.'

When the relativized locative np is also a constituent in the main clause, the relative marker has to be replaced by nan or neeke ex:8:x1622.

Or-op i koora ik-e-mik neeke ekap-o-k.\\
descend- ss. seq 1p. unm house be- pa -1p there. cf come- pa -3s\\
`It descended and came to the house/building where we were.'

Temporal adverbial clauses, which are structurally close to relative clauses, are discussed below in sec:8.3.3.1, and locative adverbial clauses in sec:8.3.3.2.
summary: Mauwake allows relativization of several noun phrase functions and follows the Noun Phrase Accessibility Hierarchy: subject and object are most frequent, while recipient, beneficiary, instrument, comitative, object of genitive/possessive, temporal, and locative NPs can also be relativized. The passage illustrates that instruments may be marked or unmarked, comitative NPs with a postposition can be relativized but those with a clitic cannot, and the object of possessive takes only the dative pronoun in relativization. Temporal and locative relative clauses are structurally like other relative clauses, though when the relativized NP is also used adverbially in the main clause, the relative marker may be replaced by locative deictics nan or neeke.

text:
Non-restrictive, or appositional, relative clauses are structurally exactly like restrictive relative clauses, but their function is different. They do not delimit the reference of the antecedent np. Instead, they give new information about it. Functionally they are like a coordinate clause added to the main clause.

Because of the structural and even intonational similarity, it is sometimes difficult to tell if a particular rc is restrictive or non-restrictive. When the antnp is a proper noun or when it includes a first or second person singular pronoun, the rc is usually non-restrictive ex:8:x1567, ex:8:x1568:

Bang=ke ekap-o-k, Ponkila aaw-o-k nain.\\
Bang= cf come- pa -3s Ponkila get- pa -3s that1\\
`Bang came, (he) who married Ponkila.'

Yo nena owowa moma marew nain miatin-i-yem. \\
1s. unm 2s. gen village taro no(ne) that1 dislike- Np - pr.1s\\
`I don't like your village, which doesn't have taro.'

The proximate demonstrative fain `this' can also function as a relative marker in the non-restrictive rc s but not in restrictive ones ex:8:x1536:

Nomokowa unowa fan-e-mik, Simbine ekap-omak-e-mik fain.\\
2s/p.brother many here- pa -1/3p Simbine come- distr / pl - pa -1/3p this\\
`Your many (clan) brothers are here, these Simbine people who came.'

When the antnp is a pronoun other than first or second singular, the rc may be either restrictive or non-restrictive ex:8:x1570.

I mua yiam ikur, fikera ikiw-e-mik nain. \\
1p. unm man 1p. refl five kunai.grass go- pa -1/3p that1\\
`There were five of us men who went to the kunai grass (= pig-hunting).' Or: `We were five men, who went pig-hunting.'
summary: Non-restrictive, or appositional, relative clauses are structurally like restrictive relative clauses, but they do not limit the reference of the antecedent noun phrase; instead, they add new information, functioning much like a coordinate clause. They can be hard to distinguish from restrictive clauses, though with proper nouns or first/second singular pronouns they are usually non-restrictive, and the demonstrative *fain* can mark non-restrictive but not restrictive relatives. When the antecedent is another kind of pronoun, the relative clause may be either restrictive or non-restrictive.

subsection: Complement clauses and other complementation strategies
text:
The prototypical function of a complement clause is as a subject or object in a main clause. In Mauwake, a complement clause proper functions as an object of a complement-taking verb ( ctv ), and occasionally as a subject in a non-verbal clause. Structurally it is a Type 2 nominalized clause: a finite clause that has the distal-1 demonstrative nain `that' occurring as a nominaliser clause-finally ( sec:5.7.2 ). The complement clause precedes the complement-taking verb. The complement clause differs from the relative clause in that none of the noun phrases inside it is an antnp or a relnp.

The division of complements into different types, ``Fact, Activity and Potential'', that provides, is crucial for the use of the different complementation strategies in Mauwake. A complement clause is normally used when a ctv needs a fact-type object complement.

Besides the regular complement clause described above, Mauwake has other complementation strategies. The indirect speech clauses are ordinary sentences embedded in the utterance clause ( sec:8.3.2.1.2 ). Medial clauses are used as the main complementation strategy for activity-type complements with perception verbs ( sec:8.3.2.2 ). Clauses with a nominalized verb are used for potential-type complements with various ctv s. The regular complement clause and the clause with a nominalized verb may occur as a subject of a clause ( sec:8.3.2.4 ).

Since one ctv can take more than one complementation strategy, the main grouping below is done according to the ctv s.
summary:
In Mauwake, a regular complement clause functions mainly as the object of a complement-taking verb and sometimes as the subject of a non-verbal clause. It is a Type 2 nominalized clause marked by the distal-1 demonstrative *nain* ‘that’ and placed before the verb; unlike relative clauses, it contains no noun phrases that function as antnp or relnp.

Mauwake distinguishes fact, activity, and potential complement types, and these determine which complementation strategy is used. Fact-type complements normally use the regular complement clause, activity-type complements with perception verbs use medial clauses, and potential-type complements use clauses with a nominalized verb; indirect speech clauses are also used as embedded sentences.

subsection: Complement clauses and other complementation strategies
text:
Some utterance verbs ( sec:3.8.4.4.6 ) are also used for thinking, so speech and thought are discussed as one group.

The status of direct quote clauses ( sec:8.3.2.1.1 ) as complement clauses is questionable, but they are discussed here because of their co-occurrence with the utterance verbs and their similarity with the indirect quotes ( sec:8.3.2.1.2 ), which are complement clauses.

The most important of the utterance verbs is na- `say, think'. It is used as the utterance verb for indirect quote complements, which in turn have grammaticalized, together with the same subject sequential form of the verb, as desiderative ( sec:8.3.2.1.3 ) and purpose clauses ( sec:8.3.2.1.4 ) and the conative construction ( sec:8.3.2.1.5 )

Direct speech

It seems to be a universal feature of direct quote clauses that they behave independently of their matrix clauses. If they are considered complement clauses of utterance verbs, their independence sets them apart from all the other complement clauses. maintains that direct speech quotes are not any kind of complementation.

A direct quote may be a whole discourse on its own, not just a clause within a sentence.

It is rather typical in Papuan languages to have a strict quote formula both before and after a quotation, or at least before it (,,,, ). It is also common that either there is no separate structure for indirect speech or that direct and indirect speech are so similar that they are often hard to distinguish from each other.

In the use of quote formulas, Mauwake is much freer than Papuan languages in general. A direct quotation in Mauwake is often preceded or followed by one of the utterance verbs. The verbs na- `say/think' and naak- `say/tell' are almost exclusively used after quotes. Enclosing a quote between two utterance verbs is not frequent ex:8:x1571:

Ne ona mua pun ma-e-k, ``Eka maneka nain=ke iwa-mi ifakim-o-k,'' na-e-k.\\
add 3s. gen man also say- pa -3s river big that1= cf come- ss. sim kill- pa -3s say- pa -3s\\
`Her husband also said, ``The big river came and killed her,'' he said.'

Most commonly, only a speech verb precedes the quote ex:8:x1578, ex:8:x1579:

Panewowa=ke ma-e-k, ``Yo nia maak-emkun opaimika efa fien-a-man.''\\
old= cf say- pa -3s 1s. unm 2p. acc tell-2/3p. ds talk 1s. acc disobey- pa -2p\\
`The old (woman) said, ``When I told you, you disobeyed me.'' '

Iiw-ep wiipa muuka nain wia maak-e-k, ``Auwa maa p-ikiw-om-aka.\\
dish.out- ss. seq daughter son that1 3p. acc tell- pa -3s 1s/p.father food bpx -go- ben - bnfy 2. imp.2p\\
`She dished out (the food) and told the children, ``Take the food to father.'''

A single utterance verb ex:8:x1580 or a whole quote-closing clause ex:8:x1583 may follow the quote. A quote-closing clause has to be used when the quotation consists of several sentences.

``No bom fain=iw mera kuum-e,'' naak-e-mik. \\
2s. unm bomb this= inst fish burn- imp.2s tell- pa -1/3p\\
` ``Blast fish with this bomb,'' they told him.'

``I muuka marew a, wiipa marew a,'' naap wia maak-e-k.\\
1p. unm son no(ne) ah daughter no(ne) ah thus 3p. acc tell- pa -3s\\
` ``We have no son, we have no daughter,'' he told them like that.'

In narratives where there are several exchanges between the participants, it is possible to leave out the utterance verb ex:8:x1581, ex:8:x1582 and even the np referring to the speaker of the utterance ex:8:x1581, if the speaker is clear enough from the context. A good speaker creates variety in the text by utilizing all these different possibilities.

Ne onak=ke, ``A, ifera feeke un-eka.'' Ne wi maak-e-mik, ``Wia, i oro-or-op un-i-yan.'' ``A, neeke-r=iw un-eka.'' ``Weetak, i oro-ora-i-yan.''\\
add 3s/p.mother Ah, salt.water here. cf fetch(water)- imp.2p add 3p. unm tell- pa -1/3p No 1p. unm rdp -descend- ss. seq fetch- Np - fu.1p Ah there. cf - = lim fetch- imp.2p no 1p. unm rdp -descend- Np - fu.1p\\
`And their mother (said), ``Ah, fetch the sea water (from) here.'' But they told her, ``No, we'll go down (to the deep sea) and fetch it.'' ``Ah, fetch it right there.'' ``No, we'll go down a long way.'' '

``Mauwa ar-e-n, amia=iya nenar-e-mik=i?'' Sarak=ke. -1mm\\
what become- pa -2s bow= com shoot.you- pa -1/3p= qm Sarak= cf \\
```What happened to you, did they shoot you with a gun?'' Sarak (asked).'

Indirect speech

Indirect speech quotes, which report speech or thought, are objects of speech verbs.

Most indirect quotes in Mauwake are syntactically identical to direct quotes. There is an intonational difference: the indirect quote is part of the intonation contour of the main clause, rather than having a contour of its own as a direct quote has. The quote is almost always followed by the utterance verb na- `say, think' ex:8:x1585; but it is also possible for the verb ma- `say' to precede it, in which case both the utterance verb and the quote have their own intonation contour ex:8:x1587. In Amele, the absence of the speech verb before the quote is the main criterion for indirect speech. In Mauwake, this cannot be used as a criterion, as the occurrence of speech verbs with direct quotes varies so much. An indirect quote is never enclosed between two utterance verbs.

Aria, Kalina, Amerika ekap-e-mik na-i-mik. \\
alright Kalina America come- pa -1/3p say- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`Alright, Kalina, they say that the Americans have come.'

Ma-e-m, nena owowa=pa ik-o-n.\\
say- pa -1s 2s. gen village= loc be- pa -2s\\
`I said (to her i ) that you j are in your own village.'

As direct quotes behave independently of their matrix clauses, they often have a separate deictic centre. But indirect quotes vary in this respect. Deictic elements, which get part or all of their interpretation from the situational context, are often the same in indirect quotes as they would be in direct quotes ex:8:x1584, ex:8:x1280:
summary:
The passage groups speech and thought together because some utterance verbs are used for both, with **na-** ‘say, think’ being the most important verb. It notes that direct quote clauses may not be true complement clauses because they behave independently of the matrix clause, while indirect quotes are complement clauses and are syntactically very similar to direct quotes, differing mainly in intonation and deictic interpretation.

In Mauwake, direct quotations often occur with utterance verbs before or after the quote, especially **na-** and **naak-** ‘say/tell’, and in narratives the verb or even the speaker noun phrase may be omitted if the context is clear. Indirect quotes are usually followed by **na-**, can sometimes be preceded by **ma-**, and are distinct from direct quotes because they are never enclosed between two utterance verbs.

subsection: Complement clauses and other complementation strategies
text:
Aite=ke manina yook-e na-eya o ook-e.\\
1s/p.mother= cf garden follow.me- imp.2s say-2/3s. ds 3s. unm follow.her- imp.2s\\
`When mother tells you to follow her to the garden, follow her.'

Ni Krais yena teeria efar ik-eka na-ep nia far-eya ona teeria wiar ik-e-man.\\
2p. unm Christ 1s. gen family 1s. dat be- imp.2p say- ss. seq 2p. acc call-2/3s. ds 3s. gen family 3. dat be- pa -2p\\
`Christ called you to be his family and (now) you are his family.'

But the deictic centre may also shift partly or completely towards that of the matrix clause. When this happens, the pronouns are the easiest to change, next the adverbs. In ex:8:x1586 a second person pronoun has replaced the proper name or third person pronoun that would have been used in a direct quote.

Sarak oo, Amerika ekap-ep Ulingan nan ik-e-mik, nefa ikum-i-mik na-i-mik oo. \\
Sarak intj America come- ss. seq Ulingan there be- pa -1/3p 2s. acc wonder.about- Np - pr.1/3p say- Np - pr.1/3p intj \\
`Sarak! The Americans have come and are in Ulingan and they say that they are wondering where you are!'

When reported by the addressee of the example clause ex:8:x1281, only the pronoun in the reported clause ex:8:x1282 is different:

No owowa ikiw-ep buk nain sesek-om-e.\\
2s. unm village go- ss. seq book that1 send- ben - bnfy 1. imp.2s\\
`When you go to the village, send the book to me.'

Yo owowa ikiw-ep buk nain sesek-om-e efa na-e-k. \\
1s. unm village go- ss. seq book that1 send- ben - bnfy 1. imp.2s 1s. acc say- pa -3s\\
`He told me to send that book to him (lit: me) when I would go to the village.'

The verbs are most resistant to deictic shift. In ex:8:x1264, even though the verb root changes, it still retains the tense and person marking of the direct quote ex:8:x1265. Both the temporal adverb and the pronoun are shifted to reflect the deictic centre of the matrix clause.

Uurika nefar ikiw-i-nen. \\
tomorrow 2s. dat go- Np - fu.1s\\
`Tomorrow I'll come (lit: go) to you.'

Ikoka efar ekap-i-nen na-e-k na weetak.\\
Later(today) 1s. dat come- Np - fu.1s say- pa -3s but no\\
`He said that he would come to me today, but he hasn't.'

Below in ex:8:x1266 also the person suffix is changed from that in ex:8:x1267 to reflect the situation of the new speech act participants.

Ona owowa=pa ik-ua.\\
3s. gen village= loc be- pa.3s\\
`She is in her own village.'

Ma-e-m, nena owowa=pa ik-o-n. \\
say- pa -1s 2s. gen village= loc be- pa -2s\\
`I said (to her) that you are in your own village.'

The deictic shift would need more study to ascertain if there are specific rules governing this variation in indirect quotes.

When the verb na- `say, think' indicates thinking, the complement clause is usually an indirect quote rather than a direct one ex:8:x1588, ex:8:x1589.

Muuka ifera me enim-i-non na-ep me uruf-a-m.\\
boy salt.water not drink- Np - fu.3s think- ss. seq not look- pa -1s\\
`Thinking that the boy wouldn't drown I didn't watch him.'

Mua pepena=ke menat=ke ek-i-ya na-ep menat ora-i-nan.\\
man inexperienced= cf tide= cf go- Np - pr.3s think- ss. seq tide descend- Np - fu.2s\\
`An inexperienced man will think that the tide is going down and will go to fish at low tide.'

Indirect non-polar questions are similar to the corresponding direct questions apart from possible adjustments to deictic elements ex:8:x1592, ex:8:x1590.

Wi uf-ow(a) epa kaaneke ik-ua na-e-k.\\
3p. unm dance- nmz place where. cf be- pa.3s say- pa -3s\\
`He asked where their dancing place was.'

O ikoka sesa kamenap aaw-i-non na-e-k.\\
3s. unm later price what.like get- Np - fu.3s say- pa -3s\\
`He asked what kind of wages he would get later.'

Polar questions, when indirect, have to be alternative questions ex:8:x1591. The verb naep may be deleted, when the indirect question is sentence-final ex:8:x1593.

Beel-al-i-non=i kamenion na-ep uruf-am-ik-ua.\\
rotten- inch - Np - fu.3s= qm or.what think- ss. seq see- ss. sim -be- pa.3s\\
`He was watching (thinking) whether it would rot or what would happen.'

Wi iwera iinan=pa ik-ok iwer(a) popoka wafur-am-ik-e-mik, eka saanar-e-k=i eewuar. \\
3p. unm coconut top= loc be- ss coconut unripe throw- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p water dry- pa -3s= qm not.yet\\
`They were at the top of the coconut palm and threw unripe coconuts (thinking) whether the water had dried or not yet.'

Desiderative clauses

It is very common in Papuan languages that an indirect quote construction with the intended action verb in future tense, imperative or irrealis form expresses a want/wish In Mauwake, the verb kookal - `like, love, desire', is mostly used with an np object, but it can take a clausal complement as well. It does not indicate intention or purpose. The complement is either type of nominalized clauses ( sec:5.7 )., desire or intention to do something. (,,, ).

In Mauwake, the future, imperative, counterfactual and nominalized forms of the main verb are possible in the complement clause. In desiderative clauses, the verb na- `say/think' is always in the medial same-subject sequential form naep; in purpose clauses, other forms are possible as well. Historically, there probably always used to be a clause with a finite verb following the clause expressing intention or desire ex:8:x367; synchronically the finite clause is often missing ex:8:x368, especially when the verb would be the same as in the complement.

Niena maa enim-u na-ep iiw-eka. \\
2p. gen food eat- imp.1d say- ss. seq dish.out- imp.2p\\
`If you want/intend to eat food, dish it out (yourselves).'

Yo opora gelemuta=ko ma-i-nen na-ep.\\
1s. unm talk little= nf say- nps - fu.1s say- ss. seq \\
`I want to tell a little story.' Or: `I'm going to tell a little story.'
summary: The passage describes how indirect and reported speech in Mauwake can show deictic shift, with pronouns changing most easily, followed by adverbs, while verbs are the most resistant and may keep the tense/person marking of the original quote. It also notes that indirect questions often mirror direct questions except for shifted deixis, polar questions become alternative questions, and desiderative clauses commonly use an indirect quote with the verb *na-* ‘say/think’ in medial sequential form to express want or intention.

subsection: Complement clauses and other complementation strategies
text:
The main verb in the complement clause is either marked for first person Purpose clauses may use other person forms as well ( sec:8.3.2.1.4 ). or is nominalized. Mauwake uses the future ex:8:x368 or imperative form ex:8:x369 of the main verb for intention or a clear/certain wish, and the counterfactual form for a wish that has less potential to be realized. The latter is also the most polite form to use, if the wish indicates a request ex:8:x370.

Haussik p-ek-u na-ep miiw-aasa nop-a-mik.\\
aidpost bp x -go- imp.1d say- ss. seq land-canoe search- pa -1/3p\\
`We/they wanted to take her to the aidpost and looked for a vehicle.'

Yo=ko wia uruf-ek-a-m na-ep.\\
1s. unm = nf 3p. acc see- cntf - pa -1s say- ss. seq \\
`I would like to see them.'

The nominalized form is mostly used in complement clauses that can also be interpreted as purpose clauses. In ``pure'' desiderative clauses it is practical to use the nominalized form especially if the first person marking in the verb might make it harder to process the meaning ex:8:x1610:

Ne o uruf-owa ne maa en-owa asip-owa na-ep=na eliw asip-uk.\\
add 3s. unm see- nmz add food eat- nmz help- nmz say- ss. seq = tp well help- imp.3p\\
`And if they want to see him and help him with food, let them help him.'

Purpose clauses

Purpose is both conceptually close and structurally similar to desiderative, and in Mauwake many of the desiderative clauses can be interpreted as purpose clauses. This is particularly so when the main verb is in the nominalized form ex:8:x371, ex:8:x345. But a truly desiderative clause even with an action nominal is never right-dislocated, whereas a purpose clause ex:8:x372 often is. The nominalized form in the main verb is common:

Weniwa=pa en-owa na-ep uuw-i-mik. \\
famine= loc eat- nmz say- ss. seq work- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`We work in order to (be able to) eat during the time of hunger.'

Wi Amerika wiam=iya irak-owa na-ep ikiw-e-mik.\\
3p. unm America 3p= com fight- nmz say/think- ss. seq go- pa -1/3p\\
`They went to fight with the Americans.'

Ona siowa ikos manina ikiw-e-mik, pika on-owa na-ep.\\
3s. gen dog with garden go- pa -1/3p fence make- nmz say- ss. seq \\
`He went to the garden with his dog, in order to make a fence.'

Future and imperative forms are also used in the purpose clause. When the subject in the purpose clause is the same as the subject of the utterance verb and the main clause, the first person future form is used for singular ex:8:x1614, ex:8:x1616 and first person dual imperative for plural ex:8:x1620.

Nain nefa maak-i-nen na-ep yo ep-a-m.\\
that1 2s. acc tell- Np - fu.1s say- ss. seq 1s. unm come- pa -1s\\
`I came to tell you that.'

No owora sesenar-i-nen na-ep Kainantu fofa ikiw-ep neeke aaw-i-nan.\\
2s. unm betelnut buy- Np - fu.1s say- ss. seq Kainantu market go- ss. seq there. cf get- nps - fu.2s\\
`To buy betelnut you will (need to) go to Kainantu marker and get it there.'

Ne haussik p-ek-u na-ep miiw-aasa nop-a-mik.\\
add aidpost bpx -go- imp.1d say- ss. seq land-canoe search- pa -1/3p\\
`And they searched for a truck (in order) to take him to the aidpost.'

When the subject of the verb in the main clause differs from that of the purpose clause, the verb inside the purpose clause has to be in the imperative ex:8:x1062-- ex:8:x1627. The whole purpose clause is structurally like a direct quote of the ``inner speech'' verb naep, so there is no deictic shift of the kind that may take place in indirect quotes.

Me yiar-uk na-ep koka=pa ik-e-mik. \\
not shoot.us- imp.3p say- ss. seq jungle= loc be- pa -1/3s\\
`We stayed in the jungle so that they would not shoot us.'

Auwa=ke o=ko amukar-inok na-ep maa naap sirar-em-ik-e-mik.\\
1s/p.father= cf 3s. unm = nf scold- imp.3s say- ss. seq thing thus make- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3\\
`They kept doing things like that so that father would scold him (and not them).'

Nain ni amis-ar-eka na-ep feenap on-i-yem.\\
that1 2p. unm knowledge- inch - imp.2p say- ss. seq like.this do- Np - pr.1s\\
`But I am doing this so that you would know.'

Efa asip-e na-ep ekap-e-m. \\
1s. acc help- imp.2s say- ss. seq come- pa -1s\\
`I came so that you would help me.'

Feenap nokar-eka na-ep yia sesek-a-k. \\
like.this ask- imp.2p say- ss. seq 1p. acc send- pa -3s\\
`He sent us to ask (you) like this.'

Yo efa miim-eka na-ep wapena wu-ami ma-e-k, \\
1s. unm 1s. acc hear- imp.2p say- ss. seq hand put- ss. sim say- pa -3s\\
`He raised his hand for them to listen to him and said, '

Ne wi popor-ar-urum-ep ik-ok ifana muutiw wu-am-ika-i-kuan, mua unuma wia miim-u na-ep.\\
add 3p. unm silent- inch - distr / a - ss. seq be- ss ear only put- ss. sim -be- Np - fu.3p man name 3p. acc hear- imp.1d say- ss. seq \\
`And they all will be quiet and listen carefully in order to hear the men's names.'

There is no raising of negation from the subordinate to the main clause ex:8:x1623.

Yo me pina=pa nia wu-ek-a-m na-ep ma-i-yem. \\
1s. unm not guilt= loc 2p. acc put- cntf - pa -1s say- ss. seq say- Np - pr.1s\\
`I am not saying (this) to put guilt on you.' (=I am saying this, but not in order to put guilt on you.)

A purpose clause does not always have the auxiliary naep. A clause with just a nominalized verb is used especially with the directional verbs ex:8:x1659, ex:8:x1658:

Yo yena emeria aaw-owa urup-e-m.\\
1s. unm 1s. gen woman take- nmz ascend- pa -1s\\
`I came up to take my wife.'

Bogia ikiw-e-mik, opaimika aakun-owa. \\
Bogia go- pa -1/3p talk talk- nmz \\
`We went to Bogia to talk.'
summary: The passage explains that Mauwake desiderative and purpose clauses are closely related and often structurally similar, with the main verb appearing in future, imperative, counterfactual, or nominalized form depending on the kind of wish or intended action. Nominalized forms are especially common in clauses that can also be read as purpose clauses, while true purpose clauses often allow right-dislocation and may use imperative forms when the subject differs from the main clause; in some cases, the auxiliary *na-ep* is omitted and only a nominalized verb is used, especially with directional verbs.

subsection: Complement clauses and other complementation strategies
text:
A clause with a nominalized verb plus a clause-final distal-1 demonstrative nain 'that' is also possible, but less common ex:8:x1633, ex:8:x1634. I have not observed a functional difference between the different purpose structures.

Tunde=pa maa muutitik uruf-owa nain soomar-e-mik.\\
Tuesday= loc thing all.kinds see- nmz that1 walk- pa -1/3p\\
`On Tuesday we walked to see all kinds of things.'

Ifemak-ep nomona iinan=pa wua-i-nan, ikoka ifera me p-ikiw-owa nain. \\
press- ss. seq stone on.top= loc put- Np - fu.2s later sea not bpx -go- nmz that1\\
`You press it down and put stones on top ( or: put it on top of stones/corals) so that the sea would not later take it away.'

Conative clauses: `try'

Instead of using a verbal construction with the verb `see' for conative modality -- expressing the attempt to do something -- which claims as almost universal for Papuan languages, Mauwake makes use of a structure where the desiderative is followed by the verb on- `do' as the verb in its reference clause ex:8:x373. Usan uses an identical construction for the same purpose.

Mukuna umuk-u na-ep on-a-mik =na me pepek.\\
fire extinguish- imp.1d say- ss. seq do- pa -1/3p= tp not enough\\
`We tried to extinguish the fire but were not able to.'

When this structure is used, it is implied that somehow or other the effort fails ex:8:x374, ex:8:x1606:

Emeria aruf-i-nen na-ep on-am-ik-eya op-a-mik.\\
woman hit- Np - fu.1s say- ss. seq do- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds hold- pa -1/3p\\
`When he was trying to hit the woman, they grabbed him.'

Wia uruf-ek-a-m na-ep on-a-k on-a-k weetak, o me wia uruf-a-k.\\
3p. acc see- cntf - pa -1s say- ss. seq do- pa -3s do- pa -3s no 3s. unm not 3p. acc see- pa -3s\\
`He tried and tried to see them, but no, he didn't see them.'

The conative structure is not used when the effort is successful ex:8:x375, and also when the `trying' is not so much an effort to do something as experimenting ex:8:x376. In these cases the verb akim- `try' is used, which is neutral as to the outcome. It requires a nominalized verb in the complement clause.

Aasa keraw-owa akim-ap akim-ap amis-ar-i-nan.\\
canoe carve- nmz try- ss. seq try- ss. seq knowledge- inch - Np - fu.2s\\
`After trying and trying to carve a canoe, you will know (how to do it).'

Weria op-ap wiinar-owa nain akim-am-ik-e.\\
planting.stick hold- ss. seq make.planting.holes- nmz that1 try- ss. sim -be- imp.2s\\
`Keep trying/learning to make planting holes with the planting stick.'

Complements of other utterance verbs

The verb ma- `say, talk' can take a regular complement clause, which is of the fact type. This clause functions as an object of the verb in the same way as an np with the head noun opora (or opaimika) `talk/story' in ex:8:x1595:

Opora gelemuta=ko np ma-i-nen na-ep.\\
talk little= nf say- Np - fu.1s say/think- ss. seq \\
`I want to tell a little story.'

The complement clause says something about the contents of the story and functions as a kind of title. This type of structure is quite common in Papuan languages treats them under relative clauses and considers them equivalents of English cleft sentences. and is used mainly in an opening or closing formula in narrative texts ex:8:x1596:

Aria yo aakisa takira en-owa gelemuta wia on-om-a-mik nain cc ma-i-yem.\\
alright 1s. unm now child eat- nmz little 3p. acc make- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p that1 say- Np - pr.1s\\
`Alright now I tell about our making a feast for the children.'

The complement ``clause'' may actually be a whole sentence, since it is possible to have medial clauses preceding the finite clause of the complement ex:8:x1597:

Tunde=pa fikera kuum-iwkin ikiw-ep waaya mik-a-m nain cc ma-i-yem.\\
Tuesday= loc kunai.grass burn-2/3p. ds go- ss. seq pig spear- pa -1s that1 say- Np - pr.1s\\
`I tell about that when they burned kunai grass on Tuesday and I went and speared a pig.'

Often the sentence has both a np containing a word for `story' and the complement clause ex:8:x1594. The relationship of these two np s is not really appositional, because the nominalized clause modifies the other np. But the nominalized clause is not a prototypical rc either, in spite of identical structure, because opora is neither an antecedent np nor a relative np that would have a function in the rc. I consider the nominalized clause a modifier of the other np, and the whole comparable to the np in ex:8:x1598. present another alternative: treating complement clauses like this and relative clauses as a single construction, where the structure only indicates that the subordinate clause is connected to an np, and the interpretation of their relationship is done pragmatically. This possibility would need more investigation in Mauwake.

Aria yo aakisa fikera ikum kuum-e-mik nain cc opora gelemuta=ko ma-i-yem.\\
alright 1s. unm now kunai.grass illicitly burn- pa -1/3p that1 story little= nf say- Np - pr.1s\\
`Alright now I tell a little story about the kunai grass that was burned by arson.'

manina uuw-owa opora \\
garden work- nmz talk\\
`garden work talk / talk (n.) about garden work'

Another complementation strategy for utterance verbs is a clause with a nominalized verb. It is used when the event expressed in the clause is regarded as potential, rather than an actual activity or a fact. The following example has two levels of complementation, as the verb in the nominalized complement also takes a nominalized complement ex:8:x1599:

I yiena miiw-aasa muf-owa ikiw-owa na-em-ik-omkun o ar-e-k. \\
1p. unm 1p. gen land-canoe pull- nmz go- nmz say- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds 3s. unm become- pa -3s\\
`While we were talking about our going to fetch a vehicle, she died (lit: became).'

The same strategy is used with the verb maak- `tell' when it is used in the sense of ordering someone to do something ex:8:x1630:
summary:
The passage describes several complementation patterns in Mauwake. Purpose clauses can contain a nominalized verb plus the distal demonstrative *nain* ‘that’, and conative ‘try’ meaning is expressed not with a verb meaning ‘see’ but with a structure involving the desiderative followed by *on-* ‘do’, which implies unsuccessful effort; for neutral trying or experimentation, the verb *akim-* ‘try’ is used with a nominalized complement.

It also shows that utterance verbs like *ma-* ‘say, talk’ can take fact-like complement clauses, often used as titles or story-openers, and these clauses may be expanded into whole sentences with medial clauses. Another strategy uses nominalized complements when the event is potential rather than factual, including in cases where *maak-* ‘tell’ means ‘order someone to do something’.

subsection: Complement clauses and other complementation strategies
text:
Emar, no muut fain uf-owa nefa maak-e-m.\\
friend 2s. unm only this dance- nmz 2s. acc tell- pa -1s\\
`Friend, I told you to dance only this.'
summary: The passage presents a sentence in which the speaker addresses a friend and says, “I told you to dance only this.” The gloss indicates a first-person past form of “tell,” with a second-person object and a nominalized “dance” phrase modified by “only this.”

subsection: Complement clauses and other complementation strategies
text:
It was mentioned above ( sec:8.2.3.4 ) that the chaining structure is used with perception verbs in Mauwake as the main complementation strategy for perception verbs, when the complement is an activity ex:8:x1512 or event ex:8:x1600. These are not genuine complement clauses, as they are not embedded in the main clause, but they perform the same function as regular complement clauses do.

Mukuruna wu-am-ika-iwkin i miim-a-mik.\\
noise put- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds 1p. unm hear- pa -1/3p\\
`We heard you making (the) noise.'

Urema maneka um-ep ika-eya uruf-a-mik. \\
bandicoot big die- ss. seq be-2/3s. ds see- pa -1/3p\\
`They saw the big bandicoot dead (=having died).'

A regular complement clause is only used with perception verbs about a past activity, when the complement clause reports a fact rather than an activity ex:8:x1628, ex:8:x1629.

Iikir-ami iwera nain emeria ar-e-p ik-ua nain cc uruf-ap \\
get.up- ss. sim coconut that1 woman become- pa -3s be- pa.3s that1 see- ss. seq \\
`He got up and saw that the coconut had become a woman, and '

Yeesus owow iinan urup-o-k nain cc uruf-ap kemel-a-mik.\\
Jesus village above ascend- pa -3s that1 see- ss. seq rejoice- pa -1/3p\\
`They saw that Jesus ascended into heaven, and rejoiced.'

When a perception verb takes an indirect question as a complement, it has to be a regular complement clause ex:8:x1631:

Ni kakala sira kamenap eliw-ar-i-ya nain cc uruf-eka.\\
2p. unm flower custom what.like good- inch - Np - pr.3s that1 see- imp.2p\\
`See how the flowers grow.'
summary: In Mauwake, chaining structure is the main complement strategy with perception verbs when the complement describes an activity or event; these are not true embedded complement clauses, but they function like them. A regular complement clause is used only for perception verbs referring to a past fact rather than an activity, and it is required for complements that are indirect questions.

subsection: Complement clauses and other complementation strategies
text:
The verbs for knowing, amisar- and paayar- together cover the cognitive area of knowing facts and skills, coming to realize, and understanding. When the complement clause indicates contents of factual knowledge, it is usually a regular complement clause ex:8:x1602.

O kaanek aaw-ep p-ekap-om-a-mik nain me amis-ar-e-k.\\
3s. where. cf get- ss. seq bpx -come- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p that1 not knowledge- inch - pa -3s\\
`He didn't know where they got it from and brought to him.'

It seems that a clause with a nominalized verb is also used as a ``fact'' complement but only when it refers to pre-knowledge of an event ex:8:x1605. It could also be understood as a ``potential'' type complement, in which case it is natural that it uses this complementation strategy. This requires more investigation.

O ikiw-owa nain amis-ar-e-n=i? \\
3s. unm go- nmz that1 knowledge- inch - pa -2s= qm \\
`Did you know about his going?'

When the complement is about knowing a skill, the verb in the complement clause is in nominalized form, or a medial clause is used ex:8:x1603, ex:8:x1849:

Nain on-owa (nain) me amis-ar-e-m.\\
that1 do- nmz that1 not knowledge- inch - pa -1s\\
`I don't know how to do that.'

Sawiter inera on-ap amis-ar-e-k.\\
Sawiter basket make- ss. seq knowledge- inch - pa -3s\\
`Sawiter knows how to make baskets.'

When the complement indicates lack of some experience, a construction with a medial clause is used. In this case, the main clause is in the negative, and the scope of the negation has to extend to the medial clause ex:8:x1604:

Owora en-ep me paayar-e-m.\\
betelnut eat- ss. seq not understand- pa -1s\\
`I'm not used to eating betelnut.' Or: `I don't know how to eat betelnut.'
summary: The verbs *amisar-* and *paayar-* cover knowing facts and skills, realizing, and understanding. Factual knowledge normally takes a regular complement clause, while knowledge of skills uses a nominalized complement or a medial clause; lack of experience is expressed with a negative main clause plus a medial clause whose negation extends to it.

subsection: Complement clauses and other complementation strategies
text:
Both types of a nominalized clause (§ sec:5.7.1, sec:5.7.2 ) may be used as subjects in verbless clauses, even though this function for complement clauses is not common. A clause with a nominalized verb is used when the activity is potential ex:8:x1636, ex:8:x1637.

Maa wiar ikum aaw-owa eliwa=ki? \\
thing 3. dat illicitly take- nmz good= cf. qm \\
`Is stealing from others good?'

Maa eneka me en-owa maa marew.\\
thing tooth not eat- nmz thing no(ne)\\
`Not eating meat is all right.'

A regular complement clause with a finite verb is used when the activity is considered a fact ex:8:x1639:

Ni unuma niam p-ir-i-man nain eliw(a) marew.\\
2p. unm name 2p. refl bpx -ascend- Np - pr.2p that1 good no(ne)\\
`That you praise yourselves (lit: lift up your own name) is not good.'
summary: Both kinds of nominalized clauses can function as subjects in verbless clauses, although complement clauses rarely do so. Nominalized verbs are used when the activity is hypothetical or potential, while a finite complement clause is used when the activity is presented as an actual fact.

text: Adverbial clauses are a very small group of subordinate clauses. They are Type 2 nominalized clauses ( sec:5.7.2 ), and they perform the same function in a clause as a temporal or locative adverbial phrase.
summary: Adverbial clauses form a very small group of subordinate clauses. They are Type 2 nominalized clauses and function in the clause like temporal or locative adverbial phrases.

text:
