The presence of the distal-1 demonstrative nain `that' indicates the pragmatic difference between the temporal clauses and those medial clauses that may get a temporal interpretation: the temporal clauses are presented as given information ex:8:x1540-- ex:8:x1624, whereas the medial clauses usually present new information ex:8:x1632, except when they occur in tail-head constructions.

Ni ifa nia keraw-i-ya nain sira kamenap on-i-man?\\
2p. unm snake 2p. acc bite- Np - pa.3s that1 custom what.like do- Np - pr.2p\\
`When a snake bites you, what do you do?'

Maa fain pakak na-e-k nain yo soran-e-m.\\
thing this bang say- pa -3s that1 1s. unm be.startled- pa -1s\\
`When this thing went ``bang!'' I got startled.'

Yo napum-ar-e-m nain eneka maay-ar-e-m. \\
1s. unm sick- inch - pa -1s that1 tooth long- inch - pa -1s\\
`When I got sick, I became hungry for meat (lit: my teeth got long).'

Yo napum-ar-ep eneka maay-ar-e-m.\\
1s. unm sick- inch - ss. seq tooth long- inch - pa -1s\\
`I got sick and became hungry for meat.'
summary: The distal demonstrative **nain** ‘that’ marks a pragmatic contrast between temporal clauses and medial clauses with temporal readings: temporal clauses typically present **given information**, while medial clauses usually introduce **new information**. An exception is tail-head constructions, where medial clauses can also carry given information. The examples illustrate this distinction, including the use of **nain** in temporal clauses and the contrast between temporal sequencing and simple coordination.

text:
Locative adverbial clauses use a clause-final deictic locative nan ex:8:x1621 or neeke ex:8:x1626 `there' instead of the demonstrative nain `that'. Note that in ex:8:x1621 the locative noun manina `garden' is not a relative np; if there were one, that would be epa `place' immediately preceding nan `there'.

I naap ikiw-ep yiena manina on-a-mik nan ik-e-mik.\\
1p. unm thus go- ss. seq 1p. gen garden make- pa -1p there be- pa -1p\\
`We went there and stayed where we had made our gardens.'

Luuwa niir-i-mik neeke soomar-e-mik.\\
ball play- Np - pr.1/3p there. cf walk- pa -1/3p\\
`We walked (to) where they play football.'

The following example is actually a locative relative clause, since it has a relative np kame `side' that has a function in both clauses ex:8:x1638:

No in-i-n kame nan urup-ep tepak iw-a-mik. \\
2s. unm sleep- Np - pr.2s side there ascend- ss. seq inside go- pa -1/3p\\
`They climbed up on the side where you sleep and went inside.'
summary: Locative adverbial clauses use a clause-final deictic locative such as **nan** ‘there’ or **neeke** ‘there’ instead of the demonstrative **nain** ‘that’. The passage also notes that **manina** ‘garden’ in one example is not a relative NP, whereas the last example is a true locative relative clause because it contains the relative NP **kame** ‘side’, which functions in both clauses.

text:
Coordinate adversative clauses were discussed in sec:8.1.3.

The topic marker - na ( sec:3.12.7.1 ) marks an adversative clause when the main clause cancels an expectation, either expressed in the text or assumed to be in the hearer's mind. Because of this, this construction is used when some effort is frustrated ex:8:x729, or when there is a strong element of surprise ex:8:x730 in the main clause.

Mukuna nain umuk-a-mik= na me pepek.\\
fire that1 quench- pa -1/3p= tp not able\\
`They tried to quench the fire, but couldn't.'

Ekap-ep uruf-a-k= na ifa maneka=ke siowa wasi-ep-pu-eya \\
come- ss. seq see- pa -3s= tp snake big= cf dog tie.around- ss. seq - cmpl -2/3s. ds \\
`He came and looked, but a snake had tied itself around the dog, and/but '

In ex:8:x1393, what the boys expect to see is a crocodile, but it turns out to be a turtle.

Takir(a) oko=ke pon muneka wu-ek-a-m na-ep urup-em-ika-eya uruf-ap tuar=ke na-ep alu-emi baurar-e-k. Takir(a) unowa ekap-ep uruf-a-mik= na pon=ke, ne unow=iya op-ap kirip-a-mik.\\
boy other= cf turtle egg put- cntf - pa -1s say- ss. seq ascend- ss. sim -be-2/3s. ds see- ss. seq crocodile= cf say- ss. seq shout- ss. sim flee- pa -3s boy many come- ss. seq see- pa -1/3p= tp turtle= cf add many= com hold- ss. seq turn- pa -1/3p\\
`A boy saw a turtle coming up (to the beach) to lay eggs and thought it was a crocodile, and shouted and fled. Many boys came and saw/looked, but it was a turtle, and they all together grabbed and turned it.'

In ex:8:x1397, a man talks to his son whom he wanted and expected to be a good person:

Aakisa yo nefa uruf-i-yem= na no mua eliw marew.\\
now 1s. unm 2s. acc look- Np - pr.1s= tp 2s. unm man good no(ne)\\
`I now look at you but you are not a good man.'

Because these clauses express a cancellation or frustration of an expectation, a negator commonly follows as the first element in the main clause, and often the negator is the only element left of the main clause, as in ex:8:x1398.

Marasin wu-om-a-mik= na weetak.\\
medicine put- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p= tp no\\
`They injected medicine in him, but no (it had no effect).'
summary: The topic marker **-na** marks an adversative clause when the main clause cancels an expectation, whether that expectation is stated in the text or assumed by the hearer. This construction is used when an effort is frustrated or when the main clause presents a surprising result, and a negator often appears first in the main clause, sometimes as the only remaining element.

text:
was the first one to clearly describe the close connection between conditionals and topics, and it has since then been attested in various languages. In many Papuan languages, the connection is very evident (,,. The protasis -- the subordinate clause expressing the condition -- provides the presupposition for the apodosis, the asserted main clause. In other words, ``it constitutes the framework which has been selected for the following discourse''.

The conditional clauses in Mauwake can be grouped into three main groups on semantic and structural grounds: imaginative, predictive, and reality conditionals. The terminology is from. Imaginative and predictive conditionals together belong to the unreality conditionals. Reality conditionals only include habitual/generic conditionals, as there are no present or past conditionals.

The protasis clause, expressing the condition, is placed before the apodosis clause, which gives the consequence. Right-dislocation of the protasis is possible but rare. The verb forms in the protasis and the apodosis depend on the type of conditional. The topic marker - na is used as the conditional marker in the unreality conditional clauses, where it is cliticized to the last element of the protasis clause, usually the verb. Reality conditional clauses do not have a conditional marker, so structurally the protasis and apodosis are ordinary juxtaposed clauses. The intonation in the protasis has a slight rise towards the end, stronger with the topic marker - na than without it.

In imaginative conditional clauses, the verb in both the protasis and the apodosis is in the counterfactual mood, which is marked by the suffix - ek. The conditional/topic marker - na is always present. The same form is used for semantically counterfactual and hypothetical conditionals. The counterfactual interpretation ex:8:x1645 is more common, but especially if there is a reference to present ex:8:x1646 or future time ex:8:x1647, it forces a hypothetical interpretation.

Yo Sek haussik ikiw- ek-a-m= na miiw-aasa=pa uroma yaki- ek-a-m.\\
1s. unm Sek hospital go- cntf - pa -1s= tp land-canoe= loc stomach wash- cntf - pa -1s\\
`If I had gone to the Sek hospital, I would have given birth in the truck.'

Yena aamun aakisa uruf- ek-a-m= na kemel- ek-a-m.\\
1s. gen 1s/p.younger.sibling now see- cntf - pa -1s= tp be.happy- cntf - pa -1s\\
`If I saw my younger brother now, I would be happy.'

Morauta iimar-ow(a) mua ik- ek-a-k= na, uurika ikiw-ep maak- ek-a-mik.\\
Morauta stand.up- nmz man be- cntf - pa -3s= tp tomorrow go- ss. seq tell- cntf - pa -1/3p\\
`If Morauta were the leader, we would go and talk to him tomorrow.'

Usually the context determines the interpretation, but without a clear context the sentence may be ambiguous ex:8:x1648:

Inasin napuma ik- ek-a-k= na sariar- ek-a-k.\\
spirit/white.man sickness be- cntf - pa -3s= tp recover- cntf - pa -3s\\
`If it were the white man's sickness This is contrasted with owow napuma `village sickness', caused by sorcery. he would recover.' Or: `If it had been the white man's sickness, he would have recovered.'

Predictive conditionals are the most frequently used and show the greatest variation morphologically. The apodosis, and consequently the whole sentence, may be either a statement with a future tense verb, or a command with an imperative verb. The verb in the protasis may be in either present or future indicative, in imperative, or in medial form. The conditional/topic marker at the end of the protasis is obligatory.

When the predictive conditional is a statement, the verb in both the protasis and in the apodosis is usually in the future tense ex:8:x1652.

No oram mokok=iw ika-i-nan=na ikoka mua lebuma ika - i - nan.\\
2s. unm just eye= inst be- Np - fu.2s= tp later man lazy be- Np - fu.2s\\
`If you just watch with your eyes (without joining the work) you will be(come) a lazy man.'

The protasis may have a medial verb form if the condition is likely to be fulfilled ex:8:x1654, or when the protasis consists of two or more clauses that are in a medial-final relationship ex:8:x1653.

Emeria sesenar-ek-a-m na-ep=na waaya ten erup naap wienak-i-non.\\
woman buy- cntf - pa -1s say/think- ss. seq = tp pig ten two thus feed.him- Np - fu.3s\\
`If/when he wants to buy a wife, he will give him (=the bride's father) twenty or so pigs.'

Yaapan me piipu-ap=na anane epaskun ika-i-nan=na no iiwawun weeser-i-nan.
\\
Japan not leave- ss. seq = tp always together be- Np - fu.2s= tp 2s. unm altogether finish- Np - fu.2s\\
`If you don't leave the Japanese but are always together, you will be finished altogether.'

Predictive conditionals allow right-dislocation of the protasis, but it is uncommon ex:8:x1662:

Owora fain aite panewowa onak-e, ekap-ep kerer-eya=na. \\
betelnut this 1s/p.mother old feed- imp.2s come- ss. seq arrive-2/3s. ds = tp \\
`Give these betelnuts to old mother to eat, if she comes and arrives here.'

In those instances where the conditional marker is attached to a predicate that is not originally a verb, the predicate needs to have medial verb marking ex:8:x1660, ex:8:x1661 ( sec:3.8.3.5 ).

Weetak-eya =na weetak.\\
no-2/3s. ds = tp no\\
`If not, then not.'

Mauw-owa manek-aya=na yia maak-i-non.\\
work- nmz big-2/3s. ds = tp 1p. acc tell- Np - fu.3s\\
`If the work is big, he will tell us.'

When the apodosis is in the imperative, there is normally some expectation that the the condition is to be fulfilled. When the likelihood is high, the medial form is used in the protasis ex:8:x1650, ex:8:x1649. Present tense ex:8:x1651 and imperative ex:8:x1656 indicate less, and future tense ex:8:x1657 the least likelihood for the condition to be fulfilled.

Wia uruf-ap=na wia maak-e.\\
3p. acc see- ss. seq = tp 3p. acc tell- imp.2s\\
`If/when you see them, tell them.'

Maa mauwa nefa maak-iwkin=na opaimika miim-e.\\
thing what 2s. acc tell-2/3p. ds = tp talk listen- imp.2s\\
`Whatever they may tell you, listen to the talk.' (Lit: `If they tell you what(ever), listen to the talk.')
summary:
The passage explains that in Mauwake, conditional clauses are closely linked to topic structure: the protasis provides the presupposed framework for the apodosis, and the conditional/topic marker **-na** is attached to the end of unreality protases. Conditional clauses are divided into **imaginative**, **predictive**, and **reality** types, with imaginative and predictive conditionals forming the unreality group; reality conditionals are habitual/generic and have no special conditional marker.

Imaginative conditionals use counterfactual verb forms in both clauses and can be interpreted as counterfactual or hypothetical depending on context. Predictive conditionals are the most common and show more morphological variation: the protasis may use present, future, imperative, or medial forms, while the apodosis may be future or imperative, and the choice of verb form reflects how likely the condition is to be fulfilled.

text:
Koora pun naap: mua oko naareke koora kua-i-ya=na o asip-e.\\
house also thus man other who. cf house build- Np - pr.3s= tp 3p. unm help- imp.2p\\
`A house is like that too: if/when any man builds a house, help him.'

Ni kirip-owa ika-inok= na kirip-eka.\\
2p. unm reply- nmz be- imp.3s= tp reply- imp.2p\\
`If you have something to reply, then reply.'

Wia uruf-i-nan=na wia maak-e.\\
3p. acc see- Np - fu.2s= tp 3p. acc tell- imp.2s\\
`If you (happen to) see them, tell them.'

Reality conditional clauses are morpho-syntactically different from the other conditional clauses in that they are not marked with the topic marker. The protasis and apodosis are juxtaposed main clauses in future tense ex:8:x1644, but this construction is mainly used to encode habitual or generic conditions. The protasis can never be right-dislocated, since it does not have the topic marker.

No inasin(a) unuma me unuf-i-nan, mua oko=ke waaya nain mik-ap nefar aaw-i-non.\\
2s. unm spirit name not call- Np - fu.2s man other= cf pig that1 spear- ss. seq 2s. dat take- Np - fu.3s\\
`If you don't call the spirit name, another man will spear the pig and take it from you.'

If there are two protasis clauses, they may be juxtaposed without a connective ex:8:x1635 or joined with the pragmatic additive ne ex:8:x1643.

Nena kuuf-i-nan, parew-i-non, eliw perek-i-nan.\\
2s. gen see- Np - fu.2s mature- Np - fu.3s well harvest- Np - fu.2s\\
`If you see it yourself and it is matured you may harvest it.'

Yo um-i-nen ne yena emeria mua oko aaw-i-non, muuka onaiya me ikiw-i-non.\\
1s. unm die- Np - fu.1s add 1s. gen woman man other take- Np - fu.3s son with not go- Np - fu.3s\\
`If I die and my wife takes another husband, she will not go (to him) with the son.'

When a sentence contains alternatives expressed by two sets of reality conditional constructions, these are joined by the pragmatic additive ne ex:8:x1642.

Yo auwa miiwa=pa mauw-i-nen, irak-owa marew, ne yo aite miiwa=pa mauw-i-nen, irak-owa ika-i-non.\\
1s 1s/p.father land= loc work- Np - fu.1s fight- nmz no(ne) add 1s 1s/p.moher land= loc work- Np -fu.1s fight- nmz be- Np - fu.3s\\
`If I work on my father's land there is no fighting (over land), but if I work on my mother's land there will be fighting.'

The same construction can encode a simple coordinate relationship, but it is less common. In spoken text a slightly falling intonation at the end of the first clause indicates a coordinate sentence ex:8:x1850.

Oko=ke pusun-emi feeke ikiw - i - non, a mua oko=ke mik - i - non.\\
other= cf run.loose- ss. sim here. cf go- Np - fu.3s ah man other= cf spear- Np - fu.3s\\
`Another (pig) will run loose and run this way, ah, another man will spear it.'
summary: Reality conditional clauses are morpho-syntactically distinct because they lack the topic marker; their protasis and apodosis are simply juxtaposed main clauses in future tense, and this form is mainly used for habitual or generic conditions. If there are two protasis clauses or alternative sets of reality conditionals, they may be linked by the pragmatic additive *ne*, and the same construction can occasionally express simple coordination, often signaled in speech by a slight falling intonation after the first clause.

Concessive clauses may look exactly like the predictive conditional clauses ex:8:x1655. If the context is not clear enough, the phrase nain pun `that too' may be added between the protasis and the apodosis for clarification ex:8:x1430.

Naapeya aara=ki e kasi=ke um-inok=na ni nain kema bagiw-ir-ap malaria sevis me wia iirar-eka.\\
therefore hen= cf. qm or cat= cf die- imp.3s= tp 2p. unm that1 liver hatred-rise- ss. seq malaria service not 3p. acc remove- imp.2p\\
`Therefore, (even) if hens or cats die, do not get angry and drive away the Malaria Service people.'

Naap yia ma-ikuan=na nain pun ni kekan-ep sira eliwa ook-eka.\\
thus 1p. acc say- fu.3p= tp that too 2p. unm be.strong- ss. seq custom good follow- imp.2p\\
`Even if they talk about us like that, be strong and follow the good custom/ways.'
summary: Concessive clauses can have exactly the same form as predictive conditional clauses, so the two may be difficult to distinguish from context alone. When the context is insufficient, the phrase *nain pun* “that too” can be inserted between the protasis and apodosis to clarify the concessive meaning.

text:
Subordinate clauses may also be coordinated with each other, although in normal speech the frequency of these constructions is low. The only subordinate clauses in the natural text data conjoined either by juxtaposition or with the additive ne are relative clauses ex:8:x1381, ex:8:x1382. The distal demonstrative nain, functioning as a relative marker, is attached to the end of each relative clause.... waaya koka=pa ika-i-ya nain rc, sokowa maneka=pa
ika-i-ya nain rc kanu-ep aap-ekap-ep fikera=pa-r=iw fiirim-eka.\\
pig jungle= loc be- Np - pr.3s that1 grove big= loc be- Np - pr.3s that1 chase- ss. seq bp x -come- ss. seq kunai.grass= loc - = lim gather- imp.2p\\
` chase the pigs that are in the jungle (and) that are in the big grove(s) and bring them and gather them right inside the kunai grass (area).'

Ne o maa kamenap on-eya wiar uruf-i-n nain rc ne wiar miim-i-n nain rc wia maak-em-ika-i-nan.\\
add 3s. unm thing how do- ss. seq 3. dat see- Np - pr.2s that1 add 3. dat hear- Np - pr.2s that1 3p. acc tell- ss. sim -be- Np - fu.2s\\
`And you will keep telling them that which you see and which you hear him do.'

The chaining structure is also used to coordinate relative clauses ex:8:x1463 and complement clauses that have a nominalized verb (5. ex:5:x1845 ), copied as ex:8:x1848 below:

Ni manina urup-ep episowa perek-a-man nain rc auwa p-ikiw-om-aka.\\
2p. unm garden ascend- ss. seq tobacco pick- pa -2p that 1s/p.father bp x -go- ben - bnfy 2. imp.2p\\
`Take to father the tobacco that you went up to the garden and picked.'

Toiyan iiriw maak-ep-pu-a-mik, uuriw yia aaw-ep Madang ikiw-owa cc nain\\
Toiyan already tell- ss. seq - cmpl - pa -1/3p morning 1p. acc take- ss. seq Madang go- nmz that1\\
`We already told Toiyan about taking us in the morning and going to Madang.'
summary: The passage says that subordinate clauses can be coordinated, but this is uncommon in normal speech. In the natural text data, the main cases are relative clauses linked by juxtaposition or by the additive ne, with the distal demonstrative nain attached to the end of each clause as a relative marker. It also notes that the same chaining structure can coordinate relative clauses and complement clauses with nominalized verbs.

text:
Three features of textual prominence, the pragmatic functions theme, topic, and focus, are discussed in this chapter. All of them play an important role in Mauwake, and they show up in morphology and/or syntax. They are not mutually exclusive: a clausal constituent may have more than one pragmatic function.

Theme, topic, and focus have been defined in linguistic literature in different and sometimes conflicting ways, so they need a definition of how they are used here.

The definitions of topic are mainly divided along two questions: whether the topic needs to be an entity -- more specifically an argument -- or not, and whether it functions on the clause or the discourse level, or both.

One classic definition describes the topic as ``the entity about which something is said, whereas the further statement made about this entity is the comment'' (, see also ). This definition treats the topic as a clause-level function and an entity, but does not specify whether this entity needs to be an argument of the verb or not. well-known definition also discusses the topic at the sentence level. Any constituent may be a topic, in fact it need not even be an entity: ``the topic sets a spatial, temporal or individual framework within which the main predication holds'' (see also ). analysis of conditionals as topics is based on this definition, as the protasis in the conditional clauses provides the presupposition for the assertion in the apodosis.

The definitions above do not touch upon topic continuity, which is an important object of study for those linguists who consider topic mainly from discourse point of view. In this case, the topic function can only be assigned to an argument of a clause. Also defines topic as ``an argument which occurs in a succession of clauses in a discourse and binds them together''. In some other approaches, this discourse topic has also been called theme or global topic. A single sentence can be said to have a topic only if the sentence constitutes at least a clause chain or a paragraph.

In the following, topic is understood in the sense that Giv\'on advocates, whereas the term theme is used to refer to Chafe's ``topic'', for which a sentence-initial position is crucial. Considering ``topicality'' in Chafe's sense, Mauwake is basically a subject-prominent language. It has the following characteristics: surface coding for the subject as the first argument and as the argument that governs verb agreement; scarcity of ``double subject'' constructions, even though they are possible; the subject controls co-referential constituent deletion; there are constraints on the ``topic'' constituent; and the frequency of topic-comment clauses is low. But Mauwake shares the following features with topic-prominent languages: there is no passivization, nor are there any empty or dummy subjects. What calls a theme is here called a left-dislocated theme.

Mauwake is a sov language and the default topic is also the syntactic subject and the semantic agent/actor, and yet the first noun phrase in a clause often is not the topic. This is because once the topic has been established, it is normally only marked by verbal suffixes, and the clause-initial position is taken by another constituent.
summary:
The passage discusses theme, topic, and focus as pragmatic functions of textual prominence in Mauwake, noting that they can appear in morphology and syntax and may overlap within a single constituent. It reviews conflicting definitions of topic in the literature, then adopts Givón’s discourse-based sense of topic while using Chafe’s sentence-initial “theme” for left-dislocated elements.  

Mauwake is described as basically subject-prominent: the subject is the first argument, controls agreement and deletion, and there are few double-subject constructions and low frequencies of topic-comment clauses. At the same time, it shares some topic-prominent traits such as lacking passivization and dummy subjects, and the clause-initial noun phrase is often not the topic because established topics are usually marked only by verbal suffixes.

text:
The position as the leftmost non-verb constituent in a sentence defines the theme in Mauwake. It may be an argument or a peripheral clause participant. When a sentence -- or the first clause in a multi-clause sentence -- consists of a verb alone, there is no theme in the sense adopted here. When the theme is an argument, it introduces what the sentence is about ex:9:x1908. When it is not an argument but a peripheral clause participant, it provides a circumstancial setting for the sentence, most commonly a locative or temporal setting ex:9:x1698. A theme forms one intonation contour with the rest of the clause.

Wi owow mua=ke wilkar wia muf-em-ik-om-a-mik.\\
3p. unm village man= cf cart 3p. acc pull- ss. sim -be- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p \\
`The village men pulled carts for them.'

Ne fraide=pa maapora puk-o-k, urera. \\
add Friday= loc party burst- pa -3s afternoon \\
`And on Friday the party started, in the afternoon.'

When the theme coincides with the subject/topic ex:9:x1908, the clause has the default word order. But when another argument is the theme, it takes the initial position, and if there is also a subject np in the same clause, it follows the theme np ex:9:x1473:

I yar O i S uruf-am-ik-omkun o koora=pa pok-ap ik-ua.\\
1p. unm 1s/p.brother.in.law 1p. unm see- ss. sim -be-1s/p. ds 3s. unm house= loc sit.down- ss. seq be- pa.3s\\
`Our brother-in-law, as we are seeing him, is sitting in his house.' (Lit: `Our brother-in-law we are seeing and he is sitting in his house.')

The sentence ex:9:x1701 is from the middle of a description about the arrival of the Japanese troops, and the goods that they brought are only mentioned in this one sentence, and the theme is neither the subject nor the topic.

Maa unowa O ifer aasa=ke p-urup-eya miiw-aasa=ke fan p-ir-am-ik-ua. \\
thing many sea canoe= cf bpx -ascend-2/3s. ds land-canoe= cf here bpx -come- ss. sim -be- pa.3s \\
`Many things were brought up (to the coast) by ships and brought here by trucks.'

In a text about a school party, dancing is first mentioned in a final verb, and then the dance becomes the theme for the following sentence ex:9:x1702:

Naap ik-ok wi Saramun=ke wiisa uf-e-mik. Uf-owa eliwa O i wiar uruf-a-mik. \\
thus be- ss 3p. unm Saramun= cf dance.name dance- pa -1/3p dance- nmz good 1p. unm 3. dat see- pa -1/3p \\
`Then the Saramun people danced wiisa. It was a good dance we saw from them.'

Very commonly, the subject only shows in the verbal suffixation, and the theme position is taken either by an object -- which may or may not be a topic -- or by an adverbial phrase. In ex:9:x1909 the theme auwa ame `father and the others' becomes a topic that continues for the next five clauses, whereas the themes of ex:9:x1910 and ex:9:x1911 do not become topics and are not mentioned any more. (In the free translation it is often not possible to reflect the theme naturally.)

Auwa ame wia maak-eya res aaw-ep merena ifa keraw-a-k nain puuk-a-mik. \\
1s/p.father assoc 3p. acc tell-2/3s. ds razor take- ss. seq leg snake bite- pa -3s that1 cut- pa -1/3p \\
`He told my father and the others, and they took a razor and made a cut into the leg that the snake had bitten.'

Maa en-owa nopa-yiaw-ep wailal-ep naap ma-e-mik...\\
thing eat- nmz search-move.around- ss. seq hunger- ss. seq thus say- pa -1/3p \\
`They searched around for food and were hungry and said like that '

Emeria naap wia aruf-i-nen na-ep on-a-k. \\
woman thus 3p. acc hit- Np - fu.1s say/think- ss. seq do- pa -3s \\
`He tried to hit the women like that.'

In a tail-head linkage construction ( sec:8.2.3.5 ) the final verb of a sentence is repeated in the beginning of the following sentence, but in a medial form. An argument ex:9:x1912, ex:9:x1913, or occasionally a peripheral ex:9:x1914, ex:9:x1915, from the final clause may be picked as the theme of the new sentence.

Owowa or-op, wailal-ep akia ik-e-k. Akia ik-ep en-em-ik-ok \\
village descend- ss. seq hunger- ss. seq banana roast- pa -3s banana roast- ss. seq eat- ss. sim -be- ss \\
`He came down to the village, was hungry, and roasted bananas. He roasted bananas and was eating them and '

Aria, wi kiiriw neeke miiw-aasa um-o-k. Miiw-a asa um-eya miiw-aasa nain on-am-ika-iwkin... \\
alright 3p. unm again there. cf land-canoe die- pa -3s land-canoe die-2/3s. ds land-canoe that1 do- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds \\
`Alright, again when they (were) there the truck broke down (lit: died). The truck broke down, and while they were working on the truck '

Yaki-ep weeser-eya owowa urup-e-mik. Owowa urup-ep o koora ikiw-o-k.\\
bathe- ss. seq finish-2/3s. ds village ascend- pa -1/3p village ascend- ss. seq 3s. unm house go- pa -3s\\
`They bathed and when it was finished they came up to the village. They came to the village and he went into the house.'...siowa wiawi nain=ke alu-owa miim-ap karu-(o)w=iw ekap-o-k. Karu-(o)w=iw ekap-ep uruf-a-k=na \\
dog 3s/p.father that1= cf make.noise- nmz hear- ss. seq run- nmz = inst come- pa -3s run- nmz = inst come- ss. seq see- pa -3s= tp \\
`The dog's owner heard the noise and came running. He came running and saw '

It is more common to have tail-head linkage where only the final verb is repeated; when the speaker repeats an argument or a peripheral as well, there is a reason for it: to give it prominence as the theme in the new sentence.

When the theme position is taken by a locative ex:9:x1699 or temporal ex:9:x1916 adverbial phrase, it normally gives a setting for the the whole sentence:

Eka mamaiya akena i yoowa me aaw-i-yen. \\
river close very 1p. unm hot not get- Np - fu.1p \\
`Very close to the river we won't get hot.'
summary:
In Mauwake, the theme is the leftmost non-verb constituent of a sentence and may be either an argument or a peripheral participant; if the sentence consists only of a verb, there is no theme. When the theme is an argument, it usually introduces what the sentence is about, but when it is a locative or temporal phrase it typically provides a circumstantial setting for the whole clause.  

If the theme coincides with the subject or topic, the clause has default word order, but if another constituent is the theme it appears first and any subject NP follows it. The passage also notes that themes can be promoted in discourse, including after tail-head linkage, where a repeated argument or peripheral is used to give prominence to the new sentence.

text:
Ikoka kuisow miiw-aasa=ke karu-eya ku-ku-ep or-om-ik-ua.\\
later one land-canoe= cf run-2/3s. ds rdp -break- ss. seq descend- ss. sim -be- pa.3s \\
`Straight away when the trucks ran (over them) they kept breaking and falling down.'

But in ex:9:x1703, the first temporal phrase is a setting for only the first clause, and the final clause has another temporal phrase. Also, in the second sentence the object is both a new topic ( sec:9.2.1 ) and fronted as the theme before the temporal adverbial. In neutral constituent order, a temporal adverbial precedes the object.

Uura feenap nain i me in-em-ik-e-mik, amirika maa me en-em-ik-e-mik. Maa uura uup-ep en-em-ik-e-mik.\\
night like.this that1 1p. unm not sleep- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p day food not eat- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p food night cook- ss. seq eat- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p\\
`On nights like this we did not sleep, in the daytime we did not eat food. The food we used to cook and eat at night.'

Other adverbial phrases may also be used in the theme position to provide a circumstantial setting ex:9:x1917, ex:9:x1918. In particular, the deictic manner adverbial naap `thus, like that' is relatively common.

Naap maak-iwkin naap ik-ua. Naap ik-ok uruf-am-ika-iwkin wia. \\
thus tell-2/3p. ds thus be- pa.3s thus be- ss see- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds no \\
`Like that they told him and like that he was. Like that he was and they watched him, but no (he did not get better).'

Wiena merena ne wapen=iw era akup-ami owowa ikiw-e-mik.\\
3p. gen foot add hand= inst road search- ss. sim village go- pa -1/3p\\
`With their feet and hands they searched the road and went to the village.'

A sentence-initial adverbial phrase that is syntactically outside the clause and also has its own slightly rising intonation contour on the last syllable is here called a left-dislocated theme. In written texts, it is separated from the rest of the clause by a comma. This clause-external pragmatic function is called theme by. He defines its function as ``specif ying the universe of discourse with respect to which the subsequent predication is presented as relevant''.

In ex:9:x1704, the left-dislocated theme consists of a relative clause where the antecedent noun soo `fish trap' has been deleted:

Aria malol=pa ifemak-i-mik nain rc, aana puuk-i-mik \\
alright deep.sea= loc press- Np - pr.1/3p that1 cane cut- Np - pr.1/3p\\
`Alright, as for those (=fishtraps) that we let down in the deep sea, we cut cane...'

There can be more than one dislocated theme for the same clause. In ex:9:x1700, there are two dislocated themes -- a temporal and a locative phrase -- plus a clause-internal theme moma `taro', which is the syntactic object of the clause:

Iiriw, owow(a) oko mua manina, moma waaya=ke anane wiar en-ow(a)=iw ika-i-ya.\\
earlier village other man garden taro pig= cf always 3. dat eat- nmz = inst be- Np - pr.3s \\
`Earlier, (in) the garden of a man from another village, his taro was always being eaten by a pig.'
summary: The passage explains that temporal or other adverbial phrases can serve as theme-setting elements, often preceding the object in neutral constituent order, and may set the context for only part of a sentence. It also notes that some sentence-initial adverbials are left-dislocated themes outside the clause, marked by a separate intonation and punctuation in writing, and that more than one dislocated theme can appear with the same clause.

text:
posited a universal topicality hierarchy, which shows features affecting the likelihood of np s being discourse topics:

enumerate
human non-human
definite indefinite
more involved participant less involved participant
1 st person 2 nd person 3 rd person
enumerate

This hierarchy can be observed in Mauwake as well: the prototypical topic refers to a referent that is human and definite, and if the first person is involved in the text, it is often the topic. And the most involved participant, the grammatical subject, is typically also the pragmatic topic.

The following three sections discuss how a new topic is introduced and maintained in a narrative text, and how it is brought back after it has been absent for a while.
summary: A universal topicality hierarchy is proposed that ranks noun phrases by how likely they are to function as discourse topics, with human, definite, and more involved or first-person participants ranking highest. The passage notes that Mauwake conforms to this pattern: prototypical topics are human and definite, first person is often topical when present, and the grammatical subject, as the most involved participant, is typically also the pragmatic topic. The following sections examine how topics are introduced, maintained, and reintroduced in narrative discourse.

text:
Even when a new topic is introduced for the first time, it is often definite, Definiteness is not an obligatory category in Mauwake. A np may be specifically marked as definite or indefinite when this feature is considered important enough, but often it is left unspecified. identifiable to the addressee: a personal pronoun ex:9:x1663, a proper name ex:9:x1664 or a relationship term ex:9:x1665, or a noun phrase ex:9:x1667.

I me amis-ar-em-ik-omkun iinan aasa iinan=pa fan ekap-emi... \\
1p. unm not knowledge- inch - ss. sim -be-1s/p. ds sky canoe sky= loc here come- ss. sim \\
`We were not aware (that anything would happen) and planes came here on the sky and '

Muakura=ke ma-e-k, `` '' \\
Muakura= cf say- pa -3s \\
`Muakura said, ``... '' '

Aria yena mua pun... iirar-iwkin owowa ekap-o-k. \\
alright 1s. gen man also... remove-2/3p. ds village come- pa -3s \\
`Alright they also dismissed my husband and he came to the village.'

Iiriw wi mua iperowa=ke feenap ma-em-ik-e-mik, emeria=ke osaiwa ar-e-mik. \\
earlier 3p. unm man middle.aged= cf like.this say- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p woman= cf bird.of.paradise become- pa -1/3p \\
`Earlier the elders kept telling this story that women had changed into birds of paradise.'

When a potential topic is introduced, it is indefinite -- the addressee is not expected to be able to identify it -- and one of the following strategies is used. The new topic may first be an object in a clause before becoming the subject in the following clause. ex:9:x1703 is repeated here as ex:9:x1668:

Uura feenap nain i me in-em-ik-e-mik, amirika maa me en-em-ik-e-mik. Maa uura uup-ep en-em-ik-e-mik.\\
night like.this that1 1p. unm not sleep- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p noon food not eat- ss. sim -be- pa -1/3p food night cook- ss. seq eat- ss. sim.be- pa -1/3p \\
`On nights like this we did not sleep, at noon we did not eat food. Food we used to cook and eat at night.'

Most commonly, the new topic is already a subject in the clause where it is introduced, and the np is either modified with the indefinite oko `other' ex:9:x1669 or marked by the neutral focus clitic - ko ex:9:x1670, which also has its origin in oko. Occasionally both of them occur on the same np ex:9:x1671.

Iiriw Malala suule maneka uuw-owa mua oko unuma Kila. \\
earlier Malala school big work- nmz man other name Kila \\
`Earlier there was a workman at the big Malala school whose name was Kila.'

Emer(a) en-ow(a) mua=ko emeria fan aaw-o-k.\\
sago eat- nmz man= nf woman here take- pa -3s\\
`A Sepik man married a wife here.'

Iiriw akena mua oko=ko fura aaw-ep koka iw-a-k.\\
earlier very man other= nf knife take- ss. seq jungle go- pa -3s \\
`Long ago a man took a knife and went into the jungle.'

The indefinite np may even have contrastive focus marking ex:9:x1666:

Pika ifara mufe-wiaw-ik-ok ifa maneka=ke siowa wiar aaw-o-k. \\
fence vine pull-move.around-be- ss snake big= cf dog 3. dat take- pa -3s\\
`As he was pulling around vines for the fence, a big snake grabbed his dog.'

Existential clauses, which mentions as one of the major strategies for introducing important topics, are possible but not very commonly employed for this function in Mauwake ex:9:x1672. Note that the neutral focus clitic - ko is also present.

Iiriw mua iperowa=ko nan Wakoruma owowa=pa ik-ua.\\
earlier man middle.aged= nf there Wakoruma village= loc be- pa.3s \\
`Earlier there was a middle-aged man in Wakoruma village.'
summary:
In Mauwake, definiteness is not an obligatory category: a noun phrase may be marked as definite or indefinite when this is important, but it is often left unspecified. Even when a topic is introduced for the first time, it is often definite because it is identifiable to the addressee, for example through a personal pronoun, proper name, or relationship term.

When a potential topic is truly new and indefinite, the language uses several strategies: it may first appear as an object before becoming the subject, or it may be introduced as a subject modified by *oko* ‘other’ or marked with the neutral focus clitic *-ko*, which may occur together. Existential clauses can also introduce important topics, but they are not commonly used for this purpose.

text:
When a potential topic, which is indefinite when first introduced, becomes established the next mention is often made with a np marked as definite by the distal-1 demonstrative nain `that'. The sentence following ex:9:x1672 in the text is ex:9:x1673.

Mua nain emeria ne muuka wiipa marew.\\
man that1 woman add son daughter no(ne).\\
`The man had no wife or children.'

Another possibility is the mere subject marking on the verb: sentence ex:9:x1674 below is continuation to the sentence ex:9:x1670 above.

Ne manina ikiw-o- k. \\
add garden go- pa -3s. \\
`And he went to the garden.'

When the topic is already definite when introduced, it is possible to make a second mention with a personal pronoun ex:9:x1919. This whole story is Text app:2:uncle in the Appendix.

Yena yaiya Tup ifa ku-o-k nain opaimika ma-i-yem. Ae, o fiker(a) gone urup-o-k. \\
1s. gen 1s/p.uncle Tup snake bite- pa -3s that1 talk say- Np - pr.1s yes 3s. unm kunai.grass middle ascend- pa -3s \\
`I tell a story about that when my uncle Tup was bitten by a snake. Yes, he went up to the middle of the kunai grass (area).'

In ex:9:x1868 the personal pronoun wi `they' in the second sentence refers to the ``weria-relatives'' (see sec:1.3.6 ), introduced as the object in the preceding sentence; a mere verbal suffix would indicate continuation with the old topic, i.e. those who sent the message.

Wiena mua weria... opaimika wia sesek-omak-e-mik. Ne wi ekap-e-mik. \\
3p. gen man planting.stick... talk 3p. acc send- distr / pl - pa -1/3p add 3p. unm come- pa -1/3p \\
`They i sent word to their i many weria-relatives j. And they j came.'

More commonly the topic, once established, is maintained as a continuing topic without an overt np or a pronoun, only via subject marking on the verb. This minimal marking conforms to claim that the heaviness of the topic marking is in inverse relation to topic continuity/predictability. The following example ex:9:x1675 is a section of a text where sawur `spirits', introduced earlier, think that there is a boy on the bed they are carrying, but the boy has already escaped. The reference to the spirits is only made by medial and final verb suffixes.

Ne aria, samapora oram akua aaw- ep ikiw-e- mik. Ikiw- ep wiena owowa=pa uruf-a- mik=na weetak, samapora muutiw akua aaw-e- mik. Aria nainiw kir-e- mik. Kir- ep ekap-em-ika- iwkin epa wiim-o-k.\\
add alright, bed just shoulder take- ss. seq go- pa -1/3p go- ss. seq 3p. gen village= loc see- pa -1/3p= tp no bed only shoulder take- pa -1/3p alright again turn- pa -1/3p turn- ss. seq come- ss. sim -be-2/3p. ds place dawn- pa -3s\\
`Alright, they carried just the bed and went. They went and in their village they looked but (to their surprise) they only carried the bed. Alright they turned back again. They turned and as they were coming, it dawned.'

The switch-reference system (§ sec:3.8.3.5, sec:8.2.3 ) together with the person/number marking in the finite verbs ( sec:3.8.3.4 ) can easily keep track of two active topics alternating with each other ex:9:x1676.

O iiwawun samor aaw-o-k. Ne nan ik-e- mik. Nan ik- ok ik- ok neeke pu-o- k. Neeke pu- eya oram akua aaw-e- mik.\\
3s. unm altogether badly get- pa -3s add there be- pa -1/3p there be- ss be- ss there. cf die- pa -3s. there. cf die-2/3s. ds just shoulder take- pa -1/3p \\
`He got really bad. They stayed and stayed there and he died there. He died there and they just carried him on their shoulders.'

In ex:9:x1676 one of the topics is in the singular, the other in the plural. But in (3. ex:3:x357 ), repeated below as ex:9:x1920, there are two third person singular topics alternating, with only the verbal marking to indicate who is doing what:

Ifakim- eya pu-ep-ik -eya om-em-ik- ua. \\
kill-2/3s. ds die- ss. seq -be-2/3s. ds cry- ss. sim -be- pa.3s \\
`When she killed him and he was dead, she was crying.'
summary: The passage explains how topic reference is maintained in the language: an indefinite topic is often reintroduced as definite with the distal demonstrative *nain* “that,” or sometimes by only marking the verb for subject. When a topic is already definite, it may be referred to by a personal pronoun, though in many cases continuing topics are left unexpressed and tracked only through verbal person/number marking. It also notes that switch-reference and finite verb marking can keep track of two alternating active topics, even when both are third-person singular.

text:
When a topic has not been active for some time in the text, there are two main strategies to re-activate it. A personal pronoun is mainly used for the major participants. For the third person singular pronoun this is the most common usage ( sec:3.5.11 ). The following example is from a text where the main participant, a man, has been killed by his spirit lover. For several sentences, the topic position is taken by the spirit woman and her parents, but in the sentence ex:9:x1921 the man, as a re-activated topic, gets up and goes to his village.

Epa wiim-eya sawur emeria nain ikiw-eya o iikir-ami owowa ekap-o-k. \\
place dawn-2/3s. ds spirit woman that1 go-2/3s. ds 3s. unm get.up- ss. sim village come- pa -3s \\
`It dawned and the spirit woman went, and he got up and came to the village.'

The sentence in ex:9:x1923 re-activates the topic, a grandmother and two grandchildren, after a gap of five clauses:

Iwera mekemkar-ep or-eya wi pikin-ep miiwa or-o-mik. \\
coconut bend- ss. seq descend-2/3s. ds 3p. unm jump- ss. seq ground descend- pa -1/3p \\
`The coconut tree bent down and they jumped down to the ground.'

In the following stretch, ex:9:x1924, the health officer, who is one of the main participants in this section of the story, is mentioned as an object noun phrase, and after two clauses he becomes the topic for just one clause. Afterwards, the men accompanying the sick man again resume as the topic....ikemika kaik-owa mua nain nop-a-mik, imen-ap maak-iwkin o miim-o-k. Aria, wi kiiriw neeke miiw-aasa um-o-k.\\
wound tie- nmz man that1 search- pa -1/3p find- ss. seq tell-2/3p. ds 3s. unm precede- pa -3s alright 3p. unm again there. cf land-canoe die- pa -3s\\
` they searched for the health officer, and when they found him and told him, he went ahead of them (to the aidpost). Alright, again when they were there the truck broke down.'

A full noun phrase is used for reactivating major participants when there are several of them and pronouns are not adequate for disambiguating between them. A noun phrase is always used when minor participants and props Participants are typically human and active in a narrative, props typically non-human and inactive. are brought back to the stage.

The example ex:9:x1677 is an extract from a story about the speaker's uncle, who was introduced with a kinship term at the very beginning of the story and only referred to by a verbal suffix or an occasional pronoun afterwards. An important prop, snake poison, which becomes a topic for a short stretch, is referred to by a full noun phrase.

Akia ik-ep en-em-ik-ok ifa marasin nain=ke kema wiar iw-a-k. Iw-aya nan miira saawirin-e-k. Ne auwa ame wia maak-eya res aaw-ep merena... nain puuk-a-mik. Puuk-ap marasin wu-om-a-mik. Marasin wu-om-a-mik=na weetak. Iiriw ifa marasin=ke kekan-e-k. Ne akia ik-e-k nain me en-e-k. Nan mukuna=pa ik-eya o nan samor aaw-o-k.\\
banana roast- ss. seq eat- ss. sim.be- ss snake poison that1= cf liver 3. dat go- pa -3s go-2/3s. ds there face become.round- pa -3s add 1s/p.father ass 3p. acc tell-2/3s. ds razor take- ss. seq leg that1 cut- pa -1/3p cut- ss. seq medicine put- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p medicine put- ben - bnfy 2. pa -1/3p= tp no earlier snake poison= cf be.strong- pa -3s add banana roast- pa -3s that1 not eat- pa -3s there fire= loc be-2/3s. ds 3s. unm there badly get- pa -3s\\
`He roasted bananas and when he was eating them the snake poison entered his liver. It entered and he felt dizzy there. And when he told my father and others, they took a razor and made a cut into the leg They made a cut and put medicine into it. They put medicine but no (it didn't help). The snake poison was already strong. And he didn't eat the bananas that he roasted. They were there on the fire and he really got bad there.'
summary: When a topic has been inactive for a while, it is reactivated either by a personal pronoun or by a full noun phrase. Personal pronouns are mainly used for major participants, especially the third person singular, while full noun phrases are used when several major participants might be confused or when minor participants and props are brought back into the discourse.

text:
The topic marker -( e) na ( sec:3.12.7.1 ) is only used with a new topic that the speaker wants to highlight. The constituent may have been briefly mentioned in an earlier clause ex:9:x1680, ex:9:x1678, or it is known from the outset as a future topic ex:9:x1679, and now it is specified as the topic for the following section of text.

Mauw-owa kamenap nain on-a-man? Mauw-owa =na sira yia nokar-e-mik, yiena kae sira nain.\\
work- nmz what.like that1 do- pa -2p work- nmz = tp custom 1p. acc ask- pa -1/3p 1p. gen 1s/p.grandfather custom that1 \\
`What kind of work did you do? - The work (was such that) they asked us about customs, our ancestral customs.'...Filip uruf-ap maak-e-k, ``Ikos ikiw-u.'' Filip=na ona owowa Suaru, \\...Filip see- ss. seq tell- pa -3s together go- imp.1d Filip= tp 3s. gen village Suaru \\
`He saw Filip and told him, ``We'll go together.'' Filip is/was from Suaru, '

Yo efa aaw-eya i owawiya ik-omkun Yaapan =ena Wewak kame=pa nan ir-a-mik. \\
1s. unm 1s. acc take-2/3s. ds 1p. unm together be-1s/p. ds Japan= tp Wewak side= loc there come- pa -1/3p \\
`He married me, and while we were together the Japanese came from the Wewak side.'

Highlighted topics are more frequent in conversations than in narratives. Since the first and second persons are more topical than the third person ex:9:x1684, ex:9:x1685, they may even get marked as topic when the discussion itself is about something else ex:9:x1686. The second person singular pronoun with the topic marker, nos-na, has acquired the meaning somewhat like `you know' in English ex:9:x1687. A highlighted topic of this kind need not be a constituent in a clause.

Nos=na? \\
2s. fc = tp \\
`What about you?' or: `What do you want?' or: `Where are you going?'

Emar, yos=na amina=ke weetak. \\
friend 1s. fc = tp saucepan= cf no \\
`Friend, I do not have a saucepan.'

Is =na yoo, takira fain ifa=ke ku-eya akua aaw-ep ekap-em-ika-i-mik yoo! \\
1p. fc = tp intj boy this snake= cf bite-2/3s. ds shoulder take- ss. seq come- ss. sim -be- Np - pr.1/3p intj \\
`We - this boy was bitten by a snake and we are coming carrying him on our shoulders.'

Mauwa ar-e-n, amia=iya nenar-e-mik=i? -Wia, nos=na, yo fiker fufa iw-ap nefa far-i-yem.\\
what become- pa -2s bow= com shoot.you- pa -1/3p= qm No 2s. fc = tp 1s. unm kunai.grass base go- ss. seq 2s. acc call- Np - pr.1s \\
`What happened to you, did they shoot you with a gun? -No, you know, I went inside the kunai grass and am calling you.'
summary:
The topic marker -(e)na is used to highlight a new topic that the speaker wants to bring to the fore, whether it has been briefly mentioned already or is known in advance as the subject of the next discourse segment. Such marked topics are especially common in conversation, and even first- and second-person pronouns may receive topic marking when they are especially topical.  

In some cases the marker has extended to fixed expressions, such as second-person singular nos=na, which can mean roughly “you know,” and the highlighted topic may even stand outside a clause, as in standalone phrases like “What about you?” or “Friend, I do not have a saucepan.”

text:
The term focus, as used here, refers to special prominence given to some constituent in a clause. In Mauwake, focus is not the same as new information, as the focused element can be either new or given information. And it cannot be contrasted with topic, as the topic may receive focus marking as well. This sec:9.3 is based on my earlier paper.

The main discussion concentrates on two focus clitics, but syntactic and phonological focusing devices are also briefly touched on.

Since focus refers to special prominence, it is possible to have clauses and sentences without any focus marking; in fact, most of the clauses do not have any. But it is also possible to have more than one focused item in a clause.
summary: In Mauwake, focus means special prominence on a constituent, and it is not equivalent to either new information or contrast with topic, since focused elements can be given or new and topics may also be focus-marked. The discussion mainly examines two focus clitics, while also briefly mentioning syntactic and phonological devices. Because focus marking is not required, many clauses have none, though a clause can contain more than one focused item.

text:
lists the following factors as necessary for focus of contrast: the knowledge that someone did something, a set of possible candidates in the addressee's mind, and the assertion as to which of these candidates is the correct one. Thus, there can be no contrast if the number of candidates is either unlimited or one. A contrastive sentence often contradicts the addressee's expectation(s), but this is not crucial; what is essential is that there is a set of possible candidates in the addressee's mind. Also, as remarks, marking a contrast is not obligatory. Even if there are more candidates than one in the addressee's mind, it is still the speaker who decides whether to overtly mark something as contrastive or not.

The contrastive focus marker in Mauwake is - ke, which cliticizes to a noun phrase ( sec:3.12.7.2 ). It can also follow a temporal or location word, although this is rare. The domain of the contrastive focus is one constituent. It is used when the np is in focus and is contrasted with something else ex:9:x1688, ex:9:x1689.

Os=ke ikiw-o-k. \\
3s. fc = cf go- pa -3s \\
`It was he who went.'

Mua bug maala nain =ke mera unowa isak-i-non, mua bug iiwa nain weetak. \\
man wind long that1= cf fish many spear- Np - fi.3s man wind short that1 no\\
`A man with big lungs will spear many fish, a man with small lungs no.´

Sometimes the use or non-use of the contrastive marker makes a difference in the interpretation of the meaning of a word. In ex:9:x1690, maneka `big' refers to the size of the man as a neutral quality, but in ex:9:x1691 either his big size is contrasted with the size of other people, or he is set apart as one of a limited set of big men, i.e., chiefs.

Mua nain maneka. \\
man that1 big \\
`That man is big.'

Mua nain maneka=ke. \\
man that1 big= cf \\
`That man is big ' or: `That man is a big man/chief.'

The main position for the contrastive focus marking is the subject ex:9:x1688, Waskia has an identical morpheme ke, labeled as a subject marker. The examples cited are very similar to those cases in Mauwake where the contrastive focus marker cliticizes to the subject. ex:9:x1689, or the non-verbal predicate of a verbless clause ex:9:x1691. In a few cases, some other constituent is marked, e.g., a contrasted object ex:9:x1692, ex:9:x1697 or an adverbial phrase ex:9:x1693, ex:9:x1694.

Ne erepam nain=ke wiena skul stua on-a-mik.\\
add four that1= cf 3p. gen school store make- pa -1/3p\\
`And the fourth one they made into their school store.'

Maa en-owa iw-e-mik, rais=ke weetak. \\
food eat- nmz give.him- pa -1/3p rice= cf no \\
`They gave him food (root crops), but not rice.'

Amirika =ke eliw ika-i-yem, uura=ke napum-ar-i-yem. \\
noon= cf well be- Np - pr.1s night= cf sick- inch - Np - pr.1s \\
`At noon I am well, at night I am sick.'

Amiten =ke ikiw-i-yem, Susure=ke me ikiw-i-yem. \\
Amiten= cf go- Np - pr.1s Susure= cf not go- Np - pr.1s \\
`I go to Amiten but I don't go to Susure.'

The contrastive focus marker is also used for subject disambiguation. When an object of a clause is fronted as the theme, the constituent order changes from sov to osv. If both the subject and object are in the third person and are realized as overt np s, this creates a potential ambiguity as to which one is which argument. The contrastive focus marker, added to the subject, may first have been used to disambiguate clauses like ex:9:x1695 and later spread as an optional marking even to clauses where the verbal suffix distinguishes the two arguments and which would not need this extra marking ex:9:x1696. Without the contrastive focus marking, the example ex:9:x1695 would mean `and my younger sibling got/took an arrow/a bullet'.

Ne yena aamun ariwa=ke aaw-o-k. \\
add 1s. gen 1s/p.younger.sibling arrow= cf get- pa -3s \\
`And my younger sibling was killed by a bullet (lit: arrow).'

Fofa=pa maa mauwa on-i-mik nain ( yos=ke) ma-i-yem. \\
market= loc thing what do- Np - pr.1/3p that1 1s. fc = cf say- Np - pr.1s \\
`I tell what we do at the market.'

Although the contrastive focus marker is very common when both the subject and object in an osv clause are np s, it is not obligatory. See the second clause of ex:9:x1702 for an example.

In other situations where there is ambiguity about the subject, the cf marker is also used. If ex:9:x1705 did not have cf marking, Pita could be interpreted as the possessor of the betelnuts and so the meaning would be `He stole Pita's betelnuts from me'.

Pita =ke owora efar ikum aaw-eya \\
Pita= cf betelnut 1s. dat illicitly take-2/3s. ds \\
`Pita stole my betelnuts, and '

In ex:9:x1706, the second cf is necessary, because otherwise `this other one' would be interpreted as an object; the real object in the second clause is marked by zero.

Ikoka masin kaanin=ke samor-ar-eya oko fain=ke asip-i-non.\\
later engine which= cf bad- inch -2/3s. ds other this= cf help- Np - fu.3s \\
`Later when any of the engines breaks this other one will help it.'

A clause can only have one constituent with contrastive focus. In a verbless clause, either the subject ex:9:x1708 or the non-verbal predicate ex:9:x1707 can be marked with it, but not both.

Yo owow(a) saria=ke.\\
1s. unm village headman= cf \\
`I am the village headman.'

Wia, yos=ke owow saria ika-i-yem. \\
no 1s. fc = cf village headman be- Np - pr.1s \\
`No, I am the village headman.'

Contrastive focus can be assigned to a constituent regardless of whether it is given or new ex:9:x1709, indefinite ex:9:x1710 or definite ex:9:x1711. Non-verbal predicates with cf are mostly new information, whereas for subjects neither givenness nor definiteness matters.
summary: The passage explains that contrastive focus requires a limited set of alternatives in the addressee’s mind, with the speaker asserting which candidate is correct; it is not necessary for the contrast to contradict expectation, and marking contrast is optional. In Mauwake, the contrastive focus marker **=ke** cliticizes mainly to noun phrases, especially subjects, but can also mark other constituents such as objects or adverbials, and its presence can change interpretation or help disambiguate subject-object relations. A clause can have only one contrastively focused constituent, and the marker can be used with given or new, definite or indefinite information.

text:
Iperuma nain me enim-eka, inasin mua=ke.\\
eel that1 not eat- imp.2p spirit man= cf \\
`Don't eat the eel, it is a spirit man.'

Iir oko mua oko=ke koora ku-ek-a-m na-ep maakara war-ep \\
time other man other= cf house build- cntf - pa -1s say- ss. seq timber cut- ss. seq \\
`Another time a man wanted to build a house and he cut timber and '

Aaya nain=ke ifa puuk-a-k. \\
sugarcane that1= cf snake change.into- pa -3s \\
`The sugarcane changed into a snake.'

In non-polar questions, it is the questioned element that is in focus. This is reflected in the question words and in the answers. When the question word is the subject ex:9:x1714 or the non-verbal predicate ex:9:x1712, it takes the cf clitic, and the corresponding constituent in the answer usually gets the focus marking as well ex:9:x1715, ex:9:x1713.

Mua naareke nefa maak-e-k?\\
man who. cf 2s. acc tell- pa -3s \\
`Who told you?'

Mua =ke me efa maak-e-mik, yena mokok=iw uruf-a-m. \\
man= cf not 1s. acc tell- pa -1/3p 1s. gen eye= inst see- pa -1s \\
`It wasn't people that told me, I saw it with my own eyes.'

Maa nain mauwa=ke? \\
thing that1 what= cf \\
`What is that thing?'

Maa nain posa=ke. \\
thing that1 turban.shell= cf \\
`That thing is a turban shell.'

The contrastive focus clitic and the question clitic - i merge into - ki when both are used with the same constituent. This happens when the non-verbal predicate of a verbless clause is questioned ex:9:x1716, in alternative questions ex:9:x1718, and sometimes in alternative statements ex:9:x1717.

Emeria fain Eema=ki? \\
woman this Eema= cf. qm \\
`Is this woman Eema?'

Emeria fain Eema=ki e emeria oko=ke? \\
woman this Eema= cf. qm or woman other= cf \\
`Is this woman Eema or another woman?'

Iwer(a) eka =ki e mauwa=ki, owora=ki, episowa =ki ika-i-non...\\
coconut water= cf. qm or what= cf. qm betelnut= cf. qm tobacco= cf. qm be- Np - fu.3s \\
`If there is coconut water, or something else, betelnut, or tobacco '
summary: The passage explains that in non-polar questions, the questioned element is in focus, which is shown by the use of the contrastive focus clitic **=ke** on the question word and often on the corresponding answer constituent. It also notes that when the focus clitic **=ke** combines with the question clitic **-i**, they merge into **=ki**, a form used when questioning the non-verbal predicate in verbless clauses, in alternative questions, and sometimes in alternative statements.

text:
The neutral focus clitic ( sec:3.12.7.2 ) most commonly occurs in irrealis-type clauses, i.e., questions ex:9:x1719, commands ex:9:x1720, negated clauses ex:9:x1721 or those with future tense ex:9:x1722, hence its original name in. But it is also used in a some realis-type clauses. Although the clitic has probably developed from the indefinite oko `a (certain), (an)other', it is added to definite noun phrases as well.

Aaya =ko niar ik-ua=i? \\
sugar= nf 2p. dat be- pa.3s= qm \\
`Do you have (any) sugar?'

Ikiw-ep maa en-owa=ko nop-aka.\\
go- ss. seq food eat- nmz = nf fetch- imp.2s\\
`Go and fetch (some) food.'

Owowa oko=ko me uf-e-mik. \\
village other= nf not dance- pa -1/3p \\
` Other villages did not dance.'

Yo aakisa opaimika=ko ma-i-nen. \\
1s. unm now talk/story= nf say- Np - fu.1s \\
`Now I will tell a story.'

In most of those few instances where the nf clitic marks a constituent in a clearly realis-type clause, that constituent is a new, indefinite np introduced as a subject ex:9:x1733, ex:9:x1732.... emer en-ow mua=ko eka en-ep momor-ar-ep \\
sago eat- nmz man= nf water eat- ss. seq fool- inch - ss. seq \\
` a Sepik man had drunk beer and became drunk and '

Nan iimar-ep ika-eya urema=ko ekap-eya miim-a-k.\\
there stand.up- ss. seq be-2/3s. ds bandicoot= nf come-2/3s. ds hear- pa -3s \\
`He was standing there and he heard a bandicoot coming.' (Lit: ` a bandicoot came and he heard it').

Any constituent in a clause can be marked as focused with the neutral focus clitic. The subject ex:9:x1733 and object ex:9:x1722 have been exemplified above, but a recipient ex:9:x1723, adverbial ex:9:x1724, ex:9:x1730, comitative, ex:9:x1725 and instrument ex:9:x1726 are also possible:

Mua nain=ko onak-e. \\
man that1= nf feed.him- imp.1s \\
`Give it to that man to eat.'

Miiw-aasa era=pa=ko me yiar samor-ar-e-k. \\
land-canoe road= loc = nf not 1p. dat bad- inch - pa -3s \\
`Our truck did not break on the road.'

Ne samor akena=ko aruf-a-mik.\\
add badly very= nf hit- pa -1/3p\\
`And they beat him very badly.'

Ikos =ko niir-u. \\
together= nf play- imp.1d \\
`Let's play together.'

Fura =iw=ko me puuk-a-mik. \\
knife= inst = nf not cut- pa -1/3p \\
`They didn't cut it with a knife.'

In a sentence the final, fully inflected verbs are already on the basis of their position more prominent than other verbs, and they cannot receive focus marking. But the medial verbs may be given extra prominence with the neutral focus clitic ex:9:x1727.

Amerika kerer-e-mik na-i-ya, ikiw-ep=ko wia uruf-ik-ua.\\
America appear- pa -1/3p say- Np - pr.3s go- ss. seq = nf 3p. acc see-be- pa.3s \\
`He says that the Americans have arrived, let's go and see them.'

Even the verbal negation particle me `not' can be marked with the nf clitic, in which case the focus is on negating the whole proposition ex:9:x1728.

Takira me=ko wia aruf-a-mik. \\
boy not= nf 3p. acc hit- pa -1/3p \\
`It is not the case that we hit the boys.'

A clause can only have one contrastive focus, Clauses with a locative adverb neeke or feeke ( sec:3.6.3 ) are an exception. but negations and especially polite requests may contain two or even three constituents marked with the neutral focus ex:9:x1729.

No=ko era=ko imen-ap=ko yia asip-e.\\
2s. unm = nf way= nf find- ss. seq = nf 1p. acc help- imp.2s\\
`If you find a way, please help us.' Or: `Please find a way to help us.'

Especially in spoken language, it is possible to reduplicate the nf clitic in a word for extra prominence ex:9:x1731.

Wi kema ma-e-mik, `` O=ko=ko amukar-ek-a-n nom. Moram me amukar-e-n?'' \\
3p. unm liver say- pa -1/3p 3s. unm = nf = nf scold- cntf - pa -2s please why not scold- pa -2s\\
`They said in their hearts, ``C'mon, you should have scolded him. Why didn't you scold him?'' '

The two focus markers are not mutually exclusive, and consequently they can co-occur in one clause ex:9:x1737.

Yos=ke maa nain=ko me aaw-e-m.\\
1s. fc = cf thing that1= nf not take- pa -1s\\
`It wasn't I who took that thing.'

The constituent with focus marking retains the same position in a clause that it has in a non-focused clause. When a personal pronoun in some other case than nominative receives neutral focus, an unmarked pronoun is added as a pronoun copy and marked with the nf clitic ex:9:x1743. When this pronoun gets fronted as a theme, it is the pronoun copy that is fronted ex:9:x1744.

Mua nain i=ko me yia far-e-k. \\
man that1 1p. unm = nf not 1p. acc call- pa -3s \\
`The man didn't call us.'

I =ko mua nain-(ke) me yia far-e-k. \\
1p. unm = nf man that1-( cf ) not 1p. acc call- pa -3s \\
` Us the man didn't call.'

More research is needed in order to establish what kind of prominence the nf clitic marks. Of the following three examples, ex:9:x1734 is a low-prominence clause with no item marked for extra prominence, in ex:9:x1735 `I' is contrasted with other people, and in ex:9:x1736 the prominence is neutral: the speaker emphasizes that (s)he didn't see, but there is no implied contrast.

Yo me uruf-a-m. \\
1s. unm not see- pa -1s \\
`I didn't see it.'

Yos =ke me uruf-a-m. \\
1s. fc = cf not see- pa -1s \\
`It wasn't I who saw it (but someone else).'

Yo =ko me uruf-a-m. \\
1s. unm = nf not see- pa -1s \\
` I didn't see it (regardless of whether anyone else did or not)'

Introduction of an indefinite topic has already been mentioned as one of the functions of neutral focus. In questions and requests the focus marking indicates politeness. And especially in many negated clauses with nf marking, there is a sense of distancing oneself from the situation ex:9:x1738.
summary: The neutral focus clitic most often appears in irrealis clauses such as questions, commands, negated clauses, and future-tense clauses, though it also occurs in some realis clauses, especially when introducing a new indefinite subject or topic. It can mark almost any clause constituent, including verbs, and may even be reduplicated for extra prominence; however, the exact type of prominence it expresses is still unclear, with uses including neutral emphasis, contrast, politeness, and distancing in negated clauses.

text:
I mua=ko me wia furew-a-mik ne yiena pun mukuna =ko me op-a-mik. \\
1s. unm man= nf not 3p. acc sense- pa -1/3p add 1p. gen also fire= nf not hold- pa -1/3p \\
`We didn't sense (any) people (there) and we ourselves didn't carry fire either.'
summary: The passage gives an example sentence showing negative clauses in which both “sense” and “hold/carry” are negated. It translates as “We didn’t sense any people there, and we ourselves didn’t carry fire either,” illustrating the use of negation with coordinated predicates.

text:
Cross-linguistically, the most common focusing device is possibly stress. Stress in Mauwake is not only a word-level feature ( sec:2.1.3.1 ); it can be employed to give prominence to a word or phrase in a clause. Default, or neutral, clause stress is on the verb or the non-verbal predicate. An extra heavy stress is used for contrastive focus especially for those constituents that seldom or never take cf marking ex:9:x1739-- ex:9:x1742.

O wowa=pa emeria unowa wia maak-e-mik. \\
village= loc woman many 3p. acc tell- pa -1/3p \\
` In the village they told it to many women.'

Owowa=pa e meria unowa wia maak-e-mik. \\
village= loc woman many 3p. acc tell- pa -1/3p \\
`In the village they told it to many women.'

Owowa=pa emeria u nowa wia maak-e-mik. \\
village= loc woman many 3p. acc tell- pa -1/3p \\
`In the village they told it to many women.'

Owowa=pa emeria unowa wia maak-e-mik. \\
village= loc woman many 3p. acc tell- pa -1/3p \\
`In the village they told it to many women (instead of hiding it from them).'

Note that in ex:9:x1742 it is only the loudness/intensity in the stressed word that distinguishes it from the neutral clausal stress.

Right-dislocation is often called a topicalizing device, but in Mauwake it can't be that, since only a few of the right-dislocated constituents are topics ex:9:x1745.

Maa nain aaw-ep iima=pa wu-om-ap om-em-ik-ua, sawur emeria nain =ke.\\
thing that1 take- ss. seq chest= loc put- ben - bnfy 2. ss. seq cry- ss. sim -be-3s. pa spirit woman that1= cf \\
`She took the thing and put it on his chest, the spirit woman (did).'

Most of the right-dislocated elements are not topics. Right-dislocation seems to be a focusing device of a special kind: the speaker decides that some constituent needs clarification or more prominence than it received, and adds it as an afterthought after the clause ex:9:x1746-- ex:9:x1748.

Saapara=pa nan suusa iw-e-mik, wiena ifa suusa nain.\\
Saapara= loc there needle give.him- pa -1/3p 3p. gen snake needle that1\\
`There in Saapara they gave him an injection, their snake (antivenene) injection.'

Aaya puuk-ap iimar-ep ik-ua, manin(a) afua=pa.\\
sugarcane change.into- ss. seq stand.up- ss. seq be- pa.3s garden old(garden)= loc \\
`It had changed into a sugarcane and was standing in the old garden.'

Ne fraide=pa maapora puk-o-k, urera.\\
add Friday= loc party burst- pa -3s afternoon\\
`And on Friday the party started, in the afternoon.'
summary: Mauwake uses stress as a common focusing device: neutral clause stress normally falls on the verb or non-verbal predicate, while extra heavy stress marks contrastive focus, especially on constituents that rarely take contrastive-focus marking. Right-dislocation is also used for prominence, but not primarily for topicalization; instead, it often functions as an afterthought that clarifies or highlights a constituent by adding it after the clause.
